title: Tissues, Cells & Organ Physiology
text:
About this book
This web-book goes with MEDC 30504, Tissues, Cells & Organ Physiology. Each chapter follows a lecture in the course, uses the course’s terms and symbols, and links to the course simulators where one fits.
It covers the cardiovascular and pulmonary blocks, with the muscle lectures and the excitable-cell material that the muscle and autonomic lectures need.

title: Tissues, Cells & Organ Physiology
text:
How to use it
Read a chapter before or after its lecture. Each one opens with goals and ends with practice questions and the key equations. Boxes marked “Background” hold material you will not be examined on.
The course exams use single-best-answer questions in the NBME style. Most give a short clinical or laboratory scenario and ask you to predict a change or explain its mechanism. The practice questions at the end of each chapter are open-ended instead, so you work through the reasoning rather than pick from a list.

title: Tissues, Cells & Organ Physiology
text:
Sources and figures
Every chapter lists its sources. Every figure was drawn for this book. Figures that redraw a classic experiment or a textbook figure say “adapted from” and cite the original. Figures from openly licensed books keep their license and credit.

title: 1  Cardiovascular Physiology Overview
text:
1.1 The course at a glance
The first part of the opening cardiovascular lecture is a single pass through the whole course. The lecture opens with a line from a teaching mentor, “concepts better caught than taught,” and that is how this material is learned: you meet the same few ideas again and again, from different directions, until they stick. The course motto makes the same point: “Facts are relatively few. Mastery can be elusive.” The work is in seeing how the pieces act on each other, so that a change in one place (a bleed, a stiff ventricle, a constricted vein) lets you predict what happens everywhere else.
This chapter names the parts of the circulation, says what each one does, and points to the chapter where each idea is developed. The Cardiac Pump chapter, which follows the same lecture, starts the detailed work.
The block covers these topics. The book groups excitable cells and muscle first. In 2026 the lectures ran in the order on the lecture’s “Flow of Major Topics” slide, which starts with the cardiac pump.

title: 1  Cardiovascular Physiology Overview
text:
1.2 Electrophysiology first
Before the heart can pump, its cells have to contract and pass an electrical signal to one another. The electrophysiology lectures cover the Na+, K+ and Ca2+ currents behind the cardiac action potential, which looks nothing like a neuron’s. They then follow how the action potential sets off contraction, and how specialized conducting tissue (muscle cells built for conduction rather than force) spreads the signal across the heart. The ECG comes later in the block.
One warning now, because it causes confusion later: the ECG is not showing action potentials. An action potential is recorded with an electrode inside one cell. The ECG is recorded on the surface of the body and reflects the summed electrical activity of the whole heart. The two can look alike, but they are different measurements.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 1  Cardiovascular Physiology Overview
text:
1.3 Cardiovascular, not cardiac
The lecture puts this block’s theme on a slide by itself: “Respect the veins… and the arteries… but mostly the veins.” The heart supplies the energy for flow, but how much blood it pumps each minute is set largely by how much blood the veins return to it. That idea, which you will meet as ventricular-vascular coupling, runs through the whole block.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 1  Cardiovascular Physiology Overview
text:
1.4 The circuit, part by part
Figure 1.1 shows the whole circuit.






Figure 1.1: The circulation as a closed circuit. The right heart pumps blood through the lungs, and the left heart pumps it through the systemic beds, which are arranged in parallel between the arteries (right) and the veins (left). Each bed has an arteriole (narrowing wedge) feeding a capillary bed. The gut and liver, and the kidney, each have two capillary beds in series. Lymphatics (dashed) return leaked fluid and protein to the veins. Adapted from Berne and colleagues, Physiology [1], as used in the 2026 lecture.




Heart. A pump that moves whatever blood is delivered to it. Engineers call this kind of pump a positive displacement pump: it traps the fluid that has filled it and forces it into the outflow pipe. The course likes a plainer picture: the heart is a “dumb sump pump.” A sump pump in a flooded basement pumps out whatever water arrives and makes no decisions of its own. The ventricle ejects a share of whatever blood fills it, and more filling means more ejected. How much fills it is the veins’ business.
Arteries. Fire hoses that distribute blood to the body. Their walls stretch a little with each beat and recoil between beats, so they store pressure and even out the pulsing output of the heart.
Arterioles. Resistance vessels at the ends of the arteries. They regulate flow the way the roller clamp on an IV line does, by narrowing the tubing. They have been called the “stopcocks” of the circulation.
Capillaries. The site of exchange: nutrients, gases and fluid move between blood and tissue here.
Veins. Storage and transport. Their main job is to hold volume: about two-thirds of the blood in the body sits in the veins at any moment.
Lymphatics. A separate system, running in parallel, that scavenges the fluid and protein that leak out of the capillaries and returns them to the veins.


1.4.1 Two circuits in series
The pulmonary and systemic circuits are connected end to end, in series, so the two sides of the heart pump the same output on average; the Cardiac Pump chapter explains why.


1.4.2 Many beds in parallel
Squint at Figure 1.1 and the dominant pattern is parallel channels: brain, heart muscle, arms, gut, kidney, skin and skeletal muscle each take their own branch off the arterial tree and drain into the veins.
That layout protects tissue. Put a clot in the artery feeding one kidney and that kidney loses its flow, but flow to the other beds barely changes. Put a large clot upstream of everything, in the main pulmonary artery, and there is no alternate path. All of the cardiac output has to pass through the lungs, so a large pulmonary embolism lodged there can kill.
A parallel layout also means that every systemic bed is supplied at about the same arterial pressure. The Hemodynamics chapter explains why, and covers the two “rule breakers,” the gut-liver and kidney circulations, where two capillary beds sit in series.


1.4.3 Design principles
The lecture’s design principles for the peripheral vascular system are these.

Parallel architecture (mostly). Artery to microcirculation to vein, with a few exceptions.
Tissue form equals function. The wall of each vessel suits its job: elastic arteries, muscular arterioles, thin capillaries, distensible veins.
Flexible and adaptive. The same system serves rest, exercise, digestion and blood loss.
Local plus central control. Each tissue bed can raise or lower its own resistance and draw blood toward itself or send it away, while the nervous system and hormones set the overall pressure.

The local part works like this:

↑ metabolic demand in a tissue → ↓ arteriolar resistance in that bed → blood flow shifts toward that bed

The Microcirculation and Local Control chapter takes this apart.

title: 1  Cardiovascular Physiology Overview
section: 1.5 How the heart and the vessels interact
text:
1.5 How the heart and the vessels interact
Picture a pressure catheter pulled back from the left ventricle into the aorta. Early in ejection, more blood enters the aorta than can run off through the arterioles, so the aorta fills, stretches and its pressure rises. When the ventricle relaxes, the aortic valve closes and the blood stored in the stretched aorta runs off toward the arterioles, so aortic pressure falls slowly until the next beat.
The distensible aorta and the resistance of the arterioles together act as a filter. The course calls this the hydraulic filter, or the Windkessel effect. By the time blood reaches the capillaries the beat-to-beat swing is essentially gone and pressure is steady (Figure 1.2). The figure also shows where most of the pressure is spent: across the small arteries and arterioles, the resistance vessels.






Figure 1.2: Pressure along the systemic circulation. The left ventricle swings between about 120 and near 0 mm Hg with each beat. In the aorta and large arteries pressure swings between about 120 and 80 around a mean near 93. The swing shrinks through the small arteries and arterioles, where mean pressure falls the most, and is gone by the capillaries. Pressure keeps falling through the veins to a few mm Hg in the right atrium. Values are illustrative. Adapted from Boron and Boulpaep, Medical Physiology [2], as used in the 2026 lecture.



Later in the block you will draw two curves on the same axes: a cardiac function curve, which shows how much the heart pumps at each right atrial pressure, and a vascular function curve, which shows how much the veins return. Where they cross is the operating point: the cardiac output and right atrial pressure at which the whole system settles (Figure 1.3). For now, notice only that the answer comes from the heart and the veins together, not from the heart alone. The Control of Cardiac Output chapter builds these curves.






Figure 1.3: A preview of the cardiac function curve and the vascular function curve. Where they cross is the operating point, here a cardiac output of 5 L/min at a right atrial pressure (Pra) of 2 mm Hg. Pms, the mean systemic filling pressure, is the right atrial pressure at which venous return falls to zero, where the vascular function curve meets the pressure axis. The lecture’s graph calls this the venous function curve and plots it against central venous pressure; this book uses vascular function curve and Pra, as the rest of the course does. Course figure, after the lecture’s preview slide.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 1  Cardiovascular Physiology Overview
text:
1.6 Microcirculation and local control
At the microcirculation, arterioles feed in and venules drain out, and O2, metabolites and fluid move between blood and tissue. Why have a circulation at all? A single-celled organism does not need one, because every part of it touches the outside world and exchange by diffusion is fast over short distances. A multicellular body has an inside and an outside, and not nearly enough surface for each cell to exchange with the environment directly. The circulation closes that gap by bringing the outside world, in the form of blood that has passed through the lungs and gut, to within a few cell widths of every cell.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 1  Cardiovascular Physiology Overview
section: 1.7 Autonomic control, integration and the special circulations
text:
1.7 Autonomic control, integration and the special circulations
The autonomic nervous system sets heart rate, contractility and the tone of arterioles and veins. Through cardiac output and SVR, these set the mean arterial pressure. Stretch receptors in the walls of the large arteries, the baroreceptors, sense that pressure, and the brainstem integrates the information and adjusts the outflow. The ANS and Extrinsic Control chapter covers this.
The last part of the block puts the pieces together and asks how the whole system responds to exercise and to injury, such as hemorrhage, heart failure and septic shock.
The special circulations lectures cover beds that break the general rules, including the coronary, cerebral, pulmonary and cutaneous circulations. These beds carry different sets of receptors and local controls, so they respond differently to the same signals. In the brain, for example, local control outweighs the nerves to its vessels.






TipWhat you need from this



Know the job of each part of the circuit, why the two sides of the heart pump the same output, why parallel beds protect tissue, and that arteries plus arterioles smooth the pulse into steady capillary flow. Everything else in this chapter is a pointer to a later one.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 1  Cardiovascular Physiology Overview
text:
1.8 Check your understanding

Imagine the kidney were placed downstream of the gut, so that blood passed through the gut’s arterioles and capillaries before reaching the kidney. What would the kidney receive, and what would happen to its flow when the gut’s arterioles dilated or constricted? How does the parallel layout avoid both problems?


Answer

The kidney would get blood that had already lost most of its pressure across the gut’s arterioles and had already exchanged O2 and nutrients with the gut. And beds in series carry the same flow, so the kidney could not set its own: when the gut’s arterioles dilated, flow through both beds would rise, and when they constricted, the kidney’s flow would fall whatever the kidney needed. In the parallel layout each bed takes its own branch off the arterial tree, so each gets arterial blood at about the same arterial pressure, and its own arterioles set its own flow.

A muscle in your leg starts working hard while the rest of you sits still. What changes in its arterioles, and what happens to blood flow to that muscle and to your kidneys?


Answer

The working muscle’s own arterioles dilate (local control), so the resistance of that bed falls and its flow rises. Like opening the roller clamp on one IV line, this changes flow in that line only. As long as arterial pressure is held up, flow to the kidneys and other parallel beds barely changes.

Blood leaves the left ventricle in spurts, but flow through a capillary is nearly steady. What two properties of the arterial system make that happen?


Answer

The distensibility of the aorta and large arteries, which store blood and pressure during systole and release them during diastole, and the resistance of the arterioles downstream. Together they form the hydraulic filter (Windkessel effect).

Where does most of the body’s blood sit at any moment, and why does that matter for the heart?


Answer

In the veins, about two-thirds of it. The heart pumps what it is given, so the veins, by controlling how much blood returns, have a large say in cardiac output.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 2  The Cardiac Pump
text:
2.1 Functional anatomy
The heart beats about 100,000 times a day and moves about 5 L of blood a minute, some 7,200 L a day. This chapter follows one of those beats. It focuses on the left side of the heart, with a few references to the right. The question it answers is the one the rest of the block keeps asking: what sets the volume of blood the ventricle ejects with each beat? The answer, which the course turns into a mantra, is preload, afterload and contractility. The Overview chapter, from the first half of the same lecture, puts the pump in its place in the circuit.
The heart is two pumps in series. Blood returning from the body enters the right atrium, crosses the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and leaves through the pulmonic valve to the lungs. Blood returning from the lungs enters the left atrium, crosses the mitral valve into the left ventricle, and leaves through the aortic valve.
There are two kinds of valve:
Valves move passively. A valve opens when the pressure behind it exceeds the pressure in front of it. It closes when blood starts to flow backward across it. For the AV valves that happens almost as soon as the pressure difference reverses. For the aortic and pulmonic valves it happens a moment later, because moving blood has momentum (see reduced ejection below). The papillary muscles do not pull the AV valves open. Every valve event in this chapter follows from these rules.
The ventricle is built of muscle fibers wrapped in layers around the chamber. When it contracts, the apex contracts before the base, which pushes blood toward the outflow tracts. The chamber shrinks in circumference and in length, and the base of the heart, where the valves sit, descends toward the apex. That descent of the base stretches the atria, which matters for the atrial pressure tracing below.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 2  The Cardiac Pump
text:
Atrioventricular (AV) valves, the tricuspid and the mitral, between each atrium and its ventricle. Their leaflets are tethered by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles, which keep the leaflets from everting (prolapsing) into the atrium when the ventricle contracts.
Semilunar valves, the aortic and the pulmonic, between each ventricle and its artery.

title: 2  The Cardiac Pump
section: 2.2 The cardiac cycle on the Wiggers diagram
text:
2.2 The cardiac cycle on the Wiggers diagram
The Wiggers diagram puts the events of one beat on a common time axis: left atrial, left ventricular and aortic pressure, left ventricular volume, the ECG and the heart sounds (Figure 2.1).






Figure 2.1: The Wiggers diagram for one beat of the left heart at 75 beats/min. From top: the phases of the cycle; aortic, left ventricular and left atrial pressure; left atrial pressure on an expanded scale, with the a, c and v waves; left ventricular volume; the ECG; and the heart sounds. Dashed vertical lines mark the four valve events. Curves come from a simple model of the left heart drawn for this book (end-diastolic volume 135 mL, end-systolic volume 65 mL, left ventricle 120/10 mm Hg, aorta about 120/75 mm Hg). Adapted from Boron and Boulpaep, Medical Physiology [1], as used in the 2026 lecture.



The textbook Wiggers diagram on the slides says isovolumetric for isovolumic, decreased ejection for reduced ejection, and decreased ventricular filling for diastasis. They are the same phases. It also draws two more heart sounds, S3 and S4, which this lecture does not teach (see the Background callout below).
Electrical activation comes before contraction. The P wave precedes atrial systole, the QRS complex precedes ventricular systole, and the T wave, ventricular repolarization, comes near the end of ejection. Ventricular systole runs from AV valve closure to semilunar valve closure. Ventricular diastole is everything else, isovolumic relaxation and all of filling, and diastasis is only the slow middle part of filling.






TipHow to learn this diagram



Do not memorize it like someone’s calendar. For each phase, ask which chamber has the higher pressure, which valves that opens or closes, and whether blood is moving. The tracings follow from the answers. Small Group 1 builds the diagram this way: first the volume curve, then the pressure curves.


The cycle is described here starting in late diastole, in the order the lecture uses.
Diastasis. The mitral valve is open and the aortic valve is closed. Blood returns slowly from the lungs into the left atrium and on into the ventricle (on the right side, from the systemic veins), so left atrial, left ventricular and venous pressures rise gradually. Meanwhile blood keeps flowing from the aorta to the periphery, and aortic pressure keeps falling, throughout diastole.
Atrial systole. Just after the P wave, the atria contract and push a final volume of blood across the open AV valves. This produces the a wave on the atrial pressure tracing (and, from the right atrium, on the jugular venous pulse). This “atrial kick” contributes about 10% of left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV) at rest (in Figure 2.1, about 11 of 135 mL). It matters more when the ventricle is stiff and hard to fill, and when the heart rate is high, because a fast rate shortens diastole and leaves less time for passive filling.
Isovolumic contraction. After the R wave, the ventricle starts to contract. Its pressure rises above atrial pressure and the mitral valve closes, which contributes to the first heart sound, S1. The aortic valve is still closed, because ventricular pressure is still below aortic pressure. With both valves closed, the ventricle squeezes a fixed volume of blood, so pressure rises steeply at constant volume, the end-diastolic volume. The closed mitral leaflets bulge back toward the atrium, which makes the c wave.
Rapid ejection. When left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, the aortic valve opens (on the right, the pulmonic valve opens when right ventricular pressure exceeds pulmonary artery pressure). Blood flows out fast, ventricular volume falls quickly, and ventricular and aortic pressures rise together to their peak, the systolic pressure, with ventricular pressure just above aortic pressure. Atrial pressure falls during this phase because the descent of the base stretches the atria.
Reduced ejection. As the ventricle empties, its pressure generation falls. Aortic pressure falls too, but more slowly, because the stretched aorta holds stored energy, and late in ejection it runs slightly above ventricular pressure. Blood keeps moving forward anyway, carried by its momentum, while the reversed pressure difference slows it down. Behind the closed mitral valve, blood returning from the lungs fills the atrium, and atrial pressure rises: the start of the v wave.
Isovolumic relaxation. As the ventricle relaxes, forward flow stops and a brief backflow closes the aortic valve, which contributes to the second heart sound, S2. Aortic valve closure marks the end of ventricular systole and the start of diastole. On the aortic tracing it leaves a small notch, the dicrotic notch (also called the incisura): the dip from the brief backflow that shuts the valve, followed by a small rebound as the aortic wall and closed valve recoil. The T wave ends just before it. The mitral valve is still closed, because ventricular pressure is still above atrial pressure, so volume stays fixed at the end-systolic volume while pressure falls steeply. Atrial pressure is still rising. Relaxation does not need filling: the pressure falls because the muscle is relaxing, not because volume changes.
Rapid ventricular filling. When ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, the mitral valve opens. Blood that had collected in the atrium rushes in. The ventricle is still relaxing, which keeps its pressure low and helps “suck” blood in, so filling is fast. Atrial pressure falls as the atrium empties. As the pressure difference between atrium and ventricle shrinks, filling slows into diastasis, and the cycle begins again.

title: 2  The Cardiac Pump
section: 2.3 The right side and the heart sounds
text:
2.3 The right side and the heart sounds
The right heart goes through the same sequence at much lower pressures (Figure 2.2). Typical ventricular pressures, systolic over end-diastolic, are 120/10 mm Hg on the left and 25/5 mm Hg on the right. These are ventricular pressures, not the arterial blood pressure. The pulmonary circuit has a much lower resistance than the systemic circuit, so the right ventricle can move the same flow at a fraction of the pressure.
Because the two circuits are in series, the output of the right ventricle equals the output of the left on average. The slides call this the continuity equation: what goes into the lungs has to come out. It is the same conservation-of-flow idea as the continuity equation Q = v × A in the Hemodynamics chapter.






Figure 2.2: (A) Left and (B) right heart pressures on the same time and pressure scales, from the same model as Figure 2.1. The right ventricle ejects the same stroke volume at about one-fifth of the pressure. (C) Physiologic splitting of S2, drawn schematically. In expiration, aortic closure (A2) and pulmonic closure (P2) are close together. In inspiration, P2 comes later and the split widens. Course figure.



On the right side the valves close a little after their partners on the left: the tricuspid valve closes after the mitral valve, and the pulmonic valve closes after the aortic valve. So:

S1 comes from closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves, at the start of ventricular systole.
S2 comes from closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves, at the end of ventricular systole. Its two parts are called A2 and P2.

Physiologic splitting of S2. Normally A2 comes just before P2, and in inspiration the gap widens enough that you can hear two sounds. The lecture’s causal chain:

Inspiration → ↓ intrathoracic pressure → ↑ venous return to the right heart → longer right ventricular ejection → later P2 → wider A2–P2 split

On expiration the extra right-sided filling goes away and the split narrows again.
The jugular venous pulse in the neck reflects right atrial pressure. It has a, c and v waves that match the left atrial events above.






NoteBackground: S3 and S4





This comes from the course’s 2018 notes. S3 and S4 appear on the heart-sounds trace of the slides’ Wiggers diagram, but this lecture does not teach them.
Two more heart sounds can occur. S3 comes in early diastole, during rapid filling, when inflow into the ventricle stops abruptly. It can be normal in children and young adults and is heard in adults with a failing, volume-overloaded ventricle. S4 comes just before S1 and is linked to atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle, for example one thickened by years of high blood pressure.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 2  The Cardiac Pump
text:
2.4 Pressure-volume relationships
The second half of the lecture leaves the time axis behind and plots left ventricular pressure against left ventricular volume. A filling curve, a systolic curve and the loop that one beat traces between them do almost all the work.

2.4.1 The diastolic pressure-volume curve: filling and preload
Fill a relaxed ventricle step by step and record its pressure at each volume. The result is the diastolic pressure-volume curve, also called the end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship (EDPVR) (Figure 2.3 A).
Its steepness tells you how hard the ventricle is to fill. Compliance is the change in volume for a given change in pressure:
\[\text{Compliance} = \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta P}\quad(\text{mL/mm Hg})\]
Its inverse, ΔP/ΔV, is stiffness. With pressure on the vertical axis, as in the course’s figures, the slope of the diastolic curve is the stiffness, and compliance is its inverse. The curve is not a straight line. At low volumes a large volume change costs little pressure, and at high volumes the same volume change costs much more. The EDPVR itself does not change as the ventricle fills. Its slope (stiffness) rises at higher volumes, so the ventricle is less compliant there. The shape comes from the passive properties of the relaxed muscle and from structures around the heart, especially the pericardium, which becomes a stiff limit at large volumes (pericardial constraint).






Figure 2.3: The diastolic pressure-volume curve (EDPVR). (A) The same 20 mL costs about 1 mm Hg at low volume and about 8 mm Hg at high volume: the curve is steeper (stiffer, less compliant) at high volume. The point where filling ends gives LVEDV (preload) and LVEDP. (B) A stiffer, less compliant ventricle. At the same LVEDP it holds less blood; at the same LVEDV its pressure is much higher. Curves from the model in Figure 2.1. Course figure.



Preload is the stretch of the resting muscle just before it contracts. In this course preload is measured as the left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV), or RVEDV for the right ventricle. Calling a volume a “load” sounds odd, but it keeps the reasoning simple: more blood in the ventricle at the end of diastole means longer fibers at the start of contraction.
Clinically, LVEDV is sometimes estimated from the left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP), which can be measured with a catheter. The two are not interchangeable. LVEDP tells you LVEDV only if you know which filling curve the ventricle is on (Figure 2.3 B). A stiff ventricle, such as one thickened by long-standing high blood pressure, holds less blood at the same filling pressure, or needs a higher pressure to hold the same volume. A high LVEDP does not by itself mean a large preload.


2.4.2 Frank-Starling and the systolic pressure-volume curve
The Cardiac Muscle chapter covers this in detail, and the lecture previews it here: a cardiac muscle fiber stretched to a longer length before it contracts develops more force. Two mechanisms contribute: the overlap of thick and thin filaments, and, more important in the heart, the greater sensitivity of the contractile apparatus to Ca2+ at longer lengths (length-dependent activation). In the intact heart, the same idea is the Frank-Starling law of the heart: the more the ventricle fills, the more force it develops in the contraction that follows.
The lecture shows it with a thought experiment. Imagine the aortic valve kept shut by a very high pressure in the aorta, so the ventricle cannot eject. Every contraction is then isovolumic, and you can record the peak pressure the ventricle develops at each filling volume (Figure 2.4 A). Fill to point 1 on the diastolic curve and contract: pressure rises straight up, at constant volume, to point A. Fill more, to point 2, and the contraction reaches B. Fill to 3 and it reaches C. The peak pressure rises with end-diastolic volume. Joining A, B and C gives the systolic pressure-volume curve, the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR).






Figure 2.4: Building the systolic pressure-volume curve. (A) With the aortic valve held shut, the ventricle contracts from three filling volumes (1, 2, 3) on the diastolic curve and develops a peak pressure (A, B, C) that rises with filling. The line through the peaks is the systolic curve (ESPVR). (B) The slope of the systolic curve is contractility. More filling moves a beat up the same line. Curves from the model in Figure 2.1. Panel A follows the experiment shown in Berne and colleagues, Physiology [2], as used in the 2026 lecture.



In this course the systolic curve is the Frank-Starling curve. Over the normal range of filling it is close to a straight line, and the lecture draws it that way. The curve from the original experiments flattens at very large volumes and then bends down. Because contractility is the slope of this curve, that flattening is a fall in contractility: past a point, the overstretched ventricle gains less force from each extra milliliter, and in a failing heart it may lose force.
Contractility is the slope of the systolic (Frank-Starling) curve (Figure 2.4 B). It is a property of the state of the muscle itself: its Ca2+ handling and the health of the tissue. Circulating adrenaline makes the line steeper (more contractility). Scar from a myocardial infarction makes it flatter (less contractility). Contractility means inotropy only. Heart rate and the speed of relaxation also affect cardiac output, but they are separate properties, and in this course a change in heart rate does not change the systolic curve.






WarningA common mistake



Over the normal range of filling, stretching the ventricle does not raise its contractility. Stretch raises the force of contraction: the beat starts from a larger volume and moves up the same Frank-Starling line, whose slope is unchanged. Contractility changes when the slope changes, as with adrenaline or injury, or where the curve flattens at very high volumes.








NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The Small Group 2 key (Question 3a) writes “increased preload/LVEDV → increased myocardial stretch → increased contractility & SV.” Over the normal range, more stretch increases the force of contraction and the stroke volume along the same Frank-Starling curve. The slope, and so contractility, does not change. Contractility falls only at very high volumes, where the curve flattens, which is what the key’s Question 3b describes.




2.4.3 The pressure-volume loop
One real beat, with the aortic valve working normally, traces a loop on these axes (Figure 2.5). The loop runs counterclockwise. Start at the lower right, at the end of filling:

Mitral valve closes (lower right corner). Filling is over. The volume here is LVEDV, the preload.
Isovolumic contraction (right side). Pressure rises straight up at constant volume.
Aortic valve opens (upper right corner), when ventricular pressure reaches aortic pressure. That pressure is the diastolic blood pressure.
Ejection (top). Volume falls as blood leaves. In rapid ejection, the right part of the top edge, pressure rises to a peak, which approximates the systolic blood pressure. In reduced ejection, the left part, pressure falls.
Aortic valve closes (upper left corner). Ejection ends at the end-systolic volume (LVESV), the blood left behind. This corner sits on the systolic curve.
Isovolumic relaxation (left side). Pressure falls straight down at constant volume.
Mitral valve opens (lower left corner), and filling moves the loop right along the bottom, close to the diastolic curve, back to the start.







Figure 2.5: The left ventricular pressure-volume loop for the beat in Figure 2.1, with the diastolic (EDPVR) and systolic (ESPVR) curves. The loop runs counterclockwise. Its width is the stroke volume, and the area inside it is the stroke work. Course figure.



The loop gives you stroke volume and stroke work, but not time.

Stroke volume is the width of the loop. SV = LVEDV − LVESV, the volume at mitral valve closure minus the volume at aortic valve closure. In Figure 2.5 it is 135 − 65 = 70 mL. The lecture puts it plainly: “stroke volume is the point.”
The area inside the loop is the stroke work, the external work the ventricle does on the blood in one beat (pressure × volume has the units of work).
There is no time on either axis. The loop cannot tell you the heart rate, how long any phase lasted, or the cardiac output. For cardiac output you need the heart rate as well:

\[\text{CO} = \text{HR} \times \text{SV}\]
At 75 beats/min, 75 × 70 mL is about 5.3 L/min.






TipTry it



Map the Wiggers diagram onto the loop. Each corner of the loop is one dashed line in Figure 2.1, each side is one phase, and the volume tracing gives the loop’s left and right edges. Small Group 1 asks you to label both diagrams with the same events.








NoteBackground: ejection fraction





Ejection fraction is the fraction of the end-diastolic volume that the ventricle ejects in one beat: SV/EDV. It is measured clinically, usually by ultrasound of the heart. It falls when contractility falls, but it also changes with preload and afterload, so it is not a pure measure of contractility. This comes from the course’s 2018 notes; the 2026 lecture works with stroke volume.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 2  The Cardiac Pump
text:
2.5 What determines stroke volume
The lecture’s mantra: when someone says stroke volume, you say preload, afterload and contractility.

Preload: the stretch of the resting muscle before it contracts, measured as LVEDV (RVEDV for the right ventricle).
Afterload: the load against which the muscle exerts its force during ejection. It is a concept, not a single measurement. It rises with the pressure the ventricle has to reach to open the aortic valve and eject (the diastolic and systolic aortic pressures), and with any resistance across the aortic valve. Arterial resistance, arterial stiffness and the size and shape of the ventricle also affect it. In the course diagrams, aortic pressure stands in for afterload.
Contractility: an intrinsic property of the muscle, its ability to develop force at a given preload and afterload, shown by the slope of the systolic curve.

Figure 2.6 changes each one in turn. Read each panel as an isolated change from the baseline beat, with the other two determinants held fixed, the valves working normally, and no reflex response yet.






Figure 2.6: Stroke volume depends on preload, afterload and contractility. Faded loop, baseline beat; solid loop, new beat. Gray bar, baseline stroke volume; green bar, new stroke volume. (A) More preload: the loop widens to the right. (B) More afterload: the aortic valve opens at a higher pressure and ejection stops at a larger volume. (C) More contractility (steeper systolic curve, dotted): ejection continues to a smaller volume. From the model in Figure 2.1. In A and C the arterial side of the model was adjusted so the aortic valve opens at the same diastolic pressure as at baseline. Course figure.











Change
What happens on the loop
Stroke volume




↑ Preload
LVEDV increases along the same diastolic curve. The systolic curve is unchanged, and LVESV is about the same if the aortic pressure is the same.
↑, because the loop widens to the right


↑ Afterload
The ventricle must reach a higher pressure before the aortic valve opens, and it stops ejecting at a larger volume, where the higher end-systolic pressure meets the same systolic curve. LVEDV and contractility are unchanged.
↓, because more blood is left at end systole


↑ Contractility
The systolic curve gets steeper. At the same LVEDV and afterload, the ventricle ejects to a smaller LVESV.
↑, because the loop widens to the left



In the model, more preload (LVEDV 135 → 149 mL) raises stroke volume from 70 to 85 mL; more afterload (diastolic aortic pressure 75 → 101 mm Hg) lowers it to 58 mL; more contractility raises it to 92 mL.
The Circulation Lab draws the left ventricular pressure-volume loop beat by beat, with the diastolic and systolic curves behind it [3]. Remove or infuse blood, or change LV systolic function or diastolic stiffness, and watch the loop move.
A wider loop after a rise in contractility means more blood was ejected. It does not, by itself, show that ejection lasted longer or that the aortic valve closed later. Those are statements about time, and the loop has no time axis. The same caution runs the other way: when contractility falls after an infarction, stroke volume falls because ejection ends at a larger volume on the flatter systolic curve, not because the aortic valve closes early.

2.5.1 The pericardium and filling
The lecture asks why it might be illegal to perform pericardiectomies on greyhounds in Florida. The lecture itself treats the story as a myth, but it teaches compliance and preload well. Remove the pericardium and the ventricle fills along a more compliant curve: at the same filling pressure it reaches a larger LVEDV. More preload gives more force of contraction and a larger stroke volume, so more cardiac output, so (in the story) a faster dog and more prize money (Figure 2.7 A). The lecture’s slide draws the shift large to make the point clear. In a normal heart the effect of removing the pericardium is modest, as in the figure. The pericardium matters most when the heart is large or when the pericardial sac fills with fluid.
That second case is cardiac tamponade. Fluid in the pericardial sac squeezes the heart from outside, so the filling curve the ventricle works on is much steeper. At the same filling pressure the ventricle reaches a much smaller LVEDV, and stroke volume falls (Figure 2.7 B). In a patient the pressures measured inside the heart actually rise, because the fluid presses on the heart from outside. LVEDV still falls, because the ventricle is distended only by the difference between the pressure inside it and the pressure in the sac. The small groups follow this case, holding end-diastolic pressure fixed as the figure does, and then add the reflex response.






Figure 2.7: The pericardium sets part of the filling curve. Dashed blue curve, the new filling curve; dashed black line, the same end-diastolic pressure in both beats. (A) Pericardiectomy: a more compliant filling curve, a larger LVEDV at the same pressure, and a larger stroke volume. (B) Tamponade: fluid in the pericardial sac makes the filling curve steeper, so LVEDV and stroke volume fall at the same pressure, before any reflex response. From the model in Figure 2.1. Course figure.



Blood loss works on the same diagram in a different way. After a hemorrhage the filling curve does not change. Less blood returns to the heart, the filling pressure falls, and the ventricle fills to a smaller LVEDV on the same diastolic curve, so stroke volume falls by the Frank-Starling mechanism. A transfusion, or fluid retained by the kidneys over days, does the reverse. Why the filling pressure falls is a story about the veins and the mean systemic filling pressure (Pms), told in the Control of Cardiac Output chapter.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The Small Group 1 key explains these cases by saying that the ventricle “equilibrates” with Pms and that the mitral valve closes sooner after hemorrhage, or later after transfusion or pericardiectomy (Questions 16, 19 and 20, and Case 4). The mitral valve closes when the ventricle starts to contract, so its timing does not depend on Pms, and the ventricle fills from the atrium, not from Pms directly. Pms affects filling by setting venous return and the filling pressure. The predictions the key reaches are right: smaller LVEDV and stroke volume after hemorrhage, larger after transfusion or fluid retention, and larger after pericardiectomy compared with the tamponade beat.
The same key (Question 17) explains the fall in stroke volume after an infarction by “earlier closing of the aortic valve.” The cause is the flatter systolic curve, which makes ejection end at a larger LVESV.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 2  The Cardiac Pump
text:
2.6 Putting it together
The ventricle is a “dumb sump pump”: within its working range it ejects more when it is given more.

↑ venous return → ↑ LVEDV (preload) → ↑ force of contraction (Frank-Starling) → ↑ stroke volume → ↑ cardiac output (at the same heart rate)

This is how the heart matches its output to what the veins return, beat by beat, without any instruction from the nervous system. The nervous system adds a second set of controls, heart rate and contractility, which the ANS and Extrinsic Control chapter covers. How the pump and the veins together settle on one cardiac output is the subject of Control of Cardiac Output.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 2  The Cardiac Pump
text:
2.7 Check your understanding

Three sets of readings come from one beat of a left ventricle: (a) ventricle 6, left atrium 8, aorta 84 mm Hg; (b) ventricle 50, left atrium 10, aorta 80 mm Hg; (c) ventricle 115, left atrium 9, aorta 113 mm Hg. For each, which of the mitral and aortic valves is open, is ventricular volume changing, and which phase could it be?


Answer


Ventricular pressure is below atrial pressure, so the mitral valve is open, and below aortic pressure, so the aortic valve is closed. Blood is entering and volume is rising: a filling phase. With pressures this low and this close, it is diastasis or atrial systole rather than the first rush of rapid filling.
Ventricular pressure is above atrial pressure, so the mitral valve is closed, and below aortic pressure, so the aortic valve is closed too. With both valves shut, volume is not changing: an isovolumic phase. One set of numbers cannot tell you which one. Isovolumic contraction and isovolumic relaxation both pass through these pressures, and only the direction of change (pressure rising or falling) separates them.
Ventricular pressure is above aortic pressure, so the aortic valve is open and the mitral valve is closed. Volume is falling: ejection, near the peak. Late in ejection the aortic pressure can sit slightly above ventricular pressure with the valve still open, because the moving blood carries on until flow reverses.


A ventricle’s end-diastolic pressure rises from 10 to 20 mm Hg. Someone concludes that its preload has doubled. Describe two different changes on the diastolic pressure-volume curve that could each give this reading, and say what you would need to know to tell them apart.


Answer

First, the ventricle could have filled further along the same curve. Preload (LVEDV) has then risen, but by much less than double, because the curve gets steeper at higher volumes. On the curve in Figure 2.3, going from 10 to 20 mm Hg takes the volume only from about 135 to about 162 mL. Second, the curve itself could have shifted up and to the left, as in a stiffer ventricle. LVEDV could then be unchanged or even smaller, so preload has not risen at all. Pressure alone cannot separate the two. You need the end-diastolic volume itself, or to know which filling curve the ventricle is on.

A classmate says, “When the heart fills more, it contracts more forcefully, so its contractility goes up.” What is right and what is wrong, and how would the two possibilities look on a pressure-volume diagram?


Answer

The observation is right: more filling gives more force of contraction and a larger stroke volume (Frank-Starling). The conclusion is wrong: contractility is the slope of the systolic curve, and filling moves the beat along the same line. More preload widens the loop to the right with the systolic line unchanged. More contractility makes the systolic line steeper and widens the loop to the left, at the same LVEDV.

Aortic pressure rises suddenly while contractility stays the same. On the first beat the aortic valve opens at a higher pressure and the ventricle ejects 12 mL less than before. Venous return to the ventricle does not change. Over the next several beats stroke volume climbs back toward its old value, still with no change in contractility. Explain how, and say where the loop ends up.


Answer

The 12 mL that was not ejected stays in the ventricle. Venous return during the next diastole adds the usual volume on top of it, so the next LVEDV is larger. More filling stretches the sarcomeres, and the beat moves along the same systolic curve to a larger stroke volume (Frank-Starling). This repeats for a few beats until stroke volume again matches what the veins return. The loop ends up shifted to the right, at a larger LVEDV and a larger LVESV, still opening at the higher aortic pressure, with stroke volume close to where it started.

A drug raises contractility and nothing else: the heart rate, LVEDV and the aortic pressure at which the valve opens stay the same. Sketch the new loop over the old one. Which corner moves, which way, and what happens to stroke volume and stroke work?


Answer

The systolic curve gets steeper. The lower right corner (mitral closure, LVEDV) and the opening pressure stay where they were. The upper left corner, where ejection ends, moves left, to a smaller LVESV on the steeper line, and usually up a little. The loop widens to the left, so stroke volume rises, and its area, the stroke work, grows. With the heart rate unchanged, cardiac output rises in proportion to stroke volume.

During a slow, deep inspiration, left ventricular stroke volume falls slightly for a few beats. Using the fact that the two ventricles are in series, explain why.


Answer

Inspiration lowers the pressure around the heart and lungs. The pulmonary vessels widen and hold more blood, so for a few beats less blood reaches the left atrium than leaves the right ventricle. Left ventricular filling falls a little, end-diastolic volume is lower, and by Frank-Starling the left ventricle ejects a little less. The extra blood held in the lungs reaches the left side over the next few beats. Because the ventricles are in series, their outputs match when averaged over a whole breath, but not beat by beat.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 3  Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells
text:
3.1 The cell membrane
Every lecture in the muscle block, and the autonomic lecture after it, assumes you know what a membrane potential is and how a cell changes it. A skeletal muscle fiber contracts because an action potential reaches it. A heart cell’s plateau, a pacemaker’s slow drift toward threshold and a smooth muscle cell’s response to norepinephrine are all changes in membrane potential made by opening or closing particular channels. This chapter builds that foundation in the order the lecture does: the membrane, the resting potential and how to calculate it, how the potential changes, and the action potential.
The plasma membrane is a lipid bilayer. Each phospholipid has a polar head group that faces water and two nonpolar hydrocarbon tails. The tails of the two layers face each other, so the middle of the membrane is a thin oily sheet with no charge.
That oily core decides what can cross on its own. Small nonpolar molecules (O2, CO2, and lipid-soluble substances such as benzene) dissolve in it and diffuse straight through. Water crosses slowly. Ions, glucose, amino acids and proteins cannot cross without help: an ion carries a charge and a shell of water molecules, and moving it into a nonpolar layer costs far too much energy. So the membrane is a barrier to charge, and that is what lets it hold a voltage.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle
3  Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells

title: 3  Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells
text:
3.1.1 How molecules cross
Figure 3.1 shows the four routes the lecture covers.






Figure 3.1: Ways across the membrane. Simple diffusion through the lipid, channel-mediated diffusion through a water-filled pore, and carrier-mediated transport, in which the carrier binds its cargo on one side and changes shape to release it on the other, are all passive: they move substances down their electrochemical gradient and use no ATP. Active transport, such as the Na+/K+ ATPase, moves ions against their gradients and uses ATP. Course figure.




Simple diffusion through the lipid, for small nonpolar molecules.
Channel-mediated diffusion. A channel is a protein with a water-filled pore that lets particular ions through, down their gradient.
Carrier-mediated transport. A carrier binds its cargo on one side, changes shape, and releases it on the other. The carrier is highly specific, and if it simply moves its cargo down a gradient it needs no ATP (glucose entering most cells works this way).
Active transport. A pump uses energy from ATP to move ions against their gradients. The one that matters most here is the Na+/K+ ATPase, which moves 3 Na+ out of the cell and 2 K+ in for each ATP it splits.

The first three are passive: they only let substances move down the gradient that already exists. The pump is what makes the gradients in the first place and keeps them there.


3.1.2 Channels are selective
A K+ channel lets K+ through and keeps Na+ out, even though Na+ is the smaller ion:



Ion
Radius (Å)




Li+
0.60


Na+
0.95


K+
1.33


Rb+
1.48



So selectivity cannot be a matter of size alone. Channels select by:

Size and shape of the narrowest part of the pore, the selectivity filter.
Charge. Charged amino acids lining the pore attract ions of the opposite charge and repel ions of the same charge, so cation channels exclude anions.
Hydration energy. In water each ion is wrapped in a shell of water molecules, and a small ion holds its shell more tightly than a large one, because its charge is concentrated in a smaller space. To pass through a narrow filter an ion has to shed some of that water, and the channel has to pay the energy back by letting the ion bind to oxygen atoms lining the pore. The K+ channel’s filter is the right size for those oxygens to sit where the water molecules around a K+ ion would sit. Na+ is too small to touch all of them, so it cannot make up the energy of losing its tightly held water, and it stays out.







NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The ion-radius table on the slides lists Rb+ as 2.48 Å. The radius of Rb+ is about 1.48 Å. The point of the table is unchanged: the radii rise from Li+ to Rb+, and the channel that passes K+ excludes the smaller Na+.




3.1.3 Channels are gated
Most channels open and close, which is called gating. The lecture lists these kinds of gate:

Ligand-gated channels open when a molecule binds them. The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction is one (see Skeletal Muscle).
Voltage-gated channels open or close when the membrane potential changes. These make the action potential.
Thermally gated channels respond to temperature, as in temperature-sensing nerve endings.
Mechanically gated channels open when the membrane is stretched or deformed, as in touch receptors and the stretch-activated channels of smooth muscle.

Some channels have no gate and stay open. The K+ “leak” channels that are open at rest are the most important of these.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle
3  Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells

title: 3  Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells
text:
3.2 Membrane potentials
The membrane potential (Vm) is the difference in electrical potential across the membrane. In this course it is always given as the inside relative to the outside, so “−70 mV” means the inside is 70 mV negative to the outside.
It is stored energy: it pushes cations into the cell and anions out, and the cell uses that push to move ions and to drive transporters. And it is a signal: neurons, muscle cells and some secretory cells communicate by changing it.

3.2.1 How a potential is generated
The lecture builds the idea in two compartments (Figure 3.2). Compartment 1 holds 0.15 M KCl and compartment 2 holds 0.15 M NaCl. Each side is electrically neutral. The membrane between them lets only K+ through.






Figure 3.2: How a K+ gradient across a membrane permeable only to K+ makes a potential. (A) At the start each side is neutral. (B) K+ diffuses from compartment 1 into compartment 2, down its concentration gradient. Each K+ that crosses leaves a Cl− behind, so a thin layer of negative charge builds on the compartment 1 side of the membrane and positive charge on the other. That charge pulls K+ back. At equilibrium the electrical pull balances the concentration gradient and net K+ flux is zero. Course figure, after the lecture’s model.



K+ is much more concentrated in compartment 1, so it starts to diffuse into compartment 2. Cl− cannot follow. Each K+ that crosses carries a positive charge away and leaves a negative charge behind, so compartment 1 becomes negative. Now two forces act on K+:

the concentration (chemical) gradient, pushing K+ from compartment 1 to compartment 2, and
the electrical gradient, pulling the positive K+ back toward the negative compartment 1.

As more K+ crosses, the electrical force grows until it exactly balances the chemical force. Net K+ movement stops. The voltage at which that happens is the equilibrium potential for K+, EK. The two forces together are the electrochemical gradient, and at the equilibrium potential it is zero for that ion.
Very few ions have to move. In a cell about 10 µm across, only about one K+ in tens of thousands crosses to set up the potential, so the concentrations inside and outside do not measurably change. And the separated charge sits in a thin layer right against the two faces of the membrane. The bulk solution on each side stays neutral.
A cell works the same way. Compartment 1 is the cytosol, rich in K+, and compartment 2 is the extracellular fluid, rich in Na+. At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K+ than to anything else, through K+ leak channels, so K+ leaves, the inside becomes negative, and the resting potential sits close to EK.


3.2.2 Measuring it
The membrane potential is measured with a fine glass microelectrode filled with salt solution and pushed through the membrane, compared with a reference electrode in the extracellular fluid. As the tip enters the cell the reading drops from 0 to the resting potential, about −70 mV in a neuron and about −90 mV in skeletal and cardiac muscle cells.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle
3  Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells

title: 3  Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells
text:
3.3 Calculating membrane potentials

3.3.1 The Nernst equation: one ion
The Nernst equation gives the equilibrium potential for one ion: the voltage at which the electrical work of moving that ion across the membrane exactly balances the chemical work of moving it down its concentration gradient. You do not need to know the derivation.
\[E_X = \frac{RT}{zF}\ln\frac{[X]_o}{[X]_i}\]
R is the gas constant, T the absolute temperature, F Faraday’s constant, z the charge on the ion including its sign (+1 for K+ and Na+, +2 for Ca2+, −1 for Cl−), and [X]o and [X]i the concentrations outside and inside. At body temperature RT/F is about 26.7 mV. Switching to base-10 logarithms multiplies the constant by 2.303, and the equation becomes
\[E_X = \frac{61\ \text{mV}}{z}\log_{10}\frac{[X]_o}{[X]_i} \quad \text{at } 37\ ^\circ\text{C}\]
At room temperature the constant is about 58 to 59 mV. A tenfold concentration gradient of a monovalent cation gives an equilibrium potential 61 mV in size at body temperature, negative inside if the ion is more concentrated inside.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The slides and the notes write EX = 61 ln([X]o/[X]i) (and 59 ln at room temperature). The 61 mV constant goes with log10, not the natural log. With ln the constant is RT/F, about 26.7 mV. Using 61 with ln gives potentials 2.3 times too large: for K+ it would give about −216 mV instead of −94 mV. The slide’s key also defines z as the number of electrons transferred. In the Nernst equation z is the charge on the ion.


Using typical concentrations for a mammalian cell (these come from the 2018 course notes):

Read each equilibrium potential as the voltage that ion is “trying” to bring the membrane to (Figure 3.3). When channels for an ion open, that ion flows in the direction that moves Vm toward its equilibrium potential. At −70 mV, opening Na+ or Ca2+ channels lets positive charge in and depolarizes the cell. Opening K+ channels lets K+ out and moves Vm toward −94 mV.






Figure 3.3: Equilibrium potentials for the four main ions (left) and resting potentials of neurons and muscle cells (right), from the concentrations in the table. Resting potentials lie close to EK because the resting membrane is most permeable to K+. Course figure.



The driving force on an ion is the difference between where the membrane is and where that ion’s equilibrium potential is, Vm − EX. At rest the driving force on Na+ is huge (−70 − 66 = −136 mV, inward), and on K+ it is small (−70 − (−94) = +24 mV, outward). Only the small Na+ leak, driven by that large inward force, keeps the resting cell from going all the way to EK.


3.3.2 The Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation: several ions at once
A real membrane is permeable to more than one ion, so the resting potential is not any single equilibrium potential. The GHK equation combines them, weighting each ion’s concentrations by its permeability (P):
\[V_m = \frac{RT}{F}\ln\frac{P_K[K^+]_o + P_{Na}[Na^+]_o + P_{Cl}[Cl^-]_i}{P_K[K^+]_i + P_{Na}[Na^+]_i + P_{Cl}[Cl^-]_o}\]
Cl− appears upside down (inside on top, outside on the bottom) because it carries a negative charge. That flip is the only trick in the equation.
The meaning is simpler than the formula: the membrane potential sits nearest the equilibrium potential of the ion the membrane is most permeable to. If only one P is large, the GHK equation collapses into the Nernst equation for that ion.
Permeability ratios were first measured in the squid giant axon: at rest, PK : PNa : PCl is about 1 : 0.04 : 0.45. Borrowing those ratios and using the mammalian concentrations in the table, the GHK equation gives about −73 mV, close to the −70 mV of a neuron. During an action potential PNa rises far above PK, and Vm swings toward ENa. Nothing about the concentrations changed. Only the permeabilities did. That is the whole basis of electrical signaling: cells change their membrane potential by opening and closing channels.
Muscle cells rest nearer −90 mV than neurons do because their resting Na+ permeability is even smaller relative to K+ (in heart and skeletal muscle, inward-rectifier K+ channels carry the resting K+ current).


3.3.3 What the pump does
The Na+/K+ ATPase does not make the resting potential directly in any large way. Because it moves 3 Na+ out for 2 K+ in, it pushes out one net positive charge per cycle and adds a few millivolts of extra negativity. Its main job is to keep the gradients. At rest Na+ leaks in and K+ leaks out all the time, and without the pump the gradients would slowly run down and the resting potential with them. So the resting potential needs both kinds of transport: the pump to build the gradients, and the open K+ channels to turn the K+ gradient into a voltage.






WarningA common mistake



“More K+ inside the cell makes the inside more positive.” It does the opposite. The inside is negative because K+ leaves. What sets the resting potential is the K+ gradient, [K+]o/[K+]i. A bigger gradient (more K+ inside or less outside) makes EK, and the resting potential, more negative. A smaller gradient, as when extracellular K+ rises, makes them less negative.


Extracellular K+. Because the resting membrane is mostly a K+ electrode, its potential is very sensitive to the K+ outside the cell, which is small and can change. Doubling extracellular K+ from 4.5 to 9 mM moves EK from about −94 to −75 mV, and the GHK resting potential from about −73 to −65 mV: the cell is partly depolarized. Raising intracellular K+ by the same amount would barely matter, because 4.5 mM more on top of 155 mM hardly changes the ratio. This is why high plasma K+ (hyperkalemia) is dangerous for the heart. The ECG chapters follow what partial depolarization does to cardiac action potentials (EKG I: Ionic Basis).
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 3  Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells
text:
3.4 Changes in membrane potential
The membrane potential is not static. The lecture uses three words, always with the inside of the cell as the frame of reference:

Depolarization: the membrane potential becomes less negative (moves toward zero, or past it).
Repolarization: it returns toward the resting potential after a depolarization.
Hyperpolarization: it becomes more negative than rest.

The lecture’s examples are two transmitters that open ligand-gated channels on a neuron (Figure 3.4 A).

Glutamate opens cation channels. At −70 mV the driving force on Na+ is large and inward, so Na+ enters and the cell depolarizes.
GABA opens Cl− channels. When ECl is more negative than the membrane potential (here −76 versus −70 mV), Cl− enters, negative charge builds inside, and the cell hyperpolarizes.

The rule behind both is the one from the Nernst section: an open channel pulls Vm toward the equilibrium potential of the ion it passes.






Figure 3.4: Changes in membrane potential. (A) A depolarization from glutamate and a hyperpolarization from GABA, schematic. (B) Graded potentials in a model neuron (Hodgkin-Huxley model, adjusted to rest at −70 mV with threshold near −55 mV). Larger stimuli give larger depolarizations, each fading back to rest. Two stimuli close together summate, reach threshold, and fire an action potential. Course figure.



These local changes are graded: a bigger stimulus opens more channels and gives a bigger change. They also fade, in time as the charge leaks back out through resting channels, and with distance as current spreads along the cell. Two of them that overlap in time can add together, which is called summation (Figure 3.4 B). If the sum reaches threshold, the cell fires an action potential.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 3  Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells
section: 3.5 Excitable cells and the action potential
text:
3.5 Excitable cells and the action potential
An excitable cell is a cell that can generate an action potential. The course covers four: neurons, skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle and smooth muscle.
An action potential is a rapid, transient change in membrane potential. In outline:

A stimulus depolarizes the membrane.
If it reaches threshold, voltage-gated channels open.
A rapid, self-limited influx of positive ions depolarizes the cell.
An efflux of positive ions repolarizes it.


3.5.1 The steps
Figure 3.5 follows a neuron’s action potential through the five steps on the lecture slides.






Figure 3.5: The action potential in a model neuron, with the five steps from the lecture. (A) Membrane potential. Numbers mark (1) threshold, (2) the rising phase, (3) the falling phase and (4) rebound hyperpolarization. The tan band is the absolute refractory period, from the upstroke through repolarization, and the gray band is the relative refractory period (5) during rebound hyperpolarization. Both are drawn schematically. (B) Na+ and K+ conductances. Hodgkin-Huxley model of the squid giant axon, adjusted so rest is −70 mV and threshold about −55 mV. The slides’ figures use somewhat different resting and threshold values; the sequence of events is what matters. Course figure.



1. Reaching threshold. A stimulus depolarizes the membrane. Depolarization opens some voltage-gated Na+ channels, Na+ enters, and that depolarizes the membrane further. Below threshold, the outward K+ leak wins and the membrane falls back to rest. At threshold (about −55 mV in a neuron), the Na+ entering just outruns the K+ leaving, and the process feeds itself.
2. Rising phase. Now positive feedback takes over: depolarization opens Na+ channels, Na+ entry depolarizes the membrane further, which opens more Na+ channels. PNa jumps far above PK, and the membrane potential races toward ENa. It overshoots zero, but it never quite reaches ENa, because K+ is still leaving.
3. Falling phase. Within about a millisecond the Na+ channels inactivate: a separate inactivation gate plugs the pore, so they close even though the membrane is still depolarized. At the same time the voltage-gated K+ channels, which open more slowly than Na+ channels, are now open. K+ leaves and repolarizes the cell.
4. Rebound hyperpolarization. The voltage-gated K+ channels also close slowly, so for a few milliseconds PK is higher than at rest and the membrane dips below the resting potential, toward EK. The notes call this the after-hyperpolarization.
5. Refractory period. An inactivated Na+ channel cannot be opened again by depolarization. It has to return to the closed state first, and it only does that once the membrane has repolarized. The Na+ channel therefore has three states:









State
Activation gate
Inactivation gate
Can depolarization open it?




Closed (resting)
shut
open
yes


Open
open
open
(already open)


Inactivated
open
shut
no, until the membrane repolarizes



During the absolute refractory period, from the upstroke through repolarization, so many Na+ channels are inactivated that no stimulus, however large, can fire a second action potential. During the relative refractory period that follows, enough Na+ channels have recovered to fire one, but some are still inactivated and extra K+ channels are still open, so it takes a stronger-than-normal stimulus. The refractory period limits how often a cell can fire and keeps an action potential moving forward (below).
The voltage-gated K+ channel in this picture has only two states, closed and open. It opens and closes slowly, but it does not inactivate.


3.5.2 All or none
An action potential is an all-or-none event. A stimulus that does not reach threshold produces only a graded potential that fades. Any stimulus that does reach threshold produces a full action potential, and a bigger stimulus does not make a bigger one. The size and shape come from the cell’s channels, not from the stimulus. Cells signal “more” by firing more often, not by firing larger spikes.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The notes say that once threshold is reached “every channel in that region participates.” Not every channel opens. What is all-or-none is the event: once the positive feedback starts, the spike runs to its full size no matter how strong the stimulus was.




3.5.3 Different cells, different action potentials
Action potentials come from time- and voltage-dependent changes in ionic permeability, and different excitable cells have different channels, so their action potentials look different (Figure 3.6).






Figure 3.6: Action potentials of three excitable cells, each on its own time scale. (A) Neuron: about 2 ms. (B) Skeletal muscle fiber: about 5 ms, from a resting potential near −90 mV. (C) Ventricular muscle cell: about 250 ms, with a long plateau. Panel A is from the model in Figure 3.5; panels B and C are drawn to match the lecture’s comparison. Course figure.




A neuron’s action potential lasts about 2 ms.
A skeletal muscle fiber’s lasts a few milliseconds and starts from about −90 mV. It is over long before the muscle reaches peak force, which matters for tetanus (Skeletal Muscle).
A ventricular muscle cell’s (a fast-response action potential) lasts about 250 ms. After a fast Na+ upstroke, L-type Ca2+ channels open and Ca2+ entry balances K+ exit for a long plateau. The plateau keeps the cell refractory until the contraction is nearly over, which is why heart muscle cannot be tetanized. The Cardiac Muscle chapter and EKG I: Ionic Basis cover its phases (0 to 4) and currents.

Not every excitable cell uses Na+ for its upstroke. Cardiac pacemaker cells in the SA and AV nodes have slow-response action potentials whose upstroke is carried by L-type Ca2+ channels, and most smooth muscle also depends on Ca2+ entry.






WarningA common mistake



Applying the neuron’s rules to every cell. A Na+ channel blocker slows the upstroke and the conduction of action potentials in cells that depend on Na+ channels (neurons, skeletal muscle, atrial and ventricular muscle, Purkinje fibers). It does not slow the SA node, so it does not slow the heart rate, and AV nodal conduction depends on the L-type Ca2+ current, not on Na+ channels. Before predicting what a drug or an ion change does, ask which channel carries the upstroke in that cell.

3  Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells

title: 3  Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells
text:
3.6 How the action potential spreads
An action potential starts at one spot and has to travel along the cell. It does this by local current (Figure 3.7).






Figure 3.7: How an action potential spreads, at one instant. (A) Membrane potential along the axon. (B) Inside the active region Na+ is entering. That positive charge flows along the inside of the cell in both directions and returns outside, completing local circuits. Ahead of the active region the current depolarizes resting membrane to threshold, so it fires next. Behind it the Na+ channels are inactivated, so the same current cannot re-excite that membrane. Farther behind, the membrane is recovering and is still relatively refractory. Drawn from the model in Figure 3.5; the rise ahead of the wave is schematic. Course figure.



Where the membrane is firing, Na+ pours in and the inside becomes positive. That charge spreads along the inside of the cell to the neighboring membrane, which is still at rest, and returns through the extracellular fluid, completing a local circuit. The current depolarizes the neighboring membrane. When that membrane reaches threshold, its own Na+ channels open and it fires, and then it depolarizes the next patch. Each patch regenerates the full action potential, so the signal does not fade with distance the way a graded potential does.
The current spreads backward as well as forward. The membrane just behind has fired a moment earlier and its Na+ channels are inactivated, so it is refractory and cannot fire again. That is why an action potential travels in one direction, away from where it started.
Between cells the same local currents can pass through gap junctions: channels that connect the cytoplasm of neighboring cells. Heart muscle cells and single-unit smooth muscle cells are linked this way, so an action potential in one cell spreads to the next and the tissue contracts together. Skeletal muscle fibers are not coupled. Each fiber is fired by its own motor nerve ending.






NoteBackground: two kinds of receptor





The 2026 lecture does not cover this. The autonomic and smooth muscle lectures build on it.

Ligand-gated ion channels (also called ionotropic receptors) are themselves channels. The transmitter binds, the channel opens, and the membrane potential changes within a millisecond. Examples: the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction and on autonomic ganglion cells, and the glutamate and GABA receptors above.
G protein-coupled receptors are not channels. The ligand changes the receptor’s shape, the receptor activates a G protein on the inside of the membrane, and the G protein changes an enzyme or a channel. The response is slower, and it is amplified, because one receptor activates many G proteins and each enzyme makes many second-messenger molecules. Adrenergic and muscarinic receptors are G protein-coupled.

The Smooth Muscle and ANS and Extrinsic Control chapters show which G protein each adrenergic and muscarinic receptor uses.

title: 3  Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells
text:
3.7 Check your understanding

A membrane separates 100 mM KCl (side 1) from 10 mM KCl (side 2) at 37 °C and is permeable only to K+. Which side becomes negative, and by how much?


Answer

K+ diffuses from side 1 to side 2, leaving Cl− behind, so side 1 becomes negative. With side 1 as “inside,” EK = 61 log(10/100) = −61 mV. If you used the slide’s form of the equation, 61 × ln(0.1), you would get −140 mV: 61 goes with log10.

Why is a neuron’s resting potential (−70 mV) close to EK (−94 mV) and far from ENa (+66 mV), and why is it not exactly at EK?


Answer

At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K+ than to Na+ (about 25 to 1), and the GHK equation weights each ion by its permeability, so Vm sits near EK. A small Na+ permeability remains, and Na+ has a large inward driving force, so the trickle of Na+ in pulls Vm a little positive of EK. The pump keeps the gradients from running down.

Extracellular K+ rises from 4.5 to 7 mM, with intracellular K+ at 155 mM. Calculate the new EK. The resting potential moves from about −73 to about −68 mV. Why does Vm move less than EK does?


Answer

EK = 61 log(7/155) ≈ −82 mV, so EK moves about 12 mV, from −94 to −82. The resting potential moves only about 5 mV. Vm is a permeability-weighted balance of all the ions the membrane passes, not EK itself. K+ has by far the largest permeability, so Vm moves the same way as EK, but the Na+ and Cl− terms in the GHK equation have not changed, and they hold Vm back from following the whole way. A cell whose resting Na+ permeability is even smaller relative to K+, such as a muscle cell resting near −90 mV, follows EK more closely.

In the heart, acetylcholine from the vagus nerve opens extra K+ channels in SA node cells. Which way does K+ move, and which way does the membrane potential change?


Answer

An open channel pulls Vm toward the equilibrium potential of the ion it passes. SA node cells sit well positive of EK, so K+ leaves the cell, positive charge is lost from the inside, and Vm moves toward EK: the cell hyperpolarizes. Starting each cycle from a more negative potential is one way acetylcholine slows the heart (ANS and Extrinsic Control).

A drug removes the Na+ channel’s inactivation gate, so the channels stay open as long as the membrane is depolarized. Which phases of the action potential change?


Answer

The rising phase is unchanged, because it depends on activation. The falling phase is slowed or lost, because Na+ inactivation is one of the two things that end the spike, so the cell stays depolarized much longer, held up by continued Na+ entry against the K+ current. Inactivation is also what makes the membrane behind a moving action potential refractory, so that protection would be lost as well.

The neuromuscular junction sits near the middle of a skeletal muscle fiber. Why does the fiber’s action potential travel toward both ends, and why does neither wave turn back?


Answer

Local current spreads both ways from the active membrane at the end plate. Membrane on both sides is at rest and can be brought to threshold, so two action potentials leave in opposite directions, one toward each end. Once each wave is moving, the membrane behind it has just fired and its Na+ channels are inactivated, so it is refractory. Only the membrane ahead can fire, and the waves stop when they reach the ends of the fiber.
