title: 4  Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics
text:
4.1 How the circulation is arranged
The circulation exists for exchange. Oxygen, nutrients, wastes and heat move between blood and tissue across the walls of the capillaries, and everything upstream of the capillaries is there to get blood to them. The course describes the system as two pumps and two exchangers: the right heart pumps blood through the lungs, where it exchanges gas with air, and the left heart pumps it through the body’s tissues, where it exchanges with cells. The Cardiovascular Physiology Overview introduces that plan. This chapter supplies the physics: what makes blood flow, what resists it, how fast it moves, and how the elastic walls of the vessels change the picture. The next chapter, Microcirculation and Local Control, takes the same ideas down to the capillary, and answers the question this lecture ends on: why a capillary one cell thick does not burst.
The right and left hearts are in series: all the blood that leaves the right ventricle passes through the lungs and returns to the left heart. The lung is a single bed on that path, although inside the lung the vessels branch into an enormous parallel network of capillaries. The Pulmonary Circulation chapter covers it.
The systemic circulation is different. The aorta gives off branches to the brain, the heart muscle, skeletal muscle, skin and the other organs, and those beds sit side by side, in parallel, between the arterial and venous systems (Figure 4.1). In most of them, arterial blood passes through a single capillary bed before it enters the veins. Within one organ the vessels are in series: artery, arteriole, capillary, venule, vein. The parallel layout lets each organ adjust its own flow by changing its own resistance, and if one branch is blocked the others still receive blood.
The course calls the kidney and liver the “rule breakers”:
Posture. Lying flat, most organ beds receive about the same arterial pressure. Standing adds the weight of a column of blood: pressures below the heart rise and pressures above it fall, in arteries and veins alike, and the leg veins distend and hold more blood. The ANS and Extrinsic Control chapter covers the reflex response.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 4  Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics
text:
Figure 4.1: Organization of the circulation. The hearts and lungs are in series; most systemic organs are parallel beds, each with one capillary bed. The kidney and the gut and liver have two capillary beds in series. Course figure.





Kidney. Blood passes through the glomerular capillaries, the efferent arteriole, and then the peritubular capillaries. The efferent arteriole’s resistance makes peritubular pressure much lower than glomerular pressure, which lets those capillaries reabsorb what the glomerulus filtered.
Gut and liver. Blood from the gut passes through its capillaries, collects in the portal vein, and passes through the liver’s capillaries before reaching the vena cava. The liver also has arterial blood from the hepatic artery. The Other Special Circulations chapter returns to the splanchnic bed.

title: 4  Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics
text:
4.2 Vessel structure and function
Three materials set what a vessel wall can do. Elastin lets the wall stretch and recoil. Collagen gives it tensile strength and limits how far it can stretch. Smooth muscle changes the vessel’s caliber. How much of each a vessel has matches its job.








Vessel
Wall
Job




Aorta and large arteries
Thick, elastic
Distribution. Their walls stretch as the heart ejects and recoil in diastole (the hydraulic filter, below).


Small, muscular arteries
More smooth muscle
Distribute blood to organs, with some role in regulating flow


Arterioles
Mostly smooth muscle around an endothelium, with sympathetic innervation
Resistance. By changing radius they set how much blood enters each capillary bed. The course calls them the circulation’s stopcocks.


Capillaries
One layer of endothelium on a basement membrane; no smooth muscle
Exchange. Density follows metabolic rate: heart muscle has a far denser network than subcutaneous tissue.


Venules
Thin layer of smooth muscle, sparse innervation
Collect capillary blood; also exchange fluid and solutes, and are where white cells leave the blood


Veins
Thin, very compliant walls with some smooth muscle; valves in the limbs
Storage. They hold most of the blood volume at low pressure. Venoconstriction shifts stored blood toward the heart.



Capillaries have no smooth muscle and cannot constrict, but their endothelial cells can change shape through actin and myosin, opening larger, leakier gaps between them. In inflammation this happens mostly in the postcapillary venules.

4.2.1 Where the blood is
Of about 5 L of blood, roughly 84% is in the systemic circulation, 9% in the pulmonary circulation and 7% in the heart. The systemic veins hold about two-thirds of the total, the arteries about 14% and the systemic capillaries only about 6%. So a modest change in venous tone moves a large volume toward or away from the heart. The Control of Cardiac Output chapter builds on this with stressed and unstressed volume.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The vessel-wall slide’s notes put more than 65% of the blood in the large capacitance veins. The volume table two slides later gives 46% in the small veins and 18% in the large veins, so the two-thirds belongs to the systemic veins as a whole.

title: 4  Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics
text:
4.3 Pressure gradients drive flow
Hemodynamics is the study of blood flow. The course uses these symbols:








Symbol
Meaning
Usual units




P
Pressure
mm Hg


Q
Flow rate: volume per unit time
mL/min or L/min


v
Mean velocity: distance per unit time (the slides write v̄)
cm/s


A
Cross-sectional area
cm²


R
Hydraulic resistance
mm Hg·min/L



Blood flows only when there is a pressure difference along a vessel. For steady flow,
\[Q = \frac{\Delta P}{R} = \frac{P_1 - P_2}{R}\]
This is the fluid version of Ohm’s law (I = ΔV/R): pressure difference plays the role of voltage, flow of current, and hydraulic resistance of electrical resistance. Friction between layers of blood turns some of its pressure energy into heat, which is why pressure falls along the way.

4.3.1 Ohm’s law for the whole systemic circulation
Apply the same law to the systemic circuit as a whole. The flow is the cardiac output. The pressure at the start is the mean arterial pressure (MAP). The pressure at the end is the pressure in the great veins as they enter the right atrium, the central venous pressure (CVP), which approximates right atrial pressure (Pra). The resistance of all the systemic vessels together, from the aortic valve to the right atrium, is the systemic vascular resistance (SVR).
\[\text{CO} = \frac{\text{MAP} - \text{CVP}}{\text{SVR}} \qquad\text{so}\qquad \text{SVR} = \frac{\text{MAP} - \text{CVP}}{\text{CO}}\]
SVR cannot be measured directly. It is calculated from MAP, CVP and cardiac output. With pressure in mm Hg and output in L/min, its unit is mm Hg·min/L. Rearranged,
\[\text{MAP} = \text{CO} \times \text{SVR} + \text{CVP}\]
Because CVP is normally only a few mm Hg, the course often writes the shorthand MAP ≈ CO × SVR. Widespread arteriolar constriction raises SVR, and if cardiac output and CVP stay the same, MAP rises. In a patient the variables often change together.
The slides note that SVR is also called total peripheral resistance (TPR). This book uses SVR.






WarningA common mistake: leaving CVP out of SVR



SVR is the driving pressure across the systemic circuit divided by the flow through it, and the driving pressure is MAP minus CVP, not MAP. In a healthy person at rest the difference is small: with MAP 93, CVP 3 and CO 5 L/min, SVR = (93 − 3)/5 = 18 mm Hg·min/L, and dividing MAP alone by CO gives 18.6.
When CVP is high, as in heart failure or fluid overload, leaving it out gives a wrong answer and can point you the wrong way. Take MAP 90, CVP 18 and CO 4. SVR = (90 − 18)/4 = 18, the same as the healthy value. Dividing MAP alone by CO gives 22.5 and suggests that resistance has risen by a quarter when it has not changed. Whenever CVP is given, subtract it.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 4  Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics
text:
4.4 Perfusion pressure and transmural pressure
Two different pressure differences act on every vessel, and they do different things (Figure 4.2).

Perfusion pressure is the difference along the vessel: upstream intravascular pressure minus downstream intravascular pressure. It drives flow along the vessel and through a tissue bed, Q = ΔP/R.
Transmural pressure is the difference across the wall at one point: pressure inside minus pressure outside, Ptm = Pinside − Poutside. A positive transmural pressure tends to distend the vessel. A negative one favors compression or collapse, depending on how stiff the wall is and how well the surrounding tissue supports it. Transmural pressure does not push blood along the vessel.







Figure 4.2: Perfusion pressure and transmural pressure in the same idealized vessel. (A) The 80 mm Hg difference along the vessel drives flow. (B) At one point, 60 mm Hg inside and 10 mm Hg outside give a transmural pressure of +50 mm Hg, which holds the vessel open. (C) With both ends at 60 mm Hg there is no flow, but the vessel stays distended. Values are illustrative. Course figure, after the 2026 lecture slide.



Panel C is the check: a high pressure inside a vessel does not by itself mean that blood is flowing. Flow needs a pressure difference from one end to the other.
Transmural pressure is what stretches a vessel, so it is the pressure in the definition of compliance later in this chapter and the stimulus for the myogenic response in the next. (The lung’s transmural pressure is the transpulmonary pressure of Respiratory Statics.) External compression lowers transmural pressure and narrows a vessel, which raises its resistance even if upstream pressure does not change.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 4  Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics
text:
4.5 Mean arterial pressure
Arterial pressure is not steady. It rises to the systolic pressure as the ventricle ejects and falls to the diastolic pressure just before the next beat. The difference between them is the pulse pressure:
\[\text{PP} = \text{SBP} - \text{DBP}\]
Ohm’s law needs one number for the pressure driving flow over the whole cycle: the mean arterial pressure, the time-average of the waveform (the area under the pressure-time curve divided by the cycle length). On a graph, MAP is the level at which the area of the waveform above the line equals the area below it (Figure 4.3). Measuring it needs an arterial catheter, so in clinic we estimate it from a cuff reading:
\[\text{MAP} \approx \text{DBP} + \tfrac{1}{3}(\text{SBP} - \text{DBP})\]
The summary slide writes the same thing as Pdia + ⅓ PP. For 120/80 mm Hg, the pulse pressure is 40 and MAP ≈ 80 + 40/3 ≈ 93 mm Hg.






Figure 4.3: MAP is the time-average of arterial pressure: in each panel the tan area above the solid mean line equals the gray area below it. (A) At a resting rate the true mean, 93 mm Hg, matches the one-third rule (dashed). (B) At 150 beats/min diastole is shortened much more than systole, the true mean rises to about 97 mm Hg, and the one-third rule underestimates it. Model waveform, 120/80 mm Hg in both panels. Course figure.



Why one-third, and not halfway? The waveform rises fast, falls fast, and then spends the long diastolic runoff, about two-thirds of each beat at rest, close to diastolic pressure, so the average sits below the midpoint. (It is not the center of mass of a triangle: a triangular pulse averages halfway up.) At fast heart rates diastole shortens, the true mean moves toward halfway, and the one-third formula underestimates MAP.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 4  Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics
text:
4.6 What sets resistance: Poiseuille’s law
For steady, laminar flow of a simple fluid through a rigid cylindrical tube, Poiseuille’s law gives the flow:
\[Q = \frac{\Delta P \, \pi r^4}{8 \eta L}\]
Comparing with Q = ΔP/R gives the resistance:
\[R = \frac{8 \eta L}{\pi r^4}\]
Here r is the tube’s radius, L its length and η the viscosity of the fluid. Resistance rises in direct proportion to length and viscosity and falls with the fourth power of the radius.
The fourth power is why radius matters so much. Halve a vessel’s radius and its resistance rises 24 = 16-fold. What that does depends on what is held constant:

If the pressure difference stays the same, flow falls to one-sixteenth.
If the flow has to stay the same, the pressure difference needed to drive it rises 16-fold.

Always identify what is being held constant before you predict a result.
Length hardly changes and viscosity changes only slowly. Radius is what the body adjusts, and the arterioles, with their thick smooth muscle, change it quickly, which is why they control flow. Blood and vessels do not meet all of Poiseuille’s assumptions (blood is a suspension of cells, vessels are elastic, flow is pulsatile), but the equation still explains why a small change in caliber has a large effect.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 4  Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics
section: 4.7 Resistances in series and in parallel
text:
4.7 Resistances in series and in parallel
The circulation combines both arrangements (Figure 4.4).
In series, the same flow passes through each segment in turn, and the resistances add:
\[R_t = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\]
Along a single tissue pathway, the artery, arteriole, capillaries and vein are in series. Because ΔP = Q × R and Q is the same through each, the largest pressure drop occurs across the segment with the largest resistance. Along most pathways that is the small arteries and arterioles.
In parallel, the branches share the same inlet and outlet pressure. Each branch takes flow according to its own resistance, and the branch flows add up to the total:
\[Q_t = Q_1 + Q_2 + Q_3 \qquad \frac{1}{R_t} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3}\]
Total resistance is lower than the resistance of any single branch. Adding an open pathway in parallel always lowers total resistance. The reciprocal of resistance is called conductance, and in parallel the conductances simply add. You will not be asked to calculate a parallel resistance on the exam, but you should understand what the equations imply.






Figure 4.4: Resistances in series and in parallel. (A) Four segments in series between 95 and 5 mm Hg. The same flow passes through each, so each segment’s share of the pressure drop is proportional to its resistance, and the arteriole, with the largest resistance, takes the largest drop. Relative resistances are illustrative. (B) Three branches in parallel share the same pressure difference. Their flows add, and the total resistance is less than that of any one branch. Course figure.



Two consequences of the parallel layout matter clinically:

One branch changes its own flow, not the whole circulation’s. A large rise in the resistance of one branch, such as cross-clamping a femoral artery during surgery, cuts that branch’s flow sharply but barely changes SVR or arterial pressure. Constricting arterioles in many beds at once, as a sympathetic reflex does, raises SVR and MAP.
Many small vessels together can have a low resistance. A single capillary has a very high resistance; billions in parallel have a much lower combined resistance. The resistance of the network depends on the number, radius and length of the individual vessels, not on aggregate area alone: ten thousand thin straws in parallel resist flow more than one wide pipe with the same total area. Capillaries are not negligible: in Figure 4.6 mean pressure falls from about 35 to about 15 mm Hg across them. But the arterioles carry the largest drop, and they are the vessels that can change.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 4  Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics
text:
4.8 Flow rate and velocity
Flow rate and velocity are different quantities, and mixing them up is one of the most common errors in this part of the course.

Flow rate (Q) is how much blood passes a point per unit time: a volume per time, such as mL/min or L/min. Cardiac output, about 5 L/min (83 mL/s), is a flow rate.
Velocity (v) is how fast the blood itself is moving: a distance per time, such as cm/s. Mean velocity is about 21 cm/s in the aorta and about 0.03 cm/s in the capillaries.

In a time t, the blood that crosses a plane in a vessel of area A fills a cylinder of area A and length d = v × t, so the volume per unit time is
\[Q = A \times v \qquad v = \frac{Q}{A}\]

4.8.1 Conservation of mass
Blood is essentially incompressible, so in a steady state the same volume passes every cross-section of an unbranched tube each second (Qin = Qout), the continuity equation. Where the tube narrows the blood moves faster; where it widens it slows (Figure 4.5), like a river through a wide, slow stretch and a narrow, fast rapid. At a branch point, the incoming flow equals the sum of the outgoing flows. Compliant vessels can store or release blood during a beat, but averaged over whole cycles inflow and outflow balance.






Figure 4.5: Continuity. The same flow, 10 cm³/s, passes through three sections of different area. The dark band in each section is the volume that passes in one second, drawn to scale: it stretches out and moves fast where the tube is narrow, and bunches up and moves slowly where the tube is wide. Course figure.





4.8.2 Why blood is slow in the capillaries
Is blood velocity higher in the aorta or in the capillaries? Many students guess the capillaries, because each is so narrow. But the aorta does not empty into one capillary. Its flow divides among about 1010 capillaries, and what matters for velocity is their aggregate cross-sectional area, about 2,800 cm². That is roughly the area of a 24-inch pizza, which the course calls the Big Benito.
With the course’s round numbers, 83 mL/s divided by the aorta’s 4 cm² gives about 21 cm/s, and divided by about 2,800 cm² gives about 0.03 cm/s, roughly 700 times slower. On the venous side aggregate area falls and velocity rises again. The slow transit through the capillaries gives time for exchange.






WarningA common mistake



“Narrow means fast” is true for one tube with the same flow through it. It is not true for a bed of many narrow tubes in parallel. Each capillary is narrow, but together they offer a huge area, and that is what sets the mean velocity. Ask which area the whole flow has to pass through.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 4  Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics
section: 4.9 Area, velocity and pressure across the circulation
text:
4.9 Area, velocity and pressure across the circulation
Figure 4.6 puts the pieces together.

Aggregate cross-sectional area rises with each generation of branching, peaks in the capillaries, and falls again as the veins converge.
Mean velocity is the mirror image, because v = Q/A and Q is the same at every level.
Pressure falls continuously from the aorta to the right atrium, because resistance dissipates it, but not evenly. The large arteries are good conduits with little resistance, so mean pressure falls only a little along them. The steepest fall is across the small arteries and arterioles, the resistance vessels. Mean pressure continues to fall through the capillaries (a representative capillary pressure is about 25 mm Hg) and the veins, reaching a few mm Hg in the vena cava. The pulsations are damped across the small arteries and arterioles and have almost disappeared by the capillaries.







Figure 4.6: Aggregate cross-sectional area, mean velocity and pressure from the aorta to the vena cava. (A, B) Values from the vascular dimensions table above, plotted on logarithmic scales. Velocity is lowest where aggregate area is greatest. (C) Representative pressures: mean pressure falls little in the large arteries and most steeply across the small arteries and arterioles. The pulsatile range (shaded) is damped across the small arteries and arterioles and has nearly vanished by the capillaries. Area and velocity data adapted from Boron and Boulpaep [1], as used in the 2026 lecture. Course figure.



Do not read velocity into the pressure curve. Low velocity follows from large aggregate area; a pressure drop reflects resistance to flow.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 4  Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics
text:
4.10 Compliance
Vessels are elastic. Compliance is the change in volume for a given change in transmural pressure:
\[C = \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta P}\]
On a graph with volume on the vertical axis and transmural pressure on the horizontal axis, compliance is the slope (Figure 4.7). A steep curve means a large change in volume for a small change in pressure: high compliance.






Figure 4.7: Compliance of an artery and a vein. Compliance is the slope of the volume-pressure curve, shown by the small triangles. The vein’s curve is steep at low pressure, so it takes up a large volume with little rise in pressure. The artery’s curve is shallow. Both become less compliant as they fill. Schematic. Course figure, after the 2026 lecture slide.



Veins are far more compliant than arteries, which is why they hold about two-thirds of the blood volume at low pressure, and why a large change in blood volume changes venous pressure comparatively little. Both become stiffer as they fill, as collagen takes up the load.






TipCheck the axes



In the Cardiac Pump lecture, the ventricle’s filling curve had pressure on the vertical axis and volume on the horizontal axis, so its slope was stiffness (ΔP/ΔV). In this lecture the axes are swapped, so the slope is compliance (ΔV/ΔP). Same idea, opposite slope. Check the axes before you read a slope. Compliance is also a different property from contractility; see the Cardiac Pump chapter.



4.10.1 The hydraulic filter
The left ventricle ejects only during systole, yet blood flows through the capillaries almost steadily. During systole the ventricle ejects faster than blood can drain through the arterioles, so part of the stroke volume is stored by stretching the aorta and large arteries. After the aortic valve closes, those walls recoil passively and keep pushing blood through the arteriolar resistance all through diastole, so pressure falls slowly and flow continues between beats (Figure 4.8).
The electrical analogy is an RC filter: a capacitor (the compliance) stores charge, and a resistor (the arterioles) limits how fast it discharges. The pair passes the average and strips out the fast fluctuations. The course calls this arrangement the hydraulic filter, also called the Windkessel effect. The Control of Cardiac Output chapter uses it to explain systolic and pulse pressure.






Figure 4.8: The hydraulic filter: a ventricle ejecting into a compliant aorta that drains through a fixed arteriolar resistance. (A) Flow leaves the ventricle in bursts. (B) With a compliant aorta (solid), pressure rises less in systole and falls less in diastole than with a stiff aorta (dashed); mean pressure is the same in both. (C) Flow through the arterioles follows pressure, so it is smoother with the compliant aorta. With no compliance it would copy the bursts in panel A. The model leaves out pressure waves that travel along the arteries. Course figure.



Arteries stiffen with age; the Control of Cardiac Output chapter works out what that does to systolic and pulse pressure, and how the pressure pulse changes as it travels along the large arteries.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 4  Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics
text:
4.11 Blood viscosity
Viscosity (η) is a fluid’s internal resistance to deformation. In Poiseuille’s law resistance is proportional to viscosity, so more viscous blood needs a larger pressure difference to keep the same flow, and the heart works harder. Water and plasma are Newtonian: their viscosity is the same however fast they flow. Blood, a suspension of cells, is non-Newtonian: its apparent viscosity depends on how it is flowing.

Hematocrit. More red cells mean more viscous blood. In polycythemia (a high hematocrit), viscosity and resistance rise; in anemia they fall.
Flow rate. Blood is shear thinning: as flow slows, its apparent viscosity rises. (Strictly, viscosity depends on the shear rate, how quickly velocity changes from one layer of fluid to the next, which falls as flow slows.) In slow flow, red cells stack into rouleaux; faster flow breaks the stacks up. The lecture’s oobleck is non-Newtonian too, but it thickens under shear, the opposite of blood.
Red cell deformability and shape. Red cells normally fold to pass through small vessels. Cells that deform poorly, such as sickled cells, raise resistance.
Temperature. Cold raises blood viscosity, as in hypothermia.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 4  Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics
text:
4.12 Laminar and turbulent flow
Normally blood flows in smooth layers, laminar flow: the layer touching the wall does not move and the central layer moves fastest, so the velocity profile is a parabola (Figure 4.9). Poiseuille’s law describes laminar flow. High velocity and abrupt narrowing, as at a stenotic valve or a plaque in a carotid artery, break the layers into chaotic eddies, turbulent flow, which wastes pressure. Turbulence makes the vessel wall vibrate: over the heart the sound is a murmur, over an artery a bruit. The normal heart sounds S1 and S2 come from valve closure, not turbulence. You will not be asked about laminar versus turbulent flow.






Figure 4.9: Laminar flow. Velocity is zero at the wall and greatest in the center, a parabolic profile. Schematic. Course figure.









NoteBackground: the pressure cost of turbulence





In laminar flow the resistance is constant, so flow rises in a straight line with perfusion pressure. Once turbulence begins, flow keeps rising with pressure but more slowly, roughly with the square root of the pressure difference, so more pressure is needed for a given flow. It does not level off at a maximum, as the lecture notes’ phrase “reaching an upper asymptote” suggests.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 4  Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics
text:
4.13 Check your understanding

Along one tissue pathway, an artery, its arterioles, the capillaries and a vein are in series. Across which segment is the largest pressure drop, and why? If the arterioles’ resistance doubled, with arterial and venous pressures unchanged, what would happen to flow through the pathway and to pressure in the capillaries?


Answer

The same flow passes through every segment in series, so each segment’s pressure drop is Q × R, and the largest drop is across the largest resistance: the arterioles (with the small arteries). Doubling arteriolar resistance raises the pathway’s total resistance, so flow falls. A larger share of the pressure is now used up across the arterioles, so capillary pressure falls. The next chapter uses this to explain how arterioles set capillary filtration.

Why is the driving pressure for flow through the systemic circulation MAP minus CVP, and not MAP alone? What would happen to systemic flow if CVP rose all the way to MAP?


Answer

Flow depends on the pressure difference between the two ends of the circuit. Blood leaves the aorta at MAP and returns to the right atrium at CVP, so the difference that drives it through SVR is MAP − CVP. Using MAP alone assumes the far end is at zero. If CVP equaled MAP there would be no pressure difference and no flow, however high the pressures were (compare Figure 4.2 C).

A classmate says MAP is halfway between systolic and diastolic pressure. What is wrong with that? What is the MAP for 150/90, and would the one-third rule over- or underestimate it at a heart rate of 160?


Answer

MAP is a time-average, and at a normal resting rate the pressure spends most of the cycle near diastolic, so the average sits about a third of the way up. For 150/90, MAP ≈ 90 + 60/3 = 110 mm Hg. At 160 beats/min diastole is shortened, the true mean moves toward halfway, and the one-third rule underestimates it.

Blood flows at 5 L/min. Why is it slower in the capillaries than in the aorta, even though each capillary is much narrower than the aorta? Why is slow capillary flow useful?


Answer

Velocity is flow divided by the area the whole flow passes through. The whole cardiac output passes through the aorta’s 4 cm², but in the capillaries it is spread over about 1010 vessels with an aggregate area of about 2,800 cm², so the blood moves about 700 times more slowly. The slow transit gives time for exchange between blood and tissue.

What is the functional advantage of veins being so much more compliant than arteries?


Answer

High compliance lets the veins hold about two-thirds of the blood volume at low pressure, and take up or give up a large volume with only a small change in venous pressure. That makes them a reservoir: venoconstriction can shift stored blood toward the heart when it is needed.

A tight cast raises the tissue pressure around the calf veins. Without using numbers, say which pressure difference decides whether the veins collapse and which decides how much blood flows through them. How can the cast reduce flow even if it does not change the pressure difference along the veins?


Answer

Collapse depends on transmural pressure, the pressure inside the vein minus the tissue pressure outside it. The cast raises the outside pressure, so transmural pressure falls, and if it falls below zero the thin-walled veins tend to collapse. Flow depends on the perfusion pressure, the difference in pressure from one end of the vein to the other, divided by the vein’s resistance. Transmural pressure does not push blood along. But a narrowed or partly collapsed vein has a smaller radius and a much higher resistance, so flow falls for the same pressure difference along it.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 5  Skeletal Muscle
text:
5.1 What skeletal muscle does
This lecture is the first of three on muscle, and the other two (Cardiac Muscle and Smooth Muscle) are built as comparisons with it. It uses the ideas from Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells: a skeletal muscle fiber is an excitable cell that rests near −90 mV and fires an action potential when its motor neuron tells it to. The question is how that action potential turns into force, and how the nervous system makes the force bigger or smaller.
Skeletal muscle moves the skeleton, but the lecture’s examples go well beyond the limbs: the extraocular muscles that point the eyes, the muscles of facial expression, the diaphragm and intercostal muscles that drive breathing (see Respiratory Statics), the muscles of the tongue and pharynx that swallow, and the pelvic floor. It holds posture. It makes heat, most obviously when you shiver. And it helps the circulation: contracting muscle squeezes the veins inside it and pushes blood back toward the heart.
The lecture ties the three muscle types to the three things that set cardiac output and blood pressure. Skeletal muscle helps venous return, which fills the heart (end-diastolic volume). Cardiac muscle sets contractility. Smooth muscle sets vascular tone, and so systemic vascular resistance (SVR).
Skeletal muscle has no pacemakers. A fiber contracts only when its motor neuron fires.

title: 5  Skeletal Muscle
text:
5.2 Structure

5.2.1 From muscle to fiber
A whole muscle is wrapped in connective tissue at every level (Figure 5.1 shows the innermost level):

Epimysium, the outermost sheath, which fuses with the tendon.
Perimysium, around each fascicle, a bundle of muscle fibers.
Endomysium, around each muscle fiber, which is one muscle cell.
Inside each fiber are many myofibrils, and each myofibril is a string of sarcomeres, the contractile units.

The connective tissue anchors the fibers to each other and to the tendon, so the force they make reaches the bone.
A skeletal muscle fiber forms when many precursor cells (myoblasts) fuse during development. The result is a long, cylindrical, unbranched cell with many nuclei. The cell is so full of actin and myosin that the nuclei are pushed to the edge, just under the membrane. That peripheral position is one way to recognize skeletal muscle under the microscope.


5.2.2 The membranes of the fiber
The fiber’s plasma membrane is the sarcolemma. At regular intervals it dives into the cell as transverse tubules (T tubules), which carry the action potential deep into the fiber. Around every myofibril is the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR), the cell’s Ca2+ store. Where the SR meets a T tubule it swells into a terminal cisterna. One T tubule with a terminal cisterna on each side is a triad. In mammalian skeletal muscle the triads sit where the A and I bands meet (the bands are defined below), so each sarcomere has two.
Cardiac muscle has a T tubule paired with one cisterna, a dyad. Skeletal muscle has fewer mitochondria than cardiac muscle, which never rests.


5.2.3 Fiber types
Not all fibers are the same. The lecture’s table, with the third column corrected:










Type I (slow)
Type IIa (fast)
Type IIb, called IIx in humans (fast)

Type I fibers are slow, oxidative and resistant to fatigue: think of postural muscles and a marathon. Type IIb (IIx) fibers are fast, glycolytic, strong, and tire quickly: think of a sprint. Type IIa fibers sit between them. “Fast” and “slow” refer to the myosin each fiber makes. The fast myosin heavy chain cycles faster. Fiber types are usually identified by staining for the myosin heavy chain, or for oxidative enzymes, which are mostly in the mitochondria.
Fatigue is not running out of ATP. ATP stays near normal in a tired fiber, and fatigue comes from ionic and metabolic changes in the working fiber.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The fiber-type table heads its columns “Type I (Slow) / Type IIa (Fast) / Type IIa or IIx (Fast),” listing IIa twice. The third column is type IIb (called IIx in humans). The next slide and the notes use I, IIa and IIb.


Most muscles contain a mixture of all three types, and the types may be more of a continuum than three boxes. Fiber type is also plastic: it depends on the motor neuron and on what the muscle is asked to do.

Reinnervation. All the fibers supplied by one motor neuron are the same type (see motor units, below), and in a normal muscle the units are interspersed, so types form a checkerboard. If a motor neuron dies, its fibers are denervated and shrink. Sprouts from a surviving neighbor can reinnervate them, and the reinnervated fibers change to the type of their new neuron. The checkerboard gives way to patches of a single type, called fiber-type grouping.
Training. Endurance training increases mitochondria and capillaries in the trained fibers. Resistance training increases fiber diameter and maximal force. Training can shift fibers between the fast subtypes.



5.2.4 The myofibril and the sarcomere
A myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres, each about 2 µm long, so there are about 5,000 per centimeter of fiber (the slide’s 10,000 per myofibril fits a fiber about 2 cm long). Each sarcomere runs from one Z line to the next and is built from two sets of overlapping filaments (Figure 5.1):

Thin filaments (actin) are anchored at the Z lines and point toward the middle.
Thick filaments (myosin) are anchored at the M line in the middle and point toward the Z lines. Their heads point away from the M line on both sides.







Figure 5.1: The sarcomere, relaxed and contracted, drawn to scale. Z lines (zigzag) bound each sarcomere; the vertical line in the middle is the M line. The A band is the length of the thick filaments and does not change. The I band (thin filament only, spanning a Z line) and the H zone (thick filament only, around the M line) both shorten as the thin filaments slide toward the M line. Filament lengths 1.6 µm (thick) and 1.0 µm (thin). Course figure.



The repeating pattern of overlap makes the bands that give striated muscle its stripes:

A band: the full length of the thick filaments. Its length is constant.
I band: the region of thin filament with no thick filament, on both sides of a Z line. It shortens during contraction.
H zone: the middle of the A band, where there is thick filament but no thin filament. It shortens and nearly disappears at full contraction.

The slides label it both H band and H zone. This book uses H zone.
In contraction the filaments do not shorten. The thin filaments slide along the thick filaments toward the M line, so each sarcomere shortens, and with it the myofibril, the fiber and the whole muscle. This is the sliding-filament mechanism.
Myosin. Each myosin molecule has two heavy chains and four light chains. The heavy chains wind together to form the long rod (tail), and each heavy chain ends in a globular head. The head carries the site that binds actin and the ATPase site that splits ATP. The light chains sit at the neck of each head, where they stabilize it and regulate its activity. Hundreds of myosin molecules bundle tail to tail into a thick filament.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The myosin slide says the light chain “forms heads responsible for binding actin.” The heavy chains form both the rod and the heads. Actin binding and ATP splitting are properties of the heavy-chain head. The light chains sit at the neck.


Actin and its regulatory proteins. Globular actin (G actin) monomers, each with a myosin-binding site, link into two strands twisted into a double helix. Lying in the groove of that helix is tropomyosin, a long rod that at rest covers the myosin-binding sites. Attached to tropomyosin at intervals is troponin, a complex of three proteins:

Troponin I binds actin strongly and helps hold tropomyosin in its blocking position.
Troponin T binds tropomyosin.
Troponin C binds Ca2+.

When Ca2+ binds troponin C, the complex changes shape and rolls tropomyosin deeper into the groove, uncovering the myosin-binding sites. That is the on switch. Skeletal and cardiac troponins have the same names and jobs, but they are molecularly distinct proteins.
A giant elastic protein, titin, runs from the Z line along each thick filament to the M line. It keeps the thick filaments centered, and it is the main source of the passive tension a stretched sarcomere develops (see length-tension, below).
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 5  Skeletal Muscle
text:
5.3 Innervation

5.3.1 The motor pathway
Voluntary movement starts with upper motor neurons in the motor cortex. Their axons descend in the corticospinal tracts, most of them crossing to the other side in the medulla, and synapse on lower motor neurons in the ventral horn of the spinal cord (or in brainstem nuclei, for the head). The lower motor neuron’s axon leaves the spinal cord in a peripheral nerve and ends on muscle fibers. That is as much neuroanatomy as this course needs.


5.3.2 The motor unit
One lower motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it supplies make a motor unit. Each fiber is supplied by only one motor neuron, but one neuron branches to many fibers: a few in a muscle that moves the eye, hundreds or more in a large limb muscle. All the fibers in one motor unit are the same fiber type, and when the neuron fires, every fiber in the unit contracts.
The nervous system grades force partly by recruitment: calling in more motor units. Units are recruited in a fixed order, from small to large, which is called the size principle. The smallest motor neurons are the easiest to fire, and they supply small numbers of type I fibers, so light, sustained tasks (posture, gentle movement) use fatigue-resistant units. As more force is needed, type IIa units join, and the largest units, with many type IIb (IIx) fibers, come in last, for brief maximal efforts. The other way to grade force is to fire each unit faster (summation and tetanus, below).


5.3.3 The neuromuscular junction
The synapse between a motor neuron and a muscle fiber is the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) (Figure 5.2). It has three parts:

The presynaptic terminal, the end of the motor neuron, filled with vesicles of acetylcholine (ACh). Each vesicle’s contents is one quantum of transmitter.
The synaptic cleft, 50 to 100 nm wide and filled with extracellular fluid. It contains acetylcholinesterase (AChE), the enzyme that breaks down ACh.
The postsynaptic membrane of the muscle fiber, the end plate, folded into junctional folds that increase its surface area. The crests of the folds are packed with nicotinic ACh receptors, 15 to 40 million per end plate. These receptors are ligand-gated cation channels: ACh opens them.







NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



One slide calls the ACh receptors “voltage gated Na channels” and the next calls them “ligand gated Na+ channels.” Nicotinic ACh receptors are ligand-gated cation channels. ACh binding opens them, Na+ enters and some K+ leaves, and the net inward current is the end-plate potential. The voltage-gated Na+ channels nearby, deeper in the folds, are what then fire the muscle action potential.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 5  Skeletal Muscle
text:
5.4 Excitation-contraction coupling
Excitation-contraction (E-C) coupling is the chain of events that links the action potential to contraction. It has two halves: getting an action potential into the muscle fiber at the NMJ, and getting Ca2+ out of the SR at the triad.

5.4.1 At the neuromuscular junction






Figure 5.2: The steps at the neuromuscular junction. Numbers on the drawing match the list. Course figure, after the lecture’s sequence.




An action potential travels down the lower motor neuron to the presynaptic terminal.
Depolarization of the terminal opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and Ca2+ enters.
Ca2+ triggers the SNARE proteins to fuse vesicles with the terminal membrane, releasing ACh into the cleft.
ACh diffuses across the cleft and binds nicotinic receptors on the end plate.
The receptors open. Na+ enters (and some K+ leaves), depolarizing the end plate. This local depolarization is the end-plate potential (EPP).
The EPP spreads to the neighboring membrane and brings it to threshold. Voltage-gated Na+ channels open and fire a muscle action potential, which spreads along the whole fiber.
Meanwhile AChE splits ACh into acetate and choline, ending the signal within a few milliseconds. The terminal takes choline back up to make more ACh.

The NMJ is built so that it does not fail. One motor neuron action potential releases enough ACh to make an EPP far larger than is needed to reach threshold: in a healthy junction every nerve impulse fires the muscle fiber. This margin is called the safety factor.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The NMJ slide says “End plate potentials can summate to reach muscle cell threshold.” At a healthy neuromuscular junction a single EPP is large enough to reach threshold by itself, so summation of EPPs is not needed. What does add up is the quanta: the ACh from each vesicle gives a tiny depolarization, and the hundred or so vesicles released by one nerve impulse together make one EPP well above threshold.




5.4.2 At the triad
The muscle action potential runs along the sarcolemma and down the T tubules, so it reaches the middle of the fiber almost as fast as the surface (Figure 5.3).






Figure 5.3: Excitation-contraction coupling at the triad. A T tubule (blue) runs between two terminal cisternae of the SR (purple). DHP receptors in the T tubule membrane are mechanically linked to ryanodine receptors (RyR1) in the SR membrane. Steps match the list on the right; step 4, at the thin filament, is not drawn. Course figure.




The action potential depolarizes the T tubule membrane.
In the T tubule membrane are dihydropyridine (DHP) receptors, voltage sensors that change shape when the membrane depolarizes. Each one is physically linked to a ryanodine receptor (RyR1), a Ca2+ channel in the membrane of the terminal cisterna across a narrow gap. The DHP receptor’s change in shape pulls the ryanodine receptor open. This is mechanical coupling.
Ca2+ flows out of the SR, down its steep gradient, and floods the cytosol around the myofibrils.
Ca2+ binds troponin C. Tropomyosin moves off the myosin-binding sites on actin, and cross-bridges start to cycle.
As long as action potentials keep coming, Ca2+ keeps being released. When they stop, SERCA (the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase) pumps Ca2+ back into the SR. Ca2+ comes off troponin, tropomyosin covers the binding sites again, and the muscle relaxes. SERCA uses ATP, so relaxation costs energy too.

Because the DHP receptor opens RyR1 directly, skeletal muscle does not need any Ca2+ to enter from outside the cell to contract. It keeps contracting for some time even with no extracellular Ca2+. Cardiac muscle is different. There the DHP receptor works as a channel: Ca2+ entering through this L-type Ca2+ channel triggers RyR2, and contraction stops without extracellular Ca2+. That is Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release (Cardiac Muscle). The skeletal DHP receptor is an L-type channel too, but contraction does not need its small Ca2+ current.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The summary slide lists “Ca+2 dependent Ca+2 release” as the skeletal muscle step. In skeletal muscle, release is by mechanical coupling of the DHP receptor to RyR1, as described above and in the notes. Ca2+-dependent (Ca2+-induced) Ca2+ release is the cardiac mechanism.


Mutations in the proteins of the triad, most often RyR1 and sometimes the DHP receptor, cause malignant hyperthermia. In a susceptible person, certain anesthetic drugs make the abnormal ryanodine receptor release Ca2+ without stopping. The muscles contract and burn ATP, partly to pump the Ca2+ back, and body temperature rises dangerously.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 5  Skeletal Muscle
text:
5.5 Cross-bridge cycling
Once the binding sites are uncovered, myosin heads attach to actin and pull. Each attach-pull-detach sequence is one turn of the cross-bridge cycle (Figure 5.4).






Figure 5.4: The cross-bridge cycle. Actin (top of each panel) and the thick filament (bottom), with the M line to the left. (A) Attached: the head is bound to actin with no nucleotide, the rigor state. (B) ATP binds and the head lets go. (C) The head splits ATP and re-cocks, still holding ADP and Pi. (D) If Ca2+ has moved tropomyosin, the cocked head binds actin. (E) Pi is released and the head tilts (the power stroke), pulling the thin filament toward the M line; ADP is released, leaving the head bound as in A. Adapted from Boron and Boulpaep, Medical Physiology [1], as used in the 2026 lecture.



A. Attached. At the end of a stroke the myosin head is bound tightly to actin, with nothing in its nucleotide site.
B. Released. ATP binds the head. Myosin with ATP bound has a low affinity for actin, so the head lets go.
C. Cocked. The head splits ATP into ADP and Pi, which stay bound. The energy released re-cocks the head into its high-energy position, pointing toward the Z line.
D. Cross-bridge. If tropomyosin has been moved, the cocked head binds a new site on actin, a little farther along.
E. Power stroke. Binding releases Pi, and the head tilts back toward its resting angle, pulling the thin filament a few nanometers toward the M line. ADP is released and the head is back at A, bound to actin and waiting for the next ATP.
ATP is used twice in a contraction: to detach and re-cock each myosin head, and to pump Ca2+ back into the SR. While Ca2+ is present and ATP keeps arriving, each head goes around this cycle many times a second, and the many heads working out of step slide the filaments smoothly. And without ATP the cycle stops at A, with every head stuck to actin. That is why muscles become rigid after death (rigor mortis).
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 5  Skeletal Muscle
section: 5.6 Muscle contraction: twitch, summation and tetanus
text:
5.6 Muscle contraction: twitch, summation and tetanus
A single action potential in a muscle fiber produces a single brief contraction, a twitch. The action potential lasts a few milliseconds. After a short latent period, while Ca2+ is released and cross-bridges attach, force rises to a peak in a few tens of milliseconds and then falls as SERCA clears the Ca2+ (Figure 5.5 A). The twitch outlasts the action potential many times over.
That mismatch is what lets the force add up (Figure 5.5).






Figure 5.5: Force in a skeletal muscle fiber (top) driven by muscle action potentials (bottom ticks). (A) One action potential gives a twitch, here about a third of the maximal force. (B) A second action potential before the first twitch has ended gives summation: a larger second contraction. (C) At a moderate firing rate the twitches fuse partly, an unfused tetanus. (D) At a high rate force rises to a smooth plateau, a fused tetanus. Schematic model: each action potential adds a brief pulse of activation, and force builds fully only when activation is sustained. Course figure, after the lecture’s comparison.




Summation. If a second action potential arrives before the muscle has relaxed, the second contraction builds on the first and reaches a higher force.
Unfused tetanus. At a moderate firing rate, the muscle partly relaxes between action potentials, so force rises with a ripple.
Fused tetanus. At a high rate there is no time to relax at all, and force rises to a smooth plateau several times larger than a single twitch.

Each action potential is still a separate, complete event. The fiber repolarizes and recovers its excitability within a few milliseconds, which is why it can fire again so soon. What adds up is the Ca2+ in the cytosol and the force. A single twitch is weak because the Ca2+ transient from one action potential is brief. SERCA clears it before the cross-bridges have had time to stretch the elastic parts of the fiber and tendon and pass their full force to the ends of the muscle. Repeated action potentials keep Ca2+ high long enough for force to build. Normal movements use unfused and fused tetani, graded by how fast the motor neurons fire, together with recruitment of more motor units.






WarningA common mistake



“In tetanus the action potentials summate.” They do not. A skeletal muscle action potential is all-or-none and over in a few milliseconds, and the next one is a separate spike from the same resting potential. What summates is the contraction: Ca2+ release and force. This is also why heart muscle cannot be tetanized. Its long action potential keeps it refractory until its contraction is nearly over.



5.6.1 Types of contraction
A contracting muscle does not always shorten.

Concentric: the muscle shortens while it contracts, because its force exceeds the load. Lifting a weight.
Isometric: the muscle contracts with no change in length, because its force equals the load. Holding a weight still.
Eccentric: the muscle lengthens while it contracts, because the load exceeds its force. Lowering a weight slowly to the ground.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 5  Skeletal Muscle
text:
5.7 Unique properties

5.7.1 Length-tension
The force a sarcomere can make depends on how much its filaments overlap, because force is proportional to the number of cross-bridges that can form. Figure 5.6 shows the relationship.






Figure 5.6: Tension against sarcomere length. Skeletal muscle (maroon): active tension, from cross-bridges, is greatest at 2.0 to 2.2 µm (shaded), where every myosin head can reach actin. It falls at longer lengths because overlap shrinks, and at shorter lengths because thin filaments overlap each other and thick filaments press against the Z lines. Passive tension (dashed), from stretching titin and connective tissue, appears only well beyond the optimum. Cardiac muscle (blue): passive tension rises steeply at lengths where skeletal muscle’s is still near zero, which keeps the heart on the rising limb of its active curve. Course figure.




At about 2.0 to 2.2 µm, overlap is optimal: every myosin head is opposite actin, and active tension is greatest.
Stretched beyond that, the thin filaments are pulled out from between the thick filaments, fewer heads can reach actin, and active tension falls. Stretched far enough, the filaments no longer overlap at all and there is no active tension.
Shorter than that, thin filaments from the two ends cross each other and get in the way, and the thick filaments eventually butt against the Z lines, so active tension falls again.
Passive tension is the force a relaxed muscle resists stretch with. In skeletal muscle it only becomes large well beyond the optimal length.

In the body, most skeletal muscles work near the top of the curve, and skeletal muscle keeps much of its force over a broad range of lengths. Cardiac muscle works over a narrower range. Its passive tension rises steeply at lengths where skeletal muscle’s is still near zero, so its sarcomeres are hard to stretch much past 2.2 to 2.3 µm, and it normally operates on the rising limb of its curve, where more stretch means more force. That is part of the cellular basis of the Frank-Starling mechanism, which the Cardiac Muscle chapter develops.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The slide’s skeletal curve reaches zero near 2.8 to 2.9 µm, while the figure here, drawn from filament overlap, reaches zero nearer 3.6 µm. You do not need either number. What matters is the shape: force peaks at 2.0 to 2.2 µm and falls on either side.
The slide also draws a cardiac active curve that falls steeply after about 2.4 µm. In the intact heart the stiff passive structures keep sarcomeres from being stretched much past 2.2 to 2.3 µm, so that falling limb is rarely reached. Figure 5.6 draws the cardiac curves only over the range the heart uses. Both pictures make the slide’s point: skeletal muscle works over a broader range of lengths than cardiac muscle.








WarningA common mistake



“Stretching the muscle increases its compliance.” On the rising limb of the length-tension curve, stretch increases the force of contraction, because more cross-bridges can form or work more effectively. Compliance describes the passive curve: how much a relaxed muscle lengthens for a given stretching force. A stretched muscle is, if anything, less compliant, because passive tension rises more steeply the more it is stretched.




5.7.2 The skeletal muscle pump
The veins of the legs run between and through muscles, and they have one-way valves that let blood move only toward the heart (Figure 5.7).






Figure 5.7: The skeletal muscle pump in a leg vein. (A) Muscle relaxed: the vein fills from below, and the valve above it is shut. (B) Muscle contracted: the muscles bulge and squeeze the vein. Blood is pushed up through the upper valve toward the heart; the lower valve shuts, so blood cannot go back down. Course figure, after the lecture’s calf muscle pump.



When the muscle contracts, it compresses the vein and drives blood up through the upper valve, and the lower valve shuts so blood cannot fall back. When the muscle relaxes, the emptied segment refills from below. Rhythmic contraction, as in walking, works like a pump in series with the heart. It increases venous return and helps fill the heart, which increases stroke volume and cardiac output. In this course, the muscle pump is treated as lowering the resistance to venous return (RVR) on the vascular function curve; Control of Cardiac Output shows how that shifts the operating point.
Standing still for a long time shows what happens without it. With no contraction to push it up, blood pools in the leg veins, venous return falls, and capillary pressure in the feet rises, which favors edema.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 5  Skeletal Muscle
text:
5.8 Check your understanding

In a muscle fiber shortening from 2.5 µm to 2.1 µm per sarcomere, which of these change length: the A band, the I band, the H zone, the thin filaments?


Answer

The I band and the H zone shorten. The A band (the length of the thick filaments) and the filaments themselves do not change. The thin filaments slide toward the M line.

A toxin blocks the ryanodine receptor. The motor nerve is stimulated. Which of these still happen: ACh release, an end-plate potential, a muscle action potential, a twitch?


Answer

ACh release, the end-plate potential and the muscle action potential are all upstream of the SR and still happen. The action potential still reaches the T tubules and still moves the DHP receptors, but Ca2+ cannot leave the SR, so troponin C is never activated and there is no twitch.

The Ca2+ in the bath around a nerve-muscle preparation is lowered to about a third of normal, not to zero. What happens to ACh release with each nerve impulse, to the size of the EPP, and to whether each impulse still fires the muscle fiber?


Answer

Less Ca2+ enters the nerve terminal through its voltage-gated Ca2+ channels with each impulse, so fewer vesicles fuse and fewer quanta of ACh are released. The EPP is smaller. Whether the fiber still fires depends on the safety factor. A normal EPP is far larger than it needs to be to reach threshold, so a somewhat smaller one can still fire the fiber on every impulse. The margin has shrunk, though. If Ca2+ falls further, the EPP in some fibers drops below threshold and those fibers stop responding to the nerve.

A drug makes SERCA pump faster, so after each action potential cytosolic Ca2+ falls back sooner than normal. What happens to the force of a single twitch, and to the firing rate needed to reach a fused tetanus? Why?


Answer

The twitch is weaker and briefer. Its Ca2+ transient is shorter, so the cross-bridges have less time to stretch the elastic parts of the fiber and tendon before the Ca2+ is gone. A fused tetanus needs cytosolic Ca2+ to stay high from one action potential to the next. With Ca2+ cleared faster, it falls further between spikes at any given rate, so the action potentials have to come closer together to keep it up. The rate needed for a fused tetanus rises.

A muscle is stretched until its sarcomeres are 2.6 µm long and then stimulated to a fused tetanus. Compared with stimulation at 2.1 µm, is the active force larger or smaller, and why? What happens to passive tension?


Answer

Active force is smaller. At 2.6 µm the thin filaments have been pulled partway out from between the thick filaments, so they overlap less of the region that carries myosin heads and fewer cross-bridges can form. The slide’s curve and the one in this chapter agree on that. Passive tension, from stretched titin and connective tissue, is just beginning to rise at 2.6 µm. At 2.1 µm it is near zero.

A patient has lost many motor neurons in one muscle and the survivors have reinnervated the orphaned fibers. What will a fiber-type stain show, and why?


Answer

Instead of the normal checkerboard of types, the stain shows large patches of fibers of a single type. Each surviving motor neuron now supplies many more fibers, and every fiber it supplies takes on the type set by that neuron.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 5  Skeletal Muscle
text:
5.9 Sources
This chapter follows the 2026 Skeletal Muscle lecture for MEDC 30504 and draws on the peer-educator notes and the 2018 course notes, corrected and updated. All figures were drawn for this book.

title: 6  Smooth Muscle
text:
6.1 Structure
Smooth muscle lines the walls of the hollow organs: arteries and veins, bronchioles, the gut, the bladder, the uterus and the ducts of the reproductive tract. It does not move bones. It changes the diameter of a tube or the volume of a bag, and it often has to hold that change for minutes, hours or a lifetime. An arteriole that sets your blood pressure is partly contracted all day. A bladder has to stay relaxed while it fills and then empty completely.
In the cardiovascular block this matters because vascular smooth muscle sets vascular tone, and vascular tone sets systemic vascular resistance (SVR), one of the three things that decide cardiac output and blood pressure. The Cardiovascular Physiology Overview and Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics chapters build on that. This chapter answers a cell-level question: how does a cell with no sarcomeres and no troponin generate force, and how do nerves, hormones, stretch and nitric oxide turn that force up and down?
The chapter assumes the sarcomere, the cross-bridge cycle and troponin regulation from Skeletal Muscle, and the membrane potential and G-protein signaling from Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 6  Smooth Muscle
text:
6.1.1 Why “smooth”
Under the light microscope skeletal and cardiac muscle are striated: their actin and myosin are lined up in sarcomeres, so the bands of every myofibril sit in register. Smooth muscle has the same two proteins but no sarcomeres, so it has no bands. That is the whole meaning of “smooth.”
A smooth muscle cell is:

fusiform (spindle-shaped), thick in the middle and tapered at both ends;
a single cell with a single, central nucleus. Smooth muscle cells do not fuse, unlike skeletal muscle fibers, which are made by fusion of many cells;
unstriated;
capable of mitosis. Of the three muscle types, only smooth muscle cells can divide. That comes back at the end of the chapter.







NoteBackground: embryonic origin





Vascular smooth muscle does not come from a single embryonic source. Depending on the vessel, it comes from neural crest, somites, the second heart field, the proepicardium, splanchnic mesoderm, or the mesothelial cells lining the pleural and peritoneal cavities. The lecture showed this to make one point: smooth muscle in different places has different ancestry, which is one reason it varies so much from organ to organ. You do not need to memorize the origins.





6.1.2 Sarcolemma and SR
The cell membrane (sarcolemma) has no T-tubules. Instead it has caveolae, small flask-shaped dips in the membrane. They play a part like T-tubules, bringing the membrane close to the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) and collecting channels and signaling proteins, but they are far less developed. The SR itself is sparse. There are no dyads and no triads.
A smooth muscle cell can get away with this because it is small and thin, a few micrometers across, so Ca2+ entering through the membrane does not have far to diffuse. It also does not need to switch on in milliseconds. A skeletal muscle fiber, by contrast, is up to 100 µm across and has to activate its whole cross-section at once, which is what the T-tubule and triad system is for.


6.1.3 The cytoskeleton
Figure 6.1 shows the parts.

Dense bodies anchor the thin filaments. Some sit in the cytoplasm and some are attached to the membrane (where they are often called attachment plaques). They do the job of the Z line in a sarcomere, and like the Z line they contain α-actinin.
Thin filaments are actin, with tropomyosin. They are part of the contractile machinery and are anchored in the dense bodies.
Thick filaments are myosin. They are part of the contractile machinery. There are many fewer of them than in striated muscle.
Intermediate filaments (vimentin and desmin) link the dense bodies into a network. They are structural and not part of the contractile mechanism, but they carry force across the cell.

Bundles of actin and myosin run between dense bodies at an angle to the cell’s long axis, in a crisscross lattice. When the bundles shorten they pull the dense bodies toward each other in many directions at once, and the cell gets shorter and fatter. Because the membrane is tied down at its attachment plaques, it puckers between them.






Figure 6.1: Smooth muscle cell structure. (A) A relaxed cell. Actin-myosin bundles (maroon) run diagonally between dense bodies in the cytoplasm and on the membrane. Intermediate filaments (dotted) link the dense bodies. (B) The same cell contracted: shorter and wider. (C) Skeletal thick filaments are bipolar, with heads that reverse at a central bare zone. Smooth muscle myosin is side-polar: along the whole filament, the heads on one side face one way and the heads on the other side face the other way. Course figure.





6.1.4 Connections between cells
Two kinds of junction join neighboring smooth muscle cells:

Gap junctions are channels made of connexin proteins that connect the cytoplasm of two cells. Ions and small molecules pass through them, so electrical activity in one cell spreads to the next.
Mechanical junctions (adherens junctions) hold cells together so that force generated in one cell is passed to its neighbors and to the surrounding connective tissue.

How many gap junctions a tissue has decides whether it behaves as one coordinated sheet or as separate cells. That distinction, single-unit versus multi-unit, comes up under neuronal regulation below.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 6  Smooth Muscle
text:
6.2 The contractile unit
The basic contractile unit of smooth muscle is a bundle of thin filaments anchored in a dense body at each end, with thick filaments between them. Myosin pulls the actin, and the dense bodies move toward each other. That much is like a sarcomere with dense bodies in place of Z lines, but two things differ.
Smooth muscle myosin is side-polar (Figure 6.1 C). In a skeletal thick filament the heads point one way on one half and the opposite way on the other half, with a bare zone in the middle. In smooth muscle the heads on one face of the filament all point one way along its full length, and those on the opposite face all point the other way. The thin filaments on the two sides slide in opposite directions, and since there is no bare zone, overlap can stay good over a much wider range of lengths. This is one reason smooth muscle can still generate force after being stretched far beyond the length at which a skeletal sarcomere would have lost all overlap.
There is no troponin in smooth muscle. In striated muscle, Ca2+ binds troponin C and moves tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin. Smooth muscle has tropomyosin but no troponin, so Ca2+ has to act some other way. It acts on the myosin, as the next section shows. The thin filament also carries caldesmon, a protein that lies along actin and tropomyosin. It modulates contraction but is not the main switch.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The figure on the contractile-unit slide labels the actin-myosin units “Sarcomeres.” Smooth muscle has no sarcomeres. The label refers to the contractile unit between two dense bodies, which works like a sarcomere but is not lined up in register with its neighbors, so it produces no striations.
The same figure calls the mechanical junction a desmosome, while the cytoskeleton slide calls it an adherens junction. The anchoring junctions between smooth muscle cells are mainly adherens-type junctions. For this course, “mechanical junction” is enough.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 6  Smooth Muscle
text:
6.3 Excitation-contraction coupling
Every muscle contracts when cytosolic Ca2+ rises. What differs between muscle types is where the Ca2+ comes from and what it binds to. Figure 6.2 summarizes smooth muscle.






Figure 6.2: Excitation-contraction coupling in smooth muscle. Ca2+ enters through membrane channels or is released from the SR. Ca2+-calmodulin activates myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), which phosphorylates the regulatory light chain of myosin and starts cross-bridge cycling. Myosin light chain phosphatase (MLCP) removes the phosphate and allows relaxation. Course figure.




6.3.1 Where the Ca2+ comes from
Cytosolic Ca2+ rises from two sources, and in smooth muscle both matter.

Across the sarcolemma. Depolarization opens voltage-gated (L-type) Ca2+ channels. Some agonists open receptor-operated channels directly, and stretch opens stretch-activated channels. Extracellular Ca2+ is about 10,000 times the resting cytosolic level, so it flows in fast once a channel opens. The lecture’s Ca2+ slide also shows nonselective cation channels, which let Na+ and Ca2+ in.
From the SR. Ca2+ that enters can bind ryanodine receptors on the SR and release more (Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release, as in cardiac muscle). Agonists acting through Gq-coupled receptors make IP3, which opens IP3 receptors on the SR. Both routes operate. Which one is larger varies from tissue to tissue, and agonists acting through α1 receptors use the IP3 route.

Because extracellular Ca2+ entry is a major source, L-type Ca2+ channel blockers relax vascular smooth muscle and lower vascular tone.


6.3.2 Ca2+, calmodulin and MLCK
In order:

The action potential, or a smaller depolarization, opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in the sarcolemma.
Ca2+ binds ryanodine receptors on the SR, which release more Ca2+ into the cytosol. (IP3 does the same through its own receptor.)
Ca2+ binds calmodulin, a small protein with four Ca2+-binding sites, which changes to its active shape.
The Ca2+-calmodulin complex (CaCM) binds and activates myosin light chain kinase (MLCK).
MLCK uses ATP to phosphorylate the regulatory light chain of myosin. That phosphorylation switches on the myosin head’s ATPase.
Phosphorylated myosin binds actin and cross-bridge cycling begins. The cycle itself is the one you learned in Skeletal Muscle.
Myosin light chain phosphatase (MLCP) removes the phosphate, and the cell relaxes.







NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



Step 5 on the excitation-contraction coupling slide reads “MLCK Phosphorylates / activates myosin light chain kinase.” MLCK does not phosphorylate itself. It phosphorylates the regulatory light chain of myosin, which activates the myosin head’s ATPase and starts cross-bridge cycling. The peer-educator notes describe the step correctly. This is errata entry 11.


So smooth muscle is regulated on the thick filament: Ca2+ switches on the myosin. Striated muscle is regulated on the thin filament: Ca2+ binds troponin on the actin filament and uncovers the binding sites. In skeletal muscle, Ca2+ acts directly and within milliseconds. In smooth muscle it acts through an enzyme cascade, which is one reason smooth muscle contracts and relaxes so slowly, over seconds rather than milliseconds.
It also means that force depends on the balance between two enzymes. MLCK adds phosphate and MLCP removes it. Anything that speeds MLCK or slows MLCP shifts the balance toward contraction, and anything that does the reverse shifts it toward relaxation. Most of the regulation in the next section works by tipping that balance.


6.3.3 Ca2+ removal
To relax, the cell has to bring cytosolic Ca2+ back down. SERCA, the Ca2+ pump in the SR membrane, pumps Ca2+ back into the SR. A Ca2+ pump in the sarcolemma (the plasma membrane Ca2+-ATPase) and the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (NCX) move Ca2+ out of the cell. NCX uses the energy of Na+ flowing in (three Na+ in for each Ca2+ out). NCX depends on the Na+ gradient that the Na+/K+-ATPase maintains (three Na+ out, two K+ in). When Ca2+ falls, Ca2+ leaves calmodulin, MLCK switches off, MLCP dephosphorylates the myosin, and the cell relaxes.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 6  Smooth Muscle
text:
6.4 Regulation of smooth muscle activity
Skeletal muscle has one input: the motor neuron. Smooth muscle has four, and a single cell may respond to all of them:

Neuronal: sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves.
Neurohormonal and pharmacological: hormones, transmitters and drugs acting on receptors.
Mechanical: stretch.
Nitric oxide, mostly from the endothelium.


6.4.1 1. Neuronal: varicosities, single-unit and multi-unit
Autonomic nerves do not form neuromuscular junctions on smooth muscle. The axon runs along or between the cells and swells every few micrometers into varicosities, which release transmitter into the space around them. Transmitter diffuses to whatever cells are near, so one varicosity can reach several cells and one cell can be reached by several varicosities. Sympathetic nerves mostly release norepinephrine and parasympathetic nerves acetylcholine. Their effects on particular organs are in Autonomic and Extrinsic Control.
How a tissue responds to its nerves depends on how its cells are connected (Figure 6.3).









Single-unit
Multi-unit




Electrical coupling
Yes, through many gap junctions
No, no gap junctions between cells


Behavior
The tissue contracts as one coordinated unit, a functional syncytium
Each cell contracts on its own nerve input


Gives
Coordinated waves of contraction
Fine, graded control


Examples
Gut (peristalsis), small arteries and arterioles (the slides: arterial smooth muscle)
Vas deferens, iris









Figure 6.3: Multi-unit and single-unit smooth muscle. (A) In multi-unit smooth muscle every cell has its own nerve supply, and the cells are electrically isolated. (B) In single-unit smooth muscle, nerve endings reach only some cells, and gap junctions spread excitation to the rest. Course figure.



The peer-educator notes call single-unit smooth muscle unitary or visceral. The terms mean the same thing.
Single-unit tissue can also contract without any nerve input. Stretch, hormones and spontaneous electrical activity can start a contraction in one cell, and gap junctions carry it across the sheet. Nerves change how strong and how frequent those contractions are, rather than starting each one.


6.4.2 2. Neurohormonal and pharmacological: same signal, different receptor
Most chemical signals reach smooth muscle through G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). A ligand binds the receptor, the G protein’s α subunit swaps GDP for GTP and separates from βγ, and the subunits act on enzymes and channels inside the cell. The background is in Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells.
The same ligand can have opposite effects, depending on which receptor it meets. Norepinephrine and epinephrine are the lecture’s examples:










Receptor

Second messenger

Lecture example

Gq
Phospholipase C makes IP3 and DAG. IP3 releases SR Ca2+

Relaxation
