The α1 pathway raises Ca2+, so it drives contraction through calmodulin and MLCK. The β2 pathway works the other way. PKA phosphorylates MLCK and makes it less active, and it also lowers cytosolic Ca2+, so the balance tips toward MLCP and the muscle relaxes. In vessels that carry both receptors, such as those in skeletal muscle, the net effect depends on which receptor dominates and on how much epinephrine versus norepinephrine arrives. Autonomic and Extrinsic Control and Other Special Circulations follow that through.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The peer-educator notes give the receptor examples as “α1, α2, β1.” The smooth muscle β receptor that relaxes vessels and airways is β2. β1 receptors are the heart’s: they raise heart rate and contractility, as the Cardiac Muscle chapter explains.


Electromechanical and pharmacomechanical coupling. There are two ways a signal can raise Ca2+. In electromechanical coupling the membrane depolarizes and voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open. In pharmacomechanical coupling an agonist raises Ca2+ without needing a change in membrane potential, by opening receptor-operated channels or by making IP3 that releases SR Ca2+. Many smooth muscles contract with no action potential at all. That is one more way smooth muscle differs from skeletal muscle, which contracts only when its motor neuron fires it.
Changing sensitivity to Ca2+. Some agonists also change how much force a given Ca2+ level produces. The same contractile receptors also activate Rho kinase, which inhibits MLCP. With less phosphatase activity, more myosin stays phosphorylated at the same Ca2+, and force rises. Figure 6.4 pulls all these routes together. Each one ends at the same two enzymes.






Figure 6.4: Signals that regulate smooth muscle. Contracting signals (left) raise Ca2+, which activates MLCK, or inhibit MLCP through Rho kinase. α2 receptors (Gi) lower cAMP and so oppose β2 relaxation. Relaxing signals (right) inhibit MLCK through cAMP and PKA, or lower Ca2+ and activate MLCP through cGMP and protein kinase G (PKG). Flat bars show inhibition. Course figure, after the lecture’s summary diagram.





6.4.3 3. Mechanical: stretch
Smooth muscle responds to being stretched. The membrane carries two kinds of stretch-sensitive channel. Mechano-gated cation channels let Na+ and Ca2+ in when the cell is stretched. The cell depolarizes, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open, and the cell contracts. Mechano-sensitive K+ channels do the opposite: they let K+ out, which hyperpolarizes the cell and relaxes it.
In arterioles, stretch-induced contraction is the basis of the myogenic response: when perfusion pressure rises and stretches the vessel wall, the smooth muscle contracts and the vessel narrows, which holds flow nearly constant. The Microcirculation and Local Control chapter covers how this contributes to autoregulation. In the gut and bladder, stretch from filling triggers contraction of single-unit muscle.


6.4.4 4. Nitric oxide
Endothelial cells make nitric oxide (NO) from L-arginine with the enzyme NO synthase. Shear stress from flowing blood is a main stimulus. Some medications release NO directly. NO is a small gas and diffuses straight across membranes into the neighboring smooth muscle cells, where it:

activates soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC), which makes cGMP from GTP;
cGMP activates protein kinase G (PKG, also called cGMP-dependent protein kinase);
PKG lowers cytosolic Ca2+. It reduces Ca2+ entry and SR release and opens K+ channels, so the membrane hyperpolarizes and voltage-gated Ca2+ channels close. PKG also activates MLCP.

Less Ca2+ means less active MLCK, and more MLCP means myosin is dephosphorylated faster. Both relax the muscle and dilate the vessel.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The nitric oxide figure labels the cGMP-dependent kinase “PGK,” and the speaker notes spell it out as “phosphoglycerate kinase.” The enzyme is protein kinase G (PKG), the cGMP-dependent protein kinase. Phosphoglycerate kinase is a glycolytic enzyme and has no role here. The arrows in the figure are right: the cGMP-activated kinase opens K+ channels, reduces Ca2+ entry and release, and so relaxes the cell.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 6  Smooth Muscle
text:
6.5 Unique properties and functions

6.5.1 Patterns of contraction
Different organs use their smooth muscle in different ways (Figure 6.5). Sphincters stay contracted most of the time and relax briefly, as when the lower esophageal sphincter opens to let a swallow through. Blood vessels and airways are partly contracted all the time: this baseline is tone, and the body adjusts it up and down. The stomach and intestines contract rhythmically (phasic contraction). The esophagus and the urinary bladder are normally relaxed and contract in brief bursts, to swallow or to void.






Figure 6.5: Patterns of smooth muscle contraction over time in different organs. Course figure, after the lecture’s slide.



Holding tone all day would be expensive if every cross-bridge used ATP at the rate skeletal muscle does. Smooth muscle has a way around that.


6.5.2 The latch state
Here phasic means a single brief contraction, the opposite of tonic; the rhythmic gut contractions above are a series of phasic contractions. In a phasic contraction (Figure 6.6 A), a brief stimulus raises Ca2+, MLCK phosphorylates myosin, cross-bridges cycle, force rises, and everything falls back as Ca2+ is removed. In a tonic contraction (Figure 6.6 B), the stimulus is sustained. Ca2+ and myosin phosphorylation peak early and then fall to a lower steady level. Force does not fall. It stays high, while only 20 to 30% of cross-bridges (that is, of myosin regulatory light chains) are phosphorylated. That is the latch state: smooth muscle can hold a contraction with minimal ATP use.
The standard explanation is that when MLCP dephosphorylates a myosin head that is still attached to actin, the head does not let go right away. It stays bound and detaches very slowly. These dephosphorylated heads, called latch bridges, keep bearing force and detach only slowly. Once one does detach, it cannot bind again until MLCK rephosphorylates it. Fewer heads are cycling, and each attached head holds on longer, so force is held for much less ATP. The muscle trades speed for economy: it holds force, but it cannot shorten quickly while in latch.






Figure 6.6: Phasic and tonic contraction. (A) A brief stimulus gives a transient rise in Ca2+, myosin light chain phosphorylation, and force. (B) During a sustained stimulus Ca2+ and phosphorylation fall to a lower steady level after their initial peak, but force stays high: the latch state. When the stimulus ends, Ca2+ falls and the muscle relaxes. Course figure, after the lecture’s slide.





6.5.3 Length adaptation
A skeletal muscle has one optimal length, set by filament overlap in the sarcomere, and force falls away on either side of it (Figure 6.7 A). Smooth muscle can work over a much wider range of lengths. Part of the reason is side-polar myosin. The other part is length adaptation: if a smooth muscle is held at a new length for a while, the cell rearranges its contractile units, adding or removing them in series, so that its length-tension curve moves and its optimal length becomes the new length (Figure 6.7 B).
That is what a bladder or a stomach needs. A full bladder can be several times its empty size and must still be able to contract strongly enough to empty.






Figure 6.7: Length-tension curves. (A) The classic length-tension relationship of skeletal muscle, with one fixed optimal length, L0 (the skeletal curve of the Skeletal Muscle chapter, with L0 taken as 2.1 µm). (B) Smooth muscle held at a new length adapts: its curve shifts so that peak force occurs near that length, shown here for 0.7 L0 and 1.3 L0. Schematic. Course figure, after the lecture’s slide.





6.5.4 Smooth muscle can divide as well as hypertrophy
Skeletal and cardiac muscle cells grow larger in response to load (hypertrophy), but they rarely or never divide. Smooth muscle cells can do both. They can proliferate (divide by mitosis). They can hypertrophy, growing larger, and in some vessels the nuclei become tetraploid or octaploid as the cell grows. They also synthesize and secrete connective tissue proteins, collagen and elastic fibers, into the wall around them.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

text:
6.6 Comparing smooth and skeletal muscle

The Cardiac Muscle chapter adds the third column.






WarningA common mistake



“Smooth muscle needs an action potential to contract.” Many smooth muscles contract with graded depolarization or with no change in membrane potential at all, through pharmacomechanical coupling (IP3 release of SR Ca2+) or stretch. “All smooth muscle acts as a syncytium” is the other one. Only single-unit smooth muscle does. Multi-unit cells, as in the iris and vas deferens, are controlled one by one.

title: 6  Smooth Muscle
text:
6.7 Check your understanding

A drug blocks MLCK completely. Can the smooth muscle contract if cytosolic Ca2+ rises? Would the answer be the same for skeletal muscle?


Answer

No. In smooth muscle, Ca2+ works only through calmodulin and MLCK: without phosphorylation of the regulatory light chain, myosin cannot cycle. Skeletal muscle would still contract, because Ca2+ there binds troponin C on the thin filament, and light chain phosphorylation only modulates force.

A strip of artery is made to contract in two ways: once by depolarizing it with a high-K+ solution, and once with an α1 agonist. An L-type Ca2+ channel blocker is then added. Which contraction is reduced more, and why?


Answer

The high-K+ contraction. It is electromechanical coupling: depolarization opens voltage-gated (L-type) Ca2+ channels, and that Ca2+ entry is almost the whole signal, so blocking the channels removes it. The α1 contraction is pharmacomechanical. Part of it also depends on Ca2+ entry, but IP3 still releases SR Ca2+ and Rho kinase still inhibits MLCP, so some force remains.

Epinephrine constricts one vessel and dilates another. How can the same hormone do both?


Answer

The response depends on the receptor. At α1 receptors (Gq), epinephrine raises IP3 and Ca2+, which activates MLCK and contracts the muscle. At β2 receptors (Gs), it raises cAMP; PKA inhibits MLCK and lowers Ca2+, so the muscle relaxes. The net effect in a vessel depends on which receptor dominates there.

A drug inhibits the enzyme that breaks down cGMP in vascular smooth muscle. Which way does vascular tone move, and through which enzymes?


Answer

Tone falls. cGMP stays high, so PKG stays active. PKG lowers cytosolic Ca2+ (less MLCK activity) and activates MLCP, so myosin is dephosphorylated and the muscle relaxes. The drug amplifies the effect of NO.

During a sustained contraction, measured myosin light chain phosphorylation falls to a quarter of its peak, but force stays near maximal. What is happening, and what does it cost the cell?


Answer

This is the latch state. Myosin heads that are dephosphorylated while attached to actin stay attached and detach very slowly, so they keep bearing force. Fewer heads are cycling and each holds on longer, so the cell uses little ATP. The price is speed: the muscle can hold force but cannot shorten quickly.

Why can a peristaltic wave travel along the intestine while each smooth muscle cell in the iris can be controlled separately?


Answer

Intestinal smooth muscle is single-unit: its cells are joined by many gap junctions, so excitation in one cell spreads to its neighbors as a wave. The iris is multi-unit: its cells have no gap junctions between them and each receives its own nerve supply, so contraction can be graded cell by cell.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

6.8 Sources

title: 7  Cardiac Muscle
text:
7.1 Structure
Cardiac output is the blood the heart pumps each minute. Along with heart rate, three things set it, and the three muscle types map onto them. The volume that fills the ventricle before it contracts (venous return, which sets end-diastolic volume) depends partly on skeletal muscle, whose pump squeezes blood back toward the heart. Vascular tone, which sets systemic vascular resistance (SVR), is the work of smooth muscle. And the strength of each beat depends on cardiac muscle. This chapter is about that third piece: how a cardiac myocyte is built, how an action potential becomes a contraction, and what lets the force of that contraction change from beat to beat.
The workload is large. At 70 beats per minute, the heart beats about 100,800 times a day, almost 37 million times a year, and about 2.8 billion times in a 75-year life. At a cardiac output of 5 L/min it pumps 7,200 L a day, close to 200 million liters in a lifetime: roughly 80 Olympic swimming pools. Most of the myocytes that do that work are the ones you were born with, because adult cardiac myocytes essentially do not divide.
This chapter builds on the sarcomere, the cross-bridge cycle and troponin regulation in Skeletal Muscle, and on the membrane potential in Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 7  Cardiac Muscle
text:
7.1.1 The heart wall
The heart wall has three layers. The outermost is the epicardium, which is the visceral layer of the pericardium. Outside it is the pericardial space, then the parietal pericardium and the tough fibrous pericardium, which anchors the heart in the chest. The middle layer, the myocardium, is the cardiac muscle. The inner layer, the endocardium, is connective tissue lined with endothelium, which separates the myocardium from the blood in the chambers.
In the ventricles the muscle fibers do not run in one direction. They wind around the chambers in spiraling layers from base to apex, and their angle changes through the thickness of the wall. When they shorten, the ventricle does not just squeeze in from the sides. It wrings, like a towel being twisted, and pushes blood out toward the valves at the base.


7.1.2 The cardiac myocyte
Cardiac myocytes are:

striated, with sarcomeres just like skeletal muscle;
branched, so each cell connects to several neighbors;
joined end to end by intercalated discs;
packed with mitochondria, which take up about 30% of the cell’s volume. The heart never rests, so it depends on a steady supply of ATP from oxidative metabolism;
usually mononucleated, with a single central nucleus (some cells have two).

Each cell is about 100 µm long, much shorter than a skeletal muscle fiber, which is one multinucleated cell that can run the length of the muscle.


7.1.3 Sarcolemma and T-tubules
The sarcolemma, the myocyte’s cell membrane, carries the transporters and channels that set the membrane potential. At each Z line it dips deep into the cell as a T-tubule (transverse tubule). The inside of a T-tubule is extracellular space: it is open to the fluid outside the cell, and its lining of negatively charged polysaccharides binds Ca2+, so the T-tubules hold a supply of extracellular Ca2+ right next to the channels that let it in. Because the T-tubules carry the membrane deep into the cell, an action potential on the surface reaches every myofibril almost at once.
Each T-tubule runs right next to the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR). In cardiac muscle a T-tubule pairs with one SR cisterna, a dyad (Figure 7.1). Skeletal muscle has triads: one T-tubule flanked by two SR cisternae. Cardiac T-tubules are also wider, there is one per sarcomere instead of two, and the SR is less extensive than in skeletal muscle. The slides write “diads”; the course term is dyad.






Figure 7.1: Triad and dyad. (A) In skeletal muscle, T-tubules (blue) enter at the junctions of the A and I bands, two per sarcomere, and each has an SR cisterna (purple) on both sides. (B) In cardiac muscle, a wider T-tubule enters at each Z line and pairs with a single SR cisterna. Thin purple lines are the SR network running between cisternae. Schematic. Course figure.





7.1.4 The sarcoplasmic reticulum
The SR is the cell’s main store of Ca2+ for contraction. Three proteins in its membrane matter here:

the ryanodine receptor (RyR2 in the heart), a Ca2+ release channel. It senses Ca2+ in the cytosol, and when Ca2+ rises near it, it opens and releases SR Ca2+;
SERCA (sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase), a pump that uses ATP to move Ca2+ from the cytosol back into the SR;
phospholamban (PLB), a small protein that regulates SERCA. Unphosphorylated, it holds SERCA back. When it is phosphorylated, the brake comes off and SERCA pumps faster.

Epinephrine and norepinephrine, acting through β1 receptors, raise cAMP and activate protein kinase A (PKA), which phosphorylates phospholamban. SERCA speeds up and Ca2+ uptake into the SR increases. You need only the result, not the steps of the cascade. The section on unique properties shows why that makes the heart beat more strongly.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The SR slide and the peer-educator notes say that phospholamban “is unique to cardiac muscle.” Phospholamban is the main regulator of SERCA in the heart, but it is also found in slow-twitch (type I) skeletal muscle and in smooth muscle. What matters for this course is that β1-adrenergic phosphorylation of phospholamban speeds Ca2+ uptake in the heart. This is errata entry 3.
The notes also say the SR “holds a large store of Ca2+ used for depolarization.” SR Ca2+ is used for contraction, not depolarization. The myocyte depolarizes because Na+ enters, and its plateau comes from Ca2+ entering across the sarcolemma through L-type channels. Releasing SR Ca2+ is the step that links the action potential to contraction. This is errata entry 19.




7.1.5 The sarcomere and troponin
The cardiac sarcomere has the same parts as the skeletal sarcomere: Z lines anchoring the thin (actin) filaments, an M line in the middle anchoring the thick (myosin) filaments, the light I band (thin filaments only), the dark A band (the full length of the thick filaments), and the H zone in the middle of the A band (thick filaments only), which narrows as the muscle shortens. The slides label it the H band. The details are in Skeletal Muscle.
Regulation is on the thin filament, as in skeletal muscle. Tropomyosin lies along the actin and covers the myosin-binding sites. The troponin complex sits on tropomyosin: troponin C binds Ca2+, troponin I inhibits actin-myosin binding, and troponin T anchors the complex to tropomyosin. When Ca2+ binds troponin C, the complex changes shape, tropomyosin moves, the binding sites are exposed, and cross-bridges form.
Cardiac troponin C has one regulatory Ca2+-binding site, and skeletal troponin C has two. Both also have two structural sites that bind Ca2+ or Mg2+, so in all cardiac troponin C has three sites and skeletal has four. The single regulatory site is the one that switches contraction on.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The sarcomere slide and the peer-educator notes say “Troponin C only has 1 calcium binding site (Skeletal muscle has 4).” That compares cardiac regulatory sites (one) with skeletal total sites (four). Compared like with like, cardiac troponin C has one regulatory site and skeletal has two, and cardiac has three sites in all and skeletal four. This is errata entry 4.


A clinical correlation. Cardiac troponin I and troponin T are cardiac-specific isoforms, different enough from the skeletal forms that blood tests can tell them apart. When cardiac myocytes are injured, as in a myocardial infarction, troponin leaks out of the dying cells and its level in the blood rises. That is why a troponin level is drawn in a patient with chest pain.


7.1.6 Intercalated discs
Where two myocytes meet end to end, their membranes form an intercalated disc. It runs in steps (Figure 7.2). The transverse parts of each step run across the long axis of the cells, and the myofibrils end there. The longitudinal parts run along the long axis. Each part holds different junctions.






Figure 7.2: An intercalated disc between two cardiac myocytes. Myofibrils (pink bands; gray lines are Z lines) end at the transverse parts of the disc, where adherens junctions (green) anchor them and desmosomes (gold) rivet the membranes together. Gap junctions (blue) lie in the longitudinal parts. Schematic. Course figure, after the lecture’s electron micrographs.



Gap junctions (longitudinal regions): communication. Each gap junction channel is made of 12 connexin proteins, six from each cell. Each set of six forms a half-channel, and the two halves line up across the narrow gap between the cells to make a channel connecting the two cytoplasms. Ions and small molecules flow freely through it. That is why the gap junction matters: when one myocyte depolarizes, current flows through the gap junctions into its neighbors and depolarizes them. The action potential spreads from cell to cell without any nerve, and the whole myocardium contracts as a coordinated unit, a functional syncytium.
Adherens junctions (transverse regions): the zipper. Cadherins span the gap between the cells. Inside each cell, α-catenin and β-catenin link the cadherins to the actin of the cytoskeleton, and the myofibrils attach here. Force generated in one cell’s sarcomeres is passed straight to the next cell.
Desmosomes (transverse regions): the rivet. The transmembrane proteins desmoglein and desmocollin bind across the gap. Inside the cell, desmoplakin connects them to desmin, an intermediate filament. Desmosomes hold the cells firmly together so they do not pull apart when the heart contracts.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 7  Cardiac Muscle
text:
7.2 Conduction system and autorhythmicity
The heart starts its own beat. Specialized cardiac cells generate the impulse and carry it through the heart in order:

Sinoatrial (SA) node, in the right atrium, the heart’s pacemaker. It fires fastest, so it sets the rate.
Internodal pathways through the atria, and Bachmann’s bundle, which carries the impulse to the left atrium.
Atrioventricular (AV) node, which delays the impulse so the atria finish contracting before the ventricles start.
Bundle of His.
Left and right bundle branches and the Purkinje fibers, which spread the impulse quickly through the ventricular walls.

These conductive cells are specialized myocytes, not nerves. They contain little actin and myosin, so they contract weakly or not at all. They are also anatomically isolated from the surrounding working myocytes: the Purkinje fibers, for example, run in bundles wrapped in connective tissue, and they connect to ordinary myocytes only at their ends.
Pacemaker cells and ordinary ventricular myocytes have different action potentials (Figure 7.3). A ventricular myocyte sits at a stable resting potential of about −90 mV until a neighbor depolarizes it. Its fast-response action potential rises sharply (phase 0), dips briefly (phase 1), holds a long plateau near 0 mV (phase 2), repolarizes (phase 3) and returns to rest (phase 4). A pacemaker cell has no stable resting potential. Its slow-response action potential starts from a maximum diastolic potential of about −60 mV and drifts upward in phase 4 until it reaches threshold, then rises slowly (phase 0) and repolarizes (phase 3).
Autonomic nerves change heart rate by changing that phase 4 drift. Sympathetic stimulation (norepinephrine at β1 receptors) steepens it, so threshold comes sooner and the rate rises. Parasympathetic stimulation (acetylcholine at M2 receptors) does two things at once: it opens K+ channels, so each cycle starts from a more negative potential, and it lowers cAMP, so the slope flattens. Both lengthen the time to threshold and slow the heart. The lecture’s figure shows only the flatter slope; both effects happen together, as Autonomic and Extrinsic Control explains.






Figure 7.3: Cardiac action potentials. (A) A pacemaker cell in the SA node has a slow-response action potential with spontaneous phase 4 depolarization. Sympathetic stimulation (maroon) steepens phase 4 and the cell reaches threshold sooner. Parasympathetic stimulation (blue) starts phase 4 from a more negative potential and flattens its slope, so the cell reaches threshold later. (B) A ventricular myocyte has a fast-response action potential with phases 0 to 4. The absolute (effective) refractory period lasts through the plateau and about midway through phase 3, and the relative refractory period covers the rest of phase 3. Schematic. Course figure.



The ionic currents behind each phase are the subject of EKG I: Ionic Basis.






WarningA common mistake



The upstroke of a slow-response action potential, in the SA and AV nodes, is carried by Ca2+ through L-type channels, not by Na+. That is why L-type Ca2+ channel blockers slow conduction through the AV node. What this means for other drugs is in Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells and EKG I: Ionic Basis.


The absolute (effective) refractory period of a ventricular myocyte lasts through the plateau and about midway through phase 3, almost as long as the contraction itself. The relative refractory period covers the rest of phase 3. The cell cannot fire again until it has largely relaxed, so the heart cannot be tetanized the way skeletal muscle can.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 7  Cardiac Muscle
text:
7.3 Excitation-contraction coupling
Excitation-contraction coupling is the chain of steps that turns the action potential into contraction. In cardiac muscle it runs in six steps (Figure 7.4).

The action potential arrives. It starts in the SA node, travels through the conduction system to the myocytes, and spreads from cell to cell through gap junctions. In each cell it runs down the T-tubules, deep into the cell, close to the SR.
L-type Ca2+ channels open. Depolarization of the T-tubule membrane opens voltage-gated L-type Ca2+ channels, and Ca2+ flows into the cell from the extracellular fluid in the T-tubule. This entry is the plateau current.
Ca2+ activates the ryanodine receptor. The incoming Ca2+ diffuses across the narrow gap of the dyad and binds RyR2 on the SR.
The SR releases a large amount of Ca2+. RyR2 opens and releases far more Ca2+ from the SR into the cytosol than came in through the L-type channels. A small trigger releases a large store: Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release.
Ca2+ binds troponin C. The troponin complex changes shape, tropomyosin moves off the myosin-binding sites on actin, and cross-bridges cycle. The sarcomeres shorten. The cross-bridge cycle is the one in Skeletal Muscle.
Ca2+ is removed and the myocyte relaxes. About 70% of the Ca2+ is pumped back into the SR by SERCA, under the control of phospholamban. NCX, the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, removes most of the rest (about 28%) from the cell, bringing three Na+ in for each Ca2+ it moves out. The last 2% or so leaves through the sarcolemmal Ca2+-ATPase and the mitochondria (the slide shows it going to the mitochondria). As Ca2+ leaves troponin C, tropomyosin covers the binding sites again.







Figure 7.4: Ca2+ handling in a ventricular myocyte. (1) The action potential depolarizes the sarcolemma and T-tubule. (2) L-type Ca2+ channels in the T-tubule let a small amount of Ca2+ in. (3) That Ca2+ opens RyR2 on the SR. (4) The SR releases a large amount of Ca2+. (5) Ca2+ binds troponin C and the myofilaments contract. (6) Ca2+ is removed: about 70% back into the SR by SERCA (regulated by phospholamban, PLB), 28% out of the cell by NCX, and about 2% by the sarcolemmal Ca2+ pump and the mitochondria. The Na+/K+ pump keeps up the Na+ gradient that drives NCX. Course figure, after the lecture’s diagram.



Two consequences follow from these numbers. First, most of the Ca2+ that activates the myofilaments comes from the SR, not from outside the cell. Extracellular Ca2+ is still essential: without the trigger there is no release, and a cardiac myocyte will not contract in Ca2+-free solution. Second, in a steady state, whatever Ca2+ enters through the L-type channels each beat has to leave the cell again, mostly through NCX. What SERCA takes back into the SR is available for the next beat.
How this differs from skeletal muscle. In skeletal muscle, the voltage sensor in the T-tubule (the dihydropyridine, or DHP, receptor) is mechanically linked to the ryanodine receptor (RyR1) and opens it directly by changing shape. No Ca2+ has to enter from outside, and skeletal muscle keeps contracting in Ca2+-free solution. In cardiac muscle the L-type Ca2+ channel is the same family of protein, but it is not physically coupled to RyR2. It works by letting Ca2+ in, and that Ca2+ opens RyR2.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 7  Cardiac Muscle
text:
7.4 Unique properties

7.4.1 Force depends on sarcomere length
As in skeletal muscle, the force a cardiac myocyte develops depends on how long its sarcomeres are when it starts to contract. In skeletal muscle, force is greatest at the length where thin and thick filaments overlap best (about 2.0 to 2.2 µm) and falls off as the sarcomere is shortened or stretched away from that length. Cardiac muscle works over a much narrower window (Figure 7.5). Its active force rises steeply as the sarcomere is stretched from about 1.8 to about 2.3 µm, and its passive tension (the force needed to stretch the resting muscle) rises steeply above about 2.2 µm. The heart normally works on the rising limb of its length-tension curve.






Figure 7.5: Length-tension curve of cardiac muscle. Solid line, active tension; dashed line, passive tension of resting muscle. Active force rises steeply between about 1.8 and 2.3 µm, and passive tension rises so steeply above about 2.2 µm that the sarcomeres in an intact heart are rarely stretched much farther. The curve is for the Ca2+ level of a normal beat. For the skeletal muscle curve, see the Skeletal Muscle chapter. Schematic. Course figure, after the lecture’s slide.









NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The length-tension slide and the peer-educator notes say that cardiac sarcomeres are shorter than skeletal sarcomeres, which “makes for narrower window of optimal contraction.” The thick filaments are the same length in both, and the sarcomere lengths overlap. The window is narrow mainly because resting cardiac muscle is so stiff: its giant elastic protein (titin) and its extracellular matrix resist stretch, so passive tension climbs steeply above about 2.2 µm and keeps the sarcomeres near the top of their working range even when the heart is very full. The rising limb is also steeper in heart muscle, because at the Ca2+ level of a normal beat a shorter sarcomere is less sensitive to Ca2+ (see the Frank-Starling mechanism below). The practical point is the same either way: the heart works over a narrow range of sarcomere lengths, on the rising part of its curve.
The slide’s cardiac curve also peaks near 2.4 µm and then falls steeply. In the intact heart, passive stiffness keeps sarcomeres from going much past 2.2 to 2.3 µm, so that falling limb is rarely reached, and the figure here draws only the range the heart uses. What matters is the shape: the heart works on the rising limb, over a narrow range, while skeletal muscle works over a broader range around its 2.0 to 2.2 µm peak.




7.4.2 The Frank-Starling mechanism
The more the ventricle fills in diastole, the more its sarcomeres are stretched, and the more forcefully it contracts. Stroke volume rises with end-diastolic volume. This is the Frank-Starling mechanism, and it lets the heart pump out whatever returns to it, beat by beat, without any nerve or hormone.
Stretch raises force in two ways. Lengthening the sarcomere toward about 2.2 µm improves the overlap of thin and thick filaments. Stretch also makes the myofilaments more sensitive to Ca2+: at a longer sarcomere length, the same Ca2+ concentration produces more force (Figure 7.6 A). In the heart the second effect is thought to be the larger one.






Figure 7.6: (A) Force developed by cardiac muscle at different Ca2+ concentrations, at a short and a stretched sarcomere length. pCa is −log[Ca2+], so Ca2+ concentration rises to the right. At the longer length the curve shifts left: the same Ca2+ gives more force. Lengths as on the lecture’s slide, measured in isolated heart muscle, which can be stretched farther than sarcomeres in an intact heart. (B) Frank-Starling curves. Moving from point 1 to point 2, more filling stretches the muscle and stroke volume rises along the same curve, with contractility unchanged. Moving from point 1 to point 3, contractility rises (for example with sympathetic stimulation) and the heart ejects more at the same end-diastolic volume, on a higher curve. A fall in contractility moves the heart to a lower curve. Schematic values. Course figure, after the lecture’s slides.



Keep the two kinds of change apart (Figure 7.6 B). More filling moves the heart along its Frank-Starling curve: force and stroke volume rise, and contractility does not change. A change in contractility moves the heart to a different curve: more (or less) force at the same end-diastolic volume. At very high filling volumes the curve flattens, so more filling adds little stroke volume, and in a failing heart stroke volume may even fall. Because contractility is the slope of the Frank-Starling curve, that flattening is a fall in contractility. The Cardiac Pump chapter shows the same distinction on the pressure-volume loop, where filling moves the loop along a fixed end-systolic pressure-volume line and a change in contractility changes the line’s slope.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The Frank-Starling slides say “Starling Curve maps contractility with stretch.” Over the normal range, greater end-diastolic stretch increases the force of contraction and stroke volume along the same curve, and contractility, the slope of the curve, stays the same. The slides’ other point, that overfilling can decrease contractility, is right: where the curve flattens at very high volumes, its slope, and so contractility, falls.








WarningA common mistake



“Stretching the ventricle increases its contractility” is wrong over the normal range of filling. Stretch increases the force of contraction through the Frank-Starling mechanism, and the slope of the curve, which is contractility, is unchanged.




7.4.3 Force depends on Ca2+
A cardiac myocyte will not contract without Ca2+, and the force it develops depends on how much Ca2+ reaches the myofilaments. In skeletal muscle a single twitch is brief and submaximal, and the body grades force by recruiting more motor units and by firing them faster, so that Ca2+ stays high (summation and tetanus). In the heart every cell contracts on every beat, and none can be tetanized, so the heart grades force partly by length (Frank-Starling) and partly by how much Ca2+ each beat releases. At normal levels the Ca2+ released in a beat fills only part of the troponin C sites, which leaves room for more.
This is where phospholamban comes back. Epinephrine and norepinephrine, through β1 receptors and PKA, phosphorylate phospholamban. SERCA pumps faster, the SR takes up more Ca2+ and holds a larger store, and the next action potential releases more Ca2+. More Ca2+ on troponin C means a stronger contraction: contractility rises. Faster Ca2+ uptake also makes the myocyte relax faster, which helps the ventricle fill when heart rate is high. Phosphorylation of phospholamban is one way adrenergic signaling increases cardiac contractility.






NoteBackground: other PKA targets





The lecture’s diagram of the β-adrenergic cascade shows that PKA also phosphorylates the L-type Ca2+ channel (more Ca2+ enters each beat), the ryanodine receptor, and troponin I (Ca2+ comes off troponin C faster, so relaxation speeds up). Acetylcholine at M2 receptors, through Gi, lowers cAMP and opposes these effects. The lecture says you do not need to memorize this part of the cascade.

title: 7  Cardiac Muscle
text:
7.6 Check your understanding

A drug blocks SERCA in a ventricular myocyte. Predict what happens to relaxation, and to the force of the beats that follow.


Answer

Relaxation slows, because the main route for clearing Ca2+ from the cytosol (about 70%) is gone and NCX has to do most of the work. Beat by beat the SR store runs down, because Ca2+ released from the SR is no longer pumped back. Less Ca2+ is released with each action potential, so less binds troponin C and force falls.

A drug blocks the gap junctions between ventricular myocytes. What happens to the spread of excitation, and why does it matter for pumping?


Answer

The action potential can no longer pass from cell to cell through the gap junctions, so excitation spreads slowly or not at all. The myocytes stop contracting together as a functional syncytium, and the ventricle cannot squeeze its blood out in one coordinated contraction.

During exercise the heart rate rises and the time between beats shrinks. How does β1 stimulation make each beat relax faster? Name the proteins PKA acts on and the pump involved, and say why faster relaxation matters at a high heart rate.


Answer

β1 receptors raise cAMP and activate PKA. PKA phosphorylates phospholamban, which takes its brake off SERCA, so SERCA pumps Ca2+ back into the SR faster. PKA also phosphorylates troponin I, so Ca2+ comes off troponin C sooner. Cytosolic Ca2+ falls faster, cross-bridges detach sooner, and the myocyte relaxes earlier in each cycle. The speed of relaxation is lusitropy, a property separate from contractility. At a high heart rate the ventricle has little time between beats to fill, and relaxing early leaves more of that time for filling.

On the Frank-Starling curves in Figure 7.6 B, a heart can reach the same larger stroke volume by moving from point 1 to point 2 or from point 1 to point 3. What is different about the sarcomeres in the two cases, and which one involves a change in contractility?


Answer

From 1 to 2, the heart fills more, so its sarcomeres start each beat longer. That raises force through better filament overlap and greater Ca2+ sensitivity, with no change in contractility: the heart stays on the same curve. From 1 to 3, sarcomere length at the start of the beat is the same, but more Ca2+ is released and bound each beat (for example after β1 stimulation phosphorylates phospholamban). The heart develops more force at the same length, which is what a rise in contractility means, so it moves to a higher curve.

Of the Ca2+ that activates contraction in each beat, most is removed by SERCA and about 28% by NCX. Why must the NCX fraction roughly match the Ca2+ that entered through the L-type channels?


Answer

In a steady state the cell cannot gain or lose Ca2+ from beat to beat. Ca2+ that came in from outside through the L-type channels has to go back out, and NCX is the main route out. Ca2+ taken back up by SERCA stays inside, in the SR, ready for the next beat.

A ventricular myocyte’s action potential lasts 250 ms and its twitch 300 ms. A second stimulus arrives either 100 ms or 320 ms after the first upstroke. Which timing fires a second action potential, and does the force of the second beat add to the first?


Answer

At 100 ms the cell is in its plateau, inside the absolute refractory period, so the stimulus fires nothing and the first twitch runs its course unchanged. At 320 ms the action potential is over and the twitch has ended, so the stimulus fires a new action potential and a new twitch. That twitch starts from a relaxed muscle, and its force does not add to the first. The cell can fire again only once it has largely relaxed, so cardiac twitches do not summate.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 8  Microcirculation and Local Control
text:
8.1 The microcirculation
Everything upstream of the capillaries exists to deliver blood to them. This chapter is about what happens when it arrives: how gases, solutes and water cross the capillary wall, where the extra fluid goes, and how each tissue adjusts the radius of its own arterioles to get the flow it needs. It builds directly on Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics, especially Poiseuille’s law, aggregate cross-sectional area and the difference between perfusion and transmural pressure. Reflex and hormonal control of the same vessels is in ANS and Extrinsic Control.
The microcirculation is the arterioles, the capillaries and the venules. In some tissues small precapillary sphincters guard the entrances to the capillaries, and short channels (metarterioles) run from arterioles across to venules. The arterioles regulate how much blood enters; the capillaries provide an enormous surface for exchange.
If you watch a living capillary bed under a microscope, red cells pass through the capillaries one after another, slowly, with no visible pulse. The pulse has been filtered out upstream by the combination of arterial compliance and arteriolar resistance, the hydraulic filter of the previous chapter. How a bed is organized varies a good deal from tissue to tissue; textbook drawings are schematic.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 8  Microcirculation and Local Control
text:
8.1.1 Arterioles: the stopcocks of the circulation
Arterioles are resistance vessels: an endothelium inside a thick coat of smooth muscle. By contracting or relaxing that muscle they change their radius, and because resistance varies with 1/r4, a small change in radius makes a large change in resistance. The course compares them to the stopcock on an IV line, which can be turned to shut one port off completely. An arteriole can constrict enough to stop flow into a tissue bed.
Raynaud phenomenon shows this in the fingers. With a mild chill the digital arterioles clamp down, the fingers turn white, and they ache because the tissue is briefly ischemic. When flow returns they flush pink, for a reason covered under metabolic control below.


8.1.2 Capillaries: built for exchange

Wall. A single layer of flattened endothelial cells, 0.2 to 0.5 µm thick, on a basement membrane, with scattered contractile pericytes inside the basement membrane. There is no smooth muscle and no outer adventitia.
Size. 5 to 10 µm in diameter, about the size of a red cell, so red cells pass in single file. Each capillary is about 0.5 to 1 mm long.
Distribution. Capillary density follows the tissue’s metabolic demand. Active tissues such as heart muscle have far more capillaries per gram than quiet ones.
Number. About 1010 capillaries in parallel, whose aggregate cross-sectional area is the 24-inch pizza (the Big Benito) of the previous chapter.

Mean velocity is total flow divided by aggregate cross-sectional area. Because that area is so large, blood moves through the capillaries at only about 0.03 cm/s, a fraction of a millimeter per second, and the slow transit gives time for exchange.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 8  Microcirculation and Local Control
text:
8.2 Crossing the capillary wall
Different substances take different routes.

Lipid-soluble substances, including O2 and CO2, diffuse straight through the endothelial cells, crossing two plasma membranes and the cytoplasm between them.
Small water-soluble solutes, such as Na+, K+, Cl− and glucose, diffuse through water-filled pathways in the clefts between endothelial cells, a few nanometers wide. (The slide calls these “intra-cellular clefts.” They are the gaps between cells.)
Plasma proteins, above all albumin, are strongly held back and normally stay in the capillary. In inflammation, as in sepsis, the barrier is injured and albumin leaks out.


8.2.1 Fick’s law: concentration drives diffusion
Solutes and gases cross the wall mainly by passive diffusion. Fick’s first law describes it:
\[J = -D\,\frac{d\phi}{dx}\]
J is the flux of solute (amount per unit area per unit time), dφ/dx is the concentration gradient across the barrier, and D is the diffusion coefficient of that solute in that barrier. The minus sign says that solute moves down its gradient, from high concentration to low. The law has the same shape as Ohm’s law: the gradient plays the role of the pressure difference, and the diffusion coefficient plays the role of a conductance. You will not calculate it, but you should be able to predict what changes the rate.







Change
Effect, with the other factors fixed




Larger concentration difference
More net flux down the gradient


More exchange surface area
More total transfer, with the barrier’s intrinsic permeability unchanged


Higher (or lower) barrier permeability
Higher (or lower) flux per unit area


Longer diffusion path
Less transfer for the same concentration difference



The numbers are large. The systemic capillaries have about 100 m² of wall, roughly half a singles tennis court. Do not confuse that with the aggregate cross-sectional area of about 2,800 cm²: the first is the area of wall available for exchange, the second the area that blood flows through. Most cells lie within about 10 µm of a capillary, and lengthening that distance even a little matters. Interstitial edema pushes cells and capillaries apart, so the diffusion path lengthens, O2 flux falls, and tissue oxygen delivery suffers.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 8  Microcirculation and Local Control
text:
8.3 Water: the Starling forces
About 20 L of fluid a day is filtered out of the capillaries and most of it comes back. The Starling equation estimates the direction and size of the net water movement across the capillary wall. The course writes it as:
\[Q_f = K\left[(P_c - P_i) - \sigma(\pi_c - \pi_i)\right]\]
A positive Qf means filtration, water moving from the capillary into the interstitium. A negative Qf means absorption.









Term

Pi

In

K

Oncotic pressure always draws water toward the side with more protein. Hydrostatic pressure pushes water away from the side where it is higher. The equation is the sum of the outward pressures minus the sum of the inward ones, scaled by K. Clinically it is never calculated, because none of its terms is measured at the bedside. Its value is in predicting what a change will do.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The slide’s speaker notes and the lecture notes write the equation as Qf = k[(Pc + πi) − (Pi + πc)], grouping the outward and inward pressures, and the supplementary slide writes the net driving pressure as (Pc − Pi) − (πc − πi). These are the same as the form above with σ = 1, rearranged. The σ term is there to show what inflammation does: a leakier wall lets protein through, σ falls, and the plasma proteins hold less water in. When the wall is intact, use σ = 1 and all three forms give the same answer.



8.3.1 Along the length of a capillary: the classical model
Capillary hydrostatic pressure falls along the capillary, from about 35 mm Hg at the arteriolar end to about 15 mm Hg at the venular end, because blood loses pressure as it flows through it. The oncotic difference stays roughly constant. In the classical model, then, the net force favors filtration near the arteriolar end and can cross over to favor absorption near the venular end (Figure 8.1).






Figure 8.1: Starling forces along a capillary in the classical model. (A) The outward hydrostatic difference (Pc − Pi) falls along the capillary as Pc falls; the inward oncotic difference (πc − πi) changes little. (B) The net driving pressure is +12 mm Hg at the arteriolar end (filtration) and −5 mm Hg at the venular end (absorption), crossing zero about two-thirds of the way along. Values from the lecture’s supplementary example, with σ = 1. Course figure.



The crossover comes from the fall in Pc, not from a change in protein concentration. (As water filters out, the protein left behind in the capillary becomes slightly more concentrated, but in this model πc is treated as roughly constant.)
This is a simplified model, and it does not describe every capillary bed. What matters is the balance: across the body, filtration exceeds absorption by about 2 to 4 L a day, and that excess has to leave the tissues another way.






NoteBackground: the classical Starling calculation





The lecture’s supplementary slide works one example, with σ = 1 and all pressures in mm Hg.

title: 8  Microcirculation and Local Control
text:
8.4 Lymphatics: the sewer system
The lymphatics are a second circulatory system, one you probably dissected past without seeing because their walls are so thin. Terminal lymphatics sit right next to the capillaries. Their openings are relatively large, so filtered protein enters along with water. Larger lymphatics have one-way valves, like veins, and smooth muscle that contracts rhythmically to pump lymph forward. Contraction of the surrounding skeletal muscle adds to the pumping. Lymph returns the net capillary filtrate, about 2 to 4 L a day, to the circulation through the thoracic duct, and with it about a quarter to a half of the circulating plasma protein each day.
Lymph flow rises as interstitial pressure rises (Figure 8.2). More filtration puts more fluid into the interstitium, Pi rises, and lymph flow increases to carry it away. That works over a useful range. At high interstitial pressures lymph flow reaches its maximum and cannot rise further. Edema develops when fluid enters the interstitium faster than the lymphatics can clear it.






Figure 8.2: Lymph flow and interstitial fluid pressure. Over the normal range, a small rise in Pi produces a large rise in lymph flow, which clears the extra fluid. Above about +2 mm Hg lymph flow is near its maximum, so further filtration accumulates as edema. Shape after the lecture’s graph. Course figure.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 8  Microcirculation and Local Control
text:
8.5 Using the Starling forces
For any situation, predict the direction of each term separately, then decide which is likely to dominate. In a real patient several can change at once.

Standing still is worse than walking. When you walk, the contracting leg muscles squeeze the valved veins and the lymphatics. That lowers venous pressure in the legs, so Pc falls, and pumps lymph away. Standing motionless (for ten hours, say, holding a retractor in a long operation) gives neither benefit, and the shoes get tight.
Compression stockings help by raising the pressure outside the capillaries. A higher Pi reduces the net outward pressure, so less fluid filters out, and the external squeeze also supports venous and lymphatic return. Wrap a hand and forearm in an elastic bandage for an hour and the arm holds less interstitial fluid when you take it off, partly because lymph flow rose.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The lecture notes say the stockings push water back into the capillaries. The slide’s own notes put it better: the main effect is less filtration and better venous and lymphatic return, not sustained reabsorption.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 8  Microcirculation and Local Control
text:
8.6 Arterioles set capillary hydrostatic pressure
Apply Ohm’s law along the pathway from artery to vein. The segments are in series, so each one’s share of the pressure drop is proportional to its resistance. Hold arterial and venous pressures fixed and change only the arterioles (Figure 8.3):

Arteriolar constriction raises the arterioles’ share of the total resistance, so more of the pressure is used up before the blood reaches the capillaries. Pc falls, and so does flow. Filtration falls and absorption is favored.
Arteriolar dilation does the reverse: less pressure is lost upstream, Pc rises, flow rises, and filtration rises.
Raising venous pressure, or resistance downstream of the capillaries, raises Pc too, because the capillaries sit between the arteriolar and venous resistances.

So the arterioles set more than flow. They also set how much fluid each capillary bed filters or reabsorbs. If an arteriole clamped down completely, the pressure on its downstream side would fall toward venous pressure.






Figure 8.3: Arteriolar tone and capillary pressure. Mean pressure along one pathway, with arterial pressure 95 mm Hg and, except for the dashed line, venous pressure 5 mm Hg. Pc is the mean pressure across the capillary segment, and flow is relative to normal. Constricting the arterioles moves more of the pressure drop upstream of the capillaries and lowers Pc; dilating them raises Pc. Raising venous pressure raises Pc with no change in arteriolar tone. Lumped resistances in series; values illustrative. Course figure.









NoteBackground: precapillary and postcapillary resistance





Treat the capillary as a node between a precapillary resistance (mostly the arterioles) and a postcapillary resistance (mostly the venules). With arterial and venous pressures fixed, Pc lies between them, closer to whichever side has the smaller resistance. Normally precapillary resistance is several times larger than postcapillary resistance, so Pc sits nearer venous pressure than the simple average of the two. Raising precapillary resistance (arteriolar constriction) or lowering postcapillary resistance moves Pc toward venous pressure. Lowering precapillary resistance or raising postcapillary resistance (venular constriction) moves it toward arterial pressure.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 8  Microcirculation and Local Control
text:
8.7 Local control of blood flow

8.7.1 Vasomotor tone
Arteriolar smooth muscle is normally partly contracted. This basal tone is what lets an arteriole both constrict and dilate. More tone narrows the vessel and raises its resistance; less tone dilates it and lowers resistance, and because of the fourth-power law a small change in radius has a large effect.
Two kinds of influence set tone:

Extrinsic influences come from outside the tissue: sympathetic nerves and circulating signals such as epinephrine, angiotensin II and vasopressin. These are covered in ANS and Extrinsic Control.
Local influences come from the tissue and the vessel itself: pressure, flow and metabolism. They need no nerves and no central control.

Their relative importance differs among tissues. Local control dominates minute to minute in the heart and brain; the skin and the splanchnic bed are under strong sympathetic control. The Coronary Circulation and Other Special Circulations chapters take each bed in turn.


8.7.2 Autoregulation
Autoregulation is the overall result of local control: blood flow through a tissue stays nearly constant across a wide range of perfusion pressures, about 20 to 150 mm Hg in the lecture’s skeletal muscle example (Figure 8.4). When perfusion pressure changes suddenly, flow first changes with it, because resistance has not had time to change. Then, over the following seconds to a minute, the arterioles adjust their radius and flow returns close to its earlier value. Below the range, the arterioles are already fully dilated and flow falls with pressure. Above it, they are fully constricted and flow rises with pressure.






Figure 8.4: Autoregulation. Filled circles: flow immediately after an abrupt change in perfusion pressure from the control level, before resistance adjusts; flow follows pressure (dashed line). Open circles: flow after local compensation. Across the autoregulatory range, about 20 to 150 mm Hg in this course, flow returns close to control. Outside the range, flow follows pressure. Schematic. The lecture’s figure shows the same pattern in skeletal muscle, from Jones and Berne [1]. Course figure.









NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The speaker notes for the autoregulation slide, and the lecture notes, give the range as 20 to 120 mm Hg. The course uses 20 to 150 mm Hg. Sources differ on the upper limit. The point to keep is that the range is wide, not narrow.


Three local mechanisms carry out autoregulation and the rest of local control: myogenic, endothelial and metabolic. Two experiments on a single isolated arteriole separate the first two, and they depend on keeping two pressures apart:

Transmural pressure is the pressure across the vessel wall, inside minus outside. It stretches the wall, and it is the stimulus for the myogenic response.
The longitudinal pressure gradient is the pressure difference along the vessel from one end to the other. It drives flow, and with flow comes shear on the endothelium.



8.7.3 A quick review: flow versus velocity
Before the experiments, one caution from the previous chapter. Mean velocity is v = Q/A, and what happens to flow and velocity when a vessel widens depends on what is held constant.








If radius increases…
Volume flow, Q
Mean velocity, v




with Q held fixed
Unchanged
Decreases (v ∝ 1/r²)


with ΔP held fixed (ideal Poiseuille tube, length and viscosity fixed)
Increases (Q ∝ r4)
Increases (v ∝ r²)


in a vascular network
Depends on how flow redistributes
Depends on Q and A



“Dilating an arteriole slows the blood” is true only if the flow through it stays the same. If the pressure difference stays the same, dilating a single tube speeds the blood up. In the body, blood turned away from one constricted bed goes largely to its neighbors, so always ask what is being held constant before predicting velocity.


8.7.4 The myogenic response: stretch causes constriction
In the first experiment an isolated arteriole is connected at both ends to fluid reservoirs at the same height, so nothing flows through it. Raising both reservoirs together raises the pressure inside the vessel, and so its transmural pressure, with no flow at all (Figure 8.5 A).
A rubber tube would simply expand. The arteriole stretches for a moment and then actively narrows, and the higher the pressure, the narrower it gets. Removing the endothelium does not change the response, so it comes from the smooth muscle itself. Relaxing the smooth muscle with sodium nitroprusside, an NO donor, abolishes the constriction and reveals the passive distension underneath: without active tone, the vessel just stretches.
Stretch opens mechanosensitive pathways in the smooth muscle that let more Ca2+ into the cell, and contraction strengthens.
↑ transmural pressure → stretch of arteriolar smooth muscle → ↑ Ca2+ entry → contraction → ↓ radius (↑ resistance) → flow held near its earlier value. The opposite happens when transmural pressure falls.






Figure 8.5: Two experiments on an isolated cardiac arteriole. (A) Myogenic response: transmural pressure is raised step by step with no flow. With active tone the arteriole narrows as pressure rises, with or without its endothelium. With the smooth muscle relaxed by nitroprusside it is passively stretched. (B) Endothelial response: the pressure gradient along the vessel, and so flow, is raised while transmural pressure is held constant. The arteriole dilates with its endothelium intact, and not at all with it removed. Pressures in cm H2O, as in the original experiments. Redrawn approximately from Kuo, Davis and Chilian [2], as used in the 2026 lecture.



The myogenic response defends a tissue’s flow against a rise in arterial pressure. It also acts when you stand: the higher transmural pressure in the arterioles of the feet makes them constrict, which limits the rise in capillary pressure and filtration below them.






NoteBackground: mechanosensitive channels





Several stretch-sensitive channels and signaling pathways link stretch of vascular smooth muscle to Ca2+ entry and contraction. Piezo1 and Piezo2 are among the mechanosensitive channels involved. Mechanosensation comes up again with the baroreceptors. No single channel accounts for the whole myogenic response, and you do not need to name them.





8.7.5 Endothelial control: shear causes dilation
Shear stress is the frictional drag of moving blood on the endothelium. The blood touching the wall does not move, so the drag depends on how steeply velocity rises from the wall toward the center: the faster the flow, the steeper that rise and the greater the drag. (Very high shear can strip endothelial cells from the wall.)
In the second experiment the transmural pressure is held constant, and the pressure gradient along the arteriole is raised step by step, so flow through it increases. Each step dilates the arteriole (Figure 8.5 B). Removing the endothelium abolishes the response, so this mechanism depends on the endothelium.
The endothelial signal is mainly nitric oxide (NO), with prostacyclin (PGI2) as a second dilator. NO diffuses into the neighboring smooth muscle, activates soluble guanylyl cyclase and raises cGMP, which relaxes the muscle. When an effect is endothelium-dependent, NO is the first candidate, and for this course it is enough to think of flow-induced dilation as NO-mediated. Nitroprusside, from the first experiment, works by supplying NO directly.
↑ flow (blood velocity) → ↑ wall shear stress → ↑ endothelial NO and PGI2 → ↑ cGMP in smooth muscle → relaxation → ↑ radius (↓ resistance). For a given flow, the wider vessel has a lower wall shear, which limits the stimulus.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The shear slide ends its chain with “↓ Velocity.” The slide’s speaker notes say not to claim that the experiment shows reduced velocity, and they are right: in the experiment flow rises, and the vessel dilates because flow rose. What the dilation reduces, for a given flow, is the shear on the wall. That is the negative feedback: more shear, more dilation, less shear per unit of flow.




8.7.6 Metabolic control: matching flow to demand
When a tissue’s metabolism rises, or its blood supply falls, local signals build up that dilate its arterioles and precapillary sphincters. The course names adenosine (from the breakdown of ATP), K+, CO2 and H+, and low O2. Resistance falls and flow into the bed rises. The extra flow improves O2 delivery and washes the vasodilator metabolites out, and as they clear, the vessels return toward their basal tone. It is feedback driven by the tissue’s own metabolism: production of the dilators is proportional to metabolic rate, and their removal is proportional to blood flow.
↓ blood flow or ↑ metabolism → ↑ local vasodilator metabolites → arteriolar dilation → ↓ resistance → ↑ flow → metabolites washed out → tone returns.
Two everyday results have names (Figure 8.6):









Active hyperemia
Reactive hyperemia




Trigger
Increased tissue metabolism
A temporary interruption of flow


When flow increases
During the increased activity
After flow is restored


Example
Working skeletal muscle
Release of an occlusion: a cuff, a pressed fingertip, Raynaud fingers rewarming


Response
Perfusion rises with demand
Flow overshoots above baseline for a while, then returns



Squeeze a fingertip hard for a minute or two and let go: the pink flush is reactive hyperemia. Metabolites accumulated while flow was stopped, and they keep the arterioles dilated until the extra flow washes them out. Both kinds of hyperemia correct a mismatch between delivery and the tissue’s needs.






Figure 8.6: Reactive and active hyperemia. (A) After a period with no flow, flow overshoots baseline when the occlusion is released and then returns. (B) During muscular work, flow rises to match the higher metabolic rate and stays up until the work stops. Schematic. Course figure.

title: 8  Microcirculation and Local Control
text:
8.8 Why don’t capillaries rupture?
Capillary hydrostatic pressure is about 25 to 35 mm Hg, held by a wall one cell thick. Why doesn’t it burst?
For a cylindrical vessel, the law of Laplace gives the tension in the wall (force per unit length of wall) needed to hold a given transmural pressure:
\[T = \Delta P \times r\]
At the same pressure, a smaller radius needs proportionally less wall tension. A capillary has a radius of about 2.5 µm, the aorta about 1.25 cm. That is a 5,000-fold difference in radius, so at equal pressure the aortic wall would have to carry 5,000 times the tension of the capillary wall.








Vessel
Illustrative radius
Relative wall tension at equal pressure




Capillary
2.5 µm
1


Aorta
1.25 cm
5,000



The tension is spread through the thickness of the wall. The wall stress, which is what the wall material actually has to withstand, is about
\[\text{wall stress} \approx \frac{\Delta P \times r}{w}\]
where w is the wall thickness. A thicker wall lowers the stress at a given pressure and radius. The aorta, with its large radius, needs a thick wall; the capillary, with its tiny radius, gets by with one cell. (For a sphere, such as an alveolus, the law of Laplace has a factor of 2, P = 2T/r; see Respiratory Statics.)
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 8  Microcirculation and Local Control
text:
8.9 Check your understanding

The arterioles feeding a capillary bed constrict while arterial and venous pressures stay the same. Trace what happens to the pressure drop across the arterioles, Pc, and net filtration. Now leave the arterioles alone and raise venous pressure instead, as in heart failure. What changes?


Answer

Constriction raises the arterioles’ share of the resistance, so a larger part of the pressure drop occurs across them, Pc falls, and net filtration falls (absorption is favored). Raising venous pressure raises Pc directly, because the capillaries sit between the arteriolar and venous resistances, so filtration rises and edema becomes more likely.

A patient with severe dehydration has lost salt and water but no protein. Which Starling term does the water loss change, and which way does fluid move between the interstitium and the capillaries? Apply the same reasoning to a child with severe protein malnutrition.


Answer

Losing water without protein concentrates the plasma proteins, so πc rises. More oncotic pressure holds water in the capillaries, net filtration falls, and fluid is drawn from the interstitium into the capillaries. (The lower blood volume also lowers Pc, which pushes the same way.) In protein malnutrition, plasma albumin is low, so πc falls. Less oncotic pressure holds water in the capillaries, filtration rises, and edema forms, in severe cases with ascites. Low albumin is only part of the story; the lecture notes that malnutrition is more complex.

In severe sepsis the capillary wall becomes leaky. Which terms of the Starling equation change, and which way?


Answer

K rises (more water crosses for a given pressure difference) and σ falls (the wall holds protein back less well). Protein leaks into the interstitium, so πi rises and the effective oncotic difference holding water in falls. All of these favor filtration, so edema forms even if Pc is normal.

Arterial pressure into a resting vascular bed rises suddenly and then stays high. Describe what happens to flow through the bed in the first few seconds and over the next minute, and name the local mechanism responsible for the change.


Answer

In the first seconds flow rises, because the pressure difference across the bed is larger and resistance has not changed yet. The higher pressure also stretches the arteriolar walls. Within seconds their smooth muscle responds to the raised transmural pressure by contracting, the myogenic response, and the arterioles narrow. Resistance rises, and flow falls back toward its earlier value even though the pressure stays high. That is autoregulation: over the range the bed can regulate, flow stays nearly constant as perfusion pressure changes.

A blood pressure cuff on the upper arm is inflated above systolic pressure for three minutes and then released. Describe the forearm blood flow over the next few minutes, and explain it.


Answer

Flow is zero while the cuff is up. After release it rises well above its earlier value, then falls back over the next minute or two: reactive hyperemia. During the occlusion, vasodilator metabolites (adenosine, K+, CO2 and H+, low O2) built up and dilated the arterioles. The high flow on release washes them out, and tone returns.

When you stand still, the column of blood above your feet raises capillary hydrostatic pressure there several-fold. Why does a vessel with a wall one cell thick still not burst? What two features of a vessel’s design keep the stress in its wall low?


Answer

Wall stress is about ΔP × r / w. A capillary’s radius is so small that the tension its wall must carry (T = ΔP × r) stays tiny even when the pressure inside rises, so a single cell layer is strong enough. The two features are a small radius and a thick wall: large vessels, which cannot have a small radius, need thick walls instead.

title: 9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling
text:
9.1 Systolic, diastolic and pulse pressure
So far the heart and the blood vessels have had their own chapters. This lecture puts them back together by asking what sets the arterial blood pressure and what sets the cardiac output. The first answer turns on the arteries: how much blood is in them and how stiff they are. The second turns on the veins, because the heart can only pump out what comes back to it. The last part of the chapter draws the heart and the vessels on one graph and uses it to predict what happens when either one changes. The ANS and Extrinsic Control chapter, next, covers the nerves that move these curves.
A blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg gives two numbers. The systolic pressure (SBP), 120, is the peak in the arteries during ejection. The diastolic pressure (DBP), 80, is the lowest pressure, reached just before the next ejection. The difference is the pulse pressure:
\[\text{PP} = \text{SBP} - \text{DBP}\]
Here PP is 40 mm Hg. Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is the time average of the waveform. At a normal heart rate it is about DBP + ⅓(SBP − DBP), about 93 mm Hg here (Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics).
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle
9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling

title: 9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling
section: 9.2 The elastic aorta: a hydraulic filter
text:
9.2 The elastic aorta: a hydraulic filter
The left ventricle ejects only during systole, about a third of each cycle at rest, yet blood flows through the capillaries all the time. During ejection the aorta and large arteries stretch and take up part of the stroke volume. During diastole the aortic valve is closed, and the stretched walls recoil and push the stored blood on toward the arterioles. The compliant arteries, together with the resistance of the arterioles downstream, smooth a pulsatile inflow into a nearly steady outflow. The course calls this a hydraulic filter. It is also called the Windkessel effect, after the German word for the air chamber that old fire engines used to turn the strokes of a hand pump into a steady jet.
If the arteries were rigid pipes, flow to the tissues would stop in diastole. A stiffer aorta stores less, so outflow and pressure swing more. The Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics chapter models this as an RC filter and draws the flows and pressures.
The filter has these benefits:

It allows perfusion during diastole. This matters most for the heart. Contraction squeezes the vessels inside the left ventricular wall, so most left coronary flow happens in diastole, driven by the diastolic pressure the aorta maintains (Coronary Circulation).
It converts intermittent flow into continuous flow.
It protects the microcirculation. By the time blood reaches the capillaries, the pressure swings are gone and the mean pressure is low.

In the lecture’s thought experiment, a valve lets pulses of water into an elastic tube. If twice as much water passed with each opening, the peak (“systolic”) pressure and the pulse pressure would both rise: stroke volume is a major determinant of both.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle
9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling

title: 9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling
text:
9.3 Pressure along the circulation
From the aorta to the capillaries, pulsations shrink and mean pressure falls, most steeply across the small arteries and arterioles, where the resistance is. The pulsations are damped by the hydraulic filter: the compliance of the arteries working against the resistance of the small arteries and arterioles. The large aggregate cross-sectional area of the capillaries slows the blood, but it is not what causes the drop in pressure (Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics).
Among the large arteries, though, systolic pressure and pulse pressure rise from the aorta toward the periphery, so a cuff on the arm reads a higher systolic pressure than the aortic root. The pressure wave travels along the arterial wall much faster than the blood itself moves, reflects back from branch points and narrowing vessels, and adds to the forward (incident) wave. Recorded pressure is incident wave plus reflected wave. This is a real change in the waveform, not a cuff artifact.
Both statements are true. Pulse pressure is amplified along the large conduit arteries, from the aorta out to the arm and leg, and damped across the arterioles and capillaries.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling
section: 9.4 Compliance: not just a property of the relaxed ventricle
text:
9.4 Compliance: not just a property of the relaxed ventricle
Compliance is the change in volume for a given change in pressure. Its reciprocal, elastance, describes stiffness:
\[C = \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta P} \qquad\qquad E = \frac{\Delta P}{\Delta V}\]
Arteries have compliance too. With age, elastin in the aortic wall fragments and collagen and calcium accumulate (the slides call it age-related medial degeneration with elastocalcinosis), so the same added volume raises the pressure more in older aortas.
That gives the course’s rule for pulse pressure (Figure 9.1). At a given stroke volume, a stiffer aorta produces a wider pulse pressure, and at a given compliance, a larger stroke volume does:
\[\text{PP} \approx \frac{\text{SV}}{C_{\text{arterial}}}\]






Figure 9.1: The same stroke volume in a compliant and a stiff aorta. In the young, compliant aorta, 70 mL raises pressure from 80 to 120 mm Hg. In the older, stiff aorta, the same 70 mL raises it from 75 to about 157 mm Hg. Stiffness widens the pulse pressure. Straight lines over the working range, with illustrative compliances of 1.75 and 0.85 mL/mm Hg. Course figure.



The approximation leaves out runoff during ejection and wave reflection, but it gets the direction right. With age, pulse wave velocity rises, so the reflected wave comes back sooner, during systole instead of diastole, and adds to the systolic peak. The aorta behaves more like a stiff pipe than a rubber hose, and systolic and pulse pressure rise with age: age-related hypertension. The slides note that the rise in arterial stiffness with age is greater in women, with elastin and collagen changes after menopause.



Pulse pressure rises with
Pulse pressure falls with




↑ stroke volume
↓ stroke volume


↓ arterial compliance (stiffer arteries)
↑ arterial compliance

9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling

title: 9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling
text:
9.5 Control of blood pressure
You can raise the pressure in a water balloon by adding water or by making the balloon stiffer. Arterial pressure works the same way: it depends on the arterial blood volume and the arterial compliance. Compliance changes over years. Minute to minute, the body controls blood pressure by changing arterial blood volume.
Arterial blood volume is set by blood in (cardiac output) and blood out, which runs off through the arterioles at a rate set by their resistance, SVR. If inflow briefly exceeds outflow, arterial volume and pressure rise until runoff catches up. So:

↑ CO → ↑ arterial blood volume → ↑ BP (if SVR is unchanged)
↑ SVR → ↑ arterial blood volume → ↑ BP (if CO is unchanged): constricted arterioles hold blood in the arteries longer

At steady state, inflow and outflow are equal, and the relation between them is Ohm’s law for the systemic circulation, as the course writes it:
\[\text{CO} = \frac{\text{MAP} - \text{CVP}}{\text{SVR}} \qquad\qquad \text{MAP} \approx \text{CO} \times \text{SVR}\]
CVP is the measured central venous pressure, which is about equal to right atrial pressure, Pra, the pressure the curves below use. The shortcut on the right works when CVP is small; when it is high, leave it in (Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics has worked examples).

9.5.1 Pulse pressure in shock
Low blood pressure has more than one pattern, and pulse pressure helps tell them apart (Figure 9.2).






Figure 9.2: Pulse pressure in three states, from a two-element Windkessel model (C dP/dt = inflow − P/R) with the same arterial compliance in each. Low-output hypotension (hemorrhage): a small stroke volume and a raised SVR give a narrow pulse pressure. High-output hypotension (sepsis): a low SVR lets the arteries run off quickly in diastole, so DBP falls, and a large stroke volume gives a wide pulse pressure, even though MAP is low. Pressures are model values; the lecture’s normal is 120/80. Course figure.




Low-output hypotension. After hemorrhage, or when the heart pumps weakly, stroke volume is small and pulse pressure is narrow. Arterioles constrict (a sympathetic reflex covered in the next chapter, ANS and Extrinsic Control), so SVR rises and partly compensates for the low CO.
High-output hypotension. In the pattern of septic shock the lecture shows, the arterioles are dilated and SVR is low. Blood runs off the arteries quickly, so diastolic pressure falls, and the heart, facing a low afterload, ejects a large stroke volume. Pulse pressure is wide even though MAP is low. A high CO partly compensates for the low SVR. Sepsis can also be a low-output state when volume is depleted or the heart is depressed.

The lesson on the slide is CO ≠ BP: a low pressure can come with a high output. The slide also writes PP ∝ SV ∝ CO. Read it as: at a given arterial compliance and heart rate, pulse pressure tracks stroke volume, and so gives a clue to cardiac output, not a measurement of it. The full shock pictures are in Cardiovascular Integration and Adaptation.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle
9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling

title: 9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling
text:
9.6 What controls cardiac output?
Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume:
\[\text{CO} = \text{HR} \times \text{SV}\]
Stroke volume depends on preload, afterload and contractility. Preload is the stretch of the ventricle before it contracts (end-diastolic volume). Afterload is the load it ejects against, roughly arterial pressure. Contractility is the force the muscle can develop at a given preload and afterload (course errata entry 2). Very fast heart rates can lower stroke volume by cutting filling time.
The rest of the chapter is about preload. The heart cannot set its own preload: how much blood returns to it depends on the vessels, so the vessels share control of cardiac output with the heart. Guyton and his colleagues showed this in the 1950s by replacing the heart of an animal with a pump and changing the vessels [1].

9.6.1 A simple model of the circulation
The lecture’s model:
