About two thirds of the blood volume sits in the veins. The rest is spread among the arteries, capillaries, heart and lungs. The course’s short version: arteries control pressure, veins control volume.

9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling

title: 9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling
text:
9.7 Mean systemic filling pressure (Pms)
Start with the heart pumping 5 L/min. Mean arterial pressure is about 102 mm Hg and venous pressure about 2 mm Hg. Now stop the heart. Blood keeps running off from the arteries into the veins, but nothing moves it back. Arterial pressure falls and venous pressure rises until they are equal and flow stops. In the lecture’s numbers they meet at 7 mm Hg (Figure 9.3).






Figure 9.3: Arterial and venous pressure at each cardiac output, from the lecture’s table. With the heart stopped (CO 0), both pressures equal Pms, 7 mm Hg. At 5 L/min, arterial pressure is 102 and venous pressure 2. Course figure.



That pressure is the mean systemic filling pressure, Pms: the pressure throughout the systemic circulation when cardiac output is zero. The slides also call it Pmc (mean circulatory pressure) or MCFP (mean circulatory filling pressure). Strictly, those terms include the pulmonary circulation and Pms refers to the systemic circulation, but the lecture treats them as the same. This book uses Pms.
Why does arterial pressure fall 95 mm Hg while venous pressure rises only 5? The same volume of blood leaves the arteries and enters the veins, and by C = ΔV/ΔP the pressure change for that volume is ΔV/C. The veins are about 20 times as compliant, so their pressure changes about one twentieth as much.
Pms cannot be measured in a routine clinical setting. A CVP line measures right atrial pressure, not Pms.

9.7.1 Stressed and unstressed volume
What sets Pms? Pour blood into an empty, floppy vein, and at first the pressure stays near zero. The blood just rounds out the vessel. Only once the vessel is full does more blood stretch the wall, and then pressure rises with each added milliliter (Figure 9.4).

Unstressed volume is the volume needed to round out the vessels before any pressure is generated.
Stressed volume is everything above that. It stretches the walls, and the walls’ recoil makes the pressure.

These terms describe how blood volume relates to the capacity of the vessels. They are not two separate pools of blood. Applying C = ΔV/ΔP to the whole systemic circulation, with no flow:
\[P_{ms} \approx \frac{\text{stressed volume}}{\text{compliance}}\]






Figure 9.4: Stressed and unstressed volume for the systemic circulation. Venoconstriction shrinks the unstressed volume, so the same volume has more stressed volume and a higher Pms. Brackets mark the unstressed (3.6 L) and stressed (1.4 L) volumes at normal venous tone. Illustrative values (5 L in the systemic circulation, compliance 0.2 L/mm Hg). Course figure.



So Pms depends on the volume of blood and on the capacity and compliance of the vessels, chiefly the veins:

↑ blood volume (transfusion, fluid retention by the kidneys) → ↑ stressed volume → ↑ Pms.
↓ blood volume (hemorrhage) → ↓ stressed volume → ↓ Pms.
Venoconstriction → smaller unstressed volume → ↑ stressed volume at the same total volume → ↑ Pms.
Venodilation does the reverse.

The lecture’s analogy is a tube of toothpaste. Squeezing the tube, or rolling it up from the bottom, raises the pressure inside without adding any toothpaste. Sympathetic venoconstriction can mobilize about 30% of the venous volume this way.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle
9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling

title: 9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling
text:
9.8 The vascular function curve
Now restart the heart and turn it up a step at a time. Each liter per minute of cardiac output moves blood from the veins into the arteries, so venous pressure falls 1 mm Hg and arterial pressure rises 19. At 5 L/min, venous pressure is 2 mm Hg and arterial pressure 102. Plotting the pressure at the right atrium against the flow gives the vascular function curve, also called the venous return curve.
Flow back to the heart obeys Ohm’s law. The upstream pressure is Pms, the downstream pressure is Pra, and the resistance is the resistance to venous return (RVR):
\[\text{VR} = \frac{P_{ms} - P_{ra}}{\text{RVR}}\]
In the lecture’s numbers, RVR = (7 − 2)/5 = 1 mm Hg·min/L. RVR is not the same as SVR. SVR is the resistance between the aorta and the right atrium. RVR is the effective resistance between the upstream pressure Pms and the right atrium, and most of it lies in the veins.
Figure 9.5 A draws the curve the way the course does, with Pra on the x-axis and venous return on the y-axis.

The x-intercept is Pms. When Pra equals Pms, there is no pressure gradient and venous return is zero.
Lower Pra means more venous return. Pra is the back pressure. On the straight part of the curve, the slope is −1/RVR.
The curve flattens at low Pra. When Pra falls below about 0, the large veins collapse where they enter the chest, so lowering Pra further adds no flow.







Figure 9.5: Vascular function curves, drawn as the course draws them. (A) Raising Pms shifts the curve right; lowering it shifts it left. RVR is unchanged, so the curves are parallel. (B) Changing RVR changes the slope around the same Pms. Course figure.



Changing Pms shifts the curve (panel A). Transfusion or venoconstriction raises Pms and shifts the curve to the right: more venous return at every Pra. Hemorrhage or venodilation shifts it to the left. In the lecture’s words, the regulation of venomotor tone, and thus Pms, is one of the principal mechanisms by which cardiac output is controlled.
Changing RVR changes the slope (panel B). A higher RVR flattens the curve around the same Pms; a lower RVR steepens it. Panel B holds Pms fixed to isolate the slope. In this course, slope changes are small next to changes in Pms and can be ignored until exercise. In exercise, metabolic dilation of the arterioles in the working muscles lowers RVR and steepens the curve, and the course also treats the rhythmic squeeze of the skeletal muscle pump, working with the venous valves, as lowering the effective RVR (Cardiovascular Adaptation to Exercise).






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The lecture’s first vascular function curves (from Berne and Levy’s Physiology) put central venous pressure on the y-axis and cardiac output on the x-axis. Later slides, and this book, flip them so Pra is on the x-axis and the curve can share axes with the cardiac function curve. The flip changes how a slope change looks: the slide’s “clockwise rotation” with more resistance is, with Pra on the x-axis, a flatter curve around Pms. Think “flatter” and “steeper,” not clockwise and counterclockwise.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle
9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling

title: 9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling
text:
9.9 The cardiac function curve
The cardiac function curve plots cardiac output against Pra (slide 45 labels it the ventricular function curve). It is the Frank-Starling relationship for the whole heart. More filling pressure fills the ventricle to a larger end-diastolic volume, the stretched muscle contracts with more force, and stroke volume and cardiac output rise. At high filling pressures, more filling adds less and less, and the curve flattens.
A change in filling moves the heart along the curve. A change in pump performance shifts the curve:

Up: more contractility; a faster heart rate, up to a point.
Down: less contractility; more afterload; a heart rate so fast that filling time is cut short.

Pra is used here as the filling pressure. It is not the same as end-diastolic volume. How much volume a given pressure produces depends on the ventricle’s filling curve (the EDPVR in The Cardiac Pump).






WarningA common mistake



Moving up a cardiac function curve does not change contractility. Extra stretch raises the force of contraction; that is the Frank-Starling mechanism. A change in contractility moves the heart to a different cardiac function curve.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle
9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling

title: 9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling
text:
9.10 Ventricular-vascular coupling: the operating point
Now put both curves on the same axes (Figure 9.6). The cardiac function curve says how much the heart will pump at each Pra. The vascular function curve says how much will return at each Pra. At steady state the two flows must match, because blood cannot pile up forever in one part of a closed circuit:
\[\text{CO} = \text{VR}\]
The only Pra where both are true is where the curves cross. That intersection is the operating point, and its coordinates are the steady-state cardiac output and Pra. The slides call it the equilibrium point.
The same Pra plays opposite roles on the two curves: a higher Pra helps the heart fill but opposes venous return. If Pra rose above the operating point for a moment, the heart would pump out more than came back, and Pra would fall back; below it, the reverse. A stronger pump lowers its own filling pressure.






Figure 9.6: Four changes on the cardiac and vascular function curves, following the lecture. Faint lines, normal curves; open circle, normal operating point; filled circle, new operating point. (A) Transfusion. (B) Reduced contractility. (C) Hemorrhage. (D) Hemorrhage with compensation: from the hemorrhage point (2), venoconstriction raises Pms part of the way back and a faster, stronger heart raises the cardiac function curve, so CO is nearly restored at a low Pra. Course figure.











Initial change
Curve that moves
New operating point




Transfusion or more venous tone
Vascular curve shifts right (Pms up)
CO up, Pra up


Hemorrhage or venodilation
Vascular curve shifts left (Pms down)
CO down, Pra down


More contractility
Cardiac curve shifts up
CO up, Pra down


Less contractility, or more afterload
Cardiac curve shifts down
CO down, Pra up



These predictions assume the other curve does not change, RVR is constant, and the heart is on the rising part of its curve.
The Circulation Lab plots the cardiac function and venous return curves while a model circulation runs [2]. Remove blood or infuse volume and watch the operating point move.
Hemorrhage shows the whole sequence. Blood loss lowers Pms, and CO falls (panel C). The baroreflex then responds. Sympathetic venoconstriction recruits unstressed volume into stressed volume and raises Pms part of the way back, while a faster, stronger heart raises the cardiac function curve (panel D). Arteriolar constriction raises SVR and helps hold MAP. A young person with these reflexes intact can lose a good deal of blood before the pressure falls. Pms acts on filling through venous return and filling pressure; the ventricle does not equilibrate with Pms (The Cardiac Pump; course errata entry 16). The integration chapter follows hemorrhage, heart failure and sepsis in detail (Cardiovascular Integration and Adaptation).

9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling

title: 9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling
text:
9.11 Finding the cause
Locating the new operating point is half the problem. The other half is saying why it moved. A common error is to find the new intersection correctly and then name the wrong change as its cause. The way the operating point moves tells you which curve moved (Figure 9.7):

If only the vascular function curve moves, the new point lies on the old cardiac function curve. The point slides along the cardiac curve, so CO and Pra move in the same direction: both up when Pms rises, both down when it falls.
If only the cardiac function curve moves, the new point lies on the old vascular function curve. The point slides along the vascular curve, so CO and Pra move in opposite directions: CO up and Pra down for a stronger heart, CO down and Pra up for a weaker one.







Figure 9.7: Reading the cause from the movement of the operating point. (A) A shifted vascular function curve (dashed) moves the point along the unchanged cardiac function curve (thick). (B) A shifted cardiac function curve (dashed) moves it along the unchanged vascular function curve (thick). Course figure.









WarningA common mistake



“The operating point moved right” does not mean “Pms rose.” A weaker heart also moves the operating point to a higher Pra, with Pms unchanged. Before you name a cause, ask which curve the new point still sits on.


Work any problem in this order:

Identify the initial disturbance. Is it in the heart (contractility, rate, afterload) or in the vessels (blood volume, venous tone, RVR)?
Shift that curve, and only that curve, and find the new intersection.
Add the compensation, which usually moves the other curve. A failing heart triggers venoconstriction and fluid retention that raise Pms; a hemorrhage triggers sympathetic stimulation of the heart.
Think through the consequences upstream and downstream: arterial pressure (from CO and SVR) and where blood is accumulating.

When both curves move, Pra may be clear while CO depends on the sizes of the two changes. More venous tone with less contractility raises Pra for both reasons, but one raises CO and the other lowers it.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle
9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling

title: 9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling
text:
9.12 Two pumps in series
The single-pump model treats the heart and lungs as one pump filled from the right atrium. The real circulation has two pumps in series, and at steady state their outputs must be equal. The lecture’s rule applies: when something changes, think through what happens upstream and downstream.
An acute fall in left ventricular contractility, as with ischemia. Left ventricular output falls while the right ventricle keeps pumping, so blood accumulates in the lungs. Left atrial pressure (Pla) rises, which restores part of the left ventricle’s output by Frank-Starling. Less venous return reaches the right heart, so Pra falls, and the higher pulmonary pressures raise the right ventricle’s afterload. At the new steady state, both ventricles pump the same, reduced cardiac output, with a higher pulmonary venous pressure. The slide traces what follows: ↓ CO → ↑ LVEDP → ↑ Ppv → ↑ Pcapillary → ↑ hydrostatic pressure, which drives filtration into the lung (the Starling forces in Microcirculation and Local Control) and can cause pulmonary edema and respiratory failure (Pulmonary Circulation).






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The two-pump slide writes “↑ PLA → ↑ PPV → ↑ PPA → ↑ PVR (↑ afterload).” Pulmonary artery pressure rises because the pressure downstream of the lungs has risen, so the right ventricle faces a higher afterload. Pulmonary vascular resistance need not change. PVR = (mPAP − PCWP)/CO, where the wedge pressure (PCWP) estimates Pla, and here both pressures rise together. Read the last step as “↑ right ventricular afterload.”


An acute fall in right ventricular output, as with tension pneumothorax. Air trapped under pressure raises intrathoracic pressure, so Pra rises even though the right heart is filling poorly. The higher Pra cuts venous return and right ventricular output. Less blood reaches the left heart, so left ventricular output falls too, though the left ventricle is normal.

title: 9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling
section: 9.13 A puzzle: orthostatic hypotension with a normal heart
text:
9.13 A puzzle: orthostatic hypotension with a normal heart
Some neurologic disorders, Parkinson’s disease among them, can cause orthostatic hypotension: blood pressure falls on standing, and the person may faint. Most of these patients have normal cardiac function. How?
Standing pools blood in the veins of the legs and abdomen. Normally the baroreflex, covered in the next chapter (ANS and Extrinsic Control), answers within seconds with sympathetic venoconstriction, which recruits that pooled blood back into the stressed volume, along with arteriolar constriction and a faster heart. If the autonomic nerves that control venomotor tone are damaged, the veins cannot constrict. The stressed volume available to drive venous return falls, the vascular function curve shifts left, and venous return, stroke volume, cardiac output and arterial pressure all fall. The heart is fine. The vessels have lost their control.






NoteBackground: why morphine can unmask blood loss





A hidden slide in the lecture asks why a young patient who has lost blood, with a normal blood pressure, may become hypotensive after a dose of morphine. The answer is the compensation in Figure 9.6 D. Young people with strong reflexes can hold Pms near normal after substantial blood loss by sympathetic venoconstriction. Morphine dilates the veins, which removes part of that compensation, so Pms, venous return and pressure fall.

9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling

title: 9  Control of Cardiac Output and Ventricular-Vascular Coupling
text:
9.14 Check your understanding

A 75-year-old has a blood pressure of 160/70 mm Hg. A 25-year-old with the same stroke volume has 120/80. What explains the difference in pulse pressure?


Answer

Pulse pressure is about SV divided by arterial compliance. The older aorta is stiffer, so the same stroke volume produces a larger rise in pressure, and the faster pulse wave returns the reflected wave during systole. Pulse pressure is 90 mm Hg instead of 40.

Two patients both have a MAP of 60 mm Hg. One has a pressure of 72/54, the other 90/45. Which is more likely to have a low cardiac output, and why?


Answer

The patient at 72/54 has a narrow pulse pressure (18 mm Hg), which suggests a small stroke volume and a low cardiac output, with SVR raised to compensate, as after hemorrhage. The patient at 90/45 has a wide pulse pressure (45 mm Hg): low SVR lets the arteries run off fast in diastole, and a large stroke volume, as in high-output sepsis. Same MAP, different cardiac outputs: CO ≠ BP.

The heart stops. Arterial pressure falls from 102 to 7 mm Hg while venous pressure rises from 2 to 7 mm Hg. Why are the changes so unequal, and what is the 7 called?


Answer

The same volume of blood leaves the arteries and enters the veins. The pressure change for a given volume is ΔV/C, and the veins are about 20 times as compliant as the arteries, so their pressure changes about one twentieth as much. The common pressure, with no flow, is the mean systemic filling pressure, Pms.

Sympathetic stimulation constricts the veins with no change in blood volume. Which curve moves, which way, and what happens to CO and Pra?


Answer

Venoconstriction shrinks the unstressed volume, so stressed volume and Pms rise. The vascular function curve shifts right. The new operating point lies on the unchanged cardiac function curve, up and to the right: CO rises and Pra rises. (In real life sympathetic stimulation also raises the cardiac function curve, which pulls Pra back down.)

After an intervention, a patient’s CO falls from 5 to 3.6 L/min and Pra rises from 2 to 3.4 mm Hg. A classmate says Pms must have risen, because the operating point moved to the right. What actually changed?


Answer

CO and Pra moved in opposite directions, so the operating point slid along the vascular function curve, and the vascular curve did not move. The cardiac function curve shifted down: contractility fell, or afterload rose. A rise in Pms would have raised both CO and Pra.

A patient’s left ventricle suddenly loses much of its contractility. Predict what happens to left atrial pressure, right atrial pressure, and the outputs of the two ventricles once a new steady state is reached.


Answer

Left atrial pressure rises as blood accumulates in the lungs, which restores some left ventricular output by Frank-Starling. Right atrial pressure falls, because less blood returns to the right heart. At the new steady state, both ventricles pump the same, reduced output.

title: 10  ANS and Extrinsic Control
text:
10.1 The control hierarchy
Every tissue controls its own arterioles. The Microcirculation and Local Control chapter showed how myogenic, metabolic and endothelial mechanisms match local blood flow to local need, minute to minute. Local control cannot defend the whole circulation, though. If every bed dilated at once, arterial pressure would fall and the brain and heart would lose their perfusion pressure. The circulation is a set of parallel beds fed by one pump, so something has to set cardiac output, hold mean arterial pressure (MAP) steady, and decide which beds get the cardiac output when there is not enough to go around. That is the job of the autonomic nervous system (ANS), with help from hormones and other organ systems. The Control of Cardiac Output chapter showed what moves cardiac output: Pms, contractility, heart rate and SVR. This chapter shows how the nerves move them. It covers the efferent side first (what the nerves do to the heart and vessels), then the afferent side (the sensors and the reflexes they drive), then a preview of extrinsic control.
Higher centers and the medulla together shape autonomic output to the circulation (Figure 10.1).
The hypothalamus is the coordinator. It sits below the thalamus, above the pituitary, and takes input from the retina, cortex, striatum, amygdala, hippocampus and spinal cord. It sets broad autonomic patterns and links cardiovascular responses to temperature control and endocrine output. It is a relay that sets the pattern, not the controller that adjusts each beat.
The limbic system provides context. The amygdala, hippocampus and cingulate cortex supply the emotional reasons to act: fear, anxiety, anticipation. That is why your heart rate rises before an exam starts, with no change in posture or blood volume.
The medullary cardiorespiratory center is the integrator. (The slide figures label it the medullary cardiovascular control center.) Clusters of neurons in the medulla (and lower pons) receive the afferent signals from the baroreceptors and chemoreceptors, combine them with input from higher centers, and set sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow in real time. The course names these nuclei:
The wiring explains the direction of the baroreflex. The NTS does not inhibit the RVLM directly. It excites the CVLM, and the CVLM inhibits the RVLM. So when the NTS gets more afferent traffic, sympathetic outflow falls. At the same time the NTS excites the vagal neurons, so parasympathetic outflow rises.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 10  ANS and Extrinsic Control
text:
Figure 10.1: The control hierarchy. Higher centers set the context and the overall pattern; the medulla integrates the afferent signals and sets sympathetic and vagal outflow moment to moment. Green arrows excite and the red bar inhibits. The NTS excites the CVLM, which inhibits the RVLM, so more afferent input to the NTS means less sympathetic outflow. Course figure.













Nucleus
Role




Nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS)
Receives the afferents in CN IX and CN X. The first stop for baroreceptor and chemoreceptor signals.


Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (DMV)
Parasympathetic (vagal) output. The nucleus ambiguus, in the ventrolateral medulla, sends most of the vagal fibers to the heart.


Rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM)
Tonically active. Drives the sympathetic preganglionic neurons in the spinal cord.


Caudal ventrolateral medulla (CVLM)
Inhibitory. When the NTS excites it, it turns the RVLM down.

title: 10  ANS and Extrinsic Control
text:
10.2 Efferent pathways
Both divisions of the ANS use two neurons in series between the central nervous system and the target. The first, the preganglionic neuron, has its cell body in the brainstem or spinal cord. It synapses in a ganglion on the second, postganglionic neuron, which runs to the target. At every autonomic ganglion, the preganglionic neuron releases acetylcholine (ACh) onto nicotinic receptors. The divisions differ in where the ganglia sit and in what the postganglionic neuron releases (Figure 10.2).






Figure 10.2: Autonomic efferent pathways. Every ganglion uses ACh on nicotinic receptors. Sympathetic postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine (NE), except those to sweat glands, which release ACh. The adrenal medulla has no postganglionic neuron: preganglionic fibers end on chromaffin cells, which release epinephrine into the blood. Course figure.




10.2.1 Sympathetic

Signals from the hypothalamus pass through the medullary center (the RVLM) and down the spinal cord to preganglionic cell bodies in the lateral horn (the intermediolateral column) of the thoracic and upper lumbar cord, T1 to L2.
The preganglionic axons leave the cord with the ventral roots and enter the sympathetic trunk (the chain of ganglia beside the vertebral column). Most synapse in the chain ganglion at the level where they left the cord. Some run up or down the chain first, which is how the head and the pelvis get sympathetic fibers even though no preganglionic neurons sit in the cervical or sacral cord. The preganglionic neurons are short.
The postganglionic neurons have their cell bodies in the chain ganglia (or, for the abdominal organs, in ganglia in front of the aorta) and send long axons to the target tissues, where they release norepinephrine (NE) onto adrenergic receptors (α1, α2, β1, β2).

Sympathetic postganglionic fibers to sweat glands are an exception: they release ACh onto muscarinic receptors (the skin’s circulation is covered in Other Special Circulations). And in the adrenal medulla, preganglionic fibers end directly on chromaffin cells, which act as modified postganglionic neurons and release epinephrine (with a little NE) into the blood. Sympathetic activation is therefore both a nerve signal to specific targets and a hormone signal to every tissue with adrenergic receptors.


10.2.2 Parasympathetic

Signals from the hypothalamus reach preganglionic neurons in the brainstem nuclei and the sacral cord (the craniosacral outflow).
The preganglionic axons are long. They run all the way to ganglia in or next to the target organ. About 75% of all parasympathetic outflow travels in the vagus nerve (CN X).
The postganglionic neurons are short. They release ACh onto muscarinic receptors on the target.










Sympathetic

Ganglia

The receptors are G protein-coupled (Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells explains what that means). The table of receptors, G proteins and second messengers (Gs and cAMP, Gi, Gq and IP3) is in Smooth Muscle. This chapter uses them without the detail.

title: 10  ANS and Extrinsic Control
text:
10.3 Autonomic control of the heart
Sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers reach the heart through the cardiac plexus, a web of nerves at the base of the heart. Sympathetic preganglionic neurons in the upper thoracic cord synapse in the cervical and upper thoracic chain ganglia (including the stellate ganglion), and the postganglionic fibers run in the cardiac nerves to the plexus and on to the SA node, the AV node and the working myocytes of the atria and ventricles. Vagal preganglionic fibers run to the plexus and synapse on postganglionic neurons on the heart itself, mostly near the SA and AV nodes and in the atria.
The nerves act on:

the SA node, which sets heart rate;
the AV node, which sets how fast the impulse passes from atria to ventricles;
the myocytes, where sympathetic input sets contractility.


10.3.1 Heart rate
The SA node fires slow-response action potentials. Phase 4 is a slow depolarization driven mostly by the funny current (If, a mixed Na+/K+ cation current through HCN channels, carried mainly by inward Na+ at diastolic potentials) and then by T-type and L-type Ca2+ current. When the membrane reaches threshold, the L-type Ca2+ current produces the upstroke. The time it takes to get from the most negative potential to threshold sets the rate. The EKG I: Ionic Basis chapter, later in the block, covers the ionic basis in full.
Sympathetic (β1). NE binds β1 receptors on SA node cells. Gs activates adenylyl cyclase and cAMP rises. cAMP increases If and the Ca2+ currents, so phase 4 is steeper and the cell reaches threshold sooner. The rate rises.
Parasympathetic (M2). ACh from vagal fibers binds M2 receptors and has two effects at the same time:

It opens K+ channels. K+ conductance rises, the membrane moves toward EK, and each cycle starts from a more negative potential.
Through Gi, it lowers cAMP. Less cAMP means less If, so the phase 4 slope flattens.

Both effects lengthen the time to threshold, and both slow the heart. The EKG I chapter draws both effects on the SA node action potential.






NoteIf you are comparing with the notes



The peer-educator notes write the vagal effect as one chain: “ACh → muscarinic receptors → ↑ K+ efflux → ↓ cAMP → slower phase 4 slope.” That reads as if K+ efflux causes the fall in cAMP. It does not. The K+ channel effect and the cAMP effect run in parallel from the same receptor (course errata entry 21). The notes also say sympathetic input acts on “the sodium channels” in pacemaker cells. Those are the HCN channels, whose funny current is carried mostly by Na+, not the fast Na+ channels of working myocytes. cAMP also increases the Ca2+ currents.


The AV node. The same receptors act on the AV node, which is also a slow-response tissue. β1 stimulation speeds AV conduction and shortens the PR interval; M2 stimulation slows it and lengthens the PR interval. Strong vagal activity can block AV conduction for a beat or more. The AV node changes conduction, not rate.






WarningA common mistake



In the SA and AV nodes the upstroke is carried by L-type Ca2+ current, not by fast Na+ current. So AV conduction depends on L-type Ca2+ channels: β1 stimulation, which increases L-type current, speeds it, and an L-type Ca2+ channel blocker slows it and lengthens the PR interval. A Na+ channel blocker does not slow the heart rate. It slows the upstroke of fast-response action potentials in atrial and ventricular muscle and in the Purkinje fibers, so it slows conduction there and widens the QRS.




10.3.2 Vagal tone dominates at rest
Both divisions are active all the time, but at rest the vagus wins. With no autonomic input at all, the SA node fires at its intrinsic rate, about 100/min. The normal resting sinus rate, 60 to 100/min and often 60 to 70 in a resting adult, sits below that because vagal tone holds it down.
The lecture shows this with a transplanted heart and with drugs. In a person with a heart transplant, the autonomic nerves to the heart are cut and do not reconnect, so the resting rate is near the intrinsic rate, about 100/min. And in healthy subjects, blocking each division with a drug shows how much each contributes (Figure 10.3). Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and removes vagal tone: the rate jumps from about 63 to about 117/min. Propranolol blocks β receptors and removes sympathetic tone: the rate falls only from about 61 to about 51/min. With both blocked, in either order, the rate settles near 100/min.






Figure 10.3: Heart rate in healthy nonathletes after autonomic blockade. Atropine (muscarinic block) raises the rate far more than propranolol (β block) lowers it, so vagal tone dominates at rest. With both blocked, the rate is the intrinsic rate of the SA node. Values read from the graph of Katona, McLean, Dighton and Guz [1], as shown in the 2026 lecture.





10.3.3 Contractility
Contractility is the force the heart muscle can develop at a given preload and afterload, which the course measures as the slope of the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship. Heart rate and relaxation are separate properties (course errata entry 2). Sympathetic stimulation raises contractility; this is the main reason sympathetic activity increases stroke volume at a given end-diastolic volume.
NE (or circulating epinephrine) binds β1 receptors on ventricular myocytes. Gs raises cAMP, and cAMP activates protein kinase A (PKA), which phosphorylates, among other proteins (Figure 10.4 A):

L-type Ca2+ channels. More Ca2+ enters during the plateau, which triggers more Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR).
Phospholamban. Unphosphorylated phospholamban holds back SERCA, the pump that returns Ca2+ to the SR. Phosphorylation removes the brake. SERCA takes up Ca2+ faster, so the SR holds more Ca2+ to release on the next beat (stronger contraction) and the cytosol clears faster (faster relaxation, which helps preserve filling time at high heart rates).

The details of excitation-contraction coupling and phospholamban are in Cardiac Muscle.
ACh at M2 receptors does the reverse through Gi: cAMP falls, phospholamban is less phosphorylated, SERCA takes up less Ca2+, and force falls. Vagal fibers go mostly to the nodes and the atria, so vagal effects on force are strongest in the atria. There, ACh also opens the same K+ channels it opens in the SA node, which shortens the action potential and lets in less Ca2+. In the ventricles, the main thing ACh does is blunt the effect of whatever sympathetic stimulation is present.






Figure 10.4: Receptor signaling. (A) In the heart, β1 receptors raise cAMP and M2 receptors lower it; M2 receptors also open K+ channels in the SA node and atria. (B) In vascular smooth muscle, α1 receptors raise intracellular Ca2+ through IP3 and cause constriction; β2 receptors raise cAMP, which inhibits myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) and causes relaxation. Course figure.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 10  ANS and Extrinsic Control
text:
10.4 Autonomic control of the vessels
Sympathetic nerves supply the smooth muscle of nearly all small arteries, arterioles and veins, and they are tonically active. Parasympathetic nerves supply only a few vessels (in the genitalia and the salivary glands), so the vascular half of autonomic control is almost entirely sympathetic. The capillaries have no smooth muscle and no nerves.
Sympathetic tone acts on veins and arterioles with different results:

Veins (venous tone). Venoconstriction shrinks the unstressed volume of the veins and moves blood into the stressed volume. Stressed volume rises, so Pms (mean systemic filling pressure) rises, venous return rises, and preload rises. About 30% of venous volume can be mobilized this way. The Control of Cardiac Output chapter explained stressed volume and Pms.
Arterioles (arterial tone). Arteriolar constriction raises SVR, which raises MAP and afterload. Constricting some beds while others stay open also redistributes cardiac output.


10.4.1 The receptor decides the response
“Sympathetic” does not mean “constriction.” What NE or epinephrine does to a vessel depends on which receptor its smooth muscle carries (Figure 10.4 B):

α1 receptors couple to Gq. Phospholipase C makes IP3, IP3 releases Ca2+ from the SR, Ca2+-calmodulin activates MLCK, and the muscle contracts. α1 is the predominant receptor in most of the peripheral circulation, on arterioles and veins alike.
β2 receptors couple to Gs. cAMP rises and inhibits MLCK, and the muscle relaxes. β2 receptors are plentiful on skeletal muscle arterioles.

The mechanism of smooth muscle contraction, and why MLCK is the switch, is in Smooth Muscle.
The two catecholamines do not reach these receptors equally. NE released from sympathetic nerves acts strongly on α1 and β1 receptors and weakly on β2. So sympathetic nerve activity constricts skeletal muscle arterioles, as it does arterioles elsewhere. Epinephrine from the adrenal medulla reaches every vessel through the blood and acts on β2 receptors as well. At the concentrations of a “fight or flight” response, it dilates skeletal muscle arterioles through β2 while it constricts the skin, gut and kidney through α1. That shift of flow toward muscle is the receptor distribution at work. During exercise, metabolic vasodilators add to it (Other Special Circulations).






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The vascular-control slides show “Epinephrine / Norepinephrine” acting on α1 and β2 receptors and say “B2 present in muscle vasculature => Dilation.” The peer-educator notes go further and list “skeletal muscle vasodilation (β2)” as an effect of sympathetic nerves, and say NE “will cause dilation” in muscle. The β2 dilation in muscle comes from circulating epinephrine. Neural NE has little effect on β2 receptors, so sympathetic nerve stimulation constricts muscle arterioles through α1. Both versions agree that receptors set the response; the difference is which catecholamine reaches the β2 receptors.
The same slides show parasympathetic “(pelvic) M2 (vasodilation)” with “(Gut).” Parasympathetic vasodilation is limited to a few beds, such as the genitalia, and ACh dilates vessels by acting on muscarinic receptors on endothelial cells, which release nitric oxide. The gut circulation is under sympathetic, not parasympathetic, control (course errata entry 14; Other Special Circulations).
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 10  ANS and Extrinsic Control
text:
10.5 Putting the efferent side together
The lecture summarizes autonomic control with the arterial version of Ohm’s law, CO = (MAP − CVP)/SVR, rearranged with CVP left out and expanded:
\[\text{MAP} \approx \text{CO} \times \text{SVR} = (\text{HR} \times \text{SV}) \times \text{SVR} = \big(\text{HR} \times (\text{EDV} - \text{ESV})\big) \times \text{SVR}\]
Each term has an autonomic handle. Sympathetic and vagal input set HR. Venous return and the compliance of the ventricle set EDV, and venous tone sets venous return. Contractility sets how far the ventricle empties, ESV. Arteriolar tone sets SVR. Sympathetic activation raises HR, EDV and SVR and lowers ESV. Vagal activation lowers HR. In the baroreflex, vagal activation and sympathetic withdrawal happen together, so the changes all reverse.






WarningA common mistake



MAP ≈ CO × SVR drops CVP. That is harmless when CVP is a few mm Hg, but when CVP is high, as in heart failure or tamponade, use SVR = (MAP − CVP)/CO, as in Peripheral Circulation and Hemodynamics.


The same summary can be drawn on the cardiac and vascular function curves (Figure 10.5). Sympathetic stimulation of the heart (rate and contractility) shifts the cardiac function curve up. Venoconstriction raises Pms and shifts the vascular function curve to the right. The new operating point has a higher cardiac output, while right atrial pressure (Pra) barely changes. These are the curves from the Control of Cardiac Output chapter.






Figure 10.5: Sympathetic activation on the cardiac and vascular function curves. β1 stimulation shifts the cardiac function curve up; venoconstriction raises Pms and shifts the vascular function curve right. Open circle, operating point before; filled circle, after. Course figure. The lecture’s summary slide reuses the hemorrhage-with-compensation graph from the Control of Cardiac Output lecture.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 10  ANS and Extrinsic Control
text:
10.6 Afferents and reflexes: the baroreceptors
The efferent nerves need information. The main sensors for the circulation are the arterial baroreceptors: stretch-sensitive nerve endings in the walls of the carotid sinus (a slight bulge where the internal carotid artery begins) and the aortic arch. Their afferent fibers run in the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) from the carotid sinus and in the vagus nerve (CN X) from the aortic arch, and both end in the NTS.
The receptors sense stretch of the arterial wall, so they report pressure. When MAP rises, the wall stretches more, the nerve endings depolarize more, and their firing rate rises. When MAP falls, firing falls.

10.6.1 The baroreceptor reflex
The reflex is a negative feedback loop that holds MAP near its set point (Figure 10.6). Follow a rise in pressure:

MAP rises and the carotid sinus and aortic arch stretch.
Baroreceptor firing rises in CN IX and CN X.
The NTS excites the CVLM, which inhibits the RVLM, so sympathetic outflow falls. The NTS also excites the vagal neurons, so vagal outflow rises.
Heart rate falls (more vagal, less sympathetic), contractility falls, arterioles dilate (SVR falls), and veins dilate (stressed volume and Pms fall, so venous return falls).
CO and SVR fall, and MAP comes back down.

A fall in pressure runs the loop the other way: less firing, less vagal and more sympathetic outflow, a faster and stronger heart, venoconstriction and arteriolar constriction, and MAP back up.






Figure 10.6: The baroreceptor reflex for a rise in MAP. Afferents in CN IX and CN X reach the NTS, which inhibits sympathetic outflow (through the CVLM and RVLM) and increases vagal outflow. The effects lower MAP back toward its set point. Course figure, after the reflex chart in Boron and Boulpaep [2], as used in the 2026 lecture.



Standing up is the everyday test. Gravity pools blood in the leg veins, venous return falls, stroke volume and CO fall, and MAP starts to drop. Within a few beats the baroreceptors fire less, and the reflex raises heart rate and contractility, constricts the veins (which pushes blood back toward the heart) and constricts the arterioles. MAP is restored before you notice. When the efferent side fails, as in some neurologic disorders that damage autonomic nerves, standing drops the pressure and can cause fainting: orthostatic hypotension, the puzzle at the end of the Control of Cardiac Output chapter.
The baroreflex is fast and strong, but it is a short-term controller. The kidneys, previewed at the end of the lecture, set blood volume over days. In hemorrhage and heart failure, the baroreflex is what produces the compensation you see in the curves (Cardiovascular Integration and Adaptation).
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 10  ANS and Extrinsic Control
text:
10.7 Afferents and reflexes: the chemoreceptors
Chemoreceptors sense the chemistry of blood and brain fluid. Their main job is to control breathing (Control of Ventilation), but they also act on the heart and vessels.

Central chemoreceptors, near the surface of the medulla, detect CO2 and pH. CO2 crosses into the brain fluid and lowers its pH.
Peripheral chemoreceptors sit next to the baroreceptors. The carotid bodies, at the carotid bifurcation, detect O2, CO2 and pH and signal through CN IX. The aortic bodies, on the aortic arch, detect O2 and CO2 and signal through CN X.


10.7.1 Two responses to the same stimulus
Low PO2, high PCO2 or low pH activates the chemoreceptors, and what happens to the heart depends on whether the person can breathe (Figure 10.7).
The integrated response, breathing freely. In a person who can breathe, the chemoreceptors drive ventilation up: the peripheral chemoreceptors alone respond to low PO2, and both central and peripheral chemoreceptors respond to high PCO2 or low pH. The larger breaths stretch the lungs, and the extra ventilation lowers PCO2. Lung stretch and the lower PCO2 both inhibit the vagal center. The net effect is less vagal outflow and tachycardia, the usual result of hypoxia in daily life. The respiratory response normally overrides the peripheral “hypoxic” bradycardia described next.
The primary response, with ventilation fixed. If breathing cannot increase, the peripheral chemoreceptor reflex shows itself directly. It is unusual in using both divisions at once: it increases vagal outflow to the heart, which causes bradycardia, and increases sympathetic outflow to the vessels, which causes vasoconstriction. The lecture’s thought exercise is a patient who is not breathing during placement of a breathing tube. PO2 falls and PCO2 rises with no rise in ventilation, and the heart slows, sometimes sharply.






Figure 10.7: The chemoreceptor reflex. (A) When breathing is free, ventilation rises (low PO2 acts through the peripheral chemoreceptors; high PCO2 and low pH act through both), and lung stretch and the lower PCO2 inhibit the vagal center, so the heart speeds up. (B) With ventilation held fixed, the peripheral chemoreceptors increase vagal outflow to the heart (bradycardia) and sympathetic outflow to the vessels (vasoconstriction). Course figure, after the reflex charts in Boron and Boulpaep [2], as used in the 2026 lecture.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 10  ANS and Extrinsic Control
text:
10.8 Extrinsic control: a preview
The lecture closes with a preview of the other organ systems that act on the circulation. Each gets its own lectures later.

The lungs and chest. Each breath changes intrathoracic pressure. Inspiration lowers the pressure around the right atrium and the great veins, which draws blood toward the heart; positive pressure in the chest does the reverse.
The kidneys. They set blood volume, and so Pms, by controlling salt and water excretion. They also release renin, which leads to angiotensin II.
Hormones. Epinephrine from the adrenal medulla acts on β1 receptors in the heart and β2 receptors in muscle vessels, as above. Angiotensin II and vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) constrict vessels and help the kidneys retain volume. Thyroid hormone raises heart rate and contractility.
Temperature. The hypothalamus controls skin blood flow through sympathetic nerves to the skin’s vessels and sweat glands.
Emotion and behavior. Limbic and hypothalamic signals change the baseline output of the medulla.
Exercise. Sympathetic activation and local metabolic vasodilation act together (Cardiovascular Adaptation to Exercise).
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 10  ANS and Extrinsic Control
text:
10.9 Check your understanding

A patient with a transplanted heart has a resting heart rate of 98/min. Why is it higher than yours, and what does that tell you about the autonomic balance at rest in a normal heart?


Answer

The transplanted heart has no autonomic nerves, so it beats at the intrinsic rate of the SA node, about 100/min. A normal resting sinus rate, often 60 to 70/min in a resting adult, is lower than that, so at rest vagal tone outweighs sympathetic tone and holds the rate down.

ACh at M2 receptors slows the SA node by two separate mechanisms. Name them, and say which part of the action potential each one changes.


Answer

It opens K+ channels, which moves the membrane toward EK, so each cycle starts from a more negative potential. And it lowers cAMP through Gi, which reduces the funny current (If) and flattens the phase 4 slope. Both lengthen the time to threshold. The K+ effect does not cause the cAMP effect; they run in parallel.

A drug blocks α1 receptors and nothing else. Predict the effect on SVR, on Pms, and, before any reflex, on MAP.


Answer

α1 receptors carry most sympathetic constriction of both arterioles and veins. Blocking them dilates the arterioles, so SVR falls, and dilates the veins, so unstressed volume rises, stressed volume falls and Pms falls. With SVR down and venous return down, MAP falls. The baroreflex then raises heart rate through β1 receptors, which the drug does not block.

During a sudden scare, blood flow to the leg muscles rises while blood flow to the skin falls. Both beds receive the same sympathetic signal. Explain the difference.


Answer

The adrenal medulla releases epinephrine into the blood. Skeletal muscle arterioles have many β2 receptors, and epinephrine acting on them raises cAMP, inhibits MLCK and dilates the vessels. Skin arterioles have mainly α1 receptors, so epinephrine and neural NE constrict them. Neural NE alone would constrict both beds; the dilation in muscle comes from circulating epinephrine.

A drug constricts arterioles and veins through α1 receptors and has no direct action on the heart. MAP rises within a minute. Trace the reflex. Why does heart rate fall, and why does MAP come back down only part of the way?


Answer

The higher pressure stretches the carotid sinus and aortic arch, and baroreceptor firing rises in CN IX and CN X. The NTS excites the CVLM, which inhibits the RVLM, so sympathetic outflow falls, and the NTS excites the vagal neurons, so vagal outflow rises. At the SA node there is more ACh at M2 receptors and less norepinephrine at β1 receptors: K+ channels open, cAMP falls, phase 4 flattens, and the rate falls. The drug has no action on the heart, so the whole fall in rate comes from the reflex. The vascular arm of the reflex helps less than usual, because withdrawing sympathetic tone cannot relax vessels whose α1 receptors the drug is still activating. Most of the correction comes from the slower, weaker heart, and MAP stays above where it started.

A sedated patient stops breathing for two minutes. PO2 falls and PCO2 rises. Does the heart rate rise or fall, and why is this different from what happens at high altitude?


Answer

It falls. With ventilation fixed at zero, the peripheral chemoreceptor reflex acts alone: it increases vagal outflow to the heart (bradycardia) and sympathetic outflow to the vessels (vasoconstriction). At altitude the person can breathe. Low PO2 drives ventilation up through the peripheral chemoreceptors (the central chemoreceptors do not sense O2), and lung stretch and the lower PCO2 inhibit vagal outflow. The net response there is tachycardia.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 10  ANS and Extrinsic Control
text:
10.11 Sources
This chapter follows the 2026 Autonomic and Extrinsic Regulation lecture for MEDC 30504 and draws on the peer-educator notes and the course’s 2018 notes on autonomic regulation, corrected and updated. All figures were drawn for this book.

2. Boron WF, Boulpaep EL. Medical Physiology. 2, updated ed. Saunders Elsevier; 2012.

title: 11  EKG I: Ionic Basis
text:
11.1 Three kinds of action potential
This is the first of three lectures that take you from ion channels to the clinical electrocardiogram. This one stays inside single cells: which channels open, in what order, and what that does to the membrane potential. The next chapter, ECG II: Vectors and Mean Electrical Axis, follows the wave of depolarization through the heart and onto the body surface, and EKG III: Clinical Interpretation reads real tracings. The course titles spell the recording both ways, EKG and ECG. This book writes ECG.
Keep one warning in mind from the start: the ECG is not an action potential. An action potential is the voltage across one cell’s membrane, recorded with an electrode inside the cell. The ECG records small voltage differences between points on the skin, made by the whole heart at once. The shapes look a little alike, and that is where the confusion starts. The second chapter explains how one turns into the other.
The membrane-potential basics (equilibrium potentials, the Nernst equation, voltage-gated channels) are in Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells, and excitation-contraction coupling is in Cardiac Muscle. This chapter uses both.
The lecture starts by setting three action potentials side by side.
The slides call these the fast and slow cardiac APs. The difference in their upstrokes comes from which ion carries the inward current: Na⁺ in fast-response cells, Ca²⁺ in slow-response cells. Most of the rest of the chapter follows from that.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 11  EKG I: Ionic Basis
text:
Skeletal muscle. A fast upstroke and a fast return, all over in 3 to 5 ms. There is no plateau.
Fast-response action potential. Found in atrial and ventricular muscle and in the His-Purkinje conduction system. The upstroke is fast, like skeletal muscle, but the cell then holds near 0 mV for 200 ms or more before it repolarizes. The whole action potential lasts about 250 to 300 ms.
Slow-response action potential. Found in the pacemaker cells of the sinoatrial (SA) and atrioventricular (AV) nodes. The upstroke is slow, there is no true plateau, and the cell never sits at a stable resting potential. Between beats it drifts upward on its own until it fires again.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 11  EKG I: Ionic Basis
text:
11.2 The fast-response action potential
Figure 11.1 shows a ventricular action potential with the main currents underneath it. By convention, inward current (positive charge entering the cell, which depolarizes it) is drawn downward, and outward current upward.






Figure 11.1: A fast-response action potential from a ventricular myocyte, with its phases numbered, and the time course of the main ionic currents below it. Inward currents are drawn downward. The current traces show when each current flows, not how large it is. Adapted from Näbauer and Kääb [1], as used in the 2026 lecture.



Phase 4, rest. Between beats the cell sits at about −90 mV, close to the K⁺ equilibrium potential. It is held there by the inward rectifier K⁺ current, IK1. The membrane at rest is far more permeable to K⁺ than to anything else, so the membrane potential stays near EK. A small inward leak of Na⁺ keeps it slightly less negative than EK itself. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, a pump that moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in for each ATP, restores the gradients that each beat runs down.
Phase 0, rapid depolarization. When a neighboring cell’s current depolarizes the membrane past threshold, about −65 mV, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open. Na⁺ rushes in, driven both by its concentration gradient and by the negative inside of the cell, and the membrane swings from −90 mV to a peak above 0 (about +20 mV) in 1 to 2 ms. This inward Na⁺ current, INa, is the largest current the cell carries, but it is brief. Within a millisecond or two the Na⁺ channels inactivate, and they stay inactivated until the cell repolarizes.
Phase 1, early partial repolarization. The transient outward K⁺ current, Ito, opens with depolarization and inactivates within a few milliseconds. K⁺ leaving the cell pulls the peak back toward 0 mV and makes the small notch at the top of the action potential.
Phase 2, the plateau. For 200 ms or more the membrane potential stays near 0 mV. This is the phase that makes cardiac muscle different. The membrane potential hardly changes because inward and outward currents are almost equal:

Inward: Ca²⁺ through L-type (“long-lasting”) Ca²⁺ channels, ICa,L. These channels respond to the depolarization of phase 0 but open slowly, so their current builds late in phase 0 and carries the plateau. The Ca²⁺ that enters here is the trigger for contraction (see the excitation-contraction coupling section below). L-type channels are the target of the Ca²⁺ channel blockers.
Outward: K⁺ through the delayed rectifier channels. They open slowly during the plateau, so their current starts small and grows.

Phase 3, repolarization. As the L-type channels inactivate and the delayed rectifier K⁺ channels open further, the outward current wins and the membrane repolarizes. There are two delayed rectifier currents, a rapid one (IKr) and a slow one (IKs). Late in phase 3, once the membrane is negative enough, IK1 comes back and finishes the job, pulling the cell back to −90 mV.

NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The slide figures show the resting potential as −96 mV and the peak as +52 mV. The peer-educator notes give −90 mV and +20 mV. These are the same action potential drawn from different sources; any value near EK for rest and somewhat above 0 for the peak is right.
hERG carries IKr and KCNQ1 (also called KvLQT1) carries IKs; inherited defects in either lengthen the QT interval.
The phase 4 notes call the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase an “exchanger” and say excess Ca²⁺ leaves by “an ATP-driven Ca pump.” The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is a pump. Most of the Ca²⁺ that leaves the cell goes out by the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger (NCX), as the calcium-cycling slide shows (28%); the sarcolemmal Ca²⁺ pump moves only a small fraction.



11.2.1 The forces on each ion
The lecture walks through the same phases in terms of the two forces on each ion, its concentration gradient and the electrical gradient. The pattern is easier to remember than the slide animations:

Phase 0. Na⁺ is at high concentration outside and the inside of the cell is negative, so both forces push Na⁺ in. That is why the current is so large and the upstroke so fast.
Phase 1 and 3. K⁺ is at high concentration inside. Whenever the membrane potential is above EK (about −94 mV), the net force on K⁺ is outward, and K⁺ leaves through any open K⁺ channel. That outward current repolarizes the cell.
Phase 2. During the plateau the inside of the cell is slightly positive, so the electrical force pushes both Ca²⁺ and K⁺ outward, though only weakly. Ca²⁺ still enters, because its concentration outside is about ten thousand times its concentration inside, and K⁺ leaves down its own concentration gradient. The two currents roughly cancel.
Phase 4. At rest the membrane sits just positive to EK, where the chemical and electrical forces on K⁺ nearly balance.



11.2.2 Why the inward rectifier matters
IK1 is called an inward rectifier because it passes current much more easily into the cell than out of it. In practice its conductance is large near the resting potential, which clamps the cell close to EK (the net current there is small, because the membrane is already near EK), and very small once the cell is depolarized. During the plateau, IK1 channels pass almost no outward current. If they did, the plateau would need a much larger inward current to hold the membrane near 0, and it would cost the cell far more ion movement. Slow-response cells have almost no IK1, which is one reason they have no stable resting potential.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 11  EKG I: Ionic Basis
section: 11.3 Three differences between cardiac and skeletal muscle
text:
11.3 Three differences between cardiac and skeletal muscle
The lecture names three:

The plateau. A cardiac action potential lasts about 300 ms; a skeletal muscle action potential lasts about 5 ms. The long cardiac action potential means the cell stays refractory through most of its own contraction, so twitches cannot fuse and the heart cannot be tetanized.
Cell-to-cell conduction. Cardiac action potentials spread directly from one cell to the next through gap junctions. Every skeletal muscle fiber needs its own motor neuron and neuromuscular junction.
Automaticity. Some cardiac cells fire on their own, with no outside trigger.

Figure 11.2 shows the first difference.






Figure 11.2: (A) In skeletal muscle each action potential lasts about 5 ms and is over long before the twitch it triggers. Stimuli 25 ms apart each produce a separate, full-sized action potential, and the forces add (tetanus). (B) In cardiac muscle the action potential lasts as long as most of the contraction. The cell is absolutely refractory (tan) until it has repolarized to about −50 mV, then relatively refractory (blue), so a second stimulus during the rise and peak of the contraction produces nothing and twitches cannot fuse. Course figure.









WarningA common mistake



In tetanus, force sums. Action potentials do not. Each skeletal muscle action potential is an all-or-none event that is over in a few milliseconds, and the next one is the same size. What adds up is the Ca²⁺ released and the force of the overlapping twitches. Cardiac muscle cannot do this because its action potential, and so its refractory period, lasts almost as long as the twitch.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 11  EKG I: Ionic Basis
text:
11.4 Excitation-contraction coupling, briefly
The action potential exists to make the heart contract. The steps, which the Cardiac Muscle chapter covers in detail, are:

The action potential spreads down the T-tubules.
L-type Ca²⁺ channels open during the plateau. This Ca²⁺ entry from outside the cell is required. Without extracellular Ca²⁺ the heart does not contract.
The entering Ca²⁺ opens ryanodine receptors (RyR2) in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which release a much larger amount of Ca²⁺: calcium-induced calcium release.
Ca²⁺ binds troponin C, tropomyosin moves off the myosin-binding sites on actin, and the cell contracts (systole).
To relax (diastole), Ca²⁺ is removed from the cytosol. About 70% goes back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum through SERCA2a, about 28% leaves the cell through NCX, and the last 1 to 2% goes through the sarcolemmal Ca²⁺-ATPase and into the mitochondria.

The sarcoplasmic reticulum’s Ca²⁺ triggers contraction. It does not depolarize the cell; Na⁺ entry does that, and the plateau is carried by Ca²⁺ entering across the sarcolemma.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 11  EKG I: Ionic Basis
text:
11.5 The slow-response action potential
Figure 11.3 shows two beats from an SA node cell. Only phases 4, 0 and 3 are labeled. There is no phase 1 notch, and the brief, sloping top of the action potential blends phase 2 into phase 3.






Figure 11.3: Slow-response action potentials from an SA node cell, with the currents that shape them. Phase 4 has no stable resting potential: the membrane depolarizes from about −60 mV toward threshold, about −40 mV, carried first by the funny current (If) and then by T-type and L-type Ca²⁺ currents while outward K⁺ current dies away. Phase 0 is carried by L-type Ca²⁺ current. Current traces are not to scale. Course figure.



Phase 4, spontaneous depolarization. The most negative point, the maximum diastolic potential, is about −60 mV, well above EK. From there the membrane depolarizes on its own. Three things push it up:

The funny current, If. It is “funny” because, unlike most voltage-gated channels, its channels open when the membrane hyperpolarizes at the end of phase 3. The channels are HCN channels, mainly HCN4 in the SA node. If is a mixed cation current, carried mainly by inward Na⁺ at diastolic potentials. It starts the slope of phase 4.
T-type (“transient”) Ca²⁺ channels open at fairly negative potentials, so their current builds in the second half of phase 4 and carries the membrane toward the L-type threshold.
L-type Ca²⁺ channels begin to open at the end of phase 4.

At the same time the outward K⁺ current left over from phase 3 is dying away, which also lets the membrane depolarize.
Phase 0, the upstroke. At about −40 mV enough L-type Ca²⁺ channels open to fire the cell. Slow-response cells have few working Na⁺ channels, and at a membrane potential this positive most of those would be inactivated anyway. So the upstroke is carried by Ca²⁺ through L-type channels, which open more slowly and carry less current than Na⁺ channels. The upstroke is slow and the peak is low, near +10 mV.
Phase 3, repolarization. Delayed rectifier K⁺ current repolarizes the cell, more slowly than in a fast-response cell. Because there is almost no IK1 to clamp the membrane at EK, it never settles at a resting potential, and phase 4 begins again at once.

What the two share: both depend on L-type Ca²⁺ channels (for the plateau in one, the upstroke in the other), and both repolarize through delayed rectifier K⁺ channels.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



One slow-response slide credits phase 0 to T-type Ca²⁺ channels; the next slide, the summary slide and the peer-educator notes credit L-type channels. Phase 0 of the slow-response action potential is carried by L-type Ca²⁺ current. T-type current helps late in phase 4.
The slides and notes say the funny current flows through “HCN1” channels. The main isoform in the SA node is HCN4. The peer-educator notes call If “Na⁺ leak + T-type Ca²⁺.” T-type Ca²⁺ current is a separate current through separate channels.








WarningA common mistake



The AV node is a slow-response tissue, so its action potentials, and conduction through it, depend on L-type Ca²⁺ current, not on Na⁺ current. That is why L-type Ca²⁺ channel blockers slow conduction through the AV node and lengthen the PR interval. Na⁺ channel blockers do not act on the AV node. They act on fast-response tissue: they slow phase 0 in the His-Purkinje system and ventricular muscle and widen the QRS. They do not slow the heart rate, because the SA node does not use Na⁺ channels to fire.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 11  EKG I: Ionic Basis
text:
11.6 Automaticity
Automaticity is the ability of a cell to fire without an outside trigger. Any cell with a phase 4 that drifts up to threshold has it. The cells that do this best sit in a hierarchy:



Pacemaker
Rate when it sets the rhythm (per minute)




SA node
60 to 100 at rest (the normal resting sinus rate)


AV node
40 to 60


Purkinje fibers
about 30 to 40



The SA node normally wins because its phase 4 reaches threshold first. Each sinus beat spreads through the rest of the heart and fires the slower pacemakers before they get there, so they never get to set the rate. They are latent pacemakers. If the SA node fails, or its impulse is blocked, the fastest remaining pacemaker takes over and produces an escape rhythm. The Purkinje fibers are the main site of ventricular escape pacemakers. Ordinary atrial or ventricular muscle can also acquire automaticity when it is diseased, and then it can fire early, producing extra beats. Escape rhythms and early beats are the subject of the third chapter.

11.6.1 How the autonomic nervous system changes the rate
With no autonomic input at all, as in a transplanted heart, the SA node fires at its intrinsic rate, about 100 per minute. At rest it is held below that by parasympathetic (vagal) tone, which is why the normal resting sinus rate is 60 to 100. Sympathetic nerves and circulating catecholamines speed it up. Both act by changing how long phase 4 takes to reach threshold (Figure 11.4).






Figure 11.4: The SA node under sympathetic (top), resting (middle) and parasympathetic (bottom) conditions. Sympathetic input steepens phase 4, so threshold is reached sooner. Parasympathetic input starts each cycle from a more negative potential and flattens phase 4, so threshold is reached later. Rates are illustrative. Course figure.



Sympathetic (β1-adrenergic). Norepinephrine from sympathetic nerves, or epinephrine from the adrenal medulla, binds β1 receptors on SA node cells. The receptor raises cAMP. cAMP binds HCN channels directly and makes them open at less negative potentials, so If is larger and the phase 4 slope steeper. β1 stimulation also increases L-type Ca²⁺ current, which shifts the firing threshold slightly more negative. Threshold comes sooner and the rate rises.
Parasympathetic (M2-muscarinic). Acetylcholine from the vagus binds M2 receptors. It has two separate effects that happen at the same time:

It opens a set of K⁺ channels, so K⁺ conductance rises and the membrane moves toward EK. Each cycle starts from a more negative potential.
It lowers cAMP, which reduces If and flattens the phase 4 slope.

Both lengthen the time to threshold, and the rate falls. The two effects run in parallel from the same receptor. The rise in K⁺ conductance does not cause the fall in cAMP.
The same receptors act on the AV node: sympathetic input speeds conduction through it and parasympathetic input slows it. In the ECG, that shows up in the PR interval. The ANS and Extrinsic Control chapter covers the reflexes that set this autonomic balance.






TipWhat you need from this



β1 steepens and M2 flattens the If slope. M2 also hyperpolarizes the cell through K⁺ channels. Everything that changes the sinus rate in the next two chapters works through the slope of phase 4, the potential it starts from, or the threshold it has to reach.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 11  EKG I: Ionic Basis
text:
11.7 Refractory periods
The action potentials so far have waited politely for the cell to finish before the next stimulus came. What happens when a stimulus arrives early? Figure 11.5 shows the answer.






Figure 11.5: Refractory periods of a fast-response cell. The three stimuli are alternatives shown on one time axis. A stimulus during the absolute refractory period (tan) produces nothing. A stronger-than-normal stimulus during the relative refractory period (blue) produces a small action potential with a slow upstroke (dashed). A normal stimulus at 620 ms, after the cell has fully recovered (whichever trace it followed), produces a normal action potential. Adapted from Boron and Boulpaep [2], as used in the 2026 lecture.



Absolute refractory period (the slides write “absolute (effective)”). From the upstroke until about halfway through phase 3 (the membrane back to about −50 mV), the cell cannot fire another action potential, however strong the stimulus. The reason is the Na⁺ channels. After they open in phase 0 they inactivate, and an inactivated channel cannot open again until the membrane repolarizes and gives it time to recover. Until enough channels have recovered, there is not enough inward current to make a new upstroke.
The absolute refractory period does two things for the heart. It prevents summation of action potentials, and so prevents tetanus. And it guarantees a period of relaxation, which is when the heart fills (diastole).
Separately from any outside stimulus, L-type Ca²⁺ channels can sometimes reopen on their own during the plateau or phase 3 and make a slow upstroke. This can set off an extra beat (the slide lists PACs and PVCs). It is most likely when the action potential is long, which is why a long QT is dangerous (see EKG III).
Relative refractory period. From about mid-phase 3 into early phase 4, the cell can fire, but only if the stimulus is stronger than normal. Some Na⁺ channels have recovered, but not all, so the upstroke is slower and the action potential smaller. Meanwhile the delayed rectifier K⁺ channels are still open and closing over time, and the extra K⁺ conductance opposes depolarization until it fades.
Both cell types have refractory periods, but they come from different channels: Na⁺ channel recovery in fast-response cells, and Ca²⁺ channel recovery in slow-response cells.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 11  EKG I: Ionic Basis
section: 11.8 Upstroke speed, resting potential and conduction
text:
11.8 Upstroke speed, resting potential and conduction
How fast an action potential spreads from cell to cell depends on how fast its upstroke is. A steep phase 0 pushes a large current into the next cell and brings it to threshold quickly. That one rule explains several clinical effects the lecture uses (Figure 11.6).






Figure 11.6: The first 30 ms of a fast-response action potential under three conditions. A Na⁺ channel blocker slows phase 0. So does a less negative resting potential, as with a high extracellular K⁺, because fewer Na⁺ channels are available at rest. Schematic. Course figure.




Na⁺ channel blockers reduce INa. Phase 0 is slower in atrial and ventricular muscle and in the His-Purkinje system, so the wave of depolarization takes longer to cross the ventricles and the QRS complex widens.
L-type Ca²⁺ channel blockers reduce the current that carries phase 0 in the SA and AV nodes. Conduction through the AV node slows and the PR interval lengthens. They also slow the SA node.
High extracellular K⁺ (hyperkalemia) or ischemia partly depolarizes the resting membrane. A less negative resting potential leaves more Na⁺ channels inactivated before the beat begins, so fewer are available for phase 0. The upstroke is slower and smaller, conduction slows, the QRS widens, and the tissue is prone to arrhythmias. Hyperkalemia also slows the SA node and can cause sinus bradycardia.







WarningA common mistake



Hyperkalemia means a high K⁺ in the extracellular fluid. Raising extracellular K⁺ shrinks the K⁺ gradient across the membrane, so EK becomes less negative and the resting potential moves up, toward 0. (Raising intracellular K⁺ would do the opposite, but that is not what happens in disease.) “Less negative” is the direction to remember: the cell is partly depolarized, and its Na⁺ channels pay for it.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 11  EKG I: Ionic Basis
text:
11.9 Check your understanding

Suppose a ventricular cell had no IK1 channels at all. What would happen to its resting membrane potential, and what would that do to its next upstroke?


Answer

The resting potential would become less negative. IK1 is what makes the resting membrane far more permeable to K⁺ than to anything else, so it holds the cell near EK. Without it, the small inward leak of Na⁺ has a larger effect and the membrane drifts up from −90 mV. More Na⁺ channels would then be inactivated before the beat, so the next upstroke would be slower and smaller. (Slow-response cells, which have almost no IK1, never settle at a resting potential for a related reason.)

The AV node conducts at about 0.05 m/s and the His bundle, a few millimeters away, at about 1 m/s. What difference in their action potentials explains most of this, and why does the slow AV node help the heart pump?


Answer

AV node cells are slow-response cells. Their upstroke is carried by L-type Ca²⁺ current, which is smaller and slower to turn on than the Na⁺ current that carries phase 0 in the His bundle, so each AV node cell brings its neighbor to threshold more slowly. (Their small fibers add resistance as well.) The delay holds the ventricles back until the atria have finished contracting and topped up ventricular filling.

A patient has sinus bradycardia from high vagal tone, and atropine blocks the muscarinic receptors on the SA node. Which two changes in the SA node action potential raise the rate?


Answer

With the M2 receptors blocked, the extra K⁺ conductance that acetylcholine opened goes away, so each cycle starts from a less negative maximum diastolic potential, closer to threshold. And cAMP is no longer held down, so If is larger and the phase 4 slope steeper. Both shorten the time to threshold.

Explain, step by step, why a less negative resting potential slows conduction in ventricular muscle even though the Na⁺ channels themselves are normal.


Answer

At a less negative resting potential, more Na⁺ channels sit in the inactivated state before the beat begins. Fewer are available to open in phase 0, so INa is smaller and the upstroke slower and lower. A slower upstroke drives less current into the next cell, which takes longer to reach threshold, so the wave of depolarization moves more slowly. Hyperkalemia and ischemia do this.

An extra stimulus reaches a ventricular cell 150 ms after its upstroke. What happens, and what is the channel explanation?


Answer

Nothing: at 150 ms the cell is in its plateau, inside the absolute refractory period. Its Na⁺ channels inactivated during phase 0 and cannot recover until the membrane has repolarized, so there is no current to make a new upstroke.

title: 12  ECG II: Vectors and Mean Electrical Axis
text:
12.1 How charge moves from cell to cell
The first chapter followed single cells. This one moves to the whole heart. Action potentials spread from cell to cell, and while some of the heart is depolarized and some is still at rest, current flows between the two regions. That current flows through the tissues of the body, and a small part of it reaches the skin, where a pair of electrodes can measure it. The question for this chapter is how the heart’s electrical activity becomes the shape on the paper, and what the shape tells you about which way the activity was going.
A 12-lead ECG is a cheap, non-invasive measure of several things at once: autonomic state (through the heart rate), the size, thickness and orientation of the heart, the conduction system, ischemia, and some non-cardiac disease. Einthoven built the first string galvanometer sensitive enough to record it from the body surface in 1903, with the patient’s limbs in buckets of salt water, work that later won him the Nobel Prize.
Cardiac cells are joined end to end at intercalated disks, and the disks are studded with gap junctions: channels made of connexin proteins that connect the cytoplasm of one cell to the next. They are not selective, and they conduct well. When one cell depolarizes, positive charge flows through the gap junctions into its resting neighbor. Part of that current discharges the neighbor’s membrane capacitance and depolarizes it toward threshold; part flows on to the next cell. Once the neighbor reaches threshold it fires its own action potential, and the process repeats down the line. This is electrotonic (passive) spread followed by regeneration, and it makes the heart act as one electrical unit. How fast it goes depends on the resistance and capacitance of the membranes, gap junctions and cytoplasm, and on how fast each cell’s upstroke is.

title: 12  ECG II: Vectors and Mean Electrical Axis
section: 12.2 What an electrode outside the cells sees
text:
12.2 What an electrode outside the cells sees
The lecture uses a model of two cells, A and B, to show how a voltage recorded outside cells differs from one recorded inside.

Inside. With one electrode inside each cell, depolarizing cell A makes it positive relative to resting cell B. The recording swings up, then fades as cell B depolarizes too. When A repolarizes first, the recording swings down.
Outside. On the outer surface, the signs are reversed. A depolarized cell has lost positive charge from its outer surface, so the outside of depolarized tissue is negative compared with the outside of resting tissue. The surface of the heart has a moving boundary, negative behind the wavefront and positive ahead of it.

That gives the three rules every ECG lead follows (Figure 12.1):

A wave of depolarization moving toward the positive electrode writes an upward (positive) deflection.
A wave of depolarization moving away from the positive electrode writes a downward (negative) deflection.
A wave moving perpendicular to the line between the electrodes writes no deflection. The lead is “blind” to it.







Figure 12.1: Extracellular recording from a strip of cells. Behind the wave of depolarization the outer surface is negative, ahead of it positive. (A) With the positive electrode ahead of the wave, the recording goes up. (B) Swap the electrodes and it goes down. (C) With the electrodes on a line perpendicular to the wave’s direction, both see the same voltage and nothing is recorded. Adapted from Boron and Boulpaep [1], as used in the 2026 lecture.



A wave of repolarization reverses the signs. Repolarized tissue is positive outside again, so a wave of repolarization moving toward the positive electrode writes a downward deflection. This is why the upright T wave is a puzzle, which the next chapter solves.
When the whole heart is at the same state, all depolarized (phase 2 everywhere) or all at rest (phase 4), there is no boundary, no current between regions, and the ECG is flat. These flat stretches are the isoelectric segments.
