title: 12  ECG II: Vectors and Mean Electrical Axis
text:
12.3 The heart as a dipole
A dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges a short distance apart. Its dipole moment is a vector: it points from the negative charge to the positive one, and its size is the charge times the separation. The boundary between depolarized and resting tissue is a sheet of tiny dipoles, each pointing from the negative, depolarized side to the positive, resting side, which is the direction the wave is moving. At any instant the ECG records the sum of all these dipoles, the heart’s net dipole vector.
The size of that vector depends on three things:

Balance between depolarized and resting tissue. If equal regions are depolarizing in opposite directions, their dipoles cancel.
How consistently the dipoles point the same way. Disorganized activation produces a small net vector.
How much tissue is depolarizing at once. A small structure such as the SA node makes a dipole too small to see on the surface ECG. The thick left ventricle makes the largest one.







NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The speaker notes describe a dipole as creating “an electromagnetic force known as a dipole moment vector.” A dipole moment is not a force. It is charge times separation, a vector, and it produces an electric field. The ECG measures that field’s voltage at the skin.


The surface ECG is a graph of the projection of this vector, over time, on the line between two electrodes. The height of a deflection depends on the vector’s size and direction, on the tissue between the heart and the skin, and on how the lead is oriented. The duration depends on how long the action potentials last and how fast they are conducted.

title: 12  ECG II: Vectors and Mean Electrical Axis
text:
12.4 The path of activation
Now follow one beat through the heart (Figure 12.2).
SA node (about 0.05 m/s). The beat starts in the SA node, high in the right atrium near where the superior vena cava enters. It fires on its own, with slow-response action potentials, and conducts slowly. The normal sinus rate is 60 to 100 per minute. The SA node is too small to show on the surface ECG.
Atria (about 1 m/s). The wave spreads radially from cell to cell through atrial muscle, and along faster bands: the interatrial band (Bachmann’s bundle) to the left atrium and internodal bands to the AV node. Atrial depolarization is the P wave. It travels from the high right atrium down and to the left, roughly along lead II, so the normal P wave is upright in lead II. The fibrous AV ring insulates the ventricles from the atria, so the only way through is the AV node.
AV node (about 0.05 m/s). The AV node sits in the right side of the interatrial septum, just above the AV ring near the tricuspid valve and the opening of the coronary sinus. Its cells are slow-response cells with small fibers, so the wave crosses it slowly. That delay lets the atria finish contracting (the “atrial kick”) before the ventricles start. The AV node makes no deflection of its own; its delay is most of the PR interval. Without the SA node, the AV node’s own rate would be 40 to 60 per minute.
His bundle and bundle branches (about 1 m/s). The His bundle emerges from the AV node on the right side of the interventricular septum. The right bundle branch runs down the right side of the septum to the right ventricle. The left bundle branch crosses to the left side of the septum and divides into the left anterior and left posterior fascicles. None of these is large enough to show on the surface ECG.
Purkinje fibers (about 4 m/s). Large-diameter fibers with fast-response action potentials spread the wave over the inner (endocardial) surface of both ventricles. They are the fastest tissue in the heart, and they are the main site of ventricular escape pacemakers.
Ventricular muscle (about 0.3 to 1 m/s). The wave then crosses the ventricular wall from endocardium to epicardium, cell to cell. Ventricular depolarization is the QRS complex. Ventricular repolarization is the T wave. Atrial repolarization happens during the QRS and is hidden by it.






Figure 12.2: The timing of activation in each part of the conduction system during one beat, lined up with a lead II ECG. The SA node, AV node, His bundle, bundle branches and Purkinje fibers produce no visible deflection. The P wave comes from atrial muscle and the QRS from ventricular muscle. Times are illustrative. Course figure.



The ECG is not the sum of these action potentials. Each tissue has its own action potential shape, but the ECG records only the voltage gradients that large masses of tissue produce as the wave crosses them.






NoteBackground: the conduction speeds in the 2018 course notes





The 2018 notes give slow-response conduction as 0.02 to 0.1 m/s, ordinary atrial and ventricular muscle as 0.3 to 1 m/s, and the Purkinje system as 1 to 4 m/s. The 2026 slides round these to 0.05 m/s for the nodes, about 1 m/s for the atria, His bundle and bundle branches, and about 4 m/s for the Purkinje fibers. The 2018 notes also say the wave reaches the AV node about 0.01 s after it leaves the SA node; the usual figure is about 0.03 s, and crossing the AV node then takes about 0.1 s. Neither time is a course number.




12.4.1 The ventricular sequence
Inside the ventricles, the order of activation sets the shape of the QRS:

The septum, left to right. The left bundle branch activates the left side of the septum first, so the first vector points to the right (and forward). Leads that look at the heart from the left, I, aVL, V5 and V6, see this small wave moving away and write a small negative q wave.
The apex and the free walls of both ventricles, from endocardium to epicardium. The left ventricle is far thicker than the right, so the net vector points down and to the left. This is the big R wave in most leads.
The base of the left ventricle and the upper septum, last. The final vector points up and back, and writes a small terminal S wave in some leads.

The vector’s tip traces a loop during the QRS, and each lead sees the loop from its own angle (Figure 12.5).

title: 12  ECG II: Vectors and Mean Electrical Axis
text:
12.5 Leads
A lead is a pair of recording points, one treated as positive and one as negative. Each lead records the projection of the heart’s vector on the line between them: positive when the vector points toward the positive end, negative when it points away.

12.5.1 The limb leads and Einthoven’s triangle
Three limb electrodes, on the right arm (RA), left arm (LA) and left leg (LL), make three standard limb leads (Figure 12.3 A):
\[\text{I} = V_{LA} - V_{RA} \qquad \text{II} = V_{LL} - V_{RA} \qquad \text{III} = V_{LL} - V_{LA}\]
Einthoven treated the three electrodes as the corners of an equilateral triangle with the heart in the middle. The triangle is insensitive to where on the limb the electrodes go: wrists or shoulders give the same picture, which is why a smartwatch can record lead I from your wrist and the finger of your other hand. Because the three leads are made from the same three electrodes, they are not independent. From the definitions, lead II equals lead I plus lead III at every instant (Einthoven’s law).






Figure 12.3: (A) Einthoven’s triangle. Each standard limb lead is the voltage of its positive electrode minus its negative one. (B) The hexaxial reference system: the six limb leads moved to a common center. The solid half of each line is the lead’s positive end. Course figure.





12.5.2 Each lead records a projection
Figure 12.4 shows a vector pointing at +60°, straight along lead II. Lead II sees all of it. Leads I and III, each 60° away, see half of it. Half plus half equals one, as Einthoven’s law requires.






Figure 12.4: (A) A dipole vector at +60° and its projections on leads I, II and III. Each lead’s shadow is the vector’s length times the cosine of the angle between the vector and the lead. (B) The resulting deflections. Course figure.



Figure 12.5 applies the same rule through a whole QRS. Lead I sees the septal vector moving away (a small q), the main vector at about 60° to its axis (a modest R), and the terminal vector moving away (a small s). Lead II looks almost straight down the main vector and writes the tallest R. aVR looks from the upper right, so almost everything moves away from it and its QRS is negative.






Figure 12.5: (A) The QRS vector loop of a normal heart in the frontal plane. The numbered arrows are the instantaneous vectors at three moments: (1) the septum, left to right; (2) the apex and free walls; (3) the last regions, at the base. The dashed arrow is the mean of all the instantaneous vectors, the mean electrical axis. (B) The QRS complexes this one loop produces in leads I, II, aVF and aVR. The loop is a model, built to match the course’s description. Course figure.





12.5.3 Augmented leads and the hexaxial system
Three more frontal-plane leads come from the same three electrodes, with no extra stickers, just arithmetic. Each augmented lead compares one limb electrode with the average of the other two: aVR (right arm positive), aVL (left arm positive) and aVF (left foot positive). Together the six limb leads look at the frontal plane every 30° (Figure 12.3 B). By convention, lead I is 0°, angles below it are positive (clockwise), and angles above it are negative.

NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The speaker notes say the augmented leads are measured against “Wilson’s central terminal.” The augmented leads use the average of the other two limb electrodes, as the same note goes on to describe for aVR. Wilson’s central terminal, the average of all three limb electrodes, is the reference for the precordial leads.

title: 12  ECG II: Vectors and Mean Electrical Axis
text:
12.6 The mean electrical axis
The mean electrical axis (MEA) is the average direction of ventricular depolarization in the frontal plane: the mean of all the instantaneous QRS vectors, shown as the dashed arrow in Figure 12.5. In a normal heart it points down and to the left, usually near +60°, because the left ventricle is thick and lies to the left and the apex points down.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The speaker note on the MEA slide defines it as “the direction of the dipole vector during the peak of ventricular depolarization (peak of R wave).” The MEA is the mean of all the QRS vectors, not the vector at one instant. In a normal heart the two point in nearly the same direction, so either definition gives about the same angle, but in a conduction delay or hypertrophy they can differ. The peer-educator notes give the correct definition, “average direction of ventricular depolarization.”



12.6.1 Normal and abnormal ranges
Figure 12.6 shows the ranges the course uses.






Figure 12.6: Ranges of the mean electrical axis. Normal is −30° to +90°, which includes the physiologic leftward axis from −30° to 0°. Left axis deviation is beyond −30° (to −90°), right axis deviation +90° to 180°, and extreme axis −90° to 180° (up and to the right). Course figure.

Physiologic leftward axis. An axis between 0° and −30° is normal. It is common when the heart lies more horizontally, as in pregnancy or obesity, and in some older or LV-dominant hearts without disease. The course calls this the physiologic leftward axis; some sources call it borderline left axis deviation. It is not left axis deviation.
The axis moves toward extra muscle and away from tissue that depolarizes late or not at all. The lecture’s causes, at a recognition level:

The slide lists a few more (atrial septal defects, pre-excitation, dextrocardia). You do not need them. The left anterior fascicle is thinner than the left posterior one, so left anterior fascicular block is the more common of the two.

title: 12  ECG II: Vectors and Mean Electrical Axis
text:
12.7 Finding the axis
The lecture teaches three methods. For each one, judge a lead by its net QRS deflection, the height of the positive part minus the depth of the negative part, not by the R wave alone. A lead with a small R and a deep S is net negative.
Vector addition. Take the net QRS deflection in two leads, mark each along its lead’s direction on the hexaxial diagram, draw perpendiculars from the two marks, and the line from the center to where they cross is the axis. With two perpendicular leads the arithmetic is easy. If lead I is net +5 mm and aVF is net +5 mm, the vector points halfway between 0° and +90°, at +45°. This is the most precise method and the slowest, and the ECG machine does it for you.
Inspection. Two shortcuts:

The lead with the tallest net positive QRS is closest to the axis.
The lead with the most isoelectric QRS (net deflection near zero) is perpendicular to the axis. The axis is then 90° from that lead, on the side of whichever perpendicular lead is positive.

A third version, the equal-R-wave method, uses two leads with R waves of the same size and direction: the axis lies midway between them. Equal R waves in II and III, for example, put the axis at +90°, along aVF.
The “ER Doc” method (lead I, then lead II). This is the quickest bedside method and the one the course prefers. It answers the clinical question, normal or not, without computing an angle.

Look at lead I. If its QRS is net negative, the vector points to the patient’s right, beyond +90° or −90°: right axis deviation (or extreme axis). If lead I is positive, the axis is somewhere from −90° to +90°.
Look at lead II. If lead I and lead II are both positive, the axis is normal, from −30° to +90°, including the physiologic leftward axis. If lead I is positive and lead II is negative, the axis is beyond −30°: left axis deviation.

Why lead II? Lead II is at +60°, so it turns negative only when the axis passes −30°, exactly the edge of normal. aVF is at +90°, so it turns negative as soon as the axis passes 0°. An axis of −15° is normal, with lead II positive, but aVF is already slightly negative (Figure 12.7).






Figure 12.7: The ER Doc method. QRS complexes in leads I, II and aVF for four axes, all from the same vector loop turned to a different angle. Shading shows the net deflection: green net positive, red net negative. At −15° (physiologic leftward axis) lead II is still positive but aVF is negative. Course figure.









WarningA common mistake



Some ECG guides use lead I and aVF. That method calls every axis between 0° and −30° abnormal, so it labels a healthy pregnant patient, or anyone with a horizontal heart, as having left axis deviation. Use lead I and lead II. If lead II is positive, the axis is normal.








NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The ECG Reading Room quick guide lists three axis options. Option 2, “R wave upright in lead I and lead II means normal axis,” is the ER Doc method; check the net QRS rather than the R wave alone. Option 3, “I, II, aVF (thumb rule),” brings aVF back in. If you use it, a negative aVF with a positive lead II is still a normal axis. The answer key’s “borderline left” axis is what this course calls the physiologic leftward axis.

title: 12  ECG II: Vectors and Mean Electrical Axis
text:
12.8 The precordial leads
The six limb leads see only the frontal plane. Six precordial (chest) leads, V1 to V6, look at the horizontal plane. Each compares one chest electrode with a central reference made by averaging the three limb electrodes (Wilson’s central terminal), so again there is no extra electrode for the negative end. Unlike the limb leads, where an electrode goes on the chest matters, because the chest electrodes sit close to the heart. V1 and V2 sit on either side of the sternum, over the right ventricle and septum; V3 and V4 are over the anterior wall; V5 and V6 are on the left side of the chest over the lateral wall. The lecture’s map of the heart’s surfaces helps here: the right atrium forms the right border, the left ventricle the left border, the right ventricle most of the front (anterior) surface, and the left ventricle most of the diaphragmatic surface.
As in the limb leads, activation moving toward a chest electrode writes an upward deflection. In V1, the septal vector moves toward the electrode (a small r), and then the large left ventricular forces move away (a deep S). In V6 the order reverses: a small q from the septum, then a tall R. Between them, the R wave grows and the S wave shrinks from V1 to V6. This is R wave progression (Figure 12.8). It reflects the change from looking across the thin right ventricle to looking straight at the thick left ventricle.






Figure 12.8: (A) The positions of V1 to V6 around the chest, seen from below. (B) Normal R wave progression: rS in V1, R and S about equal near V3 and V4, qR in V6. Model complexes from a vector loop in the horizontal plane. Course figure.




12.8.1 Contiguous leads
Leads that look at the same region of the heart are grouped. When the waveform changes in one lead, look for the same change in its neighbors. This grouping matters most when you diagnose ischemia, which is a second-year topic.

title: 12  ECG II: Vectors and Mean Electrical Axis
section: 12.9 Is the ECG a picture of the heart?
text:
12.9 Is the ECG a picture of the heart?
Not quite. The ECG is a set of projections of one moving vector, recorded from twelve directions, and it tells you about timing, direction and the amount of muscle being activated. Imaging gives anatomy. The lecture ends with body-surface maps made from dozens of electrodes, which come closer to a picture but are not used in routine care.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle
12  ECG II: Vectors and Mean Electrical Axis

title: 12  ECG II: Vectors and Mean Electrical Axis
text:
12.10 Check your understanding

A wave of depolarization travels from the left arm toward the right arm. What does lead I record, and why?


Answer

A downward (negative) deflection. Lead I’s positive electrode is on the left arm, so a wave moving from left to right is moving away from the positive electrode.

At one instant lead I reads +0.3 mV and lead III reads +0.6 mV. What does lead II read?


Answer

+0.9 mV. By Einthoven’s law, lead II equals lead I plus lead III.

In a patient’s ECG, aVL has the most nearly isoelectric QRS and lead II is strongly positive. Estimate the axis.


Answer

aVL is at −30°, so the axis is perpendicular to it, at +60° or −120°. Lead II (+60°) is positive, so the axis is about +60°. Normal.

On the hexaxial diagram, which limb lead is perpendicular to −30°, and which is perpendicular to 0°? Use your answers to explain why, once lead I is positive, the sign of lead II and not of aVF marks the boundary between a normal axis and left axis deviation.


Answer

Lead II, at +60°, is perpendicular to −30°, and aVF, at +90°, is perpendicular to 0°. A lead’s QRS changes sign when the axis crosses the line perpendicular to that lead. So lead II turns from positive to negative as the axis moves past −30°, the edge of the normal range. aVF turns negative as the axis moves above 0°, which is still inside the normal range (0° to −30° is the physiologic leftward axis). A negative aVF cannot tell normal from abnormal, and a negative lead II can.

Long-standing hypertension thickens a patient’s left ventricle. Which way does the mean electrical axis move, and what would the ER Doc method show if it moved far enough?


Answer

To the left, toward the extra muscle, because the thicker left ventricle adds more leftward dipole. If it moves past −30°, lead I stays positive and lead II turns negative: left axis deviation.

Why does the SA node produce no wave on the ECG, while the atria produce the P wave?


Answer

The size of the dipole depends on how much tissue is depolarizing at once. The SA node is tiny, so its dipole is too small to detect at the skin. The atria are a much larger mass of muscle depolarizing together.

title: 13  EKG III: Clinical Interpretation
text:
13.1 The waves and intervals
The first two chapters built the ECG from the bottom up: ion channels and action potentials, then vectors, leads and the mean electrical axis. This one reads the result, in the lecture’s six steps: measurement, rhythm analysis, conduction analysis, waveform (morphology) analysis, interpretation, and comparison with a previous ECG. Each abnormality comes back to the earlier physiology: which pacemaker is firing, where conduction is slow or blocked, and how the wave of depolarization crosses the ventricles.
You will practice all of this in the ECG Reading Room session. The course titles spell the recording both ways, EKG and ECG. This book writes ECG.
Einthoven named the waves of one beat P, Q, R, S and T (Figure 13.1).
Intervals include at least one wave; segments are the flat stretches between waves.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 13  EKG III: Clinical Interpretation
text:
P wave: atrial depolarization.
QRS complex: ventricular depolarization. A Q wave is any negative deflection before the first positive one, the R wave is the first positive deflection, and the S wave is a negative deflection after the R. Not every lead has all three.
T wave: ventricular repolarization. Atrial repolarization happens during the QRS and is hidden by it.



PR interval: from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS. It covers atrial conduction, the AV node delay, and conduction through the His bundle, bundle branches and Purkinje fibers.
PR segment: from the end of the P wave to the start of the QRS.
QRS duration: from the start to the end of the QRS.
ST segment: from the end of the QRS to the start of the T wave, when the whole ventricle is depolarized (phase 2 everywhere). The point where the QRS ends and the ST segment begins is the J point.
QT interval: from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave, measured whether or not there is a Q wave. It covers ventricular depolarization and repolarization.







Figure 13.1: One beat on standard ECG paper, with its waves, intervals and segments. The calibration pulse at the left is 1 mV tall (10 mm) and 0.2 s wide. Course figure.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 13  EKG III: Clinical Interpretation
text:
13.2 Measurement

13.2.1 The paper
An ECG is a graph of voltage against time. Standard paper runs at 25 mm/s, with 10 mm for each millivolt.



Box
Size
Time (horizontal)
Voltage (vertical)




Small box
1 mm
0.04 s (40 ms)
0.1 mV


Large box
5 mm, five small boxes
0.2 s (200 ms)
0.5 mV



Check the calibration pulse at the start of every tracing: 10 mm tall (1 mV) and usually 0.2 s wide. A standard printout shows 10 seconds of rhythm.


13.2.2 Heart rate
The lecture gives three ways to measure the ventricular rate (Figure 13.2):

From the R-R interval. Rate = 60 / (R-R interval in seconds). An R-R of 0.8 s (4 large boxes) is 75 per minute. (In milliseconds, rate = 60,000 / R-R.)
The 300 rule. Find an R wave on a heavy line and count the large boxes to the next R wave. Rate ≈ 300 / (number of large boxes): 1 box is 300, 2 boxes 150, 3 boxes 100, 4 boxes 75, 5 boxes 60, 6 boxes 50, 7 boxes about 43. The slides call this the ER-Doc method. This book keeps that name for the lead I and lead II axis method in ECG II, so here it is the 300 rule.
The 10-second rule. Count the QRS complexes on the 10-second rhythm strip and multiply by 6. The slides call this the pulmonologist method. It is the one to use when the rhythm is irregular, as in atrial fibrillation, because the other two depend on a single R-R interval.







Figure 13.2: Measuring rate. The R-R interval is 4 large boxes (0.8 s). The numbers above the strip mark the rate you would get if the next R wave fell on each heavy line. Course figure.



A rate of 60 to 100 per minute is normal, under 60 is bradycardia, and over 100 is tachycardia. These are definitions, not diagnoses: an athlete at rest may run at 50 and anyone exercising runs over 100.


13.2.3 Normal values
The course uses these normal values:








Measurement
Normal
Small boxes




PR interval
120 to 200 ms
3 to 5


QRS duration
under 120 ms (most normal QRS complexes are 80 to 100 ms)
under 3


QTc
460 ms or less; above 460 ms is prolonged



P wave
under 120 ms, under 0.2 mV
under 3 wide, under 2 tall



PR interval. A quick check: the normal PR fits inside one large box. A PR over 200 ms means conduction is delayed between the atria and the ventricles, most often in the AV node (first-degree AV block, below). A PR under 120 ms means the impulse reached the ventricles without the usual AV node delay, either through an accessory pathway that bypasses the AV node (pre-excitation) or because the impulse started in or near the AV node (a junctional rhythm).
QRS duration. A QRS of 120 ms or more is wide. It means the ventricles are being activated, at least in part, by slow cell-to-cell conduction through muscle instead of through the His-Purkinje system: a bundle branch block, an impulse that starts in the ventricle (a PVC or ventricular rhythm), an accessory pathway, or slowed conduction from hyperkalemia or a Na⁺ channel blocker.
QT interval and QTc. The QT interval mostly reflects how long ventricular action potentials last. Action potentials shorten as the heart rate rises, so the QT does too. To compare QT intervals at different rates, correct it for rate. The course uses Bazett’s formula, with the R-R interval in seconds:
\[\text{QTc} = \frac{\text{QT}}{\sqrt{\text{RR}}}\]
At a rate of 60 the R-R is 1 s, so QTc equals QT. A quick visual check is that the measured QT should be less than half the R-R interval. That check works for the uncorrected QT and only at normal heart rates.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The QRS slide says “< 100 – 110 ms / < 2.5 small boxes,” its speaker note “<100-120 msec,” and the peer-educator notes both “<120 ms” and “Normal (100-120).” The course uses QRS under 120 ms, with most normal QRS complexes 80 to 100 ms. When a question depends on a normal range, it gives you the range.
For the QTc, the slide says normal is under 460 ms, the peer-educator notes give 440 ms for men and 460 ms for women, and the Reading Room quick guide gives “<470 good, 470-500 borderline, >500 concerning.” The course value is a single cutoff: a QTc above 460 ms is prolonged. The Reading Room’s 470 and 500 ms are thresholds for the risk of arrhythmia, not normal limits.
The Reading Room quick guide gives the PR interval as “< 200 ms or 1 big box,” with no lower limit. The normal PR is 120 to 200 ms; a PR under 120 ms is abnormal too.
The QT speaker note says that “as the heart rate increases the QTc decreases inversely.” It is the measured QT that shortens as the rate rises. The QTc is the QT corrected for rate, so that the rate effect is removed.

title: 13  EKG III: Clinical Interpretation
text:
13.3 Rhythm analysis
Rhythm is read from the rhythm strip, usually lead II, which runs the full width of the printout. Lead II looks along the direction the atria normally depolarize, so it shows the P waves best.
Normal sinus rhythm meets all of these:

A P wave before every QRS, and a QRS after every P wave (P:QRS 1:1).
P waves upright in lead II (and lead I), and all the same shape. This says the impulse starts in the SA node, in the high right atrium.
A constant PR interval, within 120 to 200 ms.
A rate of 60 to 100 per minute.
A regular R-R interval.

Normal sinus rhythm describes the rhythm only. An ECG in sinus rhythm can still show a wide QRS, an abnormal axis or ischemia.

13.3.1 Changes in SA node automaticity
When the SA node fires faster or slower than normal but every other criterion holds, the rhythm is sinus tachycardia or sinus bradycardia (Figure 13.3).






Figure 13.3: Lead II rhythm strips. (A) Normal sinus rhythm at 75 per minute. (B) Sinus tachycardia at 150 per minute: still one upright P before every QRS, but the R-R is only 2 large boxes. (C) Sinus bradycardia at about 43 per minute. Course figure.



Sinus tachycardia (over 100 per minute) comes from increased SA node automaticity:

Sympathetic stimulation, fight or flight: β1-adrenergic stimulation increases If and lowers the firing threshold, so phase 4 reaches threshold sooner.
Fever (hyperthermia).
Metabolic and endocrine causes, such as an overactive thyroid.

Sinus tachycardia is usually a normal response to stress, pain, fever or exercise, not a disease in itself.
Sinus bradycardia (under 60 per minute) comes from decreased SA node automaticity:

Parasympathetic (cholinergic) stimulation, as in a vasovagal faint.
Intrinsic SA node disease (sick sinus syndrome, ischemia).
Drugs such as β-blockers.
Hyperkalemia.
Hypothermia.
Physical training: trained athletes have a slow resting rate.
Raised intracranial pressure.

The Reading Room’s first case runs through both: a patient afraid of needles goes into sinus tachycardia, then faints at the sight of blood with sinus bradycardia. The ionic basis chapter explains both mechanisms.


13.3.2 Abnormal and ectopic impulse formation
Any cardiac cell can, under the wrong conditions, fire on its own. When a cell outside the SA node fires before the next sinus beat, it produces an ectopic (out-of-place) beat (Figure 13.4).






Figure 13.4: (A) Sinus rhythm with two premature ventricular contractions (PVCs): early, wide complexes with no P wave before them, and a T wave pointing the opposite way. (B) An ectopic atrial rhythm: every P wave is negative in lead II, because the atria are being activated from below. (C) Multifocal atrial tachycardia: P waves of several shapes and PR intervals, an irregular rhythm, and a rate over 100. Lead II. Course figure.



Premature ventricular contractions (PVCs). A cell in the ventricle fires early. There is no P wave before it, because the impulse did not come from the atria, and the QRS is wide. Why wide? Ask instead why a normal QRS is narrow: the His-Purkinje system, at about 4 m/s, delivers the impulse to the inner surface of both ventricles almost at once. A PVC spreads cell to cell through muscle, outside the conduction system, at under 1 m/s, so the QRS is wide and abnormally shaped, and the T wave usually points the opposite way. In the Reading Room, the same patient’s palpitations turn out to be sinus rhythm with PVCs.
Premature atrial contractions (PACs). An atrial cell outside the SA node fires early. The P wave comes early and has an unusual shape, but the impulse reaches the ventricles through the AV node and His-Purkinje system as usual, so the QRS is narrow.
Ectopic atrial rhythm. A site lower in the atria takes over for many beats in a row, because it now fires faster than the SA node. A sinus impulse travels from the high right atrium toward lead II’s positive electrode on the left leg, so the sinus P wave is upright in lead II. An impulse from low in the atria travels upward, away from that electrode, so its P wave is negative in lead II.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia. Several atrial sites each fire on their own: at least three P wave shapes, varying PR intervals, an irregular rhythm and a rate over 100. The Reading Room’s patient has a flare of COPD.
Escape rhythms. These are the opposite case: the SA node fails or its impulses are blocked, and a slower latent pacemaker takes over because nothing faster is firing. An escape from the AV junction runs at 40 to 60 per minute with a narrow QRS; one from the Purkinje fibers or ventricle runs at about 30 to 40 per minute with a wide QRS. An escape rhythm is a backup, not the problem.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 13  EKG III: Clinical Interpretation
text:
13.4 Conduction analysis
When the P waves come from the SA node and look normal but something is wrong with how the impulse gets through, the problem is conduction. Conduction can fail at the SA node, the AV node, or anywhere in the His-Purkinje system, including one bundle branch or fascicle.

13.4.1 AV block
AV blocks are graded by how many atrial impulses get through to the ventricles (Figure 13.5).






Figure 13.5: Lead II strips of AV block. (A) First degree: every P conducts, but the PR is 0.30 s. (B) Mobitz I (Wenckebach): the PR grows longer each beat until one P is not conducted (arrow), then the cycle repeats with a short PR. (C) Mobitz II: the PR is the same before and after a P that suddenly is not conducted (arrows); the QRS is wide here, as it often is. (D) 2:1 block: every second P is not conducted, so there are never two conducted beats in a row to compare. (E) Third-degree block: P waves (triangles) at 90 per minute and QRS complexes at 42 per minute march independently. Course figure.



First-degree AV block. Every P wave is conducted, but slowly: the PR interval is over 200 ms (more than one large box) and constant. It is usually in the AV node, usually causes no symptoms, and does not need a pacemaker.
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I (Wenckebach). The PR interval gets longer with each beat until a P wave is not conducted and a QRS is dropped; after the pause the PR is short again. Progressive slowing is typical of AV node tissue, so the block is usually in the AV node. It is usually benign, often from high vagal tone (athletes, sleep), and rarely needs treatment. In the Reading Room, a patient whose smartwatch flagged an abnormal rhythm turns out to have Mobitz I.
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II. Most P waves are conducted with a constant PR interval, and then, without warning, one is not. The PR is the same before and after the dropped beat. This all-or-none failure is typical of the His bundle and bundle branches, so Mobitz II is usually below the AV node, and the QRS is often wide because the bundle branches are diseased too. Mobitz II is dangerous: it can progress suddenly to complete heart block, and it is treated with a pacemaker even in patients who have no symptoms.
2:1 AV block. When every second P wave is not conducted, there are never two conducted beats in a row, so you cannot tell whether the PR would have lengthened (Mobitz I) or stayed fixed (Mobitz II). 2:1 block is its own category and cannot be typed from the strip.
Third-degree (complete) AV block. No atrial impulses reach the ventricles. The atria follow the SA node and the ventricles follow an escape pacemaker below the block. P waves and QRS complexes are both regular but unrelated, the faster P waves marching through the QRS complexes (AV dissociation). The QRS depends on where the escape pacemaker is. If the block is in the AV node, a junctional escape below it fires at 40 to 60 per minute with a narrow QRS. If the block is lower, a ventricular escape fires at about 30 to 40 per minute with a wide QRS. Either way the rate is slow and the escape pacemaker can fail, so complete heart block can cause fainting or cardiac arrest and is treated with a pacemaker. Acquired AV block of any degree most often comes from ischemic heart disease or from drugs, among them β-blockers, digitalis and the L-type Ca²⁺ channel blockers.

NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The ECG Reading Room key gives the site of the Mobitz II case (the man who fainted at home) as the AV node. Mobitz II is usually below the AV node, in the His bundle or bundle branches, and the case’s wide QRS points that way. The peer-educator notes put it correctly: “Not an AV node problem.”




13.4.2 Bundle branch block
When one bundle branch fails, the ventricle it serves is activated late, by cell-to-cell spread from the other side of the septum, so the QRS is wide (120 ms or more) and its shape and axis change. The Reading Room’s syncope case has a left bundle branch block. Recognize that the QRS is wide and why; naming the pattern is a later topic.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 13  EKG III: Clinical Interpretation
text:
13.5 Waveform analysis

13.5.1 The P wave
A normal P wave lasts under 120 ms and is under 0.2 mV tall. Its direction in different leads tells you where the impulse started. Its size and shape can suggest atrial enlargement, which is beyond what this course asks.


13.5.2 The QRS complex and ST segment
The QRS is the place to judge width (above), axis (the ECG II chapter), and R wave progression across the precordial leads. Very large QRS voltages can mean ventricular hypertrophy; the Reading Room notes this but does not ask you to diagnose it.
During the ST segment the whole ventricle is depolarized, so in a healthy heart the segment is flat, level with the PR segment. Injured or ischemic muscle makes it rise or fall from the J point onward. ST elevation is the sign of an acute myocardial infarction (a STEMI), which is why patients with chest pain have an ECG within minutes of arrival. ST depression can mean ischemia or hypokalemia. ST changes are a second-year topic; the lecture previews them and the Reading Room does not cover them.


13.5.3 The T wave
The T wave is ventricular repolarization. A normal T wave has a shape and direction much like the P wave’s: rounded, and upright in most leads where the QRS is upright. Disease can flatten it, invert it or peak it.
Why is it upright? A wave of repolarization moving toward the positive electrode writes a downward deflection (ECG II), so if the ventricles repolarized in the order they depolarized, the T wave would point opposite to the QRS. It does not, because repolarization runs in roughly the reverse order. Epicardial cells have shorter action potentials than endocardial cells, so although the epicardium depolarizes last, it repolarizes first. Repolarization moves from epicardium to endocardium, opposite to depolarization, and a reversed wave of the opposite sign writes a deflection in the same direction (Figure 13.6).






Figure 13.6: An endocardial and an epicardial action potential from the left ventricular wall, and the voltage difference between them, which has the sign an electrode facing the epicardium records. The endocardium depolarizes first, so the QRS is upright. The epicardial action potential is shorter, so the epicardium repolarizes first and the T wave is upright too. Schematic. Course figure.



The T wave is also smaller and broader than the QRS. Repolarization is spread out over time and less organized than depolarization, so its dipoles are smaller and less aligned.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 13  EKG III: Clinical Interpretation
section: 13.6 The long QT and torsades de pointes
text:
13.6 The long QT and torsades de pointes
The QT interval matters because a long one sets up a dangerous arrhythmia. In Figure 13.7 A the QT is 0.40 s, which looks normal, but the heart rate is about 94. The R-R interval is 0.64 s, and √0.64 = 0.8, so QTc = 0.40 / 0.8 = 0.50 s, or 500 ms, well above 460 ms. The QT is too long for this heart rate.






Figure 13.7: (A) Measuring the QT and correcting it for rate. (B) Torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in which the QRS complexes seem to twist around the baseline. Lead II. Course figure.



A long QT means the ventricular action potentials are long, and long action potentials, especially if some regions repolarize later than others, can trigger extra beats during repolarization. The result can be torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia whose QRS complexes change in size and direction as if twisting around the baseline. It can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest.
Ventricular fibrillation (VF) is chaotic ventricular activity with no organized QRS complexes (Figure 13.8 D). The ventricles quiver instead of contracting, and cardiac output stops: VF is cardiac arrest. VF, and VT without a pulse, are treated by defibrillation.
Asystole is the other rhythm of cardiac arrest: no electrical activity at all, with no sinus node activity and no escape rhythm. It is not treated by defibrillation; treatment targets the cause.
The course names these causes of a long QT: many drugs (some anti-nausea drugs among them), hypokalemia, hypocalcemia and congenital long QT syndrome. Hypercalcemia and digoxin shorten the QT.
Sympathetic stimulation shortens both the PR and the QT intervals. A QT that does not shorten as the rate rises is a clue that it is prolonged.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 13  EKG III: Clinical Interpretation
section: 13.8 The ECG and the cardiac cycle
text:
13.8 The ECG and the cardiac cycle
The ECG shows electrical events, not contraction. The P wave and the QRS each come just before the contraction they trigger, by about 20 to 50 ms: the P wave before atrial contraction (the atrial kick, about 10% of end-diastolic volume at rest), and the QRS before ventricular contraction and the isovolumic contraction phase. The T wave comes during the end of ejection. The ventricle relaxes as it repolarizes, and filling begins after isovolumic relaxation. The Cardiac Pump chapter lines these up on the Wiggers diagram.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 13  EKG III: Clinical Interpretation
section: 13.9 Reentry rhythms: atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter and ventricular tachycardia
text:
13.9 Reentry rhythms: atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter and ventricular tachycardia
The end of the deck, marked optional, covers the fast rhythms that come from reentry. The Reading Room asks you to recognize two of them, atrial fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia, and to reason about where the impulse comes from (Figure 13.8; panel D, VF, is described with torsades above).






Figure 13.8: Lead II strips of four fast rhythms; VF (D) is described in the section on torsades. (A) Atrial fibrillation: a wavy baseline with no P waves, and narrow QRS complexes at irregular intervals. (B) Atrial flutter: regular sawtooth flutter waves at about 300 per minute, with every fourth one conducted here. (C) Ventricular tachycardia: regular wide complexes at about 160 per minute, no P waves. (D) Ventricular fibrillation: chaotic activity with no organized QRS complexes. Course figure.



Atrial fibrillation. The slide attributes it to micro-reentrant circuits in the atria, usually in the left atrium around the pulmonary veins. The atria are activated chaotically and do not contract. There are no P waves, only a wavy, irregular baseline, and the AV node lets impulses through at random, so the ventricular rhythm is irregularly irregular. The QRS is narrow, because the impulses that do get through use the normal conduction system. Use the 10-second rule for the rate. Losing the atrial kick costs about 10% of end-diastolic volume at rest. The bigger problem is a fast ventricular rate. In the Reading Room’s case it shortens diastole, so the ventricle fills less and stroke volume, cardiac output and mean arterial pressure fall.
Atrial flutter. A single large reentrant circuit, usually around the tricuspid valve ring in the right atrium, activates the atria about 300 times a minute. The ECG shows regular sawtooth flutter waves, best seen in lead II. The AV node cannot conduct every one, so the ventricles usually respond to every second or every fourth (2:1 or 4:1 conduction). With a fixed ratio the ventricular rhythm is regular; when the ratio varies, it is regularly irregular, as the slide says.
Ventricular tachycardia (VT). A regular, wide-complex tachycardia that starts in the ventricle, with no P waves before the QRS complexes. The complexes are wide for the same reason a PVC is. Fast VT leaves little time for filling and can quickly lead to cardiac arrest.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The atrial flutter slide calls the circuit “micro-reentrant.” Typical atrial flutter is a single macro-reentrant circuit around the tricuspid valve ring.








NoteBackground: reentry and accessory pathways (optional slides)





Reentry. An impulse that splits into two paths and meets itself on the far side normally dies out, because each wavefront runs into tissue the other has just made refractory. Reentry needs unidirectional block (usually injured tissue that blocks the impulse in one direction only) and a conduction time around the loop long enough that the tissue at the start has recovered when the impulse returns. Large, dilated hearts and slow, diseased tissue make that easier. The impulse then circles, firing the heart at the loop’s rate. Reentry underlies atrial flutter, many cases of atrial fibrillation and most ventricular tachycardia.
Accessory pathways (pre-excitation). In Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome, an extra band of muscle (the bundle of Kent) connects atrium and ventricle across the AV ring and bypasses the AV node. Part of the ventricle is activated early through the pathway, so the PR is short, and that early activation spreads slowly through muscle, so the QRS starts with a slurred delta wave. The QRS is a fusion of the early and the normal activation. The pathway can also form a reentrant loop with the AV node, or let a very fast atrial rhythm reach the ventricles unfiltered.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 13  EKG III: Clinical Interpretation
text:
13.10 Putting it together
Read every ECG in the same order:

Rate. Fast, slow or normal?
Rhythm. Regular or irregular?
P waves. Present? Upright in lead II and all the same shape? One before every QRS?
PR interval. Within 120 to 200 ms? Constant?
QRS. Narrow or wide? What is the axis?
ST segment and T wave. Flat ST? T waves upright where the QRS is upright?
QT. Is the QTc over 460 ms?
Compare with a previous ECG. A change over time, such as a new block or new ST changes, is often more important than any single finding.

Then synthesize: say where the impulse starts, whether it is conducted normally, and how the ventricles are activated.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 13  EKG III: Clinical Interpretation
text:
13.11 Check your understanding

On a strip the R-R interval is 3 large boxes and 2 small boxes. What is the heart rate?


Answer

3 × 0.2 + 2 × 0.04 = 0.68 s, and 60 / 0.68 ≈ 88 per minute, between the 300 rule’s 100 and 75.

Lead II shows a negative P wave before every QRS, with a PR interval of 100 ms. Where does the impulse start, and why is the PR short?


Answer

Low in the atria, near the AV junction. A negative P in lead II means atrial depolarization is moving up, away from lead II’s positive electrode, so it did not start in the SA node. Starting close to the AV node, the impulse spends less time crossing the atria before it reaches the node, so the PR is short.

A patient has left bundle branch block. Every beat starts in the SA node, every QRS has a normal P wave before it, and the PR interval is normal. Why is the PR normal while every QRS is wide?


Answer

Conduction is normal from the SA node through the atria, the AV node and the His bundle, so the P wave and the PR interval are normal. Below the His bundle, the right bundle still delivers the impulse quickly to the right ventricle and the right side of the septum. The left bundle carries nothing, so the left ventricle is activated late, by cell-to-cell spread through muscle from the right side of the septum, at under 1 m/s instead of the 4 m/s of the His-Purkinje system. Depolarizing both ventricles takes 120 ms or more, so the QRS is wide.

In Mobitz I the PR interval lengthens before the dropped beat; in Mobitz II it does not. What does that difference tell you about the tissue that is failing in each?


Answer

Progressive slowing is how AV node tissue fails: its slow-response cells recover slowly, so each impulse is conducted a little more slowly than the last until one fails. The His bundle and bundle branches are fast-response tissue that conducts normally right up to the beat it cannot conduct at all, so the PR stays fixed and the block is sudden. So Mobitz I points to the AV node and Mobitz II to the system below it, the level from which block can progress to complete block.

During exercise a person’s heart rate rises from 60 to 120 per minute. What should happen to the QT interval, and what would it mean if the QT stayed the same as at rest?


Answer

The QT should shorten, because ventricular action potentials shorten at faster rates and with sympathetic input. At 120 per minute the R-R is 0.5 s and √0.5 is about 0.7, so an unchanged QT would give a QTc about 40% higher than at rest (where QTc equals QT). A QT that fails to shorten as the rate rises is relatively prolonged.

In complete heart block, the QRS complexes are narrow and come at 45 per minute. Where is the escape pacemaker, and where is the block?


Answer

A narrow QRS means the ventricles are activated through the His-Purkinje system, so the escape pacemaker is in the AV junction, above the bundle branches, at its usual 40 to 60. The block is above it, in the AV node. A block below the His bundle would leave a slower ventricular escape with a wide QRS.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 14  Cardiovascular Integration and Adaptation
text:
14.1 The rules you already have
By now you have the parts. The heart’s pumping is summarized by the cardiac function curve, the vessels’ return of blood by the vascular function curve, and the reflexes that adjust both by the baroreceptor reflex. This lecture puts them to work on the problems they were built for. Something goes wrong: blood is lost, the heart weakens or cannot fill, or the vessels dilate. What changes first, what does the body do about it, and what does the fix cost? The same few rules answer every case, and the exercise chapter that follows applies them to a healthy person pushed to the limit (Cardiovascular Adaptation to Exercise).
The Control of Cardiac Output chapter built the tools: CO = VR at steady state, VR = (Pms − Pra)/RVR, and the operating point where the cardiac and vascular function curves cross (the small groups call the pair “Guyton curves”). In this course, changes in RVR are treated as minor and ignored, except in exercise, so a change in venous tone is drawn as a change in Pms, a parallel shift of the vascular function curve. The curves give CO and Pra but not blood pressure; for that you need SVR, from MAP − Pra = CO × SVR. The small groups also use a “single pump” model in which left and right atrial pressures are equal, so keep in mind that pulmonary edema depends on left atrial pressure.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 14  Cardiovascular Integration and Adaptation
text:
14.2 Three states: before, injury, compensation
Every case in this chapter has the same three states, and most mistakes come from mixing them up:

Before the insult. The person’s own normal operating point.
Injury, before compensation. Only the curve the insult acts on has moved. No reflex has acted yet.
After compensation. The reflexes have moved one or both curves, usually including the curve the insult did not touch.

The small groups ask you to label baseline, injury and compensation on every drawing. “Immediately after” an insult, before any reflex, is state 2. Once the reflexes have acted, expect state 3: a faster heart rate and a higher Pms than in state 2.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 14  Cardiovascular Integration and Adaptation
text:
14.3 Hemorrhage
The injury lecture opens with a man who cuts a large artery and bleeds briskly. How will his autonomic nervous system defend his cardiac output, and how will it defend his mean arterial pressure?

14.3.1 The injury
Blood loss removes stressed volume, so Pms falls. Figure 14.2 follows the chain on the left, the process diagram the small groups use:
hemorrhage → ↓ Pms → ↓ venous return and preload (EDV) → ↓ force of contraction → ↓ SV → ↓ CO → ↓ arterial blood volume → ↓ BP
Nothing about the heart itself has changed: its contractility and its filling curve are the same. The ventricle simply fills to a smaller end-diastolic volume because less blood comes back, and by Frank-Starling it generates less force and a smaller stroke volume (Figure 14.1 A). Pulse pressure narrows with the smaller stroke volume.






Figure 14.1: Pressure-volume loops in the two injuries of the lecture. (A) Hemorrhage before compensation: less venous return lowers the filling pressure, so the ventricle fills to a smaller end-diastolic volume on the same filling curve (EDPVR). Contractility (the ESPVR) is unchanged, and stroke volume falls. (B) Myocardial infarction: the ESPVR is flatter, so ejection stops at a larger end-systolic volume and stroke volume falls (solid). With compensation (dashed), a higher filling pressure fills the ventricle to a larger end-diastolic volume, which restores part of the stroke volume at the cost of a higher LVEDP. Faded loops are the beat before the injury. Bars show stroke volume. Loops from the model in The Cardiac Pump; illustrative values. Course figure, after the lecture’s P-V loop slides.









Figure 14.2: Hemorrhage as a process diagram. Left: the injury, before compensation. Right: the reflex compensations that follow, sorted by where they act, and the slower hormonal and renal response. The veins and heart raise CO; the arterioles raise SVR; together they defend MAP. Course figure, after the process diagrams of the small-group sessions and the integrated hemorrhage chart from Boron and Boulpaep [1] used in the lecture.



On the curves (Figure 14.3 A), only the vascular function curve moves, to the left. The operating point slides down the unchanged cardiac function curve, so CO and Pra both fall.


14.3.2 The compensating mechanisms
The lecture lists the compensating mechanisms:

the baroreceptor reflex;
the chemoreceptor reflex;
the CNS ischemic response (the slides call it the cerebral ischemic response);
reabsorption of tissue fluids;
release of endogenous vasoconstrictors: epinephrine and norepinephrine from the adrenal medulla, vasopressin from the posterior pituitary, and angiotensin II through the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system;
renal conservation of salt and water.

The baroreceptor reflex. The arterial (high-pressure) baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch fire less as MAP falls, and low-pressure receptors in the atria sense the fall in central blood volume. Sympathetic outflow rises and vagal outflow falls (ANS and Extrinsic Control has the pathway). The response reaches four targets:

Veins. Venoconstriction moves blood from unstressed to stressed volume, so Pms rises and the vascular function curve shifts right.
Heart. Heart rate and contractility rise, so the cardiac function curve shifts up.
Arterioles. Constriction raises SVR, which slows the diastolic runoff of blood from the arteries, so more blood stays in the arterial tree and MAP rises. The price is a higher afterload.
Microcirculation. Arteriolar constriction lowers capillary hydrostatic pressure and lets interstitial fluid move into the blood (below). Constriction in the gut, skin and kidney sends a larger share of the cardiac output to the brain and heart, whose vessels are under local control.

The chemoreceptor reflex. When arterial pressure falls, flow through the carotid and aortic bodies falls too. Their cells become short of O2 even though arterial PO2 is normal, and with the acidosis of poorly perfused tissue the peripheral chemoreceptors add to sympathetic drive and to breathing. Less flow to the brain lowers the pH of the brain’s extracellular fluid, which stimulates the central chemoreceptors as well.
The CNS ischemic response. If MAP falls below about 50 mm Hg, the brain itself becomes ischemic. The vasomotor neurons of the medullary cardiorespiratory center respond to their own lack of blood flow with an intense sympathetic discharge. It is a last-resort mechanism. It produces the strongest vasoconstriction the body can make, but it starts only when pressure is already dangerously low, and if perfusion of the brainstem fails for long, the vasomotor center itself stops working and outflow collapses.
Hormones and the kidneys. Epinephrine and norepinephrine from the adrenal medulla act within seconds to minutes. Vasopressin and angiotensin II constrict vessels and help the kidneys retain water and salt. Lower renal perfusion and sympathetic activity release renin, and aldosterone increases salt retention. Over hours to days, the retained fluid restores blood volume and Pms.


14.3.3 Mobilizing blood from the veins
The lecture’s summary of the venous response: increased venomotor tone lowers the capacitance of the veins, so more of the blood is stressed volume, and Pms rises. Constriction of the veins of the splanchnic bed (gut and liver) and the skin moves blood from these reservoirs toward the heart, into the central compartment. (The slide lists skin, liver and lungs. The splanchnic veins are the largest reservoir under sympathetic control, course errata entry 14; the lungs are part of the central compartment.) On the slides this is “autotransfusion”: the body transfuses itself from its own veins. In the lecture’s words, the regulation of venomotor tone is one of the principal mechanisms by which the cardiac output is controlled.
On the curves (Figure 14.3 B), take it one curve at a time, as the small groups do:

Venoconstriction raises Pms part of the way back. The vascular function curve shifts right again, and the operating point climbs back up the cardiac function curve (point 3): CO and Pra both rise from the injured state.
A faster, stronger heart shifts the cardiac function curve up. The operating point now slides up and to the left along the new vascular function curve (point 4): CO rises further and Pra falls.
Arteriolar constriction raises SVR. It does not appear on these curves, but it holds MAP up at the reduced CO.







Figure 14.3: Hemorrhage on the cardiac and vascular function curves. (A) Injury: blood loss lowers Pms from 7 to 4.5 mm Hg, and the operating point moves from 1 to 2 along the unchanged cardiac function curve. (B) Compensation: venoconstriction raises Pms to 5.5 mm Hg (point 3), and a faster, stronger heart raises the cardiac function curve (point 4). CO is partly restored, at a Pra lower than before the hemorrhage. Faint lines are the curves before the hemorrhage. Illustrative values. Course figure.



The lecture’s review answers the opening question:








Defends
Mechanism
Chain




Cardiac output
Veins
constriction → ↑ Pms → ↑ venous return → ↑ preload → ↑ SV → ↑ CO


Cardiac output
Heart
↑ heart rate and contractility → ↑ CO (less than the rise from Pms)


MAP
Veins
↑ CO (from above) → ↑ arterial blood volume → ↑ MAP


MAP
Arteries
constriction → ↑ SVR → ↑ arterial blood volume → ↑ MAP



The veins do more for cardiac output than the heart does, which is what Figure 14.3 B shows: the step from 2 to 3 is larger than the step from 3 to 4. The net result of a moderate, compensated hemorrhage is a CO below normal, a low Pra, a fast heart rate, an SVR raised enough to make up for the lower CO, and a MAP close to normal.






WarningA common mistake



The ventricle fills from the atrium. It does not “equilibrate with Pms,” and a lower Pms does not make the mitral valve close early; the valve closes when the ventricle starts to contract. After hemorrhage the lower Pms means less venous return and a lower filling pressure, so the ventricle reaches a smaller end-diastolic volume on the same EDPVR (course errata entry 16).




14.3.4 Breathing and positive pressure
Venous return rises during inspiration. The diaphragm descends, pressure in the chest falls around the right atrium and great veins, pressure in the abdomen rises, and blood moves toward the heart. The opposite happens when pressure in the chest is raised. The lecture’s clinical correlation: blood pressure and cardiac output may fall precipitously if a marginally compensated patient is intubated and given positive-pressure ventilation.
↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↑ Pra → ↓ venous return → ↓ RV end-diastolic volume → ↓ RV stroke volume → ↓ CO
Pra rises because the pressure around the heart rises. That cuts the gradient from Pms, so less blood returns. The pressure across the right ventricular wall, which is what fills it, does not rise, so the ventricle fills less. A patient whose pressure is held up by venoconstriction has no reserve left to absorb the loss of venous return.


14.3.5 The microcirculation: reabsorbing tissue fluid
The Starling equation from Microcirculation and Local Control applies here. The course writes it as
\[Q_f = K\left[(P_c - P_i) - \sigma(\pi_c - \pi_i)\right]\]
and the lecture slide writes the same balance as outward pressures (Pc + πi) minus inward pressures (Pi + πc). The lecture contrasts two cases. In severe malnutrition, plasma protein and πc fall, the inward pressure falls, and filtration rises: edema. In a low-volume state such as hemorrhage, arteriolar constriction and the low venous pressure lower Pc, the outward pressure falls, and fluid is reabsorbed from the interstitium into the capillaries.
This reabsorption is a second “autotransfusion,” from the tissues rather than the veins. Up to about 1 L of fluid per hour can be returned to the circulation. The fluid brings little protein with it, so it dilutes the plasma proteins and lowers πc, which slows further reabsorption (Figure 14.4).






Figure 14.4: Arterial pressure (solid) and plasma colloid osmotic pressure (dashed) after a rapid hemorrhage, schematic after the experiment shown in the lecture, in which 45% of the blood volume was withdrawn from cats. Pressure falls during bleeding and recovers within an hour. Colloid osmotic pressure falls steadily, because reabsorbed tissue fluid, which carries little protein, dilutes the plasma. The lecture’s figure continues to 6 h: the pressure held for about two hours and then fell steadily, because a loss this large was not compensated for long (see the decompensation box below, not examined). Approximate values. Course figure.





14.3.6 Why 1 L can be compensated and 2 L cannot
The course’s numbers explain the cliff. Total blood volume is about 5 L, and about 70% of it is in the veins. Sympathetic venoconstriction can mobilize about 30% of venous volume:
\[5\ \text{L} \times 0.7 \times 0.3 \approx 1\ \text{L}\]
So the veins can put back about 1 L of stressed volume. A hemorrhage of 1 L can be largely made up by venoconstriction, with Pms and venous return held near normal. Once the reserve is spent, every further loss comes straight out of stressed volume, and Pms, venous return and CO fall steeply (Figure 14.5).






Figure 14.5: The venous reserve in hemorrhage, in a simple model of the systemic circulation (blood volume 5 L, unstressed volume 3.6 L, compliance 0.2 L/mm Hg, so Pms starts at 7 mm Hg). Dashed: no reflexes, so each liter lost lowers Pms by 5 mm Hg. Solid: venoconstriction makes up about 85% of each liter lost, until it has recruited 1 L of unstressed volume (at about 1.2 L of blood lost, dashed line), and the heart is stimulated. Pms and CO fall slowly until then and steeply after (shaded). Illustrative values. Course figure.



A young person with healthy reflexes can lose a good deal of blood before the pressure falls. That does not mean the person is safe. The normal pressure is being held up by intense vasoconstriction, and flow to the gut, kidney and skin may already be too low. The clues are a fast heart rate, a narrow pulse pressure (a small stroke volume), cool, pale skin from cutaneous vasoconstriction, and fast breathing from chemoreceptor drive. A falling blood pressure is a late sign.






NoteBackground: decompensation (not examined)





The lecture marks these as not tested. If hemorrhage is severe or prolonged, the circulation can enter a downward spiral in which pressure, after recovering for a time, falls again and does not come back.

Acidosis from poorly perfused tissue reduces the responsiveness of the heart and vessels to catecholamines.
Cardiac dysfunction. Left coronary perfusion pressure (aortic diastolic pressure minus LVEDP) is low, tachycardia shortens diastole, and the heart’s O2 demand is high, so the heart becomes ischemic and pumps less (Coronary Circulation).
CNS depression and loss of sympathetic tone, once the brainstem is underperfused for long.
Clotting becomes abnormal: too much at first, too little later.
Organ failure, of the kidney and the liver among others.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 14  Cardiovascular Integration and Adaptation
text:
14.4 Myocardial infarction and heart failure
The lecture’s second case is a patient brought to the emergency department whose ECG shows a rate of about 115/min and ST-segment elevation: a heart attack. (The leads that show the elevation point to the injured territory and so to the artery. The lecture’s lead-and-artery table is in Coronary Circulation, in the Background box on ST changes. Reading ST changes is not examined in this course.) The question is the same as for hemorrhage. What has the injury done to the pump, and how does the body defend cardiac output and pressure?

14.4.1 The injury
An infarct lowers contractility, so the ESPVR is flatter (Figure 14.1 B). Ejection ends when the ventricle reaches the ESPVR, which now happens at a larger end-systolic volume, so stroke volume falls (course errata entry 17). Because more blood is left in the ventricle at the end of systole, the end-diastolic volume rises a little even before any reflex acts. Less stroke volume means less cardiac output and a lower arterial pressure, and the same reflexes as in hemorrhage are set off.
On the curves (Figure 14.6), the cardiac function curve shifts down, and the operating point slides down and to the right along the unchanged vascular function curve (point 2). CO falls, and Pra rises, because the heart is no longer pumping out what comes back. That combination, poor forward flow and a higher filling pressure behind the heart, is what the notes call congestion plus poor perfusion.


14.4.2 The compensation
The lecture asks what the compensation is trying to achieve. With a flatter ESPVR, the way to get stroke volume back is to fill the ventricle more. The baroreflex constricts the veins, and the low renal perfusion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, so over days the kidneys retain salt and water and raise blood volume. Pms rises, the vascular function curve shifts right, and the operating point climbs the weakened cardiac function curve (point 3). On the P-V loop (Figure 14.1 B, dashed), the ventricle fills to a larger end-diastolic volume on the same EDPVR, and stroke volume is partly restored, at a higher LVEDP. Sympathetic drive also raises heart rate and the contractility of the remaining muscle, which lifts the weak cardiac function curve a little; Figure 14.6 leaves that out to show the effect of volume alone.






Figure 14.6: Heart failure on the cardiac and vascular function curves. (1) Before the injury. (2) Lower contractility shifts the cardiac function curve down: CO falls and Pra rises. (3) Venoconstriction and fluid retention raise Pms from 7 to 10 mm Hg: CO recovers part of the way and Pra rises more. (4) Retaining still more fluid (Pms 13) raises Pra a lot for a small gain in CO, because the weak heart is on the flat part of its curve. CO stays below its value before the injury. In the single-pump model left atrial pressure rises with Pra. Illustrative values. Course figure.





14.4.3 The price: higher filling pressure
The lecture’s next question is whether these compensations are really good. Raising Pms restores CO in the only way a weak heart allows, by filling it more, and filling it more means higher filling pressures. The higher LVEDP is passed back through the left atrium and pulmonary veins to the pulmonary capillaries. Clinically it is estimated as the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP), which approximates left atrial pressure (Pulmonary Circulation describes the measurement). By the Starling equation, a higher capillary hydrostatic pressure drives filtration, and when it exceeds what the lymphatics can carry away, fluid enters the lung: pulmonary edema, seen on the chest radiograph (Pulmonary Circulation). On the right side, a higher Pra raises venous and capillary pressure in the body, which causes peripheral edema.
The weaker the heart, the flatter its curve, and the worse the trade. Going from point 3 to point 4 in Figure 14.6, more fluid buys little CO and a lot of pressure. The other compensations have prices too. Tachycardia shortens diastole and raises myocardial O2 demand, and arteriolar constriction raises afterload, which a failing ventricle handles poorly.
When the infarct is large, these effects feed on each other: the lecture’s last diagram shows the spiral of cardiogenic shock. Low cardiac output and a high LVEDP lower coronary perfusion pressure (aortic diastolic pressure minus LVEDP), the higher wall tension raises O2 consumption, the lungs become congested, the compensatory vasoconstriction, tachycardia and salt and water retention add to the load, and inflammatory mediators released after the injury lower SVR and contractility further. Ischemia spreads, and without treatment the spiral ends in organ failure and death.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 14  Cardiovascular Integration and Adaptation
text:
14.5 Cardiac tamponade
The injury lecture does not cover tamponade. The small groups do (Small Group 1, Case 3, and Small Group 2, Section 5), and this section follows them at their depth.
Fluid in the pericardial space raises the pressure around the heart. The thin-walled, low-pressure right heart is compressed first. The left ventricle, with its thick wall and higher pressure, is less affected, but less blood reaches it through the lungs.
The injury. The heart cannot fill. In the small groups’ P-V loop the ventricle fills along a stiffer curve and, at the same end-diastolic pressure, reaches a smaller end-diastolic volume (The Cardiac Pump). The process diagram is the one for any fall in preload:
↓ filling (↓ EDV) → ↓ SV → ↓ CO → ↓ arterial blood volume → ↓ BP
On the curves, the problem is in the heart, so the cardiac function curve shifts down: at any Pra the compressed heart fills and pumps less. The operating point slides down and to the right along the unchanged vascular function curve. CO falls and Pra rises. The high Pra is passed back to the jugular veins, which is why the neck veins are distended.
The compensation. The baroreflex responds as in hemorrhage. Heart rate and contractility rise, which lifts the cardiac function curve part of the way. Sympathetic venoconstriction raises Pms, which shifts the vascular function curve right and drives more blood into the compressed heart, at the cost of a still higher Pra. Arteriolar constriction raises SVR and holds MAP, and the microcirculation reabsorbs fluid and redirects flow to the brain and heart.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 14  Cardiovascular Integration and Adaptation
text:
14.6 Septic shock

14.6.1 What sepsis does to the circulation
The injury lecture does not cover sepsis. This section uses the high-output pattern on the pulse pressure and shock slide of Control of Cardiac Output and the course’s convention for drawing it on the curves.
Septic shock is a distributive shock. Inflammatory mediators act on the vessels in two ways:

Arteriolar dilation. SVR falls. Blood runs off the arteries quickly, so diastolic pressure falls, and the heart, facing a low afterload, ejects a larger stroke volume.
Venodilation and capillary leak. Dilated veins have a larger unstressed volume, and leaky capillaries let plasma escape into the tissues. Both lower stressed volume, so Pms falls and the vascular function curve shifts left.

Sympathetic drive then raises heart rate and contractility and constricts the veins as far as it can against the mediators. The cardiac function curve shifts up, and Pms recovers part of the way (Figure 14.7 A). The result, in the pattern on that slide, is a CO that is normal or high, a low Pra, a wide pulse pressure, and a low MAP.
Why is MAP low when CO is not? Because MAP − Pra = CO × SVR, and SVR has fallen more than CO has risen (Figure 14.7 B). In the course’s phrase, CO ≠ BP.






Figure 14.7: Septic shock. (A) On the curves: venodilation and capillary leak lower Pms and shift the vascular function curve left, while the lower afterload raises the cardiac function curve a little (2, dotted curves); sympathetic drive then raises the cardiac function curve further and recovers part of Pms (3). CO ends near or above normal, at a low Pra. (B) MAP from MAP = CO × SVR + Pra for three states. Compensated hemorrhage holds MAP near normal with a lower CO and a raised SVR; sepsis has a normal CO and a low MAP because SVR is low. SVR in mm Hg·min/L. Illustrative values. Course figure.



Sepsis can also be a low-output state. A patient who is septic and volume depleted, or whose heart is depressed, has a low Pms or a low cardiac function curve, a low CO and a narrow pulse pressure.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The peer-educator notes list septic shock under “flattened VR slope” and ask why sepsis causes “both ↓ Pms and ↓ slope of VR.” A flatter vascular function curve would mean a higher RVR. Sepsis lowers SVR, and SVR is not RVR. In this course, RVR changes are treated as minor and ignored except in exercise, so draw sepsis as a leftward shift of the vascular function curve (lower Pms from venodilation and fluid loss) with its slope unchanged (course errata entry 35), and put the low SVR into MAP = CO × SVR. The large effect of sepsis on venous return comes from the fall in Pms.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 14  Cardiovascular Integration and Adaptation
section: 14.7 Working back from the operating point to the cause
text:
14.7 Working back from the operating point to the cause
A common error is to find the new operating point correctly and then name the wrong cause. The Control of Cardiac Output chapter gives the rule for a single shift. With injury and compensation in the same problem, it takes a few more steps:

Name the state. Before, injury or compensated? An injury moves one curve; compensation usually moves the other. (Sepsis is the exception: its low afterload lifts the cardiac function curve a little at the same time.)
For a single shift, ask which curve the new point still sits on, using the same-direction and opposite-direction rule from Control of Cardiac Output. This test works only when one curve has moved. If Pra did not change while CO did, or the change is larger than one curve could produce, both curves moved; go to step 3.
If both moved, take them one at a time. Move one curve, find the intermediate point, then move the other. Hemorrhage with compensation in Figure 14.3 B is the model: 2 to 3 is the veins, 3 to 4 is the heart. Compared with point 1, point 4 has a lower CO and a lower Pra, which on its own would look like a vascular shift alone.
Then find the pressure. Use MAP − Pra = CO × SVR. The curves do not show SVR.












Injury: curve that moves
Injury: CO, Pra
Compensation: curve that moves
After compensation




Hemorrhage
Vascular, left (Pms ↓)
↓, ↓
Vascular right (venoconstriction), cardiac up
CO partly restored, Pra low, SVR ↑, MAP near normal


Heart failure
Cardiac, down
↓, ↑
Vascular right (venoconstriction, fluid retention)
CO partly restored, Pra high, congestion


Tamponade
Cardiac, down (impaired filling)
↓, ↑
Cardiac up (HR, contractility), vascular right
CO partly restored, Pra high (distended neck veins), SVR ↑


Septic shock
Vascular, left (Pms ↓); cardiac up a little (low afterload); SVR ↓
↓, ↓
Cardiac up, vascular part way back
CO normal or high, Pra low, SVR ↓, MAP low









WarningA common mistake



“Pra is high, so Pms must be high” is the wrong inference in heart failure. Right after the injury, Pms has not changed at all; Pra rose because the point slid down the unchanged vascular function curve. Pms rises only later, with compensation. In the same way, “CO is back to normal” after a hemorrhage does not mean the blood volume is back. It means venoconstriction and the heart have made up for it, with a raised SVR and a fast heart rate.








TipTry it



The Circulation Lab runs a hemorrhage and a tamponade in a model circulation [2]. Its starting scenarios include a 500 mL hemorrhage and pericardial fluid of 200 or 400 mL, and you can drain the fluid or replace the blood and watch the pressure-volume loop and the cardiac function and vascular function curves recover.
