title: 14  Cardiovascular Integration and Adaptation
text:
14.8 Check your understanding

Why is a normal blood pressure a poor sign that a bleeding patient is safe? Which findings appear before the pressure falls, and what does each one tell you?


Answer

Pressure is defended by venoconstriction (which restores Pms), a faster and stronger heart, and arteriolar constriction (which raises SVR), so MAP can stay near normal while blood volume is low and flow to the gut, skin and kidney is already reduced. The venous reserve is about 1 L, and once it is used up the pressure can fall quickly. Earlier signs: a fast heart rate (baroreflex), a narrow pulse pressure (small stroke volume), cool, pale skin (cutaneous vasoconstriction) and fast breathing (chemoreceptor drive). A falling pressure is a late sign.

In the days after a large heart attack, the kidneys retain salt and water, and CO and Pra both rise compared with the day of the infarct. Which curve moved? Why does each further rise in Pms buy less CO in this patient than it would in a healthy person?


Answer

CO and Pra moved in the same direction, so the operating point slid up the cardiac function curve: the vascular function curve shifted right as fluid retention raised blood volume and Pms. The weak heart’s cardiac function curve is low and flat. Each rightward shift of the vascular function curve meets it where it has almost stopped rising, so most of the extra Pms shows up as a higher Pra rather than a higher CO. A healthy heart’s curve is still rising steeply over the same range, so the same shift would raise CO much more.

One patient is compensating for a hemorrhage: Pra 2 mm Hg, CO 3.8 L/min, MAP 88 mm Hg. Another has septic shock: Pra 1 mm Hg, CO 6 L/min, MAP 60 mm Hg. Estimate the SVR of each and compare it with a normal value of about 18 mm Hg·min/L. Where does each patient’s problem lie?


Answer

SVR = (MAP − Pra)/CO. Hemorrhage: (88 − 2)/3.8 ≈ 23 mm Hg·min/L, above normal. Sympathetic arteriolar constriction has raised SVR enough to hold MAP despite the low CO; the problem is volume. Sepsis: (60 − 1)/6 ≈ 10 mm Hg·min/L, about half of normal. CO is above normal, so the low pressure is not a pump or volume problem; it comes from arteriolar dilation.

A patient with heart failure and congestion receives, on the same day, one treatment that raises contractility and another that makes the kidneys excrete salt and water. By the next morning CO has risen from 3.5 to 4.0 L/min and Pra has fallen from 14 to 6 mm Hg. A classmate says that because CO and Pra moved in opposite directions, only the cardiac function curve moved. What has the classmate missed, and what did each treatment do to the curves?


Answer

The opposite-direction rule identifies a single shift, and here two treatments each moved a curve. The treatment that raised contractility moved the cardiac function curve up; by itself that would raise CO and lower Pra. The loss of salt and water lowered blood volume and Pms and moved the vascular function curve left; by itself that would lower both CO and Pra. Taken one at a time, the two shifts add up to a Pra that falls more than the rise in contractility alone would produce and a CO that rises less. The failing heart’s curve is flat at a high Pra, so removing volume there costs little CO. The size of the Pra fall, 8 mm Hg for a modest rise in CO, is the clue that both curves moved.

A man compensating for a hemorrhage has a MAP of 70 mm Hg and a normal arterial PO2 of 95 mm Hg, yet his carotid bodies are firing hard and he is breathing fast. How can the carotid bodies sense a shortage of O2 when the arterial PO2 is normal, and what does their firing add to his compensation?


Answer

The carotid bodies respond to the O2 supply of their own cells, and that depends on how much blood flows through them as well as on its PO2. With arterial pressure low, flow through the carotid bodies falls, so their cells run short of O2 even though each milliliter of blood is normally oxygenated. Acid from poorly perfused tissue stimulates them as well. Their firing adds sympathetic drive on top of the baroreflex (more vasoconstriction and a faster heart) and drives breathing. Deeper breaths lower the pressure in the chest, which helps venous return a little.

Mean arterial pressure falls to 40 mm Hg. What response does this trigger, how does it differ from the baroreceptor reflex, and why is it called a last resort?


Answer

The CNS ischemic response. The vasomotor center itself becomes ischemic and responds with a massive sympathetic discharge, stronger than anything the baroreflex produces. The baroreflex senses arterial stretch and works across the normal range of pressures. The ischemic response begins only below about 50 mm Hg, when the brain is already underperfused, and if perfusion stays that low the center fails.

title: 15  Cardiovascular Adaptation to Exercise
text:
15.1 How much more is needed
Hemorrhage, heart failure and sepsis test how the circulation defends itself when something breaks (Cardiovascular Integration and Adaptation). Exercise tests it from the other side: nothing is broken, but the demand rises tenfold. If you want to see how a system works as a whole, and where its limits are, push it. This chapter follows the cardiovascular side. The respiratory response, O2 extraction and cardiopulmonary exercise testing are in Physiology of Exercise.
At rest a young adult consumes about 3.5 mL of O2 per kilogram per minute. At maximal exercise an average healthy young adult reaches about 35 mL/kg/min, a tenfold rise. Elite endurance athletes reach roughly 80 to 97 mL/kg/min. Some animals go much further: racehorses about 180, sled dogs about 240, and the pronghorn about 300 mL/kg/min.
Almost all the extra O2 goes to working skeletal muscle, and it has to be carried there by blood. The circulation meets the demand in two ways: it raises the cardiac output, and it sends most of that output to the muscles that need it. Muscles also pull more O2 out of each liter of blood (the arteriovenous O2 difference widens), which the pulmonary chapter covers.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 15  Cardiovascular Adaptation to Exercise
text:
15.2 The controls
Many signals act at once (Figure 15.1). The neural ones converge on the medullary cardiorespiratory center (the slide’s figure calls it the medullary cardiovascular control center), which raises sympathetic outflow and lowers vagal outflow. The local and mechanical ones act directly in the muscles and veins.






Figure 15.1: The controls of the cardiovascular response to exercise. Neural inputs (blue) converge on the medulla and raise sympathetic and lower vagal outflow to the heart, the veins and the arterioles of inactive tissues. Local and mechanical effects (tan) act in the working muscle and its veins. Course figure, adapted from Boron and Boulpaep, Medical Physiology [1], as used in the lecture.




15.2.1 Central command
The cerebral cortex sends signals to the motor neurons and, in parallel, to the medullary cardiorespiratory center. This central command is feed-forward: it raises sympathetic outflow to the heart and vessels and lowers parasympathetic outflow before any metabolic signal has had time to build up. It starts even with the anticipation of exercise. Heart rate rises at the starting line, before the race begins. It continues as long as the motor command does.
The lecture asks what central command would do on its own. A faster, stronger heart and venoconstriction would raise cardiac output somewhat. But sympathetic nerves constrict arterioles throughout the body, skeletal muscle included, so on its own central command would raise blood pressure without sending much more blood to the muscles. The large rise in muscle flow needs the next mechanism.


15.2.2 Metabolic dilation in active muscle
The major vascular adjustment to exercise is local. Contracting muscle releases metabolites (lower PO2, higher PCO2 and H+, K+, adenosine and others), and these dilate its arterioles (Microcirculation and Local Control). Blood flow through active muscle can rise about twentyfold. Circulating epinephrine from the adrenal medulla adds some β2 dilation (Other Special Circulations). The sympathetic nerves themselves constrict muscle arterioles; the vasodilator nerve fibers to active muscle drawn on the slide’s textbook figure are not part of this course.
This happens even though sympathetic outflow to the same muscle is rising. In active muscle, the local metabolites blunt the response of the arterioles to sympathetic constriction, so local control wins. That is functional sympatholysis. In inactive tissue the sympathetic signal is not opposed, and the arterioles constrict. The same rise in sympathetic outflow therefore has opposite net effects in active and inactive beds, and that is how blood is redistributed toward the muscles that need it.
Dilation of so many muscle arterioles lowers SVR. A lower SVR keeps afterload from rising much even as MAP rises and CO quadruples, which lets the stronger heart eject a larger stroke volume. Slide 9 calls this a reduction in afterload: the load is small for the flow being pumped, even though arterial pressure is a little higher than at rest. The course also treats this dilation, together with the muscle pump below, as lowering RVR, which is why exercise is the one setting where the slope of the vascular function curve matters.


15.2.3 Where the blood goes
At rest, skeletal muscle receives about 15% of a cardiac output of about 5 L/min. At maximal exercise it receives about 80% of a cardiac output four times larger (Figure 15.2).






Figure 15.2: Where the cardiac output goes as O2 consumption rises, for a 70 kg adult (3.5 to 35 mL/kg/min). Total output rises from 5 to 20 L/min. Skeletal muscle flow rises from about 15% to about 80% of the total. Gut and kidney flow falls. Heart flow rises with the heart’s own work, and brain flow stays nearly constant. Skin flow first falls, then rises as the body heats, then falls again near maximal exercise. Illustrative values. Course figure, after the figure used in the lecture.




Skeletal muscle takes most of the increase, under local metabolic control.
Heart. Coronary flow rises in proportion to the heart’s extra work, also under metabolic control (Coronary Circulation).
Brain. Flow stays nearly constant. Cerebral vessels are under local control.
Gut and kidney. Sympathetic constriction reduces their flow, and splanchnic venoconstriction moves blood from that large venous reservoir into the central circulation (Other Special Circulations).
Skin has a triphasic response. Early in exercise, sympathetic constriction lowers skin flow. As core temperature rises, the hypothalamus dilates skin vessels to lose heat, and skin flow rises. In strenuous exercise near the maximum, skin vessels constrict again, because the muscles and the blood pressure compete with temperature control for a cardiac output that can rise no further, and core temperature keeps climbing.



15.2.4 The muscle and respiratory pumps
Contracting muscle squeezes the veins inside it. One-way valves let blood go only toward the heart, so each contraction pushes blood back to the central circulation, and each relaxation lets the veins refill from the capillaries. The small groups describe the rhythmically contracting muscles with their valved veins as a second pump in series with the heart. The course lumps the skeletal muscle pump into RVR: the pump lowers the effective resistance to venous return.
Breathing helps in the same way. Each deeper, faster breath lowers the pressure in the chest around the right atrium and great veins and raises the pressure in the abdomen as the diaphragm descends, so blood moves from the abdomen into the chest.


15.2.5 The exercise pressor reflex
Contracting muscle also sends signals back to the brain. Mechanoreceptors respond to stretch and pressure in the working muscle, and chemoreceptors in the muscle (metaboreceptors) respond to the metabolites that accumulate there. Their afferents reach the medullary center and raise sympathetic outflow. This exercise pressor reflex raises heart rate, contractility and blood pressure. Its metabolite-sensing part, the muscle metaboreflex, grows when muscle flow cannot keep up with demand, for example in heavy or sustained contraction.
The arterial chemoreceptors add sympathetic drive mainly in heavy exercise, when lactic acid lowers the blood pH. In moderate exercise, arterial PO2, PCO2 and pH stay close to normal.


15.2.6 Baroreflex resetting
In exercise, blood pressure and heart rate rise together. At rest, a rise in pressure would make the baroreflex slow the heart, so the baroreflex cannot be working the same way. It is not switched off. Central command and the muscle afferents reset it to regulate around a higher pressure and over a higher range of heart rates (Figure 15.3). At the new operating point the reflex still works: a sudden fall in pressure during exercise still speeds the heart, and a sudden rise still slows it. The course’s phrase is “reset, not turned off.” The flowchart on slide 9 shows the reset reflex at work. Dilation of so many muscle arterioles tends to lower arterial pressure, the baroreceptors sense it, and the reflex raises heart rate and constricts the arterioles of inactive muscle, gut, skin and kidney.






Figure 15.3: Baroreflex resetting, schematic. Each curve shows the heart rate the baroreflex produces at each MAP. In exercise the curve shifts to higher pressures and higher heart rates. The operating point moves to a higher MAP and heart rate but stays on a steep part of the new curve, so the reflex still buffers changes in pressure. Illustrative values. Course figure.



The slides describe functional sympatholysis, the exercise pressor reflex, the muscle metaboreflex and baroreflex resetting without naming them. This chapter uses the names so each mechanism has a handle.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 15  Cardiovascular Adaptation to Exercise
section: 15.3 The heart has to keep up
text:
15.3 The heart has to keep up
Venous return can rise only if the heart pumps it on. Sympathetic stimulation through β1 receptors, together with less vagal outflow, changes three properties of the heart:

Chronotropy: heart rate rises.
Inotropy (contractility): the ESPVR steepens, so the ventricle ejects more and empties further at a given end-diastolic volume.
Lusitropy: the ventricle relaxes faster, so it fills quickly enough in a shorter diastole.

These are three separate properties. Contractility means inotropy only (course errata entry 2). All three raise cardiac output, and on the cardiac function curve all three shift the curve up.
Figure 15.4 shows how the main variables change as the work rate rises.






Figure 15.4: Cardiovascular variables during graded exercise. Heart rate rises steadily. Stroke volume rises early and then levels off, and falls a little near the maximum. Cardiac output rises with work. Systolic pressure rises much more than diastolic, so pulse pressure widens, and mean pressure rises only modestly because SVR falls by half. The arteriovenous O2 difference widens. This subject’s CO rises about threefold, less than the fourfold in the table below, so SVR falls by half rather than to a third; both are illustrations. Values read approximately from the lecture’s figure and made consistent with CO = HR × SV, MAP ≈ CO × SVR and the Fick principle. Adapted from Berne and colleagues, Physiology, 5th edition [2], as used in the lecture, where the resistance panel is labeled total peripheral resistance.

title: 15  Cardiovascular Adaptation to Exercise
section: 15.4 Exercise on the cardiac and vascular function curves
text:
15.4 Exercise on the cardiac and vascular function curves
Exercise moves both curves, and the vascular function curve changes in two ways at once. Taking the changes one at a time shows what each contributes (Figure 15.5).

Venoconstriction raises Pms (panel A). The vascular function curve shifts right. Alone, this would slide the operating point up the resting cardiac function curve: a modest rise in CO, with Pra rising too.
Muscle dilation and the muscle pump lower RVR (panel B). The vascular function curve becomes much steeper around the same Pms. With the resting heart, the operating point climbs further along the flattening cardiac function curve, and Pra rises a lot. The heart has become the bottleneck: venous return is offered, and the heart cannot pump it on without a high filling pressure.
The heart’s curve rises (panel C). Faster rate, more contractility and faster relaxation shift the cardiac function curve up. The operating point slides up and to the left along the new, steep vascular function curve, to a CO about four times rest.
The result (panel D). Compared with rest, CO has risen about fourfold while Pra is about the same. The exercise lecture in the pulmonary block quotes a six- to eightfold rise, which is what trained athletes reach. A typical young adult reaches about four times rest. The pulmonary Physiology of Exercise chapter covers the rest of that lecture: maximal heart rate, the “cardiac limited” point, and the O2 pulse as a stand-in for stroke volume.

The small group draws the heart first, following slide 11: Pra then falls before the vessels bring it back up. Either order ends at the same operating point.






Figure 15.5: Exercise on the cardiac and vascular function curves, one change at a time. Open circle: rest (CO 5 L/min, Pra 2 mm Hg). (A) Venoconstriction raises Pms from 7 to 10 mm Hg. (B) A lower RVR (1.0 to 0.4 mm Hg·min/L) steepens the vascular function curve; with the resting heart, Pra rises to about 7 mm Hg. (C) A stronger, faster heart raises the cardiac function curve, and the operating point moves to CO 20 L/min at Pra 2 mm Hg. (D) Rest and exercise compared. Illustrative values chosen to match the lecture’s CO of about 20 L/min. Course figure.



Seeing that the new operating point is higher is not the answer. In exercise, an unchanged Pra with a large rise in CO means that both curves moved: if only the vascular function curve had moved, Pra would have risen (panels A and B), and if only the heart had changed, Pra would have fallen. The Pra stays put because the vessels offer more venous return and the heart takes it away as fast as it arrives.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The flowchart of the muscle’s mechanical effects (from Boron and Boulpaep) runs: muscle pump → ↑ venous return → ↑ right atrial pressure → ↑ EDP → ↑ EDV → ↑ stroke volume. The integrated table says Pra is about unchanged in exercise. Both are right. The flowchart follows one mechanism by itself, the muscle pump acting on an unchanged heart, as in panel B of Figure 15.5. Once sympathetic stimulation raises the cardiac function curve as well (panel C), the heart pumps the extra venous return on without a higher filling pressure. Stroke volume rises from more venous return, more contractility and a low SVR, and end-diastolic volume rises only a little.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 15  Cardiovascular Adaptation to Exercise
text:
15.5 Strenuous exercise and its limits
As exercise approaches the maximum:

Heart rate approaches the person’s maximal predicted heart rate, if the person is willing to work that hard. Maximal heart rate falls with age.
Stroke volume levels off and begins to fall, because at very high rates diastole becomes too short to fill the ventricle fully.
Skin vessels constrict to keep blood in the muscles and maintain pressure, so heat loss falls and core temperature rises.
Acidosis develops as working muscle makes more lactic acid than can be cleared.

There is a maximal heart rate and a maximal cardiac output, and in health the cardiovascular system, not breathing, limits maximal exercise. The pulmonary chapter shows why the lungs have reserve left at that point.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 15  Cardiovascular Adaptation to Exercise
text:
15.6 When exercise stops
The small group’s case is a runner who collapses just after crossing the finish line of a marathon, having drunk little on the way. While she was running, her pressure was held up by the changes in both curves. Sweating had already lowered her blood volume and Pms. When she stopped, sympathetic outflow and metabolic demand fell, so heart rate and contractility began to return toward rest, and the skeletal muscle pump stopped. In the course’s convention, losing the muscle pump raises RVR, so the vascular function curve flattens. Venous return, CO and blood pressure all fell.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 15  Cardiovascular Adaptation to Exercise
section: 15.7 Is the rise in cardiac output due to the rise in heart rate?
text:
15.7 Is the rise in cardiac output due to the rise in heart rate?
The lecture’s table for a healthy young person:



State
HR (/min)
SV (mL)
CO (L/min)




Rest
70
70
4.9


Exercise
180
110
19.8



Heart rate rises about 2.6-fold and stroke volume about 1.6-fold, so it is tempting to say the heart rate did most of the work. That misses what is happening to stroke volume. If you pace a resting heart from 70 to 180/min, cardiac output barely changes: diastole shortens, the ventricle fills less, and stroke volume falls. The vessels are still returning the same amount of blood, and the heart can only pump what comes back. In exercise, stroke volume rises at a rate of 180/min. That can happen only because venous return has risen (higher Pms, lower RVR, the muscle and respiratory pumps), contractility and lusitropy have risen, and the fall in SVR has kept afterload from rising much. Heart rate matters, but the rise in cardiac output depends on the vessels returning more blood.

15.7.1 A puzzle: epinephrine and a mechanical pump
The lecture ends with an experiment in an animal model of the circulation. Epinephrine is infused:



State
HR (/min)
SV (mL)
CO (L/min)




Before epinephrine
120
35
4.2


After epinephrine
160
65
10.4



The obvious reading is that epinephrine made the heart beat faster and harder. Then the heart is replaced by a mechanical pump set to keep right atrial pressure constant, the same dose of epinephrine is given, and the cardiac output rises in the same way. The pump has no receptors for epinephrine. How is this possible?
The answer is in the venous return equation. A pump that holds Pra constant pumps out whatever arrives. Epinephrine constricts the veins, which raises Pms, so at the same Pra venous return rises (Figure 15.6), and the pump delivers it. The rise in cardiac output came from the vessels.






Figure 15.6: The pump experiment on the vascular function curve. A pump that holds Pra fixed (dashed vertical line) pumps out whatever returns. Epinephrine raises Pms (from 6.2 to 12.4 mm Hg in this illustration), so venous return at the same Pra rises from 4.2 to 10.4 L/min, the values in the lecture’s table. Illustrative values. Course figure.



So what does the heart do? The lecture gives two answers:

The blood in the peripheral vessels, chiefly the veins, has an elastic recoil pressure (Pms) that drives blood back to the heart, and Pra is the back pressure against that flow. The heart controls cardiac output by keeping Pra low.
The heart returns to the systemic circulation the blood that drains out of it into the heart and lungs, and so maintains Pms.

A healthy heart permits a high cardiac output by pumping on whatever the vessels return, without letting Pra rise. The vessels set how much returns. That is why, in exercise, the heart’s curve and the vessels’ curve have to rise together.






WarningA common mistake



Finding the new operating point is not the same as finding its cause. In the epinephrine experiment, heart rate and stroke volume both rose, yet the rise in cardiac output was produced by the veins. In exercise, a higher CO at an unchanged Pra means both curves moved. Before you name a cause, ask which curve the new point lies on. That test works only when one curve has moved: if Pra did not change while CO did, or the change is larger than one curve could produce, both curves moved, and you take them one at a time.








NoteBackground: training (not examined) and central fatigue





The lecture marks training effects as not on the test. Endurance training raises maximal O2 consumption. At rest, vagal tone is higher and sympathetic tone lower, so a trained person has a lower resting heart rate and a larger resting stroke volume. Trained muscles have lower vascular resistance, more capillaries, more mitochondria and more oxidative enzyme activity, and they extract more O2 during exercise. Maximal cardiac output is higher because maximal stroke volume is higher. Genetic factors matter as well.
Fatigue is not only a matter of the muscles and heart. The lecture shows studies in which reduced brain oxygenation and metabolism during exhausting exercise went with reduced activation of the muscles, a central fatigue that is more than motivation or willpower.

title: 15  Cardiovascular Adaptation to Exercise
text:
15.8 Check your understanding

A sprinter crouches in the blocks before the starting gun. What is happening to her heart rate and venous tone, and why can this not by itself deliver the muscle blood flow she is about to need?


Answer

Central command, a feed-forward signal from the cortex, raises sympathetic outflow and lowers vagal outflow before the race starts. Heart rate and contractility rise, and the veins constrict and raise Pms. But sympathetic nerves also constrict arterioles in skeletal muscle. The large rise in muscle flow needs local metabolic dilation, which begins only when the muscles start working.

An α1 agonist is infused into the brachial artery at the same dose on two occasions: once with the forearm at rest, and once while the subject does rhythmic handgrip exercise. Forearm vascular resistance rises much more at rest. Why?


Answer

In the exercising forearm, the contracting muscle releases metabolites (lower PO2, higher PCO2 and H+, K+, adenosine) that dilate its arterioles and blunt their response to α1 constriction. This is functional sympatholysis, and it opposes a drug at the α1 receptor just as it opposes norepinephrine from the sympathetic nerves. In the resting forearm there are no extra metabolites to oppose the drug, so the arterioles constrict fully and resistance rises a lot.

In exercise, MAP rises from about 93 to about 110 mm Hg while CO rises from 5 to 20 L/min. Roughly what has happened to SVR, and where?


Answer

MAP ≈ CO × SVR, so SVR has gone from about 93/5 ≈ 19 to about 110/20 ≈ 5.5 mm Hg·min/L, under a third of its resting value, a larger fall than in the graded-exercise figure’s subject. The fall comes from metabolic dilation of arterioles in the active muscle, which is a large share of the body’s parallel vascular beds. The constriction in gut, kidney and inactive muscle offsets only a little of it.

Suppose that during exercise the veins constricted and RVR fell as usual, but the cardiac function curve stayed at its resting position. Predict CO and Pra compared with normal exercise.


Answer

The steeper, right-shifted vascular function curve would meet the resting cardiac function curve high on its flat part. CO would rise less than normal, and Pra would rise a lot (panel B of Figure 15.5). The heart, not the vessels, would limit output, and the extra filling pressure would show up as congestion.

During a hard run, blood pressure is 160/80 mm Hg and heart rate 150/min. At rest, a pressure of 160/80 would make the baroreflex slow the heart. Is the baroreflex switched off during exercise?


Answer

No. Central command and the exercise pressor reflex reset it to regulate around a higher pressure and a higher heart rate. A sudden drop in pressure during the run would still speed the heart. The reflex is reset, not turned off.

Stroke volume rises from 70 to 110 mL in exercise even though the heart rate of 180/min shortens filling time. Name the changes that make this possible.


Answer

More venous return (higher Pms from venoconstriction, lower RVR from muscle dilation and the muscle pump, and the respiratory pump), so preload is maintained. Higher contractility, so the ventricle empties further. Faster relaxation (lusitropy), so the ventricle fills quickly enough in a short diastole. A low SVR, which keeps afterload from rising much. If the heart were paced to 180/min at rest, none of these would change, and stroke volume would fall.

title: 16  Coronary Circulation
text:
16.1 Anatomy
The heart pumps for everyone else, and it has to be perfused like everyone else. It is a special case for two reasons. Its muscle uses a great deal of O2 and already takes most of the O2 out of the blood it receives, so it has almost no reserve except more flow. And the muscle that needs the flow squeezes its own vessels shut every time it contracts. Heart disease is the leading cause of death in the United States, and most of it is coronary heart disease: a mismatch between what the myocardium needs and what the coronary arteries can deliver. This chapter is about that balance of supply and demand.
Both coronary arteries arise from the root of the aorta, just above the aortic valve. Their openings sit behind the valve cusps, in the sinuses of the aortic root. When the ventricle relaxes and the valve closes, the column of blood falling back toward the ventricle fills the sinuses and the coronary arteries with it.
The left main coronary artery is short. It divides into two branches that together supply most of the left ventricle and the septum:
The right coronary artery (RCA) runs in the right atrioventricular groove. Its right marginal branch supplies the right ventricle. Near the back of the heart it usually gives off the posterior descending artery (PDA), which runs toward the apex in the posterior interventricular groove. The RCA largely serves the right ventricle, but it also serves part of the left: the inferior (posterior) wall and the back of the septum, about a quarter of the left ventricle. The left ventricle is so much larger than the right that the artery serving the right heart ends up supplying some of it too.
Dominance is named for the artery that gives off the PDA. In most people (roughly two-thirds to four-fifths, depending on the source the lecture uses) the PDA comes from the RCA: a right-dominant heart. In a smaller group it comes from the circumflex (left dominant), and in the rest both contribute (codominant). Small branches from the dominant artery supply the AV node, so in a right-dominant heart an RCA blockage can impair AV conduction as well as the inferior wall. Figure 16.1 summarizes the territories.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 16  Coronary Circulation
text:
the left anterior descending (LAD) artery, running down the front of the heart in the interventricular groove, with diagonal branches over the anterior wall and septal branches into the front of the septum;
the left circumflex artery, running around the left side in the atrioventricular groove, with left marginal branches to the lateral wall.









Figure 16.1: Coronary territories on a short-axis slice through both ventricles, as if looking up from the apex, in a right-dominant heart. The LAD supplies the anterior wall and the front of the septum, the circumflex the lateral wall, and the RCA the right ventricle, the inferior wall and the back of the septum through the PDA. Boundaries vary between people. Schematic. Course figure.




16.1.1 Into the wall
The large coronary arteries are epicardial: they run on the surface of the heart. From them, intramural arteries dive straight through the muscle toward the inside of the wall and branch as they go, ending in a dense network just under the endocardium, the subendocardial plexus (Figure 16.3 A). Every vessel inside the wall is surrounded by muscle that contracts with each beat. The deepest vessels, at the end of the line, sit where the squeeze is strongest. That geometry explains most of what follows.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 16  Coronary Circulation
text:
16.2 Perfusion

16.2.1 A high-demand organ
At 70 beats per minute and 5 L/min, the heart beats about 100,000 times a day and pumps about 7,200 L a day, about 2.8 billion beats over 75 years. It never rests, and it runs almost entirely on aerobic metabolism.
At rest the heart extracts about 70 to 80% of the O2 delivered to it. The body as a whole extracts about 25%. Coronary venous blood is therefore much more desaturated than mixed venous blood, and the heart cannot take much more O2 out of each milliliter of blood when its needs rise. O2 delivery to the myocardium is flow dependent: when the heart needs more O2, coronary blood flow has to rise, and flow, not extraction, is the step that limits how much O2 the myocardium can use (Figure 16.2).






Figure 16.2: Why coronary flow tracks demand. (A) The heart extracts 70 to 80% of the O2 delivered to it at rest, the body as a whole about 25%. (B) Myocardial O2 consumption rises in proportion to coronary blood flow. The line assumes a fixed arterial O2 content of 20 mL/dL and extraction of 0.7; the lecture shows measurements that fall along such a line. Schematic. Course figure.









NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The speaker notes for the slide comparing organs say the heart “consumes almost 100% of the oxygen delivered.” The heart extracts about 70 to 80% at rest (course errata entry 20). Some O2 always remains in coronary venous blood. The point to keep is the one the slide makes: extraction is already high, so more O2 has to come from more flow.




16.2.2 The pressure gradient changes through the cardiac cycle
Flow into the wall needs a pressure difference: the pressure in the epicardial arteries (aortic pressure) minus the pressure the vessels inside the wall are exposed to.
In diastole, the ventricle is relaxed. Aortic pressure is about 80 to 90 mm Hg, and the pressure around the intramural vessels and the subendocardial plexus is close to ventricular diastolic pressure, about 5 to 10 mm Hg. Blood flows readily from the aortic root into the wall.
In systole, the left ventricle generates about 120 mm Hg, as much as the aorta. The contracting muscle compresses the intramural vessels, most of all in the inner layers next to the high-pressure cavity. The pressure difference driving flow into the inner wall falls to about zero, and left coronary flow nearly stops.
The right ventricle generates only about 25 mm Hg in systole. Aortic pressure is higher than RV pressure in systole as well as diastole, so the right coronary circulation keeps flowing through the whole cycle (in health).






Figure 16.3: (A) The coronary vessels of the left ventricular wall. Epicardial arteries on the surface send intramural arteries through the muscle to the subendocardial plexus. In systole the contracting muscle compresses them, most strongly near the endocardium. (B) The pressure difference driving flow into the inner wall (aortic minus ventricular pressure), using the lecture’s values (aortic pressure 80 to 90 mm Hg in diastole and 120 in systole; LV 5 to 10 in diastole and about 120 in systole; RV 5 to 10 in diastole and about 25 in systole). The inner left ventricular wall is perfused in diastole; the right ventricle in both phases. Course figure, after the lecture’s slides.



Figure 16.4 shows what this does to flow. Aortic pressure is highest in systole, yet left coronary flow is lowest then. It falls to nearly zero during isovolumic contraction, when the ventricle squeezes hardest on a closed chamber, recovers only partly during ejection, and is greatest in diastole, peaking early in diastole as the muscle relaxes while aortic pressure is still high. Right coronary flow follows aortic pressure and is, if anything, a little higher in systole.






Figure 16.4: Aortic pressure and left and right coronary blood flow through one cardiac cycle at 75 beats per minute. Left coronary flow is least during systole and greatest in diastole. Right coronary flow continues through systole because aortic pressure exceeds RV pressure. Schematic; values approximate. Course figure, after the lecture’s figure.



The point to carry forward is the one the course states: the left ventricle is perfused only in diastole; the right ventricle is perfused in systole and diastole. Strictly, the outer layers of the left ventricular wall get some flow during ejection, as Figure 16.4 shows; the inner layer gets essentially none. That is why the Control of Cardiac Output chapter cares about diastolic pressure: the elastic aorta keeps pressure up after the valve closes, and that diastolic pressure is what fills the left coronary arteries.


16.2.3 Left coronary perfusion pressure
Because the left ventricle fills its coronary bed in diastole, its perfusion pressure is the diastolic pressure difference:
\[\text{Left coronary perfusion pressure} = \text{aortic DBP} - \text{LVEDP}\]
Aortic diastolic pressure (DBP) pushes blood in. Left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP), the pressure inside the relaxed chamber at the end of filling, is the back pressure that the inner wall and its vessels sit against. With a DBP of 80 and an LVEDP of 8 mm Hg, the perfusion pressure is 72 mm Hg.
Anything that lowers DBP (hemorrhage, vasodilation, a leaky aortic valve) or raises LVEDP (a failing or stiff ventricle, too much filling) lowers left coronary perfusion pressure. A third factor is not in the equation but matters as much: time. The left ventricle is perfused only while it is in diastole, so a fast heart rate, which shortens diastole far more than systole, cuts the time available for flow.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The peer-educator notes add “R side coronary perfusion pressure = aortic diastolic pressure − RV pressure.” The course equation is for the left side only. The right ventricle is perfused in both systole and diastole, so its driving pressure is aortic pressure minus RV pressure through the whole cycle (about 120 − 25 in systole and 85 − 7.5 in diastole, using the lecture’s 5 to 10 mm Hg for both ventricles in diastole), not a diastolic value alone.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 16  Coronary Circulation
text:
16.3 Regulation
Coronary flow is set the way flow is set anywhere: by arteriolar radius. The question is which signals control the radius. As in every special circulation in this block, there are two sets of controls, systemic (autonomic and hormonal) and local, and the useful question is which one wins.

16.3.1 Systemic regulation
The autonomic nervous system acts on the heart in several places at once (the ANS and Extrinsic Control chapter has the detail):








Effector
Sympathetic (NE, epinephrine)
Parasympathetic (ACh)




SA node
β1: faster rate
M2: slower rate


AV node
β1: faster conduction
M2: slower conduction


Myocardium
β1: more contractility
M2: slightly less contractility


Coronary vessels
α1: constriction; β2: dilation
little direct effect



Taken alone, the vascular row predicts that sympathetic activation should lower coronary flow. α1 receptors on coronary smooth muscle constrict the vessels, and the faster heart rate shortens diastole. Yet during exercise or stress, when sympathetic activity is high, coronary flow rises, often several-fold. The rest of the table explains why. Sympathetic stimulation makes the heart beat faster and harder, which raises myocardial O2 demand, and the metabolic dilators that demand produces overwhelm the direct α1 constriction. The net effect of sympathetic activation on the coronary arteries is dilation, through local control.


16.3.2 Local regulation: mechanical (myogenic)
Like other arterioles, coronary arterioles respond to stretch. When perfusion pressure rises, the arteriolar wall is stretched, mechanosensitive channels in the smooth muscle let in Ca2+, and the arteriole constricts. When perfusion pressure falls, there is less stretch and it dilates. Flow is held nearly constant across a range of perfusion pressures (Figure 16.5), which the lecture shows as roughly 60 to 120 mm Hg in its coronary example. Below the range the arterioles are already maximally dilated, and flow falls with pressure. The mechanism is the same myogenic response described in Microcirculation and Local Control, where the course’s general autoregulatory range is 20 to 150 mm Hg. Limits differ between beds and sources; what matters is that flow stays steady across normal pressures and falls once pressure drops below the range.






Figure 16.5: Coronary autoregulation. Across the autoregulatory range, resistance rises with perfusion pressure, so flow changes little. Below it the arterioles are maximally dilated and flow follows pressure. Schematic, using the 60 to 120 mm Hg range of the lecture’s coronary figure. Course figure.



The myogenic response protects the heart when arterial pressure changes. It does not match flow to the heart’s work. That is the job of metabolic control.


16.3.3 Local regulation: metabolic, the dominant control
When the myocardium works harder, or its O2 supply falls short, local dilators build up and widen the coronary arterioles. The lecture names two: adenosine, from the breakdown of ATP in the myocytes, and nitric oxide (NO), from the endothelium (the Microcirculation chapter calls this endothelial control). The slides call these mechanisms “myogenic autoregulation” and “metabolic autoregulation”; the course keeps “autoregulation” for the overall result. NO activates guanylyl cyclase in the smooth muscle, cGMP rises, and the muscle relaxes (the Smooth Muscle chapter has the pathway). Resistance falls, flow rises, and the extra flow brings O2 and washes the metabolites out. Production of the dilators rises with metabolic rate and their removal rises with flow, so flow settles where supply matches demand.
This is the dominant control of coronary flow. Local metabolic control outweighs autonomic control in the heart, which is why coronary flow rises in proportion to myocardial O2 use (Figure 16.2 B) even when sympathetic activity is high. The same is true of the brain (Other Special Circulations). It makes sense: the brain and heart cannot afford to have their supply turned down by a reflex that is defending blood pressure for the rest of the body.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 16  Coronary Circulation
text:
16.4 Cardiac ischemia: supply versus demand
Ischemia is O2 delivery that falls short of O2 demand. Severe or prolonged ischemia kills muscle (infarction). Any cause of ischemia either lowers supply or raises demand.

16.4.1 Decreased supply

Coronary artery obstruction. An atherosclerotic plaque narrows the artery. If its fibrous cap ruptures, a clot forms on it and can block the artery completely, and the muscle beyond the blockage dies. A narrowed artery may supply enough flow at rest but not enough when demand rises, because its downstream arterioles are already partly dilated to make up for the narrowing.
Decreased systemic pressure. Hemorrhage or shock lowers aortic diastolic pressure and with it coronary perfusion pressure.
Decreased O2-carrying capacity. Flow can be normal and delivery still low if each milliliter of blood carries less O2. Arterial O2 content is CaO2 = (1.39 × Hb × SaO2) + (0.003 × PaO2), in mL O2/dL with Hb in g/dL, as the Transport of O2 and CO2 chapter teaches it, so anemia or low saturation lowers delivery at any flow. The coronary slide writes the constants as 1.34 and 0.0031; sources round them differently, and the difference is less than 1 mL/dL.



16.4.2 Increased demand
Four things raise myocardial O2 demand, and each also works against supply:








Increased
Raises demand because
Also affects supply because




Heart rate (tachycardia)
More beats per minute
Diastole shortens, so the left ventricle has less time to be perfused


Contractility
Harder contraction uses more ATP
Greater pressure on the intramural arteries and subendocardial plexus during systole


Preload
More stretch means higher wall tension (Laplace)
Higher LVEDP raises the pressure around the inner wall and lowers perfusion pressure


Afterload
The ventricle must generate more pressure to eject
It is met by more contractility, with the compression that brings



Even so, the healthy heart copes. Higher contractility and afterload raise aortic pressure, which raises coronary perfusion pressure, and metabolic dilation of the arterioles makes up the rest. Ischemia appears when compensation is limited, usually by coronary artery disease: the narrowed artery cannot deliver the extra flow, so a demand the healthy heart would meet easily, such as climbing stairs, outruns supply. The third CV small group (Applied Physiology Cases 3) works through the same reasoning after a myocardial infarction: the occluded vessel lowers flow regionally, a falling DBP lowers perfusion pressure, a faster heart rate shortens perfusion time, and a rising LVEDP raises wall tension and squeezes the subendocardial branches.


16.4.3 The subendocardium is injured first
Ischemia appears first in the inner layer of the left ventricular wall, the subendocardium. Three facts from earlier in the chapter combine:

Systolic compression is strongest next to the cavity, so the inner layer gets essentially no flow in systole and depends entirely on diastole.
In diastole, LVEDP presses on the inner layer from the cavity side. When LVEDP rises, the inner layer’s perfusion pressure falls first.
The subendocardial vessels are at the end of the intramural arteries, the farthest point from the epicardial supply, while wall stress and O2 demand are highest in the inner layers.

So when supply falls or demand rises across the whole heart, as in hemorrhage, severe anemia or a fast tachycardia, the injury is subendocardial. Only when an epicardial artery is blocked completely does the injury extend through the full thickness of the wall (transmural) in that artery’s territory.






TipWhat you need from this



Be able to sort any cause of ischemia into supply or demand, and to say how heart rate, contractility, preload and afterload each change both sides. For the left ventricle, think of three things: aortic diastolic pressure, LVEDP and time in diastole.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 16  Coronary Circulation
text:
16.5 Assessing perfusion and function
The lecture closes with how ischemia is detected in the clinic. These are previews; later courses teach them as clinical skills.
The ECG. Ischemic and injured muscle changes the ECG: the ST segment, the T wave and, after an infarction, pathological Q waves. The details are below as background; the EKG III chapter explains why the ST segment is normally flat.






NoteBackground: ST changes and coronary territories





Ischemia confined to the subendocardium tends to depress the ST segment. Transmural injury tends to elevate it (Figure 16.6). The lecture previews how the leads that show ST elevation point to the injured territory, and so to the artery. ST depression is often diffuse and does not localize this way. Reading ST changes is a second-year skill and is not examined in this course.








Leads
Region of the left ventricle
Usual artery




II, III, aVF
Inferior
RCA (in right-dominant hearts), sometimes circumflex


V1, V2
Septal

V3, V4
Anterior
LAD

Lateral
Circumflex or a diagonal of the LAD









Figure 16.6: The ST segment. (A) Normal: flat and level with the PR segment. (B) ST depression, as in ischemia limited to the subendocardium. (C) ST elevation, as in transmural injury. Synthetic traces on standard ECG paper. Course figure.






Echocardiography. Ultrasound shows the walls moving. Ischemic or infarcted muscle contracts weakly or not at all, so a region that moves poorly points to the artery that supplies it.
Nuclear studies and stress testing. A radioactive tracer that is taken up in proportion to blood flow shows which regions are underperfused. Studies are often done at rest and after exercise on a treadmill, or after a drug that mimics exercise, because a narrowed artery may supply enough at rest and fall short only when demand rises: the supply-and-demand problem of this chapter.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 16  Coronary Circulation
text:
16.6 Check your understanding

A patient has a right-dominant heart. Which artery supplies the inferior wall of the left ventricle, and why might a blockage there slow AV conduction?


Answer

The right coronary artery, through the posterior descending artery. The AV node is supplied by small branches of the dominant artery, so in a right-dominant heart an RCA blockage can make the AV node ischemic as well.

In chronic pulmonary hypertension the right ventricle thickens and develops much higher systolic pressures than normal. Right coronary flow now falls in systole and arrives mostly in diastole, the pattern of the left ventricle. Which layer of the right ventricular wall is now most at risk of ischemia, and why has the right ventricle’s O2 demand risen?


Answer

The subendocardium. Systolic compression is strongest next to the cavity, so once RV pressure is high the inner layer gets little flow in systole and depends on diastole, as the inner layer of the left ventricle does. Its vessels are also at the far end of the intramural arteries. Demand has risen because afterload is up: the right ventricle must generate a much higher pressure to eject into the pulmonary artery. It meets that load with more contractility and with a thicker wall, more muscle that uses O2.

Norepinephrine acting on α1 receptors constricts coronary arteries. Why, then, does coronary blood flow rise when sympathetic activity rises during exercise?


Answer

Sympathetic stimulation also raises heart rate and contractility (β1), which raises myocardial O2 demand. The myocardium releases adenosine and NO, and this metabolic dilation is much stronger than the direct α1 constriction. Local metabolic control outweighs autonomic control in the heart, so the net effect is dilation and higher flow.

A failing left ventricle fills at an LVEDP of 25 mm Hg instead of 8. Why does the subendocardium become ischemic before the outer layers of the wall?


Answer

LVEDP is the pressure in the relaxed cavity, and it presses directly on the inner layer and the subendocardial plexus. The inner layer gets almost no flow in systole, so it depends on diastole, and in diastole its vessels now sit against a back pressure of 25 instead of 8. Its perfusion pressure falls first and most. The outer layers lie farther from the cavity and also get some flow during ejection. At the same time the stretched ventricle has a higher wall tension (Laplace), so demand rises, and wall stress and O2 demand are highest in the inner layers. The subendocardial vessels are also the farthest point from the epicardial supply.

A patient loses a large volume of blood, and her losses are replaced with saline. Her blood pressure and heart rate return to normal, but her hemoglobin is now half its usual value. Is her heart at risk from a supply problem or a demand problem, and why can’t her heart simply extract more O2?


Answer

Supply: each milliliter of blood carries about half as much O2 (CaO2 depends on [Hb]), so delivery falls at any flow. The heart already extracts 70 to 80% of the O2 it receives, so extraction has little room to rise. The only way to restore delivery is more coronary flow, which metabolic dilation provides until the arterioles are fully dilated. If demand rises beyond that, as with exercise or a tachycardia, the subendocardium becomes ischemic first.

Why is a fast heart rate more dangerous to the left ventricle than to the right?


Answer

The left ventricle is perfused only in diastole, and a faster heart rate shortens diastole much more than systole. The right ventricle is also perfused in systole, because aortic pressure stays well above RV pressure, so losing diastolic time costs it less.

title: 17  Other Special Circulations
text:
17.1 Cerebral circulation
Every organ is perfused from the same arterial pressure, so the share of the cardiac output each one gets is set by the resistance of its own arterioles. Two sets of signals compete to set that resistance. Systemic control (sympathetic nerves and circulating hormones) serves the whole body: it defends arterial pressure and moves blood where the body as a whole needs it. Local control (myogenic, metabolic and endothelial mechanisms, from Microcirculation and Local Control) serves the tissue itself. In each bed, one of them usually wins, and which one wins depends on what the organ is for. This chapter takes four beds in turn, asking the same questions of each: why does it matter, how is it built, and who is in charge? The heart and the lungs have their own chapters (Coronary Circulation and Pulmonary Circulation).
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 17  Other Special Circulations
text:
17.1.1 Why it matters
The brain is about 2% of body mass but accounts for about 20% of the body’s basal metabolic rate (Figure 17.1). It stores almost no O2 or glucose, so it depends minute by minute on its blood supply, and it is extremely sensitive to ischemia. Neurons start to fail within minutes of losing flow, well before endothelial cells, glia and the other cells around them. The anatomy (the circle of Willis and its branches) is not tested in this lecture.






Figure 17.1: Share of body mass and share of basal metabolic rate for several organs. The brain, heart, kidneys and liver use far more energy than their mass would suggest. Values approximate, from the lecture’s figure. Course figure.





17.1.2 Systemic regulation
Two reflexes from the ANS and Extrinsic Control chapter protect the brain’s supply, but they do it by acting on the rest of the circulation:

The baroreceptor reflex. Stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch sense arterial pressure. A fall in pressure raises sympathetic output to the heart and vessels and restores arterial pressure, the pressure the brain is perfused from.
The chemoreceptor reflex. Central chemoreceptors in the medulla detect CO2 and pH. Peripheral chemoreceptors detect O2 and CO2 (aortic bodies) or O2, CO2 and pH (carotid bodies). They drive ventilation and sympathetic output.

The cerebral arterioles themselves get little effective sympathetic control. Their tone is set locally.


17.1.3 Local regulation
Myogenic control. Cerebral arterioles constrict when perfusion pressure rises and dilate when it falls, holding cerebral blood flow near 50 mL/100 g/min across perfusion pressures from about 50 to 150 mm Hg (Figure 17.2). Below the range, the arterioles are fully dilated and cannot dilate further, flow falls with pressure, and the brain becomes ischemic. Above it, pressure forces the arterioles open, flow rises, and fluid is pushed out of the vessels into the brain (vasogenic edema). The brain’s range, as the lecture gives it, has a higher lower limit than the course’s general statement that local control holds flow steady from about 20 to 150 mm Hg (Microcirculation and Local Control); the limits differ between beds, and the point in each is that flow stays steady across normal pressures. The brain sits inside a rigid skull, so holding flow and volume steady also protects it from a dangerous rise in pressure inside the cranium.
The pressure that perfuses the brain is arterial pressure minus the pressure inside the skull, the intracranial pressure (ICP):
\[\text{Cerebral perfusion pressure} = \text{MAP} - \text{ICP}\]
With ICP fixed, cerebral perfusion pressure follows blood pressure.
Chronic hypertension shifts the range. In someone who has lived with high blood pressure for years, the cerebral arteries remodel and the whole autoregulatory curve shifts to the right. Higher pressures are tolerated without forced dilation, but the lower limit rises too. The lecture asks why this matters when hypertension is treated as an emergency: lowering such a patient’s pressure quickly to a “normal” value can put it below their lower limit, and the brain becomes ischemic at a pressure a normotensive person would tolerate.






Figure 17.2: Cerebral autoregulation. In a normotensive person, flow stays near 50 mL/100 g/min from about 50 to 150 mm Hg of perfusion pressure. In chronic hypertension the curve shifts to the right, raising both limits. Schematic; the shifted limits are illustrative. Course figure, after the lecture’s figures.



Metabolic control. Flow follows activity region by region. Clenching a hand raises flow in the motor area for that hand, and reading, talking or reasoning each raises flow in a different set of regions. Active neurons release metabolic signals that dilate the arterioles nearby. The strongest chemical regulator of cerebral flow, though, is CO2: a rise in arterial PCO2 lowers the pH around the cerebral arterioles and dilates them, and a fall (as with hyperventilation) constricts them.
Cerebral blood flow is largely locally mediated: local > systemic. The brain sets its own flow, and the systemic reflexes help by keeping arterial pressure within the range the brain can autoregulate across.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 17  Other Special Circulations
text:
17.2 Skeletal muscle circulation

17.2.1 Why it matters
Skeletal muscle is about 42% of body mass and about 20% of the resting metabolic rate. At rest its flow is modest, but in exercise its metabolic rate rises many-fold and its blood flow can rise about 20-fold. Because the bed is so large, its arterioles are also a big part of SVR: tightening or loosening them changes arterial pressure for the whole body. The anatomy of the muscle microcirculation is not tested.


17.2.2 Systemic regulation
Skeletal muscle arterioles carry two kinds of adrenergic receptor (Figure 17.3):

α1 receptors, which constrict. Norepinephrine (NE) acts mainly on α1 receptors and has little effect on β2.
β2 receptors, which dilate. Epinephrine acts on both, and β2 receptors respond to it at lower concentrations.

NE is the transmitter that sympathetic nerves release onto the arterioles, so sympathetic nerve activity constricts muscle arterioles. Epinephrine reaches them through the blood from the adrenal medulla and dilates them through β2. The ANS and Extrinsic Control chapter explains why neural NE does not dilate muscle vessels.
As exercise starts, sympathetic outflow rises, and NE constricts the arterioles of inactive muscle and of the gut and skin. In the muscle that is working, metabolic dilation begins at once and overrides the NE constriction there, which the course calls functional sympatholysis (Cardiovascular Adaptation to Exercise). Circulating epinephrine adds some β2 dilation as exercise continues.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The muscle slides say that because NE is the primary neurotransmitter, “vasoconstriction dominates in early exercise,” and the peer-educator notes say the same. That holds for muscle that is not working, and in anticipation of exercise before metabolites have built up. In the working muscle itself, metabolites blunt the α1 constriction from the start, and flow rises with the first contractions. Both versions agree on the overall result the slides emphasize: during exercise, working muscle is vasodilated.




17.2.3 Local regulation
Working muscle produces CO2 and H+, uses O2, and releases adenosine, and its endothelium releases NO. All of these dilate the arterioles. Metabolic dilation predominates during exercise, and the overall result is vasodilation of the arterioles in working muscle, against a sympathetic drive that is high. The same sympathetic drive keeps arterioles constricted in muscle that is not working and in the gut and skin, so flow is directed to the muscles doing the work. The Cardiovascular Adaptation to Exercise chapter puts this together for the whole body.






Figure 17.3: Three signals act on a skeletal muscle arteriole. Sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine, which constricts through α1 receptors. Circulating epinephrine dilates through β2 receptors. Metabolites from working muscle dilate, and in working muscle they predominate. Course figure, after the lecture’s slides.



Skeletal muscle: local > systemic during exercise. At rest, when metabolic signals are low, sympathetic tone sets muscle arteriolar resistance, which is how the baroreflex uses this large bed to adjust SVR.






WarningA common mistake



“Sympathetic activation dilates muscle vessels” mixes up the two catecholamines. Sympathetic nerves release NE, which constricts through α1. Dilation in exercising muscle comes from metabolites, helped by circulating epinephrine on β2 receptors.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 17  Other Special Circulations
text:
17.3 Splanchnic circulation

17.3.1 Why it matters
The splanchnic circulation supplies the stomach, intestines, spleen, pancreas and liver. It carries absorbed nutrients to the liver and on to the rest of the body (“you are what you eat”). It is also the body’s largest reservoir of blood at rest, more than 25% of the blood volume, most of it in compliant veins. That reservoir can be moved into the central circulation when the body needs it.


17.3.2 Anatomy
Two features are unusual (Figure 17.4):

Multiple organs, each with its own arteries, and each can be regulated separately.
Capillary beds in series. Blood from the gut, spleen and pancreas passes through their capillaries, collects in the portal vein, and then passes through a second capillary bed, the sinusoids of the liver, before reaching the vena cava. The liver also receives arterial blood from the hepatic artery. The detailed anatomy is not tested.







Figure 17.4: The splanchnic circulation. Blood passes through the capillaries of the gut, spleen and pancreas, then through the portal vein to the liver sinusoids, a second capillary bed in series, before reaching the inferior vena cava. The hepatic artery adds arterial blood to the liver. Schematic. Course figure, after the lecture’s figure.





17.3.3 Regulation
The splanchnic bed is under strong sympathetic control. Sympathetic fibers from the prevertebral ganglia release NE onto α1 receptors on the splanchnic arterioles and veins:

Arteriolar constriction reduces gut blood flow and raises SVR.
Venoconstriction squeezes blood out of the splanchnic veins into the central circulation. That raises stressed volume and Pms (mean systemic filling pressure), and with it venous return and cardiac output (the Control of Cardiac Output chapter explains Pms).

This is how the body borrows splanchnic blood in hemorrhage and exercise. Parasympathetic nerves increase gut motility and secretion but have little direct effect on the splanchnic vessels and do not control splanchnic venous tone.
Local control also operates. Exocrine and paracrine signals, metabolic control (the rise in metabolism when the gut is digesting), and a myogenic response all act on splanchnic arterioles. The rise in gut blood flow after a meal comes mostly from these local vasodilators, released by the active tissue. The lecture’s list of individual splanchnic vasodilators and vasoconstrictors does not need to be memorized.
Even so, the splanchnic bed differs from the brain and heart. It is a major target of systemic reflexes, and sympathetic activation can cut its flow sharply when the rest of the body needs the blood. The course groups it with the skin as a predominantly autonomically controlled bed: systemic > local.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The splanchnic slides list parasympathetic “Arterial Dilation / Venodilation” and say “*Predominantly Parasympathetically Mediated,” the summary slide lists “Splanchnics (Parasympathetics),” and the peer-educator notes say parasympathetic signals are dominant in the gut at rest. The main autonomic control of the splanchnic circulation is sympathetic (course errata entry 14). Sympathetic α1 constriction of the arterioles and veins is what lets the body shift splanchnic blood to the central circulation. The slides are right that this bed, unlike the brain and heart, is under strong autonomic control; the controlling division is sympathetic.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 17  Other Special Circulations
text:
17.4 Cutaneous circulation

17.4.1 Why it matters
Skin is not very active metabolically, and its O2 needs are small. Yet it is highly vascular and its flow is highly dynamic: total skin blood flow can fall to nearly zero in the cold and rise to about 7 L/min in severe heat. The reason is thermoregulation. Skin blood flow is controlled mainly for the body’s temperature, not for the skin’s own needs.


17.4.2 How skin blood carries heat away
Warm blood from the core brings heat to the surface, where it can leave the body:

Convection: heat carried away by moving air (or water). It depends on air flow over the surface and on blood flow within the skin.
Conduction: direct transfer of heat to whatever touches the skin. It depends on the temperature difference and on how well the neighboring material conducts and absorbs heat. Water does both far better than air, which is why cold water chills you faster than air at the same temperature.
Sweat uses several routes at once. Water on the skin conducts heat well; evaporation (the change from liquid to gas) absorbs a great deal of heat; and the vapor carries it away by convection.

All of these depend on blood flow to the skin. Sweat on a skin with no blood flow would cool only the skin.


17.4.3 Anatomy: apical and non-apical skin
All skin has the usual arteriole, capillary bed and venule. Apical skin (the glabrous skin of the palms and soles, and the lips, nose, ears and face) has an extra pathway: arteriovenous anastomoses (Figure 17.5 A). These are direct connections from arteriole to venule with no capillary bed, so they deliver no O2 or nutrients to the tissue. They exist for thermoregulation. When they open, a large flow of warm blood passes just under the surface, which is why the face, ears, nose and hands look red and flushed when you are hot. Non-apical (hairy) skin, covering most of the body, has no anastomoses. The anatomy itself is not tested; what the anastomoses do is.






Figure 17.5: Apical and non-apical skin. (A) Apical skin has arteriovenous anastomoses that bypass the capillaries. Sympathetic adrenergic fibers constrict its arterioles and anastomoses through α1 receptors. (B) Non-apical skin has no anastomoses. Its arterioles get the same constrictor fibers, plus sympathetic cholinergic fibers to the sweat glands, whose activity also produces active vasodilation. Adapted from Boron and Boulpaep, Medical Physiology [1], as used in the lecture.





17.4.4 Regulation
Sympathetic constriction. Sympathetic adrenergic fibers release NE onto α1 receptors on the arterioles of all skin and on the anastomoses of apical skin. At rest these fibers are tonically active. More sympathetic activity, as in a “fight or flight” response, the start of exercise, cold, or hemorrhage, constricts skin vessels and lowers skin blood flow, moving blood away from the metabolically slow skin toward organs that need it.
Thermoregulation. Temperature is sensed in two places. Local skin temperature is sensed by C fibers that carry the signal up the spinothalamic tract. Core temperature is sensed in the brain, by the hypothalamus, and in the spinal cord. The hypothalamus integrates both and sends its commands out through sympathetic nerves.
When the body is too warm, two things happen:

Sympathetic constrictor tone falls. In apical skin, this withdrawal of tone is how the anastomoses open.
In non-apical skin, a second set of sympathetic fibers comes into play. These are the one notable exception to the rule that postganglionic sympathetic neurons release NE: sympathetic cholinergic fibers release acetylcholine onto sweat glands. Sweating starts, and the skin arterioles actively dilate, far more than withdrawal of constrictor tone alone could produce. The lecture suggests the dilation is mediated by bradykinin; the mediator is not settled, and you do not need it.

When a sympathetic response and a heat load arrive together, as in sustained exercise on a hot day, both signals are present. α1 constriction tries to lower skin flow while the cholinergic vasodilator system tries to raise it, and the vasodilation is dominant. Skin blood flow rises and heat is shed, at the cost of a lower SVR and less blood in the central circulation. Near maximal exercise the balance tips back, and skin vessels constrict again to defend blood pressure and muscle flow. The Cardiovascular Adaptation to Exercise chapter follows that tradeoff.
Overall, the skin is a predominantly autonomically controlled bed: systemic > local, and the control is sympathetic.
Local control exists too. Skin shows reactive hyperemia: the flush after pressure on the skin is released. It has C-fiber mediated responses: local warming or injury makes sensory nerve endings release vasodilators into the nearby skin. And NO from the endothelium contributes to local dilation.


17.4.5 People who struggle with thermoregulation
People with a spinal cord injury lose sympathetic control of the skin below the level of the injury, so they can neither sweat nor redirect skin blood flow there, and they overheat or chill easily. Older adults have weaker skin vasodilator and sweating responses. Young children depend on adults to control their surroundings and can overheat quickly.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 17  Other Special Circulations
text:
17.5 Summary: who is in charge?

The pattern makes sense. The brain and heart cannot let a reflex that is defending blood pressure for the rest of the body turn down their own supply, so their own metabolism sets their flow. The gut and skin can tolerate a temporary cut in flow, so they are where the sympathetic system finds blood to move: the gut gives up its large venous reservoir, and the skin gives up flow it was using mostly for heat. The kidney appears in the lecture’s summary as locally controlled; this lecture does not cover the renal circulation.

title: 17  Other Special Circulations
text:
17.6 Check your understanding

A man with long-standing hypertension arrives with a blood pressure of 220/120 mm Hg. His blood pressure is lowered within minutes to 120/80. He becomes confused. Explain, using his autoregulation curve.


Answer

Chronic hypertension has shifted his cerebral autoregulation curve to the right, so the lower limit of his range is higher than normal. A mean pressure that a normotensive person would tolerate falls below his lower limit, his cerebral arterioles are already fully dilated, and cerebral blood flow falls with pressure. The brain becomes ischemic.

During a hemorrhage, which of the four beds in this chapter have their flow cut by the sympathetic response, and which are spared? How does the splanchnic bed help beyond reducing its own flow?


Answer

The skin and the splanchnic bed are cut sharply by α1 constriction (so is resting skeletal muscle). The brain and heart are spared because local control predominates there. The splanchnic veins also constrict and push blood from this large reservoir into the central circulation. That raises stressed volume and Pms, which supports venous return and cardiac output.

An hour after a large meal, blood flow to the small intestine has risen substantially. What causes the rise, and what would a burst of sympathetic activity (say, a sprint for the bus) do to it?


Answer

Local metabolic and paracrine vasodilators released by the digesting tissue. Parasympathetic nerves raise motility and secretion, but they are not what dilates the vessels. A burst of sympathetic activity constricts splanchnic arterioles through α1 and cuts gut flow, because systemic control predominates in this bed.

You sit in a hot room at rest. How does blood flow rise in your fingertips, and how does it rise in the skin of your forearm?


Answer

Fingertips are apical skin. Their arteriovenous anastomoses open mainly because sympathetic adrenergic constrictor tone is withdrawn. The forearm is non-apical skin. Withdrawal of constrictor tone helps, but most of the rise comes from active vasodilation through sympathetic cholinergic fibers, the same fibers that make you sweat.

A person takes a drug that blocks both β1 and β2 receptors and then exercises. Does blood flow to the working leg muscles still rise? Which signal is lost and which remains?


Answer

It still rises. The drug removes the β2 dilation from circulating epinephrine (and limits the rise in heart rate and contractility, so cardiac output rises less). Metabolic dilation in the working muscle does not depend on β receptors, and it is the predominant signal during exercise, so the arterioles still dilate.

A head injury raises intracranial pressure while mean arterial pressure is unchanged. What happens to cerebral perfusion pressure, and how do the cerebral arterioles respond at first?


Answer

Cerebral perfusion pressure (MAP − ICP) falls. As long as it stays within the autoregulatory range, the arterioles dilate (less stretch, myogenic response) and flow is held near normal. If ICP rises far enough that perfusion pressure falls below the lower limit, the arterioles are fully dilated and flow falls.

title: 18  Pulmonary Circulation
text:
18.1 Two blood supplies
All of the cardiac output passes through the lungs. The right ventricle pumps the same 5 to 6 L/min as the left, through a circuit in series with the systemic circulation, yet it does so at about one sixth of the pressure. This lecture, taught in the cardiovascular block, asks why the pulmonary circulation is built for low pressure and how it stays that way when flow rises. The pulmonary block returns to the same vessels from the gas-exchange side in Ventilation and Perfusion, which covers what blood flow distribution and hypoxic vasoconstriction do to V/Q matching and arterial blood gases.
The lung has two circulations:
The bronchial circulation is part of the systemic circulation. It feeds the lung’s own tissue, the way the coronary arteries feed the heart. Some bronchial venous blood drains into the pulmonary veins and so mixes, unoxygenated, with blood leaving the lungs; the V/Q chapter counts it as part of the normal small shunt.
The pulmonary circulation’s principal role is to expose blood to air. The pulmonary arteries branch alongside the airways into a capillary network that wraps the alveoli in an enormous, thin surface. The pulmonary circulation also has other jobs:
