title: 18  Pulmonary Circulation
text:
18.2 A low-pressure circuit
The pulmonary and systemic circulations carry the same flow, about 6 L/min in the lecture’s example. Systemic arterial pressure is about 120/80 mm Hg. Pulmonary arterial pressure is about 20/10 mm Hg, with a mean of about 14.
Low pressure suits the lung’s job in three ways:

It prevents pulmonary edema. Pulmonary capillary walls are thin so that gas can cross them quickly. At systemic pressures, the Starling forces (from Microcirculation and Local Control) would push fluid out of these capillaries into the interstitium and the alveoli, and fluid in the alveoli blocks gas exchange.
It aids gas exchange. Thin-walled, low-pressure vessels can spread into a large, thin exchange surface.
It facilitates forward flow into the left heart. The right ventricle only has to generate a low pressure to pump the whole cardiac output, so it can be a thin-walled pump that fills at a low right atrial pressure. A low Pra keeps the driving pressure for venous return high (VR = (Pms − Pra)/RVR, from Control of Cardiac Output).


18.2.1 Pulmonary vascular resistance
The same Ohm’s law that gives systemic vascular resistance gives pulmonary vascular resistance. For the systemic circulation, SVR = (MAP − CVP)/CO: the pressure drop from the aorta to the right atrium, divided by flow, in mm Hg·min/L. For the lungs, the pressure drop runs from the pulmonary artery to the left atrium:
\[\text{PVR} = \frac{\text{mPAP} - \text{PCWP}}{\text{CO}} \times 80\]
mPAP is the mean pulmonary artery pressure, the equivalent of MAP. PCWP, the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, stands in for left atrial pressure, the outflow pressure, just as CVP does for the systemic circuit. Multiplying mm Hg·min/L by 80 converts the result to the units clinicians use, dyn·s·cm−5. Normal PVR at rest is 80 to 150 dyn·s·cm−5.
With the lecture’s resting values (mPAP 14 mm Hg, PCWP 5 mm Hg, CO 6 L/min):
\[\text{PVR} = \frac{14 - 5}{6} \times 80 = 120 \ \text{dyn·s·cm}^{-5}\]
The same flow passes through both circuits, but the pressure drop across the lungs is about 9 mm Hg, against roughly 90 mm Hg across the systemic circulation, so PVR is far lower than SVR. You need to know that SVR is much higher than PVR, not the exact ratio, and you do not need to memorize the factor of 80.


18.2.2 Measuring the wedge pressure
Left atrial pressure is hard to measure directly, so it is estimated with a pulmonary artery catheter. A thin catheter with a small balloon near its tip is passed through a vein into the right atrium, through the right ventricle and out into the pulmonary artery. When the balloon is inflated, the flowing blood carries it forward until it wedges in a small branch (Figure 18.1). Nothing flows beyond the wedged balloon, so the blood ahead of it forms a still column that connects through the capillaries and veins to the left atrium. With no flow there is no pressure drop along that column, and the pressure at the catheter tip approximates left atrial pressure. Pressures can be recorded in each chamber as the catheter passes through.






Figure 18.1: Measuring the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure. The catheter passes through the right atrium and right ventricle into the pulmonary artery, and its balloon wedges in a small branch. Blood beyond the balloon stops moving, so the pressure at the tip approximates left atrial pressure. Schematic. Adapted from Leff and Schumacker, Respiratory Physiology: Basics and Applications [1], as used in the lecture.



A high PCWP means a high left atrial pressure, and that pressure is passed back to the pulmonary capillaries. Their hydrostatic pressure rises, filtration rises, and fluid enters the interstitium and then the alveoli: pulmonary edema, as when a failing left ventricle fills at a high LVEDP (Microcirculation and Local Control has the Starling forces).
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 18  Pulmonary Circulation
text:
18.3 How PVR is regulated
Most of what changes PVR is passive: gravity, the pressure inside the vessels, and the volume of the lung around them. One active mechanism, hypoxic vasoconstriction, matters a great deal.

18.3.1 Gravity and the West zones
The pulmonary vessels are flexible, and their pressures are low enough that gravity matters. In an upright person, the column of blood adds pressure toward the base of the lung and subtracts it toward the apex. Vessels at the base are more distended, and blood flow per alveolus rises from the apex toward the base.
Alveolar pressure, by contrast, is about the same everywhere in the lung. Comparing the pressure in the pulmonary arteries (Pa), in the alveoli (Palv) and in the pulmonary veins (Pv) gives three zones of flow, named for West (Figure 18.2). The slides write alveolar pressure as PA; this book uses Palv, as in the pulmonary chapters, to keep it apart from Pa.

Zone 1: Palv > Pa > Pv. Alveolar pressure exceeds the pressure in the capillaries and squeezes them shut. The region is ventilated but not perfused: dead space. Zone 1 is typically not present in health. It appears when vascular pressures fall or alveolar pressure rises (Ventilation and Perfusion).
Zone 2: Pa > Palv > Pv. Roughly the upper third of the upright lung. The capillaries are open at their arterial end but squeezed at their venous end, so flow is set by Pa − Palv, not by the arterial-venous difference. The capillaries act as a Starling resistor: a collapsible tube whose flow depends on the pressure outside it. These vessels are the flexible reserve of the lung. A higher Pa opens more of them, and higher alveolar pressure squeezes them.
Zone 3: Pa > Pv > Palv. The lower lung. Capillaries are open along their whole length, flow is set by Pa − Pv, and this zone has the greatest blood flow.

Use the zone numbers for the order of the three pressures. When you describe regions of the normal upright lung, the apex and the base are the clearer words, because in health the apex still has some blood flow. The Ventilation and Perfusion chapter follows what the zones do to V/Q and gas exchange.






Figure 18.2: The zones of flow in the upright lung. Left: the order of arterial (Pa), alveolar (Palv) and venous (Pv) pressure in each zone and what sets flow there. Right: blood flow rises from apex to base; zone 1 has none. Zone 1 is drawn large to show it; the healthy lung has little or none. Schematic, after West [2], as used in the lecture.





18.3.2 Passive regulation: recruitment and distension
When cardiac output rises, in exercise for example, pulmonary artery pressure rises only a little, so PVR must fall. Two passive mechanisms lower it (Figure 18.3):

Recruitment. At rest some capillaries, mostly in the upper lung, are collapsed or barely open. A small rise in pulmonary arterial pressure opens them. Each newly opened vessel is another resistance in parallel, so total resistance falls.
Distension. Vessels that are already open widen as pressure inside them rises, and by Poiseuille’s law a small increase in radius lowers resistance a lot.

The course emphasis is on recruitment over distension: when flow rises, the lung mainly opens more vessels rather than over-stretching the ones already open. More open capillaries also means more surface for gas exchange.






Figure 18.3: Recruitment and distension, with four hypothetical vessels. (A) At rest two are collapsed and two modestly filled. (B) Recruitment: a rise in pressure opens the collapsed vessels, adding channels in parallel. (C) Distension: vessels already open widen. Both lower PVR. Course figure, after the lecture’s slide.



The result is that in health a small increase in pulmonary arterial pressure produces a large increase in blood flow, and resistance falls as pressure rises (Figure 18.4). The lecture’s table for a healthy young man shows it:




Rest
Exercise

Cardiac output nearly triples while mean pulmonary artery pressure rises by 6 mm Hg, and PVR falls to less than half. The reserve is not unlimited. Once most vessels are open, further rises in flow need larger rises in pressure. At rest, a mean pulmonary artery pressure above about 20 mm Hg is pulmonary hypertension.






Figure 18.4: Pressure, flow and resistance in the pulmonary circulation. (A) A small rise in mean pulmonary artery pressure produces a large rise in flow. (B) So PVR falls as pressure rises, from 120 dyn·s·cm−5 at the lecture’s resting values. Schematic, with left atrial pressure held at 5 mm Hg; the shaded band is the normal resting range. The exercise column of the table also has a higher wedge pressure, so its PVR (50) is lower than this curve gives at 20 mm Hg. Course figure, after the lecture’s figures from Boron and Boulpaep [3].





18.3.3 Lung volume
Lung volume also changes PVR, and it acts on two kinds of vessel in opposite directions (Figure 18.5):

Alveolar vessels are the capillaries in the alveolar walls. As the lung inflates, the alveoli enlarge and their walls stretch, and the capillaries running in those walls are stretched thin and compressed. Their resistance rises with lung volume and is highest at TLC.
Extra-alveolar vessels are the larger arteries and veins that run through the lung tissue outside the alveolar walls. As the lung inflates, pleural pressure becomes more negative and the surrounding lung tissue pulls outward on their walls, so they are pulled open. Their resistance falls with lung volume and is highest at low volumes, near RV, where they narrow.

Total PVR is the sum of the two in series. It is lowest near FRC, the volume at which a person spends most of the breathing cycle, and rises toward both RV and TLC: a U-shaped curve.






Figure 18.5: Pulmonary vascular resistance and lung volume. Extra-alveolar vessels are pulled open as the lung inflates; alveolar vessels are squeezed by stretched alveolar walls. Total resistance, the sum, is lowest near FRC. Schematic. Course figure, after the lecture’s figure from Boron and Boulpaep [3].









NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The peer-educator notes say that inhalation “increases alveolar volume and pressure” and compresses the capillaries. During a normal inspiration alveolar pressure falls slightly below atmospheric (the Respiratory Statics chapter explains why). What compresses the alveolar vessels is the stretch of the enlarging alveolar walls around them, not a rise in alveolar pressure. The prediction is the same: alveolar vessel resistance rises as the lung inflates.




18.3.4 Active regulation: hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
The one strong active control of the pulmonary vessels is O2. When the alveolar PO2 in a region of the lung falls, the small pulmonary arteries supplying that region constrict. This is hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV). It is the opposite of what systemic arterioles do, which dilate when their tissue is hypoxic. HPV is local: the pulmonary vascular smooth muscle responds to the low O2 around it, without nerves or circulating signals.
The lecture shows why it helps with a model of two alveoli, each receiving half the cardiac output, with mixed venous blood 75% saturated (Figure 18.6):

Both alveoli ventilated. Blood leaving each alveolus is fully saturated, and the blood reaching the left atrium is about 100% saturated.
One alveolus blocked, as by pneumonia or a mucus plug, with no HPV. Half the flow passes an alveolus with no fresh gas and leaves it still 75% saturated. Mixed with the 100% blood from the good alveolus, the blood reaching the left atrium is (75 + 100)/2 = 87.5% saturated.
With HPV. The vessels to the hypoxic alveolus constrict and flow shifts to the ventilated one. If the blocked unit now gets a quarter of the flow, the mix is 0.25 × 75 + 0.75 × 100 ≈ 94%.

HPV matches perfusion to ventilation (“V/Q matching”) and protects arterial saturation when the hypoxic region is limited. The Ventilation and Perfusion chapter covers how it shapes shunt and PaO2.






Figure 18.6: The two-alveolus model of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. (A) Both alveoli ventilated: blood reaching the left atrium is about 100% saturated. (B) One alveolus unventilated with no HPV: half the flow stays 75% saturated and the mix is 87.5%. (C) With HPV, flow shifts away from the hypoxic alveolus and the mix is about 94%. Saturations are the lecture’s. Course figure, after the lecture’s slides.



When the whole lung is hypoxic, HPV cannot redirect blood anywhere better. Arteries constrict throughout the lung, and the effect is a rise in total PVR.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 18  Pulmonary Circulation
text:
18.4 Two diseases that raise PVR
Emphysema (in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease). Large regions of the lung are poorly ventilated, so alveolar hypoxia is widespread and chronic. HPV acts across the whole lung and raises PVR, and the destruction of alveolar walls also removes capillaries from the bed, leaving fewer vessels in parallel.
Pulmonary embolism. A clot carried from the systemic veins lodges in the pulmonary arteries and blocks them. The pulmonary circulation is in series with the rest of the circulation, so the whole cardiac output must still pass through the lungs. Blocked vessels are removed from the parallel network, and the remaining vessels have to carry the whole cardiac output, so PVR rises abruptly. The ventilated alveoli beyond the clot get no flow, which adds dead space (the V/Q chapter).






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The peer-educator notes describe pulmonary embolism as “acute hypoxia due to block in blood vessels from blood clot → increase PVR to compensate.” The rise in PVR is not a compensation. The clot itself obstructs the vessels, which raises PVR, mainly mechanically, and the alveoli downstream are ventilated but not perfused. Hypoxemia, when it occurs, is a result of the embolism and the redistribution of flow, not the cause of the rise in PVR.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 18  Pulmonary Circulation
section: 18.5 Why PVR matters: the right ventricle
text:
18.5 Why PVR matters: the right ventricle
The right ventricle is built for the low-pressure pulmonary circuit: a thin-walled, crescent-shaped chamber wrapped around the left ventricle. A rise in PVR is a rise in its afterload, and how it copes depends on how fast the rise happens (Figure 18.7).
Acute increase in PVR, as with a large pulmonary embolism. The thin right ventricle cannot suddenly generate a much higher pressure. It dilates and is overloaded: it fails as a pump, its stroke volume falls, and its filling pressure (Pra, measured as CVP) rises. The dilated right ventricle also pushes the septum toward the left ventricle.
Chronic increase in PVR, as in emphysema with chronic hypoxia. Given months or years, the right ventricle adapts the way any muscle does to a sustained load: it hypertrophies and learns to live at higher pressures. Over time, though, it can still dilate and fail. Right ventricular enlargement and failure caused by lung disease is cor pulmonale.






Figure 18.7: The right ventricle and PVR, in short-axis sketches. (A) Normal: a thin-walled RV crescent. (B) Acute rise in PVR: the RV dilates and fails, and the septum is pushed toward the LV. (C) Chronic rise in PVR: the RV wall hypertrophies (cor pulmonale). Schematic. Course figure, after the lecture’s slide.



The lecture’s closing point ties this back to the two pumps in series: the left ventricle can only pump what the right ventricle gives it. If the right ventricle cannot push the cardiac output through a high PVR, left ventricular filling falls and systemic cardiac output falls with it, however healthy the left ventricle is. Patients with severe elevations of PVR can have “right-heart-limited” circulations. The Control of Cardiac Output chapter shows the same coupling from the left side, where a failing left ventricle raises left atrial and pulmonary pressures and loads the right ventricle.






TipWhat you need from this



Know that PVR is low and SVR much higher, how to calculate PVR from mPAP, PCWP and CO, and the three things that keep PVR low or change it: recruitment (and distension) as flow rises, lung volume (lowest PVR near FRC), and hypoxic vasoconstriction (regional for V/Q matching, global as a cause of high PVR). Then be able to say what an acute and a chronic rise in PVR do to the right ventricle.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 18  Pulmonary Circulation
text:
18.6 Check your understanding

A large clot blocks the artery to the left lower lobe. The alveolar capillaries there lose their flow. Which blood supply keeps the bronchial walls of that lobe alive, and why does it still have flow?


Answer

The bronchial circulation. Bronchial arteries come off the aorta and run at systemic pressure, independent of the pulmonary artery, and they supply the airways and supporting tissue, the non-gas-exchanging parts of the lung.

A person takes a maximal breath to TLC and holds it, then later breathes out all the way to RV. How does PVR at each volume compare with PVR at FRC, and which vessels are responsible?


Answer

PVR is higher at both. At TLC the alveolar vessels in the stretched alveolar walls are squeezed and lengthened, so their resistance is high. At RV the extra-alveolar vessels are no longer pulled open by the surrounding tissue and narrow, so their resistance is high. The sum is lowest near FRC.

A climber goes to high altitude, where every alveolus has a low PO2. What happens to her PVR and right ventricle over the first two weeks, and how would the right ventricle look if she lived there for years?


Answer

Hypoxic vasoconstriction acts throughout the lung, because every region is hypoxic, so total PVR rises. Over the first weeks the right ventricle faces a higher afterload and must generate a higher pulmonary artery pressure. Over years of sustained high PVR it adapts the way muscle does to a chronic load: its wall hypertrophies. That is the chronic pattern, unlike the dilation and failure of an acute rise in PVR.

A patient has had one lung removed. At rest her pulmonary artery pressure is nearly normal. Predict what happens to her mean pulmonary artery pressure during exercise compared with a person with two lungs, and explain why.


Answer

It rises more. With one lung, the whole cardiac output already passes through half the vascular bed, so many of the vessels that would normally be recruited are already open. During exercise there is little reserve left to recruit, so the rise in flow needs a larger rise in pressure.

Why does a sudden large pulmonary embolism raise CVP and lower systemic arterial pressure, even though the left ventricle is healthy?


Answer

PVR rises abruptly. The thin right ventricle cannot generate the higher pressure, so it dilates and fails: its stroke volume falls and its filling pressure (CVP) rises. Less blood reaches the left heart, and the left ventricle can only pump what the right ventricle delivers, so systemic cardiac output and arterial pressure fall.

Why does the pressure at the tip of a wedged pulmonary artery catheter approximate left atrial pressure, and not pulmonary artery pressure?


Answer

The inflated balloon stops flow in the branch it occludes. With no flow, there is no pressure drop along the still column of blood between the catheter tip and the left atrium, so the tip reads the pressure at the far end of that column, left atrial pressure. Pulmonary artery pressure is upstream of the balloon and is cut off from the tip.
crumbs: Cardiovascular physiology, excitable cells and muscle

title: 19  Respiratory Physiology Introduction
text:
19.1 Breathe in, breathe out
The respiratory block opens with a short tour. The point of the tour is a framework: when the details of pressures, partial pressures and dissociation curves start to pile up, you should be able to say which part of the system you are in and which of the two jobs it serves. This chapter covers that tour. The next one, Respiratory Statics, starts the details.
Take a deep breath in, then let it out. To breathe in, you used your muscles, mostly the diaphragm, to make the chest bigger. That lowered the pressure around the lungs, the lungs expanded, and air was sucked in through the open airway. To breathe out, you did nothing. You relaxed, and the system sprang back to where it rests. You can also breathe out forcibly, using expiratory muscles, but quiet breathing spends all of its energy on inspiration.
That is most of respiratory mechanics in two sentences. We are negative-pressure breathers: we pull air in by lowering the pressure around the lungs, not by pushing it in. Keep that picture in mind when the pressure symbols multiply in the statics and dynamics chapters.

title: 19  Respiratory Physiology Introduction
section: 19.2 Why we need lungs at all
text:
19.2 Why we need lungs at all
A single cell living in water gets its O2 by diffusion. Outside the cell, O2 is high and CO2 is low. Inside, the mitochondria use O2 and make CO2. Each gas moves down its gradient across the membrane, and nothing else is needed (Figure 19.1 A).






Figure 19.1: Why a multicellular body needs lungs and a circulation. (A) A single cell exchanges O2 and CO2 with its surroundings by diffusion alone. (B) In the body, ventilation brings fresh air to the alveoli and removes CO2, gas diffuses between the alveoli and the blood, and the circulation carries O2 to the tissues and CO2 back to the lungs. Course figure.



A cell in your kidney or your calf muscle is far from fresh air, so the body does the same job in stages (Figure 19.1 B). Bulk flow of air (ventilation) brings air rich in O2 to the alveoli. O2 diffuses across the thin alveolar-capillary barrier into the blood and binds to hemoglobin. The circulation carries it to the tissues, where it diffuses out to the cells that use it. CO2 makes the reverse trip, and the same bulk flow of air blows it off. The intent in the mitochondria is the same as in the single cell. The body just needs several organs to keep the gradients in place.
The cardiovascular block ended with the blood going round and round. This block assumes that and asks how the lungs load O2 into that blood and take CO2 out of it.

title: 19  Respiratory Physiology Introduction
text:
19.3 Two jobs: oxygenation and ventilation
The lungs do two things.

Oxygenation is getting O2 from the air into the arterial blood. Its end point is the arterial PO2 (PaO2) and the saturation of hemoglobin.
Ventilation is getting CO2 out of the body. Its end point is the arterial PCO2 (PaCO2).

Both happen in the same lungs with the same breaths, but what controls each one is different, so the course teaches them as if they were in separate silos. Once you know how each works, the later lectures put them back together and ask how a problem with one affects the other. When you meet a patient who is short of breath, the first question the course teaches you to ask is: is this a problem of oxygenation, of ventilation, or both?

title: 19  Respiratory Physiology Introduction
text:
19.4 The parts of the system
The respiratory system has these parts:

The lungs: the airways, which conduct air, and the alveoli, where gas exchange happens.
The chest wall: the ribs, the intercostal muscles, and everything else that surrounds the thorax. The diaphragm counts as part of the chest wall. It forms the floor of the thorax, and it is also the main muscle of inspiration. It does most of the work in quiet breathing, with help from the intercostal and scalene muscles, and more neck muscles join in when you breathe hard.
The pleural space: the thin, closed space between the lungs and the chest wall. It holds almost no fluid, and because it is sealed, it links the two. When the chest wall is pulled outward, pleural pressure falls, the lungs are pulled outward with it, alveolar pressure falls below the pressure at the mouth, and air rushes in.

The course compresses the mechanics into one phrase: the chest wall wants to be big, and the lungs want to be small. Linked by the pleural space, they settle at a volume where the two pulls balance. That resting volume, at the end of a quiet breath out, is the functional residual capacity (FRC). The lecture calls FRC the starting point of respiratory physiology, the way mean systemic filling pressure (Pms) was the starting point of the circulation’s Guyton curves.
Because the system has three parts, a problem can sit in only three places: the lung, the chest wall, or the muscles. The course uses that idea all through the block, from the pressure-volume curves of statics to the pulmonary function tests at the end.

title: 19  Respiratory Physiology Introduction
text:
19.5 A map of the block
Figure 19.2 lays the lectures along the path that O2 takes. Each box is one or more chapters of this book.






Figure 19.2: The pulmonary block as a path from the air to the mitochondria. Mechanics moves the air, ventilation sets the gas in the alveoli, gas exchange moves it into the blood, and transport carries it to the tissues. Control of ventilation sits underneath and adjusts the whole chain. Course figure.



Mechanics. Respiratory Statics names the lung volumes and capacities and explains the pressure-volume curves of the lung, the chest wall and the whole respiratory system, and how the muscles set the largest and smallest volumes. Respiratory Dynamics I makes the system move: how pleural pressure, alveolar pressure and flow change through one quiet breath. Respiratory Dynamics II adds the airways. Ohm’s law returns from the cardiovascular block (pressure difference = flow × resistance), and airway resistance is what goes wrong in common diseases such as asthma. It also explains why even healthy people hit a limit on how fast they can breathe out.
Ventilation. Alveolar Ventilation follows air from the atmosphere to the alveoli. Minute ventilation is tidal volume times breathing rate (V̇E = VT × RR), much as cardiac output is stroke volume times heart rate. Part of each breath only fills the conducting airways, so it is alveolar ventilation (V̇A) that matters. The alveolar gas equation gives the alveolar PO2, and V̇A sets the PaCO2.
Gas exchange. Diffusion covers how gas crosses the alveolar-capillary barrier, written as Fick’s law of diffusion. Ventilation and Perfusion covers the matching of air to blood. Where there is a lot of blood flow there should be a lot of ventilation. A unit with blood flow but no air (shunt) or air but no blood flow (dead space) wastes effort.
Transport. Transport of O2 and CO2 covers hemoglobin, O2 content, and the Fick principle, V̇O2 = Q̇ × (CaO2 − CvO2). O2 delivery is cardiac output times arterial O2 content. Pulmonary Acid Base adds the link between CO2 and pH.
Control. Control of Ventilation covers how the brainstem senses CO2, pH and O2 and adjusts breathing, mostly without your noticing. Ask someone to think about their breathing and it gets messed up.
Putting it together. Physiology of Exercise revisits exercise from the respiratory side: if cardiac output rises several-fold, the same extra blood flows through the lungs, and ventilation has to keep up. Think Like a Respiratory Consultant brings the whole block to the patient through pulmonary function testing. The pulmonary circulation was taught in the cardiovascular block; see Pulmonary Circulation.
The tour also named the lung volumes and capacities (tidal volume, FRC, TLC, RV, vital capacity); Respiratory Statics defines them.
Pulmonary function tests run through the whole block. A full set is spirometry, lung volumes from a body box, and the diffusing capacity. This is not the clinical part of the curriculum, but disease is a useful counterexample: seeing how emphysema or interstitial lung disease breaks the normal physiology makes the normal physiology clearer. The course uses those diseases as labels for physiological patterns, not to teach their treatment.






TipHow to work in this block



The lecture compares respiratory physiology to the game Othello: a minute to learn, a lifetime to master. There are not that many facts, but they combine in many ways. Work with a pencil. Most of the graphs in this block are curves that bend, and you learn them by drawing them, moving them, and drawing them again.

title: 19  Respiratory Physiology Introduction
section: 19.6 Two scaffolds you will fill in
text:
19.6 Two scaffolds you will fill in
Two frameworks organize the clinical end of the block. This section is a preview: the hypoxemia framework is taught in Ventilation and Perfusion, and the hypercapnia framework in Pulmonary Acid Base and Think Like a Respiratory Consultant. It helps to see their shape now (Figure 19.3).






Figure 19.3: The two frameworks of the block. (A) Hypoxemia, sorted by the A–a gradient into causes that lower alveolar PO2 and causes that impair gas exchange. (B) Hypercapnia, a ventilation problem, as an imbalance between the strength of the respiratory system and the load it has to move. Course figure.




19.6.1 Oxygenation: why is the PaO2 low?
Hypoxemia means a low PaO2. To work out why, the course starts from the alveolar gas equation, which gives the PO2 in the alveoli:
\[P_AO_2 = (P_B - P_{H_2O})\,F_iO_2 - \frac{P_aCO_2}{R}\]
Here PB is barometric pressure, PH2O is water vapor pressure (47 mm Hg), FiO2 is the fraction of O2 in inspired air (0.21 for room air), and R is the respiratory exchange ratio (about 0.8). The Alveolar Ventilation chapter derives it.
If you know the PAO2 and measure the PaO2, the difference between them is the A–a gradient (PAO2 − PaO2). It sorts hypoxemia into two groups.

A–a gradient normal: the alveolar PO2 itself is low. Either barometric pressure is low (high altitude), the inspired O2 fraction is low (for example, a confined space where another gas has displaced O2), or the patient is hypoventilating, so CO2 builds up in the alveoli and takes the place of O2 (a high PaCO2 in the equation). The lungs pass on what they receive, and what they receive is too little.
A–a gradient raised: the alveolar gas is fine, but O2 is not getting into the blood. The causes are diffusion limitation, ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch and shunt.

A low O2 content in mixed venous blood, as in heart failure or fever, makes each of these gas-exchange problems worse, because the blood that escapes full exchange arrives with less O2 to begin with. In normal lungs it causes almost no hypoxemia on its own.
Later lectures add a second branch point: does the PaO2 rise with supplemental O2? Hypoxemia from V/Q mismatch or diffusion limitation improves. Hypoxemia from shunt responds poorly, because the shunted blood never meets the extra O2.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The Intro hypoxemia slide lists “Poor venous saturation/admixture” as a fourth cause of a raised PAO2 − PaO2. A low mixed venous saturation lowers PaO2 only through blood that passes a shunt, low V/Q units, or a diffusion-limited barrier. It makes those three mechanisms worse rather than standing as a mechanism of its own, which is how the Ventilation and Perfusion lecture presents its shunt case. The course errata make the same correction.




19.6.2 Ventilation: why is the PaCO2 high?
Hypercapnia means a high PaCO2. The PaCO2 is set by how fast CO2 is made and how fast alveolar ventilation clears it:
\[P_aCO_2 \propto \frac{\dot{V}CO_2}{\dot{V}_A}\]
A high PaCO2 almost always means the alveolar ventilation is too low for the CO2 being made. The course asks why with a balance. On one side is the strength of the system: the drive from the brainstem, the nerves and the respiratory muscles. On the other is the load: stiff lungs, narrowed airways, a heavy or stiff chest wall, or a large amount of CO2 to clear. When the load outweighs the strength, ventilation falls behind. The course’s shorthand is “won’t breathe” (drive is low, as with opioids) versus “can’t breathe” (the muscles cannot move the load). Pulmonary Acid Base and Think Like a Respiratory Consultant work through it.

title: 19  Respiratory Physiology Introduction
text:
19.7 Check your understanding

You hold your breath at the end of a quiet exhalation and relax every muscle. Why does your chest neither shrink nor expand?


Answer

You are at FRC. The lungs pull inward and the chest wall pulls outward, and at this volume the two pulls are equal, so no muscle force is needed to hold it. The pleural space links them, so they must share one volume.

Which of the two lung functions does each of these measure: the PaCO2, the PaO2, the hemoglobin saturation?


Answer

PaCO2 measures ventilation. PaO2 and saturation measure oxygenation. A patient can have a problem with one and not the other, which is why the course asks “oxygenation or ventilation?” first.

A climber on a high mountain has a low PaO2. Her lungs are healthy. Would you expect her A–a gradient to be normal or raised, and why?


Answer

Normal. Barometric pressure is low, so the alveolar PO2 is low, and healthy lungs pass that low PO2 on to the blood. The gradient between alveolus and artery is not the problem; the alveolar PO2 is.

A patient breathes in normally but cannot breathe out forcibly. Can she still exhale a quiet tidal breath? Why?


Answer

Yes. Quiet expiration is passive. When the inspiratory muscles relax, the respiratory system’s net inward recoil above FRC (the lungs’ inward pull now exceeds the chest wall’s outward pull) pushes the air back out and returns the system to FRC. Expiratory muscles are only needed to breathe out below FRC or faster than recoil alone allows.

You are handed four numbers for a patient: SaO2, PaCO2, FEV1 and PaO2. Which would you look at to decide whether the problem is one of oxygenation or of ventilation, and which job does each report on?


Answer

PaO2 and SaO2 report on oxygenation, and PaCO2 reports on ventilation, so those three answer the question. FEV1 reports on neither directly. It measures how fast air can be blown out of the lungs, which is mechanics: a low FEV1 can lead to a ventilation or an oxygenation problem, or to neither.

title: 19  Respiratory Physiology Introduction
text:
19.9 Sources
This chapter follows the 2026 Respiratory Physiology Introduction lecture for MEDC 30504, given as the opening of the first statics session, and draws on the 2025 recording of the same lecture and the course’s lecture notes, corrected and updated. All figures were drawn for this book.

title: 20  Respiratory Statics
text:
20.1 Lung volumes and capacities
As the introduction set out, the lungs have two jobs, ventilation (moving CO2 out) and oxygenation (getting O2 into the blood). Both depend on moving air in and out, and that depends on mechanics. Statics is the part of mechanics that deals with the respiratory system when nothing is moving: the forces that hold the lungs at a given volume when the airway is open and air is not flowing. Dynamics, the next chapter, adds airflow and airway resistance.
A volume is a single, non-overlapping slice of the lung’s air. A capacity is the sum of two or more volumes. Figure 20.1 shows them on a spirometer tracing.
FRC is the volume at the end of a quiet expiration, when the respiratory muscles are relaxed. It is the starting point for every quiet breath, and most of this chapter is about why it sits where it does.
Volumes scale with body size, age and sex. Hutchinson, who built the first practical spirometer, showed in 1846 that vital capacity rises with height [2]. A patient’s measured values are compared with predicted values from reference equations and reported as percent predicted.

title: 20  Respiratory Statics
text:
Figure 20.1: Lung volumes and capacities on a spirometer tracing. The subject breathes quietly, takes the deepest possible breath, breathes out as far as possible, then returns to quiet breathing. Values are for a healthy young adult in the Respiratory Mechanics Lab [1]: TLC 6.0 L, FRC 3.0 L, RV 1.5 L, VT 0.5 L. Course figure.











Volume
What it is
Typical (L)




Tidal volume (VT)

0.5


Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV)
Extra air you can breathe in after a normal inspiration
2.5


Expiratory reserve volume (ERV)
Extra air you can breathe out after a normal, passive expiration
1.5


Residual volume (RV)
Air still in the lungs after a maximal expiration
1.5






Capacity

Typical (L)

3.0

20.1.1 What spirometry can and cannot measure
A spirometer measures air that moves through the mouth. Older spirometers collected exhaled air in a bell floating in water. Most modern ones measure flow, with a pneumotachograph or a turbine or ultrasonic sensor, and integrate it to get volume.
Either way, a spirometer can only measure air that comes out. RV never leaves the lung, so spirometry cannot measure RV, and it cannot measure any capacity that contains RV: FRC and TLC. Spirometry gives VT, IRV, ERV, IC and VC. To get the rest, you need one more number, and the usual one is FRC. It is measured at the end of a quiet breath, which takes no effort, so it is the most reproducible starting point. Once FRC is known, RV = FRC − ERV and TLC = FRC + IC. A full set of pulmonary function tests is three tests: spirometry, lung volumes (usually by body box) and the diffusing capacity, which a later chapter covers.


20.1.2 Measuring FRC with a body box
In body box plethysmography the patient sits in a sealed, transparent box and breathes through a mouthpiece [3, 4]. At the end of a quiet expiration (at FRC), a shutter closes the mouthpiece and the patient makes small panting efforts against it. No air enters or leaves the lungs, so the lung gas is simply compressed and decompressed.
Boyle’s law says that for a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, P1V1 = P2V2. Here the pressures must be absolute pressures, not pressures relative to the atmosphere. For the gas in the lungs:

Before the effort: P1 is barometric pressure, Patm (strictly, barometric pressure minus water vapor pressure), and V1 = FRC, the unknown.
During an effort to breathe in: the chest enlarges by a small ΔV, so the lung gas expands and its pressure, measured at the mouth, changes by ΔP (it falls, so ΔP is negative).

So Patm × FRC = (Patm + ΔP)(FRC + ΔV). Multiplying out, dropping the tiny ΔP × ΔV term, and solving:
\[\text{FRC} = -\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta P}\,P_{atm}\]
ΔP comes from the mouthpiece gauge. ΔV comes from the box: when the chest enlarges, it squeezes the gas in the box, and the rise in box pressure is calibrated to volume. On the outward pant everything runs in reverse: the lung gas is compressed, the patient gets smaller and box pressure falls. The lecture slide shows that pant, and the arithmetic comes out the same.






TipWhat you need from this



You will not be asked to do the body box calculation. Know that spirometry cannot measure RV, FRC or TLC, that the body box measures FRC using Boyle’s law, and that once you have FRC, spirometry gives you everything else.








NoteBackground: gas dilution





FRC or TLC can also be measured by having the patient breathe a known amount of an inert gas such as helium. The gas mixes into the lung air, and its fall in concentration gives the volume it mixed into (C1V1 = C2V2). Dilution only counts gas that is in contact with the open airways. In obstructive disease some gas is trapped behind closed or narrowed airways, so dilution underestimates lung volume. The body box compresses all the gas in the chest, so it counts trapped gas that dilution misses.

title: 20  Respiratory Statics
text:
20.2 Pressures, units, and transmural pressure
Respiratory pressures are small, so they are measured in centimeters of water. One cm H2O is the pressure that holds up a 1 cm column of water. It is about 0.74 mm Hg (1 mm Hg ≈ 1.36 cm H2O). From here on, all pressures are relative to atmospheric pressure, so “0” means atmospheric and “−5” means 5 cm H2O below it.
What matters for any elastic structure is the pressure difference across its wall, the transmural pressure:
\[P_{tm} = P_{in} - P_{out}\]
A positive transmural pressure pushes the wall outward and distends the structure. The lung, the chest wall and the airways each have one, and it is the transmural pressure, not the absolute pressure on either side, that sets their volume. In the dynamics chapters, Ptm is used for the airway wall: airway pressure minus pleural pressure.

title: 20  Respiratory Statics
text:
20.3 Pressure-volume curves
The best way to see what holds the lungs at a given volume is to plot volume against the pressure needed to hold each structure at that volume with its muscles relaxed. Figure 20.2 shows the three curves the course uses (the small-group keys call them compliance curves). On these plots, pressure to the right of zero means the structure is being held expanded against its tendency to shrink, and pressure to the left means it is being held compressed against its tendency to spring out.






Figure 20.2: Relaxation pressure-volume curves of the lung (orange), chest wall (blue) and whole respiratory system (maroon). At each volume the system’s pressure is the sum of the lung’s and the chest wall’s. Curves come from the Respiratory Mechanics Lab statics model [1]. The chest wall curve is fit to the measurements of Rahn and colleagues [5], and the lung curve uses the exponential form of Salazar and Knowles [6], extended below the range they fit.



The chest wall wants to be big. The relaxed chest wall rests at about 4.75 L, 72% of the way from RV to TLC [5]. Below that volume it recoils outward, and above it, it recoils inward. That is a property of its anatomy: ribs, cartilage and muscle that have been sprung inward. The diaphragm and the abdomen below it count as part of the chest wall.
The lung wants to be small. At zero transpulmonary pressure, a lung removed from the chest shrinks to a small “minimal volume,” below RV. It never empties completely, because its small airways pinch shut at low volume and trap some gas. At every volume in the chest it recoils inward, and the recoil grows as it is stretched. A later section explains where the recoil comes from.
The pleural space links them. The lung and chest wall are not attached to each other. They are coupled by the thin, sealed film of fluid in the pleural space. When one moves, it pulls the other with it, so they always share the same volume. At FRC, the lung pulls inward with 5 cm H2O and the chest wall pulls outward with 5 cm H2O. The two pulls make the pleural pressure negative: about −5 cm H2O at FRC. That is an average. In an upright person it is more negative at the apex and less negative at the base, which matters in the ventilation-perfusion chapter.
A pneumothorax shows what happens when the seal breaks. Air enters the pleural space, pleural pressure rises to atmospheric, and each structure goes its own way: the lung collapses toward its minimal volume and the chest wall springs outward.
The respiratory system curve is the lung and chest wall together, which is what you feel as a whole person. Because they share one volume, their pressures add at each volume: the system’s pressure is the lung’s recoil pressure plus the chest wall’s. Below the chest wall’s resting volume, the chest wall springs outward and helps, so the system needs less pressure than the lung alone and its curve lies to the left of the lung curve. Above it, the chest wall also has to be stretched, so the system needs more pressure than the lung alone and its curve crosses to the right. In Figure 20.2 the crossing is near 4.75 L.
FRC is where the system’s pressure is zero: the volume where the lung’s inward recoil and the chest wall’s outward recoil cancel, with no muscle effort. The course calls FRC “the Pms of the respiratory system”: like mean systemic filling pressure in the circulation, it is the state the system settles into when nothing is driving it.

title: 20  Respiratory Statics
text:
20.4 The single-alveolus model
Treat the whole lung as one balloon (the alveolus) inside a box (the chest wall), connected to the mouth by one airway (Figure 20.3). Four pressures describe it.








Symbol
Name
Meaning




Palv
Alveolar pressure
Pressure of the gas inside the alveoli. Written PA on the lecture slides.


Ppl
Pleural pressure
Pressure in the pleural space, just outside the lung


Ptp
Transpulmonary pressure
The lung’s transmural pressure: Ptp = Palv − Ppl


Pel
Elastic recoil pressure
The inward pressure the lung’s recoil generates; set by lung volume and by the lung’s tissue and surface forces



The lung’s recoil squeezes the gas inside it, so alveolar pressure sits Pel above pleural pressure:
\[P_{alv} = P_{pl} + P_{el}\]
Rearranging, Ptp = Palv − Ppl = Pel. The pressure distending the lung is matched by the lung’s own recoil at that volume. What changes during a breath is Ppl. Palv follows it, and air flows until the new volume’s recoil catches up.
The order of events is always the same. The muscles are the only lever: they change Ppl, the change in Ppl changes Palv, Palv drives flow, flow changes volume, and volume changes Pel.






Figure 20.3: The single-alveolus model. (A) At FRC with the glottis open and no flow. (B) The instant inspiration begins: the inspiratory muscles have lowered pleural pressure, but almost no air has entered yet, so Pel is unchanged. Pressures in cm H2O relative to atmosphere. Course figure, after the lecture’s model.



At FRC (panel A). No air is flowing, so alveolar pressure equals mouth pressure, 0. The lung’s recoil at FRC is about 5 cm H2O. So Ppl = Palv − Pel = 0 − 5 = −5, and Ptp = 0 − (−5) = 5.
Starting a breath (panel B). The diaphragm contracts (with help from the intercostal muscles) and lowers pleural pressure, say to −7. At that instant almost no air has entered, so lung volume, and with it the lung’s recoil, is essentially unchanged at 5. Alveolar pressure becomes Ppl + Pel = −7 + 5 = −2, which is below mouth pressure, so air flows in. As air enters, lung volume and recoil rise and alveolar pressure climbs back toward 0, where flow stops. We are negative-pressure breathers: we breathe in by lowering the pressure around the lung, not by pushing air in.
Ptp is still 5 because lung volume has not changed yet. The total difference between the mouth and the pleural space is 7 cm H2O: 5 of it holds the lung at its current volume and 2 drives air through the airways, by the same Ohm’s law as in the circulation (ΔP = flow × airway resistance).
Quiet expiration takes no muscle work. The inspiratory muscles relax, pleural pressure rises back toward −5, and the larger recoil at the higher volume pushes Palv above zero, so air flows out. In a forced expiration, the expiratory muscles push pleural pressure above zero. The next chapter follows the whole breath with numbers.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The lecture slides write Ptp = 0 − (−7) = 7 at the start of inspiration and say that Ptp now exceeds Pel. That 7 is calculated with Palv still at 0, so it is the mouth-to-pleural pressure: the total pressure the muscles have put across the lung and airways. Once Palv has fallen to −2, Palv − Ppl is 5, equal to Pel. Both ways give the same Palv of −2 and the same answer: air flows in.
The slides also write the same relation as PA = Pel − Ptp, where the slides’ Ptp (calculated with Palv = 0) is just −Ppl. That is Palv = Ppl + Pel rearranged. In this course, work problems with Palv = Ppl + Pel.
You may later meet a third convention, mostly in critical care, where “transpulmonary pressure” means airway-opening pressure minus pleural pressure. With no flow, all of these give the same number.








TipTry it



The Respiratory Mechanics Lab draws these curves and lets you take a 0.5 L breath from FRC, with Ppl, Palv, Ptp and Pel updated as the breath runs [1].

title: 20  Respiratory Statics
section: 20.5 Compliance and the work of breathing
text:
20.5 Compliance and the work of breathing
Compliance is how much volume you get for a change in pressure: the slope of a pressure-volume curve.
\[C = \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta P}\]
A compliant lung inflates a lot for a small pressure. A stiff lung has low compliance. Near FRC, the lung and the chest wall each have a compliance of roughly 0.2 to 0.3 L/cm H2O, and the respiratory system about half of either, because their pressures add at each volume [5, 7].
Two details matter:

Compliance falls as the lung gets bigger. The lung curve in Figure 20.2 flattens near TLC. Each extra liter takes more pressure.
Overall versus specific compliance. Compliance depends on how much lung there is. A person who has had a lung removed has about half the overall compliance, but the remaining lung is normal tissue. Dividing compliance by the volume it was measured at (usually FRC) gives specific compliance, which describes the tissue itself. Diseases that make the lung stiff, such as fibrosis, lower specific compliance.

Pressure times volume has the units of work (force per area × volume = force × distance). The more pressure a breath needs, the more work it takes. In a stiff, fibrotic lung the recoil at rest might be 12 cm H2O instead of 5, so Ppl sits near −12 at FRC, and taking a breath means pulling it to about −14 instead of −7. Every breath takes more work, and a bigger breath, as in exercise, costs more still. That is why people with stiff lungs first notice breathlessness on exertion. So what sets the lung’s recoil, and how does the body keep it low?

title: 20  Respiratory Statics
section: 20.6 What sets the lung’s elastic recoil
text:
20.6 What sets the lung’s elastic recoil
The lung’s recoil has two sources: the elastic tissue in its walls (elastin and collagen), and surface tension at the thin layer of liquid lining every alveolus.

20.6.1 Air versus saline
Von Neergaard separated the two in 1929 by inflating isolated lungs with air and then with saline [8]. Saline removes the air-liquid interface and leaves only tissue forces. Figure 20.4 shows the result.






Figure 20.4: Pressure-volume curves of an isolated lung inflated with saline and with air. Solid lines, inflation; dashed lines, deflation. The tan band between saline and air deflation is the extra pressure surface tension adds. The gray band between the two air limbs is hysteresis. Schematic adapted from von Neergaard’s experiment [8]; similar curves appear in West and Luks [7].



Three things stand out:

The saline-filled lung inflates with far less pressure. Surface tension accounts for more than half of the recoil of an air-filled lung.
Starting from collapse, almost no air enters until the pressure reaches an opening pressure. Then volume rises quickly.
The air-filled lung shows hysteresis: inflation and deflation follow different curves, so at any pressure the lung holds more volume on the way down than on the way up. Two things cause it. Opening collapsed alveoli takes more pressure than keeping open ones open, and the surfactant film has higher tension while it is being stretched than while it is being compressed. The saline-filled lung shows almost no hysteresis.

Tissue forces still matter. They are what change in fibrosis, where scar makes the tissue itself stiff.


20.6.2 Surface tension and the law of Laplace
Water molecules attract each other. A molecule inside the liquid is pulled equally in all directions, but one at the surface is pulled only sideways and inward. The surface behaves like a stretched sheet that tries to make its area as small as possible. That pull, force per unit length of surface, is the surface tension (T).
In a sphere, surface tension squeezes the gas inside. The law of Laplace gives the pressure needed to keep the sphere open:
\[P = \frac{2T}{r}\]
The smaller the sphere, the more pressure it needs. That would make a lung lined only with water unstable. Alveoli of different sizes are connected through the airways, so the gas in them is at the same pressure. If a small and a large alveolus had the same surface tension, the small one would need more pressure to stay open than the large one, and it would empty into the large one (Figure 20.5 A). Left alone, the lung would tend toward a few overinflated alveoli and many collapsed ones, and inflating it would take a great deal of work.
Real alveoli are not separate bubbles. They share walls and hold one another open, which also resists collapse. The two-bubble picture is a simplification, but it shows why surface tension has to be controlled.






Figure 20.5: The law of Laplace for two connected alveoli. (A) With the same surface tension, the small alveolus needs twice the pressure of the large one and empties into it. (B) Surfactant lowers tension more in the smaller alveolus, so the pressures match and both stay open. Arbitrary units. Course figure.





20.6.3 Surfactant
Surfactant solves the problem [9]. Type II alveolar cells secrete it. It is mostly phospholipid, chiefly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC), with a small amount of surfactant proteins. Each molecule has a water-loving head that sits in the lining liquid and water-fearing tails that point into the air. The molecules collect at the surface, push water molecules apart, and weaken their attraction.
Surface tension is measured in dyn/cm (the same as mN/m). Water at body temperature is about 70 dyn/cm. A surfactant film left undisturbed settles near 25 dyn/cm. When the film is compressed, as when an alveolus shrinks during expiration, tension falls close to zero. Measured in intact lungs, it runs from near zero at low volumes to about 30 dyn/cm near TLC [10].
The effect depends on how crowded the surfactant is. The amount on an alveolus barely changes from one breath to the next, so:

When an alveolus is small, the same surfactant covers less surface and packs tightly, so surface tension is low. Small alveoli stop emptying into large ones (Figure 20.5 B).
When an alveolus is large, the surfactant is spread thin and surface tension rises, which adds to the lung’s recoil at high volume. Most of the flattening near TLC comes from the tissue, though: the collagen network reaches its limit, which is why the saline curve in Figure 20.4 flattens too.

The overall result is a more compliant lung, less work per breath, and alveoli that fill more evenly.
Premature infants are born before their type II cells make enough surfactant. Their lungs are stiff, their alveoli collapse, and breathing takes more work than they can sustain: neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Avery and Mead linked the syndrome to a lack of surfactant in 1959 [11]. Treatment includes giving surfactant directly into the airway.
In adults, inflammation from pneumonia, sepsis or injury can flood the alveoli with fluid and wash out or inactivate surfactant. This is the acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). The lungs become heavy and stiff, alveoli collapse, and blood flows past collapsed alveoli without picking up oxygen. The V/Q chapter calls that shunt.

title: 20  Respiratory Statics
section: 20.7 What sets FRC, TLC and RV
text:
20.7 What sets FRC, TLC and RV
Each of the three volumes that spirometry cannot see is set by a balance of forces (Figure 20.6).






Figure 20.6: The respiratory system curve (maroon), with faint lung and chest wall curves. The red dashed lines show the recoil each muscle group can just hold against at each volume. The inspiratory muscles (right) hold the system expanded against its inward recoil. The expiratory muscles (left) hold it compressed against its outward recoil. Where a line meets the system curve, the muscles can go no further: TLC at upper right, RV at lower left. The lines slope because each muscle group is weaker at the volume where it is shortest. Curves come from the Respiratory Mechanics Lab statics model [1]. Muscle strength is set so that the maximal mouth pressures (recoil plus muscle pressure) are about −110 cm H2O at RV and +200 cm H2O at TLC, between the values Black and Hyatt reported for young men and women [12].



FRC: lung versus chest wall, with no muscles. FRC is where the lung’s inward recoil equals the chest wall’s outward recoil with the muscles relaxed. Change either curve and FRC moves. Change only the muscles and FRC does not.
TLC: the inspiratory muscles versus the inward recoil of the system. Above about 4.75 L, the chest wall’s resting volume, both the lung and the chest wall recoil inward, and the inspiratory muscles have to overcome both. TLC is the volume where the strongest inspiratory effort can go no further. The inspiratory line slopes because of length-tension, which you met in the muscle block: as the lung fills, the diaphragm flattens and shortens, so it can generate less force.
You will also read that TLC is set by the elastic properties of the lung. Near TLC the lung is so stiff that more effort buys very little volume (in the model, the lung supplies 34 of the system’s 37 cm H2O of recoil at TLC), so a stiff lung lowers TLC and a floppy one raises it. But the muscles still set the end point, which is why weak muscles lower TLC even when the lung is normal.
RV: the expiratory muscles versus the chest wall, or the airways. In a young adult with healthy airways, RV is the volume where the expiratory muscles can squeeze the chest wall no smaller: the compressed chest wall becomes very stiff [13]. In lecture you heard that the flat bottom of the curve is where airways collapse. That is the limit in older adults and in obstructive lung disease: small airways close before the chest wall limit is reached and trap gas behind them, so RV rises. It is also why a lung taken out of the chest never empties. The dynamics chapter explains airway closure.

title: 20  Respiratory Statics
text:
20.8 Disease patterns
Restrictive diseases lower TLC: the lungs are small. Obstructive diseases narrow the airways and slow expiratory flow, which spirometry shows as a low FEV1/FVC (next chapter). Some obstructive diseases, emphysema above all, also make the lungs big.
A restrictive pattern can come from three places: a stiff lung, a stiff or loaded chest wall, or weak muscles. For any case, work through the same steps:

Is the problem in the lung, the chest wall or the muscles?
Which curve moves, and which way?
What happens to TLC, FRC and RV, and to the work of breathing?

Figure 20.7 shows four cases.






Figure 20.7: Lung volumes in four conditions, from the Respiratory Mechanics Lab statics model [1]. Thin dashed lines show the healthy curve that changed and the healthy respiratory system. Red dashed lines are the muscle limits. (A) Pulmonary fibrosis: lung compliance reduced. (B) Emphysema: lung compliance increased. (C) Obesity: an inward load on the chest wall. (D) Respiratory muscle weakness: muscle strength reduced to 25%. The static model does not include airway closure, so it does not show the rise in RV that air trapping causes in emphysema.



Pulmonary fibrosis (a lung problem). Scar makes the lung tissue stiff, so the lung curve shifts down and to the right and flattens, and the lung’s recoil at every volume rises. The lung wins the tug-of-war with the chest wall, so FRC falls, and the system reaches the inspiratory muscle limit sooner, so TLC falls. RV falls a little; the small-group keys mark it decreased. The change is small because in a young adult the chest wall, which fibrosis does not change, sets RV. The main problem is the tissue, not the surfactant.
ARDS (a lung problem). Lost surfactant and extra lung water make the lung stiff through surface forces as well as tissue. On the air-filled lung’s pressure-volume loop (as in Figure 20.4), both limbs shift right and flatten: filling the lung and keeping it open both take more pressure.
Emphysema (a lung problem). Smoking, or less often alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, destroys alveolar walls and their elastic connections, so the lung loses recoil: its curve shifts up and to the left and steepens. The chest wall wins, so FRC rises (hyperinflation) and TLC rises. RV rises even more, because without the outward pull of surrounding tissue the small airways close early and trap gas. The dynamics chapter covers that part. People with emphysema are short of breath even though their lungs are easy to stretch. At a high FRC the diaphragm starts every breath flattened and short, at a poor point on its length-tension curve.
Chest wall and abdominal restriction (a chest wall problem). The lung is normal, but the chest wall is stiffer or loaded. Examples include a circumferential burn whose scar binds the chest, kyphoscoliosis, and anything that keeps the diaphragm from descending: obesity, pregnancy, ascites or a large upper abdominal mass. The chest wall curve shifts to the right, so it no longer springs outward as much, and FRC falls. In obesity FRC falls while RV changes little, so ERV shrinks the most. TLC falls less, and in the model it barely changes.
Respiratory muscle weakness (a muscle problem). The lung and chest wall are normal, so their curves do not move, and FRC, which needs no muscle, stays normal. Weak inspiratory muscles cannot pull the system as far, so TLC falls. Weak expiratory muscles cannot squeeze it as far, so RV rises. Read in percent predicted, TLC is low, FRC normal and RV high, a rising pattern the small groups call the step-up pattern. Diseases that weaken the respiratory muscles, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis or myasthenia gravis, show this pattern. In long-standing weakness FRC can drift down a little, because the lung and chest wall stiffen over time.
The Respiratory Mechanics Lab has each of these as a preset, along with kyphoscoliosis [1].

title: 20  Respiratory Statics
text:
20.9 Check your understanding

A patient’s spirometry shows a vital capacity of 4.5 L, and the lab also wants her FRC. Why can a body box measure FRC when the spirometer cannot? Use Boyle’s law.


Answer

A spirometer measures only air that comes out, and FRC includes RV, which never leaves the lung. In the body box the shutter closes at the end of a quiet expiration, at FRC, and the patient pants against it. No air enters or leaves, so the gas in the chest is only compressed and decompressed. By Boyle’s law (P1V1 = P2V2, with absolute pressures), the pressure change at the mouth and the small change in chest volume, read from the box, give the volume of gas being squeezed: FRC. The box compresses all the gas in the chest, so it counts RV too. Then TLC = FRC + IC and RV = FRC − ERV.

What is pleural pressure at FRC, and why is it negative? What happens to it during a forced expiration?


Answer

About −5 cm H2O. At FRC the lung pulls inward with 5 cm H2O and the chest wall pulls outward with 5, and the sealed pleural fluid between them is pulled on from both sides, so its pressure is below atmospheric. In a forced expiration the expiratory muscles squeeze the chest and push Ppl above zero. Palv = Ppl + Pel then rises well above mouth pressure, and air flows out fast.

Partway through a quiet inspiration, Ppl is −7 cm H2O and the lung’s elastic recoil is 6 cm H2O. What are Palv and Ptp, and is air moving?


Answer

Palv = Ppl + Pel = −7 + 6 = −1 cm H2O, below mouth pressure, so air is still flowing in. Ptp = Palv − Ppl = −1 − (−7) = 6, equal to Pel. If you calculated 0 − (−7) = 7, that is the mouth-to-pleural pressure the slides call “Ptp”. It exceeds Pel by the 1 cm H2O that is driving flow.

A woman has large-volume ascites. Why does her FRC fall more than her TLC?


Answer

FRC is the volume where the lung’s inward recoil and the chest wall’s outward recoil balance, with no muscle effort. The fluid pushes the diaphragm up and loads the chest wall from below, so the chest wall springs outward less and that balance point moves to a smaller volume. TLC is set by how far the inspiratory muscles can pull the system. They can still pull most of the way against the extra load, so TLC falls less. The lung itself is normal.

In emphysema, why does RV rise more than FRC or TLC?


Answer

In a young adult with healthy airways, RV is set by the expiratory muscles squeezing a chest wall that becomes very stiff when compressed. In emphysema the small airways have lost the surrounding tissue that holds them open, and the lung’s recoil is weak, so they close early during expiration, before the chest wall limit is reached. Gas is trapped behind them. RV is then set by airway closure, and it rises the most.

Why are the smallest alveoli of a premature infant the first to collapse?


Answer

With too little surfactant, surface tension stays high and about the same in large and small alveoli. By the law of Laplace (P = 2T/r), a small alveolus then needs more pressure to stay open, so it empties into its larger neighbors. Surfactant normally prevents this by lowering tension most in the smallest alveoli.

title: 21  Respiratory Dynamics I
text:
21.1 The single-alveolus model
Respiratory Statics held the respiratory system still. The lungs want to be small, the chest wall wants to be big, and the pleural space links them, so they settle at FRC, which the course calls the Pms of the respiratory system. This chapter makes the system move. It follows the single alveolus through one quiet breath with numbers at every step, then adds two wrinkles that the single alveolus leaves out: the lung is not the same from top to bottom, and air has to travel through airways that resist its flow. Respiratory Dynamics II takes the airways further.
The model is the one from statics: one alveolus (the whole lung) in a box (the chest wall), open to the mouth through one airway. Mouth pressure, which is atmospheric, is set to 0, so every pressure is relative to the atmosphere. Air flows into the alveolus when alveolar pressure is below 0 and out when it is above 0.
The rule from statics carries through every step:
\[P_{alv} = P_{pl} + P_{el}\]
The lung’s recoil squeezes the gas inside it, so alveolar pressure sits Pel above pleural pressure. That makes Ptp = Palv − Ppl = Pel at every moment, during flow as well as at rest.
Causes and effects run in one direction. The muscles change Ppl. Ppl and the lung’s recoil set Palv. Palv drives flow. Flow changes volume, and volume changes Pel. Pel depends only on how big the lung is, so at the instant a muscle contracts or relaxes, Pel has not had time to change.

Inspiration is shaded white and expiration gray. The pressures use the lecture’s numbers (Pel 5 cm H2O at FRC and 9 at end inspiration), and airway resistance is set so that Palv reaches about −1 and +1.
