Pressures are in cm H2O, rounded to whole numbers as on the slides. Walk through it.
A. At FRC. No air is moving, so Palv equals mouth pressure, 0. The lung’s recoil at FRC is 5, so Ppl = Palv − Pel = −5, and Ptp = 0 − (−5) = 5.
The first instant of inspiration: a thought experiment. Imagine the diaphragm contracts and lowers Ppl in one step, here to −6 (slide 8). No air has entered yet, so lung volume and Pel are still at their FRC values. Palv = Ppl + Pel = −6 + 5 = −1. That is below mouth pressure, so air begins to flow in. Nothing else has to happen for inspiration to begin; lowering Ppl is the whole act. The size of the step is arbitrary: statics and slide 3 use −7, which gives Palv −2. In a real breath Ppl and Palv fall smoothly together from the first moment, as in Figure 21.1, and flow builds as Palv falls.
B. During inspiration. The muscles keep lowering Ppl, and air keeps flowing in. As the lung fills, Pel rises. By 3,300 mL, Ppl is −8 and the lung’s recoil has risen to 7, so Palv is −1 and air is coming in near its fastest rate. The muscles have to keep pulling Ppl down just to stay ahead of the rising recoil.
C. End inspiration. At 3,500 mL the lung’s recoil is 9. The inspiratory muscles have pulled Ppl to −9 and hold it there. Palv = −9 + 9 = 0, so flow stops. This is the turnaround point: Palv has to pass through 0 for flow to change direction.
D. Expiration. The inspiratory muscles relax. Ppl rises toward its relaxed value. In the instant they relax, the lung is still at 3,500 mL with Pel 9, so as soon as Ppl rises above −9, Palv = Ppl + 9 rises above 0 and air flows out. At 3,300 mL on the way out, Ppl is −6 and Pel is 7, so Palv is +1. No muscle is pushing. The recoil that the breath in stored in the stretched lung is what pushes the air out.
E. Back at FRC. Air flows out until volume is back to 3,000 mL, Pel is back to 5, Ppl is back to −5 and Palv is back to 0. The system is where it started, with no muscle effort, ready for the next breath.
Notice three things on the traces. Pleural pressure is negative throughout a quiet breath: it falls from −5 to about −9 and comes back, and never becomes positive. Alveolar pressure is negative during inspiration, positive during expiration, and 0 at the turnarounds. And at the same lung volume, Ppl is more negative on the way in (−8 at B) than on the way out (−6 at D). The 2 cm H2O difference is the pressure needed to move air through the airways, first one way and then the other. The last section of this chapter comes back to it.






TipWhy we say inspiration is active and expiration passive



In quiet breathing, all the muscle work goes into inspiration: lowering Ppl against the lung’s rising recoil. Expiration is relaxation. The lung’s recoil, larger at the higher volume, pushes the air out. Expiratory muscles come in only when you need to breathe out faster than recoil allows or below FRC. Then, in a forceful expiration, Ppl becomes positive. Respiratory Dynamics II follows that case.








NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



Dynamics I slide 3, like the statics slides, computes Ptp as 0 − (−7) = 7 at the start of inspiration, says “Ptp exceeds Pel”, and writes PA = Pel − Ptp. That 7 is calculated with Palv still at 0, so it is the pressure from the mouth to the pleural space. Once Palv has fallen to −2, Palv − Ppl is 5, equal to Pel. Both methods give Palv = −2 and the same answer: air flows in. In the lecture this was described as “the textbook way”, with Palv = Ppl + Pel as “the other way to think about it”. This book and the course errata use Palv = Ppl + Pel, so Ptp always equals Pel. The walk-through slides start the breath with a smaller step (−6 instead of −7); both give Palv = Ppl + 5.
The slides that walk through the breath (slides 7 to 12) give Ptp = Palv − Ppl directly, as this chapter does. Two of them do not fit the rest. Slide 9 gives Ptp 6 and slide 11 gives Ptp 8, both at 3,300 mL, but the lung has one recoil at one volume, so Ptp must be the same at the same volume going in and going out. The errata keep 3,300 mL and correct them to the values in the table above: Ppl −8 and Palv −1 on the way in, Ppl −6 and Palv +1 on the way out, Ptp 7 both times. The Dynamics I notes table has the same problem in its early- and mid-inspiration rows, and the errata correct it the same way.








NoteIf you are comparing with the statics chapter: how stiff is the lung?



The lecture’s numbers make Pel rise from 5 to 9 cm H2O as volume rises from 3,000 to 3,500 mL. That is a lung compliance of 0.5 L ÷ 4 cm H2O = 0.125 L/cm H2O. Respiratory Statics gives 0.2 to 0.3 L/cm H2O near FRC, and the measured traces from Boron and Boulpaep [1] shown in the same lecture use 0.2 (transpulmonary pressure from 5 to 7.5 for 0.5 L). The lecture’s numbers are rounded to keep the arithmetic easy. A normal lung is closer to 0.2, the value statics and the measured traces use; 0.125 would be on the stiff side of normal. With 0.2, end-inspiratory Ppl would be −7.5 instead of −9. The logic of the breath is the same either way. Use whatever numbers a question gives you.








NoteBackground: what the traces look like when they are measured





The lecture showed the same breath as it looks when the pressures are measured, from Boron and Boulpaep [1]. The shapes are the same as Figure 21.1: pleural pressure falls during inspiration and rises during expiration, alveolar pressure dips below zero and then rises above it, and flow peaks early in each phase. The lecture said this one was “just for fun”, not something to know. What you should be able to do is draw Figure 21.1 yourself from the rule Palv = Ppl + Pel: the lecture suggested printing the blank traces as a worksheet and filling in each moment.









TipTry it



The Respiratory Mechanics Lab takes a 0.5 L breath from FRC and updates Ppl, Palv, Ptp and Pel as the breath runs.

title: 21  Respiratory Dynamics I
section: 21.3 Wrinkle 1: the lung is not the same from top to bottom
text:
21.3 Wrinkle 1: the lung is not the same from top to bottom
The single-alveolus model treats every alveolus alike. In an upright person they are not. Pleural pressure is more negative at the apex of the lung, about −10 cm H2O, than at the base, about −2.5 (Figure 21.3 A). The reason is the weight of the lung. The lung hangs in the chest like a Slinky held from its top end. The coils near the top carry the weight of everything below them and are stretched wide apart. The coils near the bottom carry little and sit close together.
So at FRC the alveoli at the apex are held more open (larger Ptp) than those at the base. The apical alveoli are bigger.
Bigger does not mean they ventilate more. What matters for ventilation is how much each alveolus changes during a breath. Figure 21.3 B puts both regions on the lung’s pressure-volume curve. A breath lowers pleural pressure by about the same amount everywhere. The apex starts high on the curve, where it is flat, so the same fall in Ppl adds little volume. The base starts low, on the steep part, so it adds more. Per unit of lung, the base gets more of each breath than the apex.






Figure 21.3: Regional differences in the upright lung. (A) Pleural pressure is about −10 cm H2O at the apex and −2.5 at the base, so apical alveoli are larger at FRC. (B) On the lung’s pressure-volume curve the base starts on the steep part. The same 4 cm H2O fall in pleural pressure raises the base by about 20% of its maximal volume and the apex by about 10%. Lung curve from the Respiratory Mechanics Lab statics model [2]. Course figure.



That matches where the blood goes. Blood flow in the upright lung is also greatest at the base. Sending more air to the places that get more blood is the start of ventilation-perfusion matching, which the Ventilation and Perfusion chapter covers, along with what happens when the matching fails.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



In the 2026 lecture, the smaller basal alveoli were explained by interstitial fluid that settles toward the base with gravity. The standard explanation, and the one the Dynamics I notes give, is the weight of the lung itself: it makes pleural pressure less negative at the base (about −2.5 cm H2O) than at the apex (about −10), so the basal alveoli are held less open. The conclusion is the same either way: basal alveoli are smaller at FRC and expand more with each breath. You do not need to explain why pleural pressure differs from apex to base; know that it does and what it does to regional ventilation.

title: 21  Respiratory Dynamics I
text:
21.4 Wrinkle 2: airway resistance
So far the breath has been mostly about compliance: how much Ppl has to fall to stretch the lung by a tidal volume. That part of the pressure is set by the lung’s recoil. But air also has to move through the airways, and the airways resist flow. The pressure needed for that follows Ohm’s law, as blood flow did:
\[\dot{V} = \frac{\Delta P}{R_{aw}}\]
Here ΔP is the difference between mouth and alveolar pressure, and Raw is airway resistance.
Figure 21.4 separates the two parts. The dashed line (B on the slides) is the pleural pressure the breath would need if the airways had no resistance: it just tracks the lung’s recoil, −Pel, and falls and rises with volume. The solid line (B′) is the real pleural pressure with normal airway resistance. During inspiration it is more negative than the dashed line, because Ppl also has to pull Palv below zero to draw air through the airways. During expiration it is less negative than the dashed line, because Palv must be above zero to push air out. The shaded gap between them is the resistive part of the pressure. It is largest when flow is fastest, and zero at the turnarounds, when there is no flow.






Figure 21.4: Pleural pressure through one breath. Dashed (B): the pressure needed with no airway resistance, set by elastic recoil alone. Solid (B′): with normal airway resistance. Dotted: inspiration with airway resistance tripled, at the same flow. The shaded gap between B and B′ is the pressure that moves air through the airways. The slide draws the expiratory gap wider. In quiet breathing the two are close to equal; the gap on the way out grows when the airways are narrowed or expiration is forced, for the reasons in Respiratory Dynamics II. Course figure.



The greater the airway resistance, the further Ppl has to swing to keep the same flow. The dotted line in Figure 21.4 shows inspiration with airway resistance tripled: to move the same 500 mL in the same time, Ppl has to fall to about −10.5 instead of −9. That is more work for the inspiratory muscles on every breath.
You can see this at the bedside. A patient in respiratory distress from an asthma exacerbation has narrowed airways. You see accessory muscles working: the neck muscles, tugging at the trachea, help lower pleural pressure further on the way in, because the diaphragm alone cannot overcome the resistance, and the abdominal muscles contract to push air out on the way out. Up to a point the patient keeps the same flow and volume by working harder. Beyond it, they cannot.
In asthma the wheeze is heard first in expiration, not inspiration. Pleural pressure is higher on the way out, so the airways are pushed open less, and they are narrowest late in expiration, when the lung is smallest. Resistance is a bigger problem on the way out. Respiratory Dynamics II explains why.

title: 21  Respiratory Dynamics I
text:
21.5 Check your understanding

At end inspiration in a quiet breath, Ppl is −8 cm H2O and no air is flowing. What are Palv, Pel and Ptp?


Answer

No flow means Palv = 0. Then Pel = Palv − Ppl = 0 − (−8) = 8, and Ptp = Palv − Ppl = 8, equal to Pel.

Partway through a quiet expiration, the lung’s recoil is 6 cm H2O and Palv is +0.5. What is Ppl? Is any muscle pushing the air out?


Answer

Ppl = Palv − Pel = 0.5 − 6 = −5.5 cm H2O. No. Ppl is still negative, which means the chest is not squeezing the lung. The lung’s own recoil is pushing the air out. A positive Ppl would mean expiratory muscles were working.

A tidal breath passes through the same lung volume twice, once on the way in and once on the way out. At that volume, which of Pel, Ptp, Ppl and Palv are the same both times, and which differ?


Answer

Pel is set by volume, so it is the same, and Ptp equals Pel, so it is the same too. Palv is negative on the way in and positive on the way out. Ppl = Palv − Pel, so it is more negative on the way in. The difference is the pressure that drives flow through the airways.

The difference in pleural pressure from the top of the lung to the bottom comes from the lung’s weight. In an upright person it makes the base gain more volume per breath than the apex. Why does ventilation become more even from top to bottom when the same person lies supine?


Answer

How large the pleural pressure difference is depends on how tall the lung is in the direction of gravity. Upright, that height runs from apex to base. Supine, it runs from front to back, a much shorter distance, so the difference in pleural pressure between the highest and lowest alveoli is smaller. Alveoli at the top and bottom then start at more similar places on the lung’s pressure-volume curve, and the same fall in pleural pressure during a breath adds more similar volumes to each.

A drug relaxes airway smooth muscle and widens the airways. With the same tidal volume and the same inspiratory flow, what happens to the lowest pleural pressure reached during inspiration? What happens to Pel at end inspiration?


Answer

Lower airway resistance needs a smaller pressure difference for the same flow, so Palv dips less below zero and Ppl does not have to fall as far: its lowest value is less negative. Pel at end inspiration does not change. It depends on the lung’s volume and stiffness, not on the airways.

During a quiet expiration, expiratory flow peaks early, soon after the inspiratory muscles relax, and then slows as the lung empties toward FRC. Use Palv = Ppl + Pel and V̇ = Palv / Raw to explain that shape.


Answer

When the inspiratory muscles relax, Ppl rises back from its most negative value while the lung is still near its largest volume, so Pel is still close to its peak of 9. Palv = Ppl + Pel turns positive, and it is largest early in expiration, so flow, Palv / Raw, peaks then. As air leaves, volume falls and Pel falls with it, back toward 5 at FRC, and Palv shrinks toward zero. With a smaller pressure difference between the alveoli and the mouth, flow slows. The lung’s own recoil supplies the push throughout.

title: 22  Respiratory Dynamics II
text:
22.1 Anatomic determinants of airway resistance
Respiratory Dynamics I ended with one airway and one number for its resistance: the more resistance, the further pleural pressure has to swing to move the same air. Real airways are not one tube. They branch about 23 times between the trachea and the alveoli, they change size as the lung fills and empties, and they are not rigid. This chapter takes the pieces of airway resistance one at a time, puts them together along the airway tree and across lung volumes, and then uses them to explain why everyone, healthy or not, has a limit on how fast they can breathe out. That limit is what spirometry measures.
Keep the volumes from Respiratory Statics in front of you. You will need TLC, FRC, RV and vital capacity (VC = TLC − RV) throughout.

title: 22  Respiratory Dynamics II
text:
22.1.1 Radius: Poiseuille’s law
Poiseuille studied the flow of liquid through narrow rigid tubes. For smooth, laminar flow he found:
\[\dot{V} = \frac{(P_1 - P_2)\,\pi r^4}{8\eta l} \qquad\text{so}\qquad R = \frac{8\eta l}{\pi r^4}\]
where r is the radius, l the length of the tube, and η the viscosity of the gas. Longer tubes and more viscous gas raise resistance. Radius matters most, because it enters as the fourth power. Halve the radius and resistance rises 16-fold (Figure 22.1). If you remember one thing from Poiseuille’s law, make it radius, because a small change in airway caliber, from bronchospasm, mucus or swelling, makes a large change in resistance.






Figure 22.1: Poiseuille’s law: resistance rises with the fourth power of falling radius. A 20% narrowing more than doubles resistance, and halving the radius raises it 16-fold. Course figure.



The law assumes three things the airways only partly satisfy:

Laminar flow. Not all airflow in the lung is laminar (next section).
A Newtonian fluid, whose viscosity does not change with velocity. Air comes close enough.
Rigid, circular tubes. The trachea is close to that. Smaller airways are floppy, and their size changes with the pressures around them, which is the root of expiratory flow limitation.

Poiseuille’s law also predicts that resistance should be highest in the narrowest airways. It is not, for reasons that take the rest of this section.


22.1.2 Flow type: laminar, turbulent and transitional
In laminar flow, the gas moves in smooth layers, like a calm river. The layer touching the wall does not move, and each layer slides past the next, so velocity is highest in the center and the profile is parabolic (Figure 22.2 A). Laminar flow is quiet and is the most efficient way to move gas through a tube: flow is proportional to the driving pressure, as Poiseuille’s law says.
In turbulent flow, the layers break up into eddies, like white water. Changing the direction of any bit of gas takes force, so turbulent flow needs more pressure for the same flow. Flow then rises only with the square root of the driving pressure (Figure 22.2 B). Turbulent flow is noisy. The breath sounds you hear with a stethoscope come from turbulence in the large airways.






Figure 22.2: Laminar and turbulent flow. (A) In laminar flow, velocity is highest in the center and zero at the wall. In turbulent flow, eddies form and the profile is blunt. (B) Laminar flow rises in proportion to driving pressure. Once flow becomes turbulent, it rises only with the square root of pressure, so each further increase in flow costs more pressure. Arbitrary units. Course figure.



Whether flow is laminar or turbulent is predicted by the Reynolds number:
\[Re = \frac{D\,v\,\rho}{\eta}\]
where D is the tube diameter, v the average velocity, ρ the gas density and η its viscosity. Turbulence is likely when Re is above about 2,000. You do not need to calculate Re. You do need its variables: a wider tube, a faster velocity or a denser gas makes turbulence more likely. In the airways, density and viscosity barely change, so diameter and velocity decide. The lecture’s example, a 3 cm tube at 150 cm/s, gives Re about 2,950. A real adult trachea is about 2 cm across, and the answer is similar, about 2,400: still turbulent. The same variables explain why a low-density gas, a helium-oxygen mixture (heliox), lowers resistance where flow is turbulent.
Transitional flow is a mixture, with eddies forming where an airway divides. Every branch point disturbs the flow a little. The airways branch in a repeating, self-similar pattern, like ferns and snowflakes.


22.1.3 Cross-sectional area and velocity
Each airway is narrower than its parent, but each generation has twice as many airways as the one before. Their total cross-sectional area, all the airways of one generation added together, rises steeply toward the periphery; the Alveolar Ventilation chapter plots it by generation. It is the same idea as the aggregate cross-sectional area of the capillaries in the cardiovascular block.
The airways are in series, so the same total flow passes through every generation. Velocity is flow divided by area, so as total area rises, velocity falls (Figure 22.3). It is highest in the first few generations below the trachea (about generations 2 to 4), where the total area dips a little, and by the terminal bronchioles the gas is barely moving. A smaller diameter and a much lower velocity give the small airways a low Reynolds number, so flow in them is laminar.






Figure 22.3: Average gas velocity along the airway tree at a flow of 0.5 L/s. Velocity is highest in the first few generations, where total cross-sectional area dips slightly, and falls steeply toward the alveoli as total area rises. Velocities are flow divided by total area, with areas from Weibel’s symmetric airway model, the model the Alveolar Ventilation lecture uses. Course figure.





22.1.4 Series and parallel
Resistances in series add. Resistances in parallel add as reciprocals, so every extra parallel path lowers the total:
\[R_T = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + \dots \qquad \frac{1}{R_T} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3} + \dots\]
The generations of the airway tree are in series, and the airways within each generation are in parallel. A single bronchiole has a high resistance, but there are so many of them side by side that the combined resistance of a whole generation of small airways is small.


22.1.5 Where the resistance lies
Put the pieces together and you get Figure 22.4 A. Resistance is highest in the medium-sized bronchi, the first several generations beyond the trachea, where the airways are still few, flow is fast, and the flow is turbulent or transitional. It falls toward the periphery. The small airways, despite their size, contribute little, and the respiratory zone almost nothing.
That has a clinical cost. Disease in the small airways can be well advanced before it raises total airway resistance enough to measure, because the small airways contributed so little to begin with.






Figure 22.4: Where airway resistance lies, and how it changes with lung volume. (A) Resistance of each airway generation: highest in the medium bronchi, small in the many parallel small airways. (B) Airway resistance falls as the lung fills, because the lung tissue tethers the airways open. Normal Raw at FRC is below 2 cm H2O/L/s. Schematics drawn to the shapes of the curves on the lecture slides. Course figure.





22.1.6 Measuring airway resistance
The pulmonary function lab measures airway resistance in the body box while the patient makes small, fast pants around FRC; resistance needs flow, so it is measured while air is moving. It is a single number for the whole lung, so it describes one lung volume and says nothing about how resistance changes across a breath. Normal Raw is less than 2 cm H2O/L/s. You do not need to know how the measurement is made, or to calculate resistance at a particular place in the airways.


22.1.7 Lung volume and tethering
Airways are not free-standing tubes. They run through the lung tissue, and the alveolar walls around them are attached to their outer walls. When the lung expands, that tissue pulls outward on every airway, which holds them open. This is tethering, or radial traction. So the larger the lung, the wider the airways and the lower the resistance; as the lung empties toward RV, the airways narrow and resistance climbs steeply (Figure 22.4 B). That is one reason Raw is measured at a standard volume, FRC.
Breathing in and out differ too. At any given lung volume, pleural pressure is more negative during inspiration than during expiration, so airway transmural pressure is larger and the airways are wider on the way in. Late in expiration the lung is also smaller, so tethering holds the airways open less. That explains a bedside sign. In asthma, where the airways are narrowed, the wheeze (the sound of turbulent flow through narrowed airways) is heard first in expiration. As an exacerbation worsens, wheeze is heard in both phases. In a very severe attack the chest can fall nearly silent, because so little air is moving. So “no wheeze” in a patient short of breath is either very good news or very bad, and you have to listen for breath sounds to tell which.






TipWhere we are




Poiseuille is a start: radius matters most for any single airway.
Flow in the large airways is turbulent, and turbulent flow needs more pressure. Flow in the small airways is laminar.
Total cross-sectional area rises toward the periphery, so velocity falls.
The parallel arrangement keeps the combined resistance of the small airways low. Most resistance is in the medium bronchi.
Resistance falls as lung volume rises, because the tissue tethers the airways open.

Airway resistance is not a fixed number. It changes with where you are in the tree, with lung volume, and between inspiration and expiration. So does the pressure inside the airway, which is the next topic.

title: 22  Respiratory Dynamics II
text:
22.2 Expiratory flow limitation
Most airflow limitation, in health and in disease, happens during expiration. On the way in, the muscles pull the lung open and the airways with it, so inspiration rarely limits flow. On the way out, everything runs the other way.
Quiet expiration is passive. The inspiratory muscles relax and the lung’s recoil pushes air out. A forced expiration adds the expiratory muscles, chiefly the abdominal and internal intercostal muscles, which squeeze the chest and push pleural pressure above zero. This section follows a forced expiration from TLC, the maneuver spirometry uses.

22.2.1 Pressure falls along the airway
Air has to flow from the alveolus to the mouth, so the pressure inside the airway must fall all along the way, from Palv in the alveolus to 0 at the mouth. Two things produce that fall.

Friction. Gas sliding along the airway wall loses energy as heat, so pressure falls along the length of every airway. The Darcy-Weisbach equation describes it; you do not need it.
Velocity (the Bernoulli effect). As gas moves from the wide periphery into the narrow central airways, it speeds up. Its kinetic energy rises, so its pressure has to fall: energy is conserved, and what goes into speed comes out of pressure. The lecture showed the idea with a strip of paper that rises when you blow across the top of it. The slide notes say this velocity effect matters more than friction during a forced expiration, and in the large central airways at high flow it does. The two together produce the pressure gradient that moves the air.



22.2.2 Airway transmural pressure
Statics defined the transmural pressure of any wall as inside minus outside. For an airway inside the chest, the outside is the pleural space:
\[P_{tm} = P_{aw} - P_{pl}\]
where Paw is the pressure inside the airway at that point. When Ptm is positive, the airway is pushed open. When it is negative, because pleural pressure is higher than the pressure inside the airway, the airway is squeezed and narrows. Compare it with transpulmonary pressure, Ptp = Palv − Ppl, which is the same idea applied to the alveolus.


22.2.3 A forced expiration in numbers
Figure 22.5 follows the lecture’s numbers.
At TLC, before the effort (A). No air is flowing, so Palv = 0. Holding the lung at TLC takes a pleural pressure of about −30 cm H2O, so the lung’s recoil is 30 (Palv = Ppl + Pel = −30 + 30 = 0). Every airway has a Ptm of 0 − (−30) = +30 and is held wide open.
The first instant of a forced expiration (B). The expiratory muscles contract hard and push Ppl to about +60. The lung has not yet emptied, so Pel is still 30, and Palv = 60 + 30 = 90. Pressure falls along the airway from 90 toward 0 at the mouth, but at this instant it stays at or above 60 inside the chest, so Ptm is not negative and the airways stay open. Flow is high. Within a moment, as flow builds, the point where airway pressure meets pleural pressure appears in the central airways, where cartilage resists the squeeze.
Later in the breath, at a lower volume (C). The lung has emptied some, so its recoil has fallen, say to 20. The muscles are still pushing, and Ppl is still +60. Now Palv = 60 + 20 = 80, and as pressure falls along the airway it drops below 60 while the airway is still inside the chest. There Ptm is negative: pleural pressure is higher than the pressure inside the airway, and the airway is squeezed narrower. This is dynamic airway compression.






Figure 22.5: A forced expiration with the lecture’s numbers. (A) At TLC with no flow: Ppl −30, Pel 30, Palv 0. (B) The expiratory muscles raise Ppl to +60; Palv = 60 + 30 = 90, and airway pressure inside the chest stays at or above pleural pressure. (C) At a lower volume, recoil has fallen to 20, so Palv is 80. Airway pressure falls below +60 before the airway leaves the chest, Ptm turns negative, and the airway narrows. Course figure, after the lecture’s model.



Now push harder. Raise Ppl from 60 to 80. Palv rises by 20, but so does the pressure squeezing the airway. The extra effort narrows the compressed segment further and adds almost nothing to flow. Past a certain effort, expiratory flow is limited, and more effort does not raise it. Everyone, healthy or not, reaches this limit in a forced expiration. The narrowed region that sets the limit is called the flow-limiting segment.






NoteIf you are comparing with the notes



The Dynamics II notes call the point along the airway where Paw equals Ppl the equal pressure point. The lecture slides do not use the term; they speak of the flow-limiting segment and dynamic airway compression. Both describe the same thing: downstream of the place where airway pressure falls to pleural pressure, Ptm is negative and the airway tends to narrow.




22.2.4 Which airways collapse
Whether an airway narrows when its Ptm goes negative depends on its wall (Figure 22.6). The trachea and main bronchi have cartilage rings and narrow only a little. Further out, the bronchi have only scattered cartilage plates, and the bronchioles have none. They depend on tethering, and when Ptm is negative they narrow and can collapse.






Figure 22.6: How airway size depends on transmural pressure. The cartilage-ringed trachea keeps most of its area even with a negative Ptm. Bronchi and bronchioles narrow steeply when Ptm falls below zero. Schematic drawn to the shape on the lecture slide. Course figure.



Lung volume decides where the flow-limiting segment sits. At high volume the lung’s recoil is large, so Palv is far above Ppl, airway pressure stays above pleural pressure for much of the way out, and the place where it finally drops below pleural pressure is in the large central airways, near the trachea. The cartilage there resists compression. As the lung empties, recoil falls, airway pressure reaches pleural pressure sooner, and the flow-limiting segment moves out into smaller, more collapsible airways. Tethering weakens too, because the lung is smaller. So flow limitation tightens as the breath goes on. At high volume, flow is limited in the central airways mainly because their total cross-section is smallest and gas velocity is highest there, not because a single wide trachea has a high resistance.
At very low volumes some small airways close completely and trap gas behind them. In a young adult the chest wall stops a forced expiration before this matters much, but with age, and in obstructive disease, airway closure is what sets RV, as Respiratory Statics explained.


22.2.5 Effort independence
Figure 22.7 shows the same idea as it is measured. In panel A, each curve is one lung volume, as the slide notes describe. Flow starts once Ppl rises far enough that Palv = Ppl + Pel exceeds zero, which at a high volume, with a large Pel, is while Ppl is still negative. At middle and low volumes flow then rises with effort and levels off: past a modest effort, pushing harder adds no flow. Near TLC it keeps rising, which is why peak flow depends on effort. In panel B, three forced expirations from TLC with different effort reach different peaks early in the breath, but after the first part they all follow the same descending line to RV.






Figure 22.7: Expiratory flow limitation as it is measured. (A) Isovolume curves: each is one lung volume (percent of vital capacity). Flow begins where Palv = Ppl + Pel reaches zero, so at Ppl = −Pel. At middle and low volumes flow levels off with more effort; near TLC it keeps rising. (B) Forced expirations from TLC with different effort: a harder effort gives a higher peak, but later in the breath every effort follows the same curve. Schematics drawn to the shapes on the lecture slides. Course figure.



So the first part of a forced expiration, near TLC, depends on effort, which is why the technician shouts at the patient to blow as hard and fast as possible. The rest of the curve is effort independent. It is set by the lung’s recoil and the airways’ resistance and collapsibility, not by the muscles. That is what makes spirometry useful: the late part of the curve reports on the lungs and airways, whatever the patient’s effort.


22.2.6 Disease: early flow limitation
Small and medium airways (asthma, emphysema). In asthma, airway smooth muscle constricts and the airways are inflamed and narrowed. With narrower airways, flow limitation starts earlier in the breath and is more severe: the descending limb of the expiratory curve sags inward, a shape called scooping (Figure 22.8 A). Emphysema reaches the same result by a different route. Lost elastic recoil lowers Palv at every volume, and lost alveolar walls weaken the tethering that holds small airways open, so they collapse early. In mild disease, wheeze is heard first at the end of expiration, at low volume, where flow limitation is tightest. This is typical of asthma.
A narrowed trachea. A lesion in the trachea, for example a stenosis after a long intubation, behaves differently. The trachea is rigid, so its narrowing does not change with transmural pressure. Every bit of air leaving the lung must pass through it, so it sets a ceiling on flow. Early in a forced expiration, when the lungs could produce their highest flows, the ceiling cuts the peak off and the curve is flat-topped. Later, when flows fall below the ceiling anyway, the curve rejoins the normal one (Figure 22.8 B). A fixed narrowing caps inspiratory flow too, so both limbs of the loop are flattened. The low, flat early part can look like a poor effort. Think Like a Respiratory Consultant comes back to this pattern.

title: 22  Respiratory Dynamics II
section: 22.3 Spirometry: the flow-volume loop and the volume-time curve
text:
22.3 Spirometry: the flow-volume loop and the volume-time curve
Spirometry records a forced vital capacity maneuver. The patient breathes quietly, takes the deepest possible breath to TLC, then blows out as hard and fast as possible, all the way to RV, and then breathes back in fully. The same data can be drawn two ways.
The flow-volume loop plots flow against volume, with no time axis. By the course’s convention, expiratory flow is drawn upward and inspiratory flow downward, and volume runs with TLC on the left and RV on the right. The expiratory limb rises to a sharp peak just after the breath starts and then falls in a nearly straight line to zero at RV. The inspiratory limb is a smooth, rounded curve below the axis. The tidal breaths before the maneuver show as a small loop that starts and ends at FRC.
The volume-time curve plots volume exhaled against time for the forced expiration. Two numbers come from it:

FVC (forced vital capacity): the total volume exhaled from TLC to RV.
FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 second): the volume exhaled in the first second.

In health FEV1/FVC is 0.70 or more; a young adult is often near 0.8. A ratio below about 0.70 is obstruction (Think Like a Respiratory Consultant). Spirometry cannot measure RV (statics again), so on its own it cannot place the loop on an absolute volume scale. Lung volumes from a body box let you draw the loops at their true volumes, as Figure 22.8 A does.






Figure 22.8: Spirometry patterns. (A) Flow-volume loops drawn on absolute lung volume, with TLC on the left. Obstruction: the loop starts at a high volume and the expiratory limb is scooped, with low flows. Restriction: the loop is small and shifted to low volume, with a steep expiratory limb. (B) A fixed narrowing of the trachea caps flow in both directions; late expiratory flow is normal. (C) Volume-time curves. The numbers are illustrative. Course figure.




22.3.1 Normal, obstructive and restrictive patterns
Obstructive (asthma, emphysema). The patient has trouble getting air out. Flow limitation starts early, so the expiratory limb is scooped. On the volume-time curve, the curve rises slowly and may still be rising at 6 seconds. FEV1 falls, FVC usually falls less, and so the ratio FEV1/FVC is low. A low FEV1/FVC is what defines obstruction. Many obstructed patients also have large lungs, with a high RV and FRC and sometimes a high TLC, but lung size is not the definition.
Restrictive (interstitial lung disease and pulmonary fibrosis, as examples of a stiff lung). The lungs are small, so FVC is low. Scarring stiffens the lung and raises its elastic recoil, so the lung empties quickly: more recoil gives a higher Palv at every volume. Flow at a given volume can be normal or high, and the expiratory limb is steep. FEV1 falls along with FVC, and FEV1/FVC is normal or high.

Telling a restrictive pattern from a small FVC caused by air trapping takes lung volumes, and telling one obstructive disease from another takes the diffusing capacity and the response to a bronchodilator. That full interpretation framework is taught in Think Like a Respiratory Consultant. The PFT lab and the Respiratory Mechanics Lab let you draw these loops yourself.






WarningA common mistake



“Obstruction means big lungs” is not the definition. Obstruction is a low FEV1/FVC. Emphysema usually raises TLC, RV and FRC, but a patient with asthma can be clearly obstructed with a normal TLC. The Dynamics II notes list “↑ RV, ↑ FRC, ↑ TLC” for obstructive patterns. Those often go with obstruction, but the ratio decides it.

No one can model every airway under every condition, so the course asks you to know each mechanism and which way it pushes resistance, not to calculate a resistance at a particular place.

title: 22  Respiratory Dynamics II
text:
22.5 Check your understanding

The trachea is the single widest airway, yet the medium bronchi a few generations below it carry more of the total airway resistance. Explain, using radius, the number of airways in parallel and the type of flow.


Answer

Each medium bronchus is much narrower than the trachea, and resistance rises with the fourth power of falling radius, so each one has a far higher resistance on its own. Airways side by side share the flow and divide the resistance among them, but in these early generations there are still too few of them to make up for their narrowness. Gas velocity is also highest in these generations, where the total cross-sectional area dips a little, so flow is turbulent or transitional, with eddies at each branch point, and it needs more pressure for the same flow than laminar flow would.

During a forced expiration from TLC, where along the airways does the flow-limiting segment first form, and which way does it move as the lung empties toward RV? Why?


Answer

Early in the breath, at high volume, the lung’s recoil is large, so Palv is far above Ppl and airway pressure stays above pleural pressure for most of the way out. It falls below pleural pressure only in the large central airways near the trachea, where cartilage resists compression. As the lung empties, recoil falls, Palv starts closer to Ppl, and airway pressure reaches pleural pressure a shorter distance from the alveoli. The flow-limiting segment moves out toward the periphery, into smaller, more collapsible airways, and tethering is weaker because the lung is smaller. Flow limitation tightens as the breath goes on.

A patient with mild asthma has a wheeze only at the end of expiration. Using lung volume and airway transmural pressure, explain why the wheeze appears there first.


Answer

At the end of expiration the lung is at its smallest, so tethering holds the airways open least and the lung’s recoil, which keeps airway pressure above pleural pressure, is lowest. Pleural pressure is also higher than at the same volume on the way in, so airway transmural pressure is smaller. The narrowed airways are therefore at their narrowest, and turbulent flow through them is the wheeze. In quiet breathing Ppl stays negative, so Ptm stays positive and nothing is flow limited; in a forced or labored expiration Ppl turns positive and compresses the airways further. During inspiration, the more negative pleural pressure holds the airways wider.

In emphysema the lung loses elastic recoil and the alveolar walls that tether the small airways. Predict what happens to the expiratory limb of the flow-volume loop and to FEV1/FVC, and give the two reasons.


Answer

The expiratory limb is scooped and flows are low, and FEV1/FVC falls (obstruction). First, with less recoil, Palv is lower at every volume, so airway pressure drops below pleural pressure sooner and the flow-limiting segment reaches the small airways early in the breath. Second, without tethering, those small airways collapse more easily when Ptm is negative.

Peak expiratory flow depends on how hard the patient blows, but the rest of a forced expiration does not. Why is the peak different? Name a patient whose peak flow would be low while the later part of the curve is normal.


Answer

Near TLC the lung’s recoil is large, so airway pressure stays above pleural pressure along most of the airways, and where it does fall below, in the central airways, cartilage resists compression. Flow there is not yet limited by dynamic compression, so a higher pleural pressure raises Palv and flow together; the isovolume curves near TLC keep rising with effort. Lower in the vital capacity the flow-limiting segment forms and more effort adds no flow. Peak flow is low with a normal later curve after a poor effort or with weak expiratory muscles. A fixed narrowing of the trachea does the same: it caps the early high flows, and the curve rejoins the normal one once flows fall below the cap.

title: 22  Respiratory Dynamics II
text:
22.7 Sources
This chapter follows the 2026 Respiratory Dynamics II lecture for MEDC 30504 (given with the 2025 slides) and draws on the course’s Dynamics II notes, the Small Group 1 key, the PFT lab slides and the 2018 course notes, corrected and updated. All figures were drawn for this book.

title: 23  Alveolar Ventilation
text:
23.1 From air to alveolus: the airways
The earlier chapters were about moving air: the forces that hold the lung at a volume (Respiratory Statics) and the pressures that drive flow through the airways (Respiratory Dynamics I and II). This chapter asks what that air movement does to the gas in the alveoli. Air that reaches the alveoli has less O2 in it than the air you breathed in, and how much less depends on three things: barometric pressure, the fraction of O2 you breathe, and how fast you breathe out CO2. The next two chapters follow the O2 across the alveolar wall (Diffusion) and into hemoglobin (Transport of O2 and CO2).
The lecture is built around two questions about Mount Everest. In 2019 a photograph of a long queue of climbers below the summit ridge, at about 8,800 m, went around the world. Nearly everyone in that line was breathing bottled O2. Why? And in May 1978, Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler reached the summit without it, when many physiologists thought that could not be done. How? By the end of the chapter you will be able to answer both with one equation.
The airways are a tree of branching tubes. Ewald Weibel’s simplified model numbers the branches by generation [1]. The trachea is generation 0. It divides into the two main bronchi (generation 1), then the lobar and segmental bronchi, and so on. At each generation the tubes become narrower, shorter and more numerous.
Each branch is narrower than its parent, but the number of branches doubles at every generation, so the total cross-sectional area rises steeply toward the periphery (Figure 23.1). The trachea is about 2.5 cm2. The terminal bronchioles together are about 180 cm2, and the alveolar sacs about 10,000 cm2, the size of a table 4 feet across. That is cross-sectional area, the area the air moves through, not the surface area for gas exchange that the diffusion chapter uses.
The airways are in series, so the same total airflow passes through every generation. Linear velocity is flow divided by area, so it is highest where total area is smallest, in the lobar and segmental bronchi (generations 2 to 4), and falls toward zero past the terminal bronchioles. There, gas moves the last few millimeters by diffusion rather than by bulk flow. Bulk flow (convection) brings fresh air down the conducting airways, and diffusion finishes the job over a distance short enough to be fast. Airway resistance and expiratory flow limitation belong to Respiratory Dynamics II. Most airway resistance sits in the medium-sized bronchi.

title: 23  Alveolar Ventilation
text:
Conducting zone, generations 0 to 16: trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and the terminal bronchioles, the smallest airways without alveoli. These airways carry air but do not exchange gas. Together they hold about 150 mL.
Respiratory zone, generations 17 to 23: respiratory bronchioles (with occasional alveoli budding from their walls), alveolar ducts (completely lined with alveoli), and alveolar sacs. The lung beyond one terminal bronchiole is an acinus. From a terminal bronchiole to the farthest alveolus is only a few millimeters, about the length of a crayon tip.








Figure 23.1: Total cross-sectional area of the airways by generation (log scale, black), from Weibel’s model A [1], as plotted in the 2026 lecture. The dashed line is relative air velocity, calculated as the smallest total area divided by the area at each generation. The same total flow passes through every generation, so velocity is highest where total area is smallest (generations 2 to 4) and falls toward zero in the respiratory zone. Course figure.










NoteIf you are comparing with the notes



The airway table in the 2025 Ventilation notes puts gas diffusion at generations “11–23”. Generations 11 to 16 are small bronchi and bronchioles that only conduct air. The respiratory zone begins at generation 17, as the slides say. The trachea is generation 0.

title: 23  Alveolar Ventilation
text:
23.2 Ambient air: Dalton’s law
Dry air is a mixture of gases, and each gas exerts its own partial pressure. Dalton’s law says the partial pressures add up to the total, the barometric pressure (PB, also written Patm):
\[P_B = P_{N_2} + P_{O_2} + P_{Ar} + P_{CO_2}\]
The partial pressure of each gas is the total pressure times that gas’s fraction of the dry mixture. For O2 at sea level, where PB is 760 mm Hg:
\[P_{O_2} = P_B \times F_{IO_2} = 760 \times 0.209 \approx 159\ \text{mm Hg}\]
The slides use 0.209 (more exactly 0.2093) to make 159.1 come out. From here on, as in the course, round FiO2 to 0.21. Nitrogen is about 78% of dry air, argon about 0.93%, and CO2 only about 0.04%, a partial pressure of about 0.3 mm Hg. For gas exchange you can treat inspired CO2 as zero.

title: 23  Alveolar Ventilation
section: 23.3 Inspired air: water vapor dilutes the other gases
text:
23.3 Inspired air: water vapor dilutes the other gases
As air passes through the nose, mouth and upper airways, the moist mucosa warms it to 37 °C and saturates it with water vapor. The saturated vapor pressure of water depends only on temperature, not on barometric pressure or on the weather outside. At 37 °C it is 47 mm Hg. That is why you use 47 at sea level, in Chicago and on the summit of Everest, and why breathing cold dry winter air does not change it: by the time the air reaches the lower airways it is at body temperature and 100% humidity.
The total pressure in the airways is still PB, so water vapor takes 47 mm Hg of it and every other gas shares what is left. The inspired PO2 (PIO2, written PiO2 on the slides) is:
\[P_{IO_2} = (P_B - P_{H_2O}) \times F_{IO_2} = (760 - 47) \times 0.21 \approx 149\ \text{mm Hg}\]
Humidification alone costs about 10 mm Hg of PO2. Inspired air, in this course, is that humidified gas sitting in the trachea. No gas exchange happens there.

title: 23  Alveolar Ventilation
section: 23.4 Alveolar gas: the alveolar gas equation
text:
23.4 Alveolar gas: the alveolar gas equation
In the alveolus two things happen that do not happen in the trachea. O2 leaves the gas for the blood, and CO2 arrives from the blood. Alveolar PO2 (PAO2) is therefore the inspired PO2 minus the O2 that has left. You cannot measure the O2 that left directly, but you can estimate it from the CO2 that came in, because the two are linked by metabolism. That gives the alveolar gas equation (also called the alveolar air equation):
\[P_{AO_2} = (P_B - P_{H_2O})\,F_{IO_2} - \frac{P_{aCO_2}}{R}\]
The first term is PIO2. The second is the O2 the alveolus has given up, estimated from the CO2 it has received.

PaCO2 stands in for PACO2. The equation really needs alveolar PCO2 (PACO2). CO2 equilibrates almost completely between alveolar gas and capillary blood (the diffusion chapter explains why), so PACO2 and arterial PCO2 (PaCO2) are essentially equal. PaCO2 is the one you can measure, with an arterial blood gas drawn from the radial artery. At rest it is about 40 mm Hg. Capital A means alveolar; lowercase a means arterial.
R converts CO2 in to O2 out. R is the respiratory exchange ratio: CO2 given off divided by O2 taken up, V̇CO2/V̇O2. At steady state it equals the respiratory quotient of the tissues and is set by what fuel they burn. On a mixed Western diet R is about 0.8, so for every 0.8 molecules of CO2 that enter the alveolus, 1 molecule of O2 leaves. On pure carbohydrate R is 1.0.







Figure 23.2: PO2 falls at each step from air to alveolus at sea level. Water vapor takes 47 mm Hg of the total pressure, and in the alveolus O2 leaves for the blood as CO2 arrives. Course figure.



The slides show the effect of diet with PaCO2 held at 40:

Pure carbohydrate (R = 1.0): PAO2 = 149 − 40/1.0 = 109 mm Hg
Western diet (R = 0.8): PAO2 = 149 − 40/0.8 = 149 − 50 = 99 mm Hg

The course rounds the sea-level value to 100 mm Hg (Figure 23.2). Use R = 0.8 unless you are told otherwise.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



Slide 14 is headed “Respiratory Quotient (R)”, and the speaker notes and Small Group 2 call R the respiratory exchange ratio (RER). This course uses respiratory exchange ratio (R) for the term in the alveolar gas equation, as the small groups do. At steady state the two ratios are equal, so the number is the same.



23.4.1 Why the equation is useful clinically
Every term on the right side is known or measurable: PB (760 at sea level, 747 in Chicago), PH2O (47), FiO2 (0.21 on room air, more on supplemental O2), PaCO2 (from a blood gas) and R (0.8). So you can calculate PAO2 at the bedside. Compare it with the measured arterial PO2 and you have the A–a gradient, PAO2 − PaO2. The Ventilation and Perfusion chapter uses the A–a gradient to sort the causes of hypoxemia. One distinction matters already: PAO2 is calculated and is about 100 mm Hg at sea level in anyone with a normal PaCO2 on room air. The normal arterial PO2 is 80 to 100 mm Hg, a little lower, by the A–a gradient.


23.4.2 Three places to use it
Sea level. PAO2 = 0.21 × (760 − 47) − 40/0.8 = 0.21 × 713 − 50 ≈ 100 mm Hg.
Chicago. PB is 747 mm Hg, which the small groups use. PAO2 = 0.21 × (747 − 47) − 50 = 0.21 × 700 − 50 = 97 mm Hg. (One memory aid: the Boeing 747, and Boeing’s headquarters used to be in Chicago.)
An airplane cabin. Commercial aircraft are pressurized not to sea level but to about 7,000 ft, where PB is about 586 mm Hg. FiO2 is still 0.21; only the total pressure has fallen. PAO2 = 0.21 × (586 − 47) − 50 = 113 − 50 = 63 mm Hg. Most healthy people do fine at that.
The summit of Everest. PB is 253 mm Hg (measured on West’s 1981 American Medical Research Expedition). With room air and a normal PaCO2:
\[P_{AO_2} = 0.21 \times (253 - 47) - \frac{40}{0.8} = 43.3 - 50 = -6.7\ \text{mm Hg}\]
A negative partial pressure cannot exist. The equation is telling you that this steady state (room air, PaCO2 40, R 0.8) is impossible in a living climber: on these numbers nobody could stand on the summit breathing air. Something in the equation has to change. PB is fixed on the summit, which leaves two terms. FiO2 can go up, or PaCO2 can come down.
The answer to question 1: raise FiO2. With bottled O2 at an FiO2 of 1.0, PAO2 = (253 − 47) × 1.0 − 50 = 206 − 50 = 156 mm Hg, higher than at sea level. That is why nearly everyone in the queue carries a bottle. Climbers’ masks do not really deliver 100% O2, but the direction is the point.






WarningA common mistake



Supplemental O2 raises FiO2, and PAO2 rises with it. It does not lower PaCO2 or “displace” CO2 from the alveolus. PaCO2 is set only by how much CO2 you make and how much fresh air reaches your alveoli, which is the next section. A patient who is breathing too little can have a normal O2 saturation on supplemental O2 while PaCO2 keeps rising.








NoteBackground: the simplified equation at high FiO2





The equation in this course is the simplified form. The full form has a small correction term that depends on FiO2 and R. On room air the correction is about 2 mm Hg and is ignored. At FiO2 1.0 the R correction drops out altogether, because no nitrogen is left to be concentrated, and the full equation gives 206 − 40 = 166 mm Hg on the summit rather than 156. The course and the small groups use the simplified equation at every FiO2, and no conclusion changes.



Messner and Habeler had no bottle, so their FiO2 was 0.21, and nothing changes PB on the summit. The only term left is PaCO2. To see how a climber can change it, you need to know what sets PaCO2.

title: 23  Alveolar Ventilation
section: 23.5 Minute, alveolar and dead space ventilation
text:
23.5 Minute, alveolar and dead space ventilation
Start at the end of a quiet expiration, at functional residual capacity (FRC), about 3,000 mL of gas in the lungs. A quiet breath adds a tidal volume (VT) of about 500 mL. Minute ventilation (V̇E) is the volume breathed per minute:
\[\dot{V}_E = V_T \times RR = 500\ \text{mL} \times 15/\text{min} = 7{,}500\ \text{mL/min}\]
Not all of that air reaches the alveoli. The last 150 mL of each breath in stays in the conducting airways, and on the next expiration it is the first to leave, unchanged. That volume is the anatomic dead space (VD): ventilated, but not taking part in gas exchange. The rest of the breath, VT − VD = 350 mL, is the fresh air that reaches the respiratory zone each breath (the slides write it VA; it is the alveolar part of the breath, not the volume of the alveoli). Those 350 mL mix with the 3,000 mL already there, which is why alveolar gas composition barely changes from one breath to the next.
Per minute, with dots marking rates:
\[V_T = V_D + V_A \qquad \dot{V}_E = \dot{V}_D + \dot{V}_A\]
\[\dot{V}_A = \dot{V}_E - \dot{V}_D = (V_T - V_D) \times RR\]









Per breath
Per minute (× 15)

VT = 500 mL
V̇E = 7,500 mL/min

VD = 150 mL
V̇D = 2,250 mL/min

V̇A = 5,250 mL/min



Pulmonary blood flow, the cardiac output, is about 5,000 mL/min, so alveolar ventilation and blood flow are about equal: the whole lung’s ventilation-perfusion ratio is about 0.8 to 1. This lecture’s numbers give about 1; the V/Q lecture’s slides use 0.8, which corresponds to an alveolar ventilation of about 4 L/min. Both are reasonable whole-lung values, and the Ventilation and Perfusion chapter explains why the ratio varies from apex to base.
The anatomic dead space is only part of the story. Alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused also waste ventilation, and anatomic plus alveolar dead space is the physiologic dead space. In healthy people alveolar dead space is very small, so physiologic dead space is about the same as anatomic dead space. Pulmonary embolism is the classic way to add alveolar dead space. The V/Q chapter shows how to measure it with the Bohr equation.






WarningA common mistake



Dead space is not residual volume. Residual volume is the gas left in the whole lung after a maximal expiration, about 1.5 L, most of it in alveoli. Anatomic dead space is the 150 mL in the conducting airways that never reaches an alveolus on a given breath.



23.5.1 Fast versus deep breathing
You can double minute ventilation in two ways: double the rate or double the depth. Figure 23.3 compares them.

Fast: 500 mL × 30/min = 15,000 mL/min. Each breath still loses 150 mL to dead space, so V̇A = 350 × 30 = 10,500 mL/min.
Deep: 1,000 mL × 15/min = 15,000 mL/min. Dead space rises a little, to about 170 mL, because the expanding lung pulls the airways open, but the conducting airways are much stiffer than the respiratory zone, so nearly all the extra volume goes to the alveoli. V̇A = 830 × 15 = 12,450 mL/min.







Figure 23.3: Three breathing patterns. Fast and deep breathing give the same minute ventilation, 15 L/min, but deep breathing delivers more fresh air to the alveoli and wastes a smaller fraction of each breath (VD/VT). Numbers from the 2026 lecture. Course figure.



Measured at the mouth the two patterns look identical, yet the deep pattern ventilates the alveoli about 20% more. The dead space fraction, VD/VT, shows why: 150/500 = 0.3 for the fast pattern and 170/1,000 = 0.17 for the deep one. Normal VD/VT at rest is about 0.3. Think of dead space as an ATM fee: a fixed charge every time you make a withdrawal, whatever the amount, so it is cheaper to take out more money less often. This is one reason people breathe deeper before they breathe faster when they start to exercise. The Physiology of Exercise chapter picks this up.

title: 23  Alveolar Ventilation
section: 23.6 What sets PaCO2: the alveolar ventilation equation
text:
23.6 What sets PaCO2: the alveolar ventilation equation
Measuring V̇A as V̇E − V̇D is simple on paper, but dead space is hard to measure. The lecture gets at alveolar ventilation another way: follow the CO2.
Inspired air has almost no CO2, and the dead space adds none, because no gas exchange happens there. So every molecule of CO2 you breathe out came from the alveoli. The CO2 leaving per minute is alveolar ventilation times the fraction of CO2 in alveolar gas:
\[\dot{V}_{CO_2} = \dot{V}_A \times F_{ACO_2}\]
V̇CO2 is strictly CO2 output, the volume of CO2 in expired gas per minute. At steady state it equals the body’s metabolic CO2 production, so the same symbol is used for both. Production rises with exercise, fever and infection. Notice that V̇CO2 is a gas exchange rate, not a ventilation.
Two steps you already know turn that fraction into the PaCO2 on a blood gas:

Fraction to pressure (Dalton’s law again): PACO2 = FACO2 × (PB − 47).
Alveolus to artery: CO2 equilibrates across the alveolar wall, so PaCO2 ≈ PACO2.

Substitute and rearrange to get the alveolar ventilation equation:
\[P_{aCO_2} = \frac{\dot{V}_{CO_2}}{\dot{V}_A} \times K \qquad \text{so} \qquad P_{aCO_2} \propto \frac{\dot{V}_{CO_2}}{\dot{V}_A}\]
K is a constant that folds in the unit conversions (0.863, with V̇CO2 in mL/min and V̇A in L/min). You do not need its value. What you need is the proportionality: PaCO2 rises in proportion to CO2 production and falls in proportion to alveolar ventilation. Think of it as a clearance equation, with the lungs as the excretory organ for CO2.
The lecture’s resting numbers are a V̇CO2 of 250 mL/min and a V̇A of about 5 L/min, which hold PaCO2 at about 40 mm Hg.

Halve V̇A (2.5 L/min) and PaCO2 doubles, to about 80: hypoventilation.
Double V̇A (10 L/min) and PaCO2 halves, to about 20: hyperventilation.

Other lectures in the course, and the transport and exercise chapters, use 200 mL/min as a typical resting V̇CO2 (with a V̇O2 of 250, that gives R = 0.8). Only the proportions matter here.
A single arterial blood gas therefore tells you whether alveolar ventilation is keeping up with CO2 production. Hyperventilation and hypoventilation are defined by PaCO2, not by how fast or how hard someone is breathing. PaCO2 below 40 means V̇A is more than V̇CO2 requires; above 40 means it is less.






Figure 23.4: PaCO2 against alveolar ventilation, drawn from PaCO2 = 0.863 × V̇CO2/V̇A. At rest (V̇CO2 250 mL/min) a V̇A of about 5.4 L/min holds PaCO2 at 40. Mild exercise triples V̇CO2, which triples PaCO2 at every V̇A; to hold PaCO2 at 40, V̇A must also triple, to about 16 L/min. Course figure.



Figure 23.4 shows the relationship as a hyperbola. During exercise the curve moves. Mild exercise triples V̇CO2 to about 750 mL/min, so at any V̇A the PaCO2 is three times higher. That is the same as saying it takes three times the V̇A to reach any given PaCO2, so “three times higher” and “three times farther right” are the same move for this curve. If V̇A stayed at 5 L/min during exercise, PaCO2 would climb toward 130. In healthy people it does not, because ventilation rises in step with V̇CO2 (Control of Ventilation, Physiology of Exercise).






WarningA common mistake



The two words are easy to swap, and even experienced clinicians do it out loud. Tie each to the blood gas. An opioid overdose slows breathing, so alveolar ventilation falls and PaCO2 rises: that is hypoventilation. A climber on Everest breathes hard, alveolar ventilation rises, and PaCO2 falls: that is hyperventilation. Rapid shallow breathing can be fast and still be hypoventilation, because a larger share of each small breath is dead space.

title: 23  Alveolar Ventilation
section: 23.7 Alveolar ventilation sets both alveolar gases
text:
23.7 Alveolar ventilation sets both alveolar gases
Alveolar ventilation appears in the alveolar ventilation equation, which sets PACO2, and PACO2 appears in the alveolar gas equation, which sets PAO2. Put the two together and you can plot both alveolar gases against V̇A (Figure 23.5).






Figure 23.5: Alveolar PO2 (maroon) and PCO2 (blue) against alveolar ventilation at sea level on room air, drawn from the alveolar ventilation equation (V̇CO2 250 mL/min) and the alveolar gas equation (R 0.8). The dots are rest. Hypoventilation raises PACO2 and lowers PAO2; hyperventilation does the reverse. PAO2 can approach but never exceed inspired PO2. Course figure, after the graph used in the 2026 lecture.



As V̇A falls, PACO2 rises and PAO2 falls. As V̇A rises, PACO2 falls and PAO2 rises. The curves are close to mirror images, but not exact ones. With R = 0.8, each 1 mm Hg fall in PaCO2 raises PAO2 by 1/R, about 1.25 mm Hg, so a 10 mm Hg fall in PaCO2 buys 12.5 mm Hg of PAO2.
Both curves flatten at high V̇A. Once PACO2 is low, more ventilation buys little more O2, and PAO2 can never exceed PIO2, about 149 mm Hg at sea level. The crossing point of the two curves has no meaning. (These curves are not the hemoglobin dissociation curve of the transport chapter, although they have a similar look.)
The same picture explains hypoventilation as a cause of hypoxemia. A patient with an opioid overdose hypoventilates, PaCO2 rises, and PAO2 falls with it. The lung itself is normal, so the arterial PO2 falls in step with PAO2 and the A–a gradient stays normal.

title: 23  Alveolar Ventilation
section: 23.8 Everest solved: only PaCO2 can change
text:
23.8 Everest solved: only PaCO2 can change
Back to Messner and Habeler. PB and FiO2 were fixed. The one term they could change was PaCO2, by raising alveolar ventilation. Suppose a climber hyperventilates hard enough to drive PaCO2 down to 8 mm Hg:
\[P_{AO_2} = 0.21 \times (253 - 47) - \frac{8}{0.8} = 43.3 - 10 \approx 33\ \text{mm Hg}\]
Not comfortable, but positive, and enough to stay alive (Figure 23.6). These are close to real numbers. On West’s 1981 expedition, alveolar gas sampled on the summit had a PACO2 of about 7.5 mm Hg and a PAO2 of about 35 mm Hg.






Figure 23.6: Alveolar PO2 from the alveolar gas equation (R 0.8, PaCO2 40 unless stated). On the Everest summit, room air with a normal PaCO2 gives an impossible negative value. Bottled O2 fixes it by raising FiO2 (the easy way). Hyperventilating to a PaCO2 of 8 fixes it by lowering the CO2 term (the hard way). Course figure.



The hard way has costs. Breathing enough to hold PaCO2 at 8 takes a great deal of work, and the respiratory muscles tire. It also causes a severe respiratory alkalosis, only partly offset over days of acclimatization as the kidneys excrete bicarbonate (Pulmonary Acid Base). And a PAO2 of 33 is a starting point with almost no margin. What it means for the blood comes in the next two chapters: the diffusion chapter asks whether capillary blood can even reach 33, and the transport chapter shows what hemoglobin does at that pressure.
So the two answers are:

The climbers in line (the easy way): bottled O2 raises FiO2 and PAO2 rises to about 156 mm Hg.
Messner and Habeler (the hard way): with FiO2 and PB fixed, they hyperventilated, lowering PaCO2 to about 8 and raising PAO2 to about 33 mm Hg.

title: 23  Alveolar Ventilation
text:
23.9 Hypoxemia from a low PAO2
Hypoxemia means a low arterial PO2. The alveolar gas equation names the causes that work by lowering PAO2 first:








Cause
Term in the equation
Example

PB
Altitude, the airplane cabin, Everest


Low FiO2
FiO2

In all three the lung is normal, so the A–a gradient is normal: PaO2 is low because PAO2 is low. Raising FiO2 corrects the hypoxemia in all three, although in hypoventilation it leaves the high PaCO2 untouched. The other causes of hypoxemia (diffusion limitation, V/Q mismatch and shunt) widen the A–a gradient. They come in the Diffusion, Ventilation and Perfusion and Think Like a Respiratory Consultant chapters, which assemble the full framework.

title: 23  Alveolar Ventilation
text:
23.10 Check your understanding

A student in Chicago works the alveolar gas equation for a January day at −20 °C and a humid July day at 32 °C, and wants to use a different PH2O for each. What would you tell her?


Answer

Use 47 mm Hg for both. By the time inspired air reaches the lower airways it has been warmed to 37 °C and fully saturated, and the saturated vapor pressure of water depends only on temperature. Outside temperature and humidity do not matter. Only the barometric pressure (747 in Chicago) and FiO2 set PIO2.

A swimmer breathes through a snorkel that adds 150 mL to his dead space, and he keeps the same VT (500 mL) and rate (15/min). What happens to his minute ventilation, alveolar ventilation, PaCO2 and PAO2 if his CO2 production does not change?


Answer

Minute ventilation is unchanged at 7,500 mL/min. Dead space is now 300 mL, so only 200 mL of each breath reaches the alveoli and V̇A falls from 5,250 to 3,000 mL/min. PaCO2 rises in proportion, by 5,250/3,000 ≈ 1.75, to about 70 mm Hg. By the alveolar gas equation PAO2 falls, to roughly 150 − 70/0.8 ≈ 62 mm Hg. To keep PaCO2 normal he has to take deeper breaths, which is why long snorkels do not work.

Two patients each lose 1 L/min of alveolar ventilation, and CO2 production does not change in either. One starts at a normal V̇A of about 5.4 L/min and a PaCO2 of 40. The other is already hypoventilating, at a V̇A of about 2.7 L/min and a PaCO2 of 80. Whose PaCO2 rises more, and why? Use the shape of Figure 23.4.


Answer

The patient who is already hypoventilating. PaCO2 ∝ V̇CO2/V̇A is a hyperbola, flat at high V̇A and steep at low V̇A. For the first patient, 1 L/min is under a fifth of his V̇A, and PaCO2 rises from 40 to about 49 (40 × 5.4/4.4). For the second, the same 1 L/min is more than a third of his V̇A, and PaCO2 rises from 80 to about 127 (80 × 2.7/1.7). A small further fall in breathing, from a sedative for example, is far more dangerous in a patient who is already on the steep part of the curve.

Hyperventilation raised PAO2 from impossible to about 33 mm Hg on Everest. Why can’t a healthy person at sea level use the same trick to raise PAO2 to 200?


Answer

PAO2 = PIO2 − PaCO2/R, and PIO2 at sea level is about 149. Even if hyperventilation drove PaCO2 toward zero, PAO2 could only approach 149, and the curves in Figure 23.5 flatten long before that. On Everest the CO2 term (50 mm Hg at a normal PaCO2) was larger than the whole PIO2 of 43, so shrinking it made all the difference. To go above PIO2 you have to raise PIO2 itself, with a higher FiO2 or a higher PB.

After surgery, a patient on supplemental O2 (FiO2 0.40) is getting drowsier from pain medication. Her pulse oximeter reads 99%. Why doesn’t that reassure you about her breathing?


Answer

The oximeter reports O2, and the extra FiO2 keeps PIO2 high, so PAO2 and her saturation can stay normal even as alveolar ventilation falls. Supplemental O2 does nothing to the CO2 term: PaCO2 ∝ V̇CO2/V̇A, so if V̇A halves, PaCO2 doubles whatever the FiO2. Only a measurement of PaCO2 (a blood gas) tells you whether her ventilation is keeping up.

Explain in two sentences why all the CO2 in an exhaled breath comes from the alveoli, and why that makes CO2 useful for measuring alveolar ventilation.


Answer

Inspired air contains almost no CO2, and no gas exchange takes place in the conducting airways, so the dead space adds none. The CO2 leaving per minute is therefore V̇A × FACO2, which lets you work out alveolar ventilation from CO2 output and alveolar (or arterial) PCO2 without having to measure the dead space.
