title: 24  Diffusion
text:
24.1 A barrier built for exchange
The Alveolar Ventilation chapter brought O2 from ambient air to the alveolus, where PAO2 is about 100 mm Hg. This chapter takes it across the blood-gas barrier into the pulmonary capillary blood, a distance of well under a micrometer that still takes a whole lecture. The next chapter (Transport of O2 and CO2) covers what hemoglobin does with the O2 once it arrives.
Diffusion is passive. No pump or transporter in the barrier moves O2 or CO2, and no energy is spent. Each gas moves only down its own partial pressure gradient. Keep one question from the last lecture in mind as you read: if alveolar and arterial PO2 are both about 100 mm Hg, where is the gradient that drives O2 into the blood?
It is thin. On an electron micrograph of a pulmonary capillary, the barrier has two sides. On the thin side, the alveolar epithelium and the capillary endothelium share one fused basement membrane, and the whole barrier is only 0.2 to 0.3 µm thick. Most gas exchange happens there. On the thick side there is more interstitium, with bundles of collagen between the epithelium and the endothelium. Edema fluid collects first on the thick side, which spares the thin side for a while (you met edema formation in Microcirculation).
It is large. The lung has several hundred million alveoli. Repeated branching into acini packs a surface of about 50 to 100 m2 into the chest, roughly half a singles tennis court.
The capillaries are a sheet, not tubes. In the systemic circulation, capillaries are usually drawn as separate tubes between an arteriole and a venule. In the alveolar wall the capillaries are so densely interconnected that blood flows as a sheet about one red cell thick, a little like a waffle fry, with flow in every direction through the side channels. The aggregate cross-sectional area is large, so resistance is low and blood moves slowly. At rest a red cell spends about 0.75 s in a pulmonary capillary, and at any moment only about 70 mL of blood is in the whole capillary bed, spread across that huge surface.
Small holes in the alveolar walls, the pores of Kohn, connect neighboring alveoli. They allow collateral ventilation, so an alveolus whose airway is blocked can still get some air from its neighbors. They are also one path by which bacteria and fluid spread from alveolus to alveolus in lobar pneumonia.

title: 24  Diffusion
text:
24.2 Fick’s law of diffusion
The rate at which a gas crosses a sheet of tissue (V̇gas) is proportional to the area of the sheet (A), to a diffusion constant for that gas in that tissue (D), and to the partial pressure difference across it (P1 − P2), and inversely proportional to the thickness (T):
\[\dot{V}_{gas} = \frac{A \cdot D}{T}\,(P_1 - P_2)\]
This has the same shape as Ohm’s law: flow equals a driving pressure divided by a resistance, with T/(A·D) playing the part of the resistance. The lung maximizes A and minimizes T. Figure 24.1 shows the thickness term at work: with the same gradient, a barrier half as thick has a profile twice as steep and moves twice as much O2.






Figure 24.1: Barrier thickness in Fick’s law. Both barriers have the same gradient, PO2 100 in alveolar gas and 40 in capillary blood. Halving the thickness doubles the slope of the PO2 profile across the barrier and doubles the transfer. Fibrosis and interstitial edema thicken the barrier. Course figure.




24.2.1 The diffusing capacity, DL
In a patient you cannot measure the area or the thickness of the barrier. So for clinical work the area, thickness and diffusion constant are lumped into one number, the diffusing capacity of the lung (DL):
\[\dot{V}_{gas} = D_L\,(P_1 - P_2)\]
DL is a property of the lung and of the gas in question. It does not depend on the partial pressures. You calculate it from a measured transfer and a measured gradient, but if you double the gradient the transfer doubles and DL stays the same.
Now the question from the start of the chapter. If P1 is alveolar PO2 and P2 is arterial PO2, and both are 100, the equation seems to say no O2 moves. The gradient is along the capillary. Blood enters at a PO2 of about 40, so at the start of the capillary the gradient is about 60 mm Hg. It shrinks as the blood loads O2 and is close to zero a third of the way along. P2 is the capillary PO2, averaged along the capillary, not the arterial value.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



Slide 8 writes Fick’s law for the lung as V̇gas = DL (PA − Pa), with arterial PO2 as P2. In a normal lung PA and Pa are about equal, so read P2 as capillary partial pressure averaged along the capillary, as the slide 8 notes explain. The course map writes DL (P1 − P2). Both give the same DL.

title: 24  Diffusion
section: 24.3 What sets D: solubility and molecular weight
text:
24.3 What sets D: solubility and molecular weight
The diffusion constant depends on the gas:
\[D \propto \frac{\text{solubility}}{\sqrt{\text{molecular weight}}}\]
A gas that dissolves well in the barrier crosses it faster, and a lighter molecule diffuses faster. The solubility that counts here is solubility in the barrier, which is mostly water. Physical solubility in water or plasma ranks the gases the same way, and Figure 24.2 shows those values.
Why CO2 diffuses about 20 times faster than O2. CO2 is about 24 times as soluble as O2. It is also heavier (molecular weight 44 against 32), which slows it a little: √(44/32) ≈ 1.17. So CO2 diffuses about 24 ÷ 1.17 ≈ 20 times faster. Molecular weight alone would favor O2; solubility outweighs it. In practice this means CO2 is almost never diffusion limited, and a high PaCO2 is not explained by a diffusion problem. A high PaCO2 means hypoventilation.






Figure 24.2: Physical solubility of three gases: dissolved gas against partial pressure, measured in blood. The slope of each line is the solubility. CO2 (0.067 mL/dL per mm Hg) is far more soluble than O2 (0.003), so at a PCO2 of 40 about 2.7 mL/dL of CO2 is dissolved, while at a PO2 of 100 only 0.3 mL/dL of O2 is. N2 is less soluble than O2, and ether is drawn for contrast. The barrier is mostly water, so these solubilities also rank the gases for D. (These rounded values give a ratio of 0.067/0.003 ≈ 22; with unrounded constants it is 22 to 24, and the lecture uses 24.) What the blood does with a gas after it arrives, such as binding it to hemoglobin, is a separate question, in the box below. Course figure.









WarningA common mistake



Two different solubilities matter in this lecture, and they are easy to run together.

Solubility in the barrier is part of D. A gas that dissolves well in the membrane crosses it faster.
Solubility or binding in the blood is not part of DL. It sets how fast the partial pressure in the capillary blood rises as the gas arrives. A gas that dissolves well in blood, or binds to something in it, can be taken up in large amounts while its blood partial pressure barely rises. The gradient stays large and the gas keeps moving, but it takes longer to reach equilibrium.

A gas that is soluble in the membrane but poorly soluble in blood equilibrates fastest. CO, which binds hemoglobin, is the extreme case and never equilibrates (later in this chapter).


Helium dissolves very poorly in blood, so almost none of it leaves the lung during a breath-hold or a rebreathing test. That is why it is used to measure lung volumes by helium dilution (Respiratory Statics).

title: 24  Diffusion
section: 24.4 At least ten layers from alveolus to hemoglobin
text:
24.4 At least ten layers from alveolus to hemoglobin
Fick’s law treats the barrier as one wall. On the way from alveolar gas to hemoglobin, an O2 molecule actually crosses at least ten layers (Figure 24.3): the liquid lining the alveolus; the type I epithelial cell (a membrane, cytoplasm, and another membrane); the interstitium; the capillary endothelial cell (membrane, cytoplasm, membrane); the plasma; and the red cell (membrane and cytoplasm). Not all of them are membranes. Each has its own diffusing capacity, and PO2 falls a little across each one.






Figure 24.3: The path of O2 from alveolar gas to hemoglobin. Layer widths are not to scale. The layers from the surface liquid through the red cell cytoplasm make up the membrane part of the diffusing capacity, DM; each is a resistance (1/D), and resistances in series add. Binding to hemoglobin is a final step, θ·Vc. Course figure, after the lecture’s figure redrawn from Boron and Boulpaep [1].



Each layer is a resistance, one over its diffusing capacity, and resistances in series add. Together the layers from the surface liquid through the red cell make up the membrane part of DL, written DM. Thicken any one of them and DM falls. The interstitium is the layer that thickens in fibrosis and where edema fluid collects first.
Once O2 has crossed every membrane it is still only dissolved in the red cell. One more step remains, and it is not a membrane: O2 has to combine with hemoglobin. That step acts like one more resistance, the hemoglobin part, written θ·Vc:

θ is how fast the hemoglobin in 1 mL of blood takes up the gas, per mm Hg. It depends on how fast the gas reacts with hemoglobin and on how much hemoglobin there is.
Vc is the pulmonary capillary blood volume, about 70 mL at rest. Together, θ·Vc says how much hemoglobin is exposed to alveolar gas and how fast it binds.

The membrane and hemoglobin parts act in series, so their resistances add:
\[\frac{1}{D_L} = \frac{1}{D_M} + \frac{1}{\theta \cdot V_c}\]
The arithmetic is beyond this course. The idea you need is that the hemoglobin side can limit DL as well as the barrier. Things that lower θ·Vc lower DL even when the membrane is normal: anemia (less hemoglobin) and loss of capillary bed, as with a pulmonary embolism (less Vc). Things that raise θ·Vc raise DL: exercise recruits and distends pulmonary capillaries and so raises Vc (recruitment and distension: Pulmonary Circulation), and polycythemia raises hemoglobin.

24.4.1 Measuring DL with carbon monoxide
The PFT lab measures the diffusing capacity with carbon monoxide (DLCO), by the single-breath method. The patient takes one breath of a dilute CO mixture, holds it for 10 seconds, and breathes out. The difference between inspired and expired CO gives the rate at which CO disappeared into the blood. CO is used because hemoglobin takes it up so avidly that the capillary PCO stays essentially zero (the next section shows why). The gradient is then simply the alveolar PCO, and the equation collapses to:
\[D_{LCO} = \frac{\dot{V}_{CO}}{P_{ACO}}\]
A normal DLCO is about 25 mL/min/mm Hg. For CO the membrane and hemoglobin resistances are about equal, which is why DLCO falls in anemia and the lab corrects it for the patient’s hemoglobin. DLCO rises in exercise because of capillary recruitment and distension. How DLCO helps sort lung diseases is part of Think Like a Respiratory Consultant.

title: 24  Diffusion
text:
24.5 Perfusion limitation and diffusion limitation
Follow a red cell into a pulmonary capillary. It has about 0.75 s to cross at rest. How fast the partial pressure of a gas rises in that blood decides what limits its transfer. Figure 24.4 shows the two extremes.






Figure 24.4: Two ways a gas can behave in the pulmonary capillary, as partial pressure in capillary blood relative to alveolar partial pressure. (A) Nitrous oxide does not bind to hemoglobin, so blood can hold only a little of it and reaches alveolar PN2O early; transfer is perfusion limited. (B) Carbon monoxide is taken up by hemoglobin as fast as it arrives, so capillary PCO stays near zero; transfer is diffusion limited. Schematic. Course figure.



Perfusion limited: nitrous oxide (N2O). N2O crosses the barrier easily and does not bind to hemoglobin, so blood can hold only a little of it compared with O2 or CO. The first N2O to cross raises the blood’s PN2O quickly, and blood and alveolar gas reach equilibrium early in the capillary, well before O2 does. After that the gradient is zero and nothing more crosses, however good the barrier is. The only way to take up more N2O is to bring more blood, so its uptake is limited by perfusion.
Diffusion limited: carbon monoxide (CO). Hemoglobin binds CO so avidly that almost every CO molecule that reaches the red cell is taken up at once, and very little stays free in the plasma. The capillary PCO therefore stays close to zero all the way along, the gradient never closes, and end-capillary PCO is far below alveolar PCO. Uptake is limited by how fast CO can cross the barrier, which is why it is the gas used to measure DL.






WarningA common mistake



It is tempting to think that because CO binds hemoglobin so avidly, the blood must end up with a high PCO. It is the opposite. Partial pressure in blood is set only by the dissolved gas. Bound CO does not count, so avid binding keeps PCO near zero, and that is why CO never equilibrates. Its molecular weight (28, lighter than O2) has nothing to do with it.



24.5.1 Where O2 and CO2 fall
O2 lies between the two extremes. It binds hemoglobin, but far less avidly than CO, so capillary PO2 does rise. In a normal lung at rest, blood enters at a mixed venous PO2 of about 40 and reaches alveolar PO2, 100, within about the first third of the capillary, by about 0.25 s (Figure 24.5). For the remaining two thirds no more O2 moves. At rest, O2 transfer is perfusion limited, and the unused length of the capillary is a large diffusion reserve.
CO2 moves the other way: blood enters at a mixed venous PCO2 of about 46 mm Hg (slide 15 rounds it to 45) and falls to the alveolar 40 in about the same time. CO2 is perfusion limited too. Its gradient is only about 6 mm Hg, roughly a tenth of the starting gradient for O2, so its 20-fold higher diffusivity is what lets it equilibrate just as quickly. “40 to 100 for O2, 46 to 40 for CO2” are good anchor numbers.






Figure 24.5: Capillary PO2 and PCO2 in a normal lung at rest. (A) O2: blood enters at 40 mm Hg and reaches alveolar PO2 (100) well within the first third of the 0.75 s transit; the shaded part is the diffusion reserve. (B) CO2: blood enters at about 46 mm Hg and falls to the alveolar 40 in about the same time. The O2 curve comes from a simple model of O2 loading that uses the course’s dissociation curve; the CO2 curve is schematic. Course figure.



Look at the shape of the O2 curve. It starts slowly, then rises steeply, then flattens. The flattening is the gradient closing as capillary PO2 approaches alveolar PO2. The slow start comes from hemoglobin. Between 40 and 60 mm Hg the blood is on the steep part of the O2 dissociation curve, where hemoglobin takes up a large amount of O2 for each mm Hg rise in PO2. Most of the O2 that crosses the barrier binds to hemoglobin instead of raising plasma PO2, so PO2 climbs slowly at first. Above about 60 mm Hg the dissociation curve is flat, hemoglobin is nearly full, and each bit of O2 that crosses raises PO2 quickly. This is the same reason CO equilibrates slowly, in a milder form. Hemoglobin’s affinity for O2 is not lower on the steep part of the curve.

title: 24  Diffusion
text:
24.6 When O2 becomes diffusion limited
The reserve can be used up in three ways: a thicker barrier (low DL), less time in the capillary, or a smaller gradient. Figure 24.6 shows all three.






Figure 24.6: Capillary PO2 along the capillary for a normal diffusing capacity and for a DL of one quarter and one eighth of normal. (A) At sea level, the normal lung equilibrates early, and even with the 0.25 s transit of heavy exercise it still reaches alveolar PO2. A lung with a low DL reaches equilibrium only late or not at all, and with a short transit it leaves the capillary well below alveolar PO2. (B) At altitude (13,500 ft, alveolar PO2 about 50, mixed venous about 25) the gradient is smaller and the blood loads on the steep part of the dissociation curve, so even the normal lung needs most of the transit time and falls short with exercise. Curves from the same model as Figure 24.5, after the figures from West’s Respiratory Physiology [2] used in the 2026 lecture. The model holds DL constant. Real blood binds O2 faster when hemoglobin is less saturated, so at altitude the normal lung equilibrates somewhat sooner than drawn: slide 22 shows it equilibrating by about 0.45 s. Both show the normal lung falling short when transit is cut to 0.25 s.



A thickened barrier. In pulmonary fibrosis, scar thickens the alveolar walls and interstitium, the diffusion path lengthens, and DL falls. Capillary PO2 rises more slowly. If the gradient has not closed by the time the blood leaves, transfer is diffusion limited: blood that entered at 40 might leave at 80 while alveolar PO2 is 100. End-capillary PO2 ends below alveolar PO2, which raises the A–a gradient. A very abnormal lung is diffusion limited even at rest.
Exercise: less time. During exercise cardiac output rises, and because all the blood must pass through the lungs, the transit time through the pulmonary capillaries can fall to about 0.25 s. A normal lung at sea level still equilibrates, so in most healthy people the lung at sea level stays perfusion limited even with hard exercise. A lung with a low DL no longer has time, and blood leaves well below alveolar PO2. This is why a patient with interstitial lung disease can look fine sitting in a chair and desaturate walking down the hall, and why clinicians check O2 saturation during exercise, often with a six-minute walk test.
Altitude: a smaller gradient. Fick’s law says transfer is proportional to the partial pressure difference. At altitude FiO2 is still 0.21, but PB is lower, so inspired and alveolar PO2 are lower. At 13,500 feet PAO2 is about 50 and mixed venous PO2 is roughly 20 to 25, so the starting gradient is about 25 to 30 mm Hg instead of 60. The blood is also loading on the steep part of the dissociation curve the whole way, which slows the rise in PO2 further. At rest the normal lung still just equilibrates. With exertion, transit time falls and end-capillary PO2 stays below alveolar PO2. Strenuous exercise at altitude is one of the few situations that makes a healthy person diffusion limited.
Combinations. In patients it is usually a combination: a thickened barrier plus exertion, or lung disease plus altitude, including the cabin of an airliner pressurized to 7,000 ft.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The 2025 Diffusion notes (section IX) have a column “Response to 100% O2” in the perfusion versus diffusion limitation table. Ignore that column. Perfusion and diffusion limitation describe whether a gas reaches equilibrium before the blood leaves the capillary, a property that applies to every gas, and a response to O2 means nothing for N2O, CO2 or CO. Hypoxemia from diffusion limitation does improve with supplemental O2, because a higher PAO2 widens the gradient across the barrier. The Ventilation and Perfusion chapter sorts the causes of hypoxemia by their response to O2.



24.6.1 A question from Everest
In 2009, Grocott and colleagues drew arterial blood from healthy climbers at 8,400 m on Everest, breathing ambient air [3]. Barometric pressure was 272 mm Hg. Inspired PO2 was 0.21 × (272 − 47) ≈ 47 mm Hg, and hyperventilation had driven PaCO2 down to about 13, so by the alveolar gas equation PAO2 was about 47 − 13/0.8 ≈ 30 mm Hg. The measured arterial PO2 averaged 24.6 mm Hg, below the alveolar value. At sea level capillary PO2 reaches alveolar PO2. Why didn’t it up there?
The gradient that drives O2 across the barrier starts out tiny, smaller even than in Figure 24.6 B, and the blood is loading on the steepest part of the dissociation curve. Capillary PO2 rises slowly and runs out of transit time before it reaches alveolar PO2, worse with any exertion. Most likely, at this altitude O2 transfer becomes diffusion limited even in a healthy lung.
This does not change how altitude is classified. At rest, altitude is a cause of hypoxemia from a low PAO2 with a normal A–a gradient, which is how the Alveolar Ventilation chapter and Small Group 2 count it. Diffusion limitation appears on top of that when transit time shortens, as in exercise at altitude, or at the most extreme altitudes. Small Group 2 uses one climber from the same camp as a teaching case with round numbers: PaCO2 12, PAO2 32 and PaO2 30 mm Hg, an A–a gradient of 2. The transport chapter uses him.

title: 24  Diffusion
text:
24.7 Check your understanding

A disease halves the alveolar surface area and also doubles the thickness of the barrier. By how much does O2 transfer change if the gradient is unchanged? Which term of the diffusing capacity changed?


Answer

V̇gas ∝ A·D/T × (P1 − P2). Halving A halves transfer, and doubling T halves it again, so transfer falls to a quarter. Both changes are in the membrane part of DL (DM). In reality the gradient would not stay fixed: as transfer fell, end-capillary PO2 would fall below alveolar PO2 if the reserve ran out.

The starting gradient for CO2 in the pulmonary capillary is only about 6 mm Hg, against about 60 for O2. Why does CO2 still equilibrate as fast as O2?


Answer

CO2 is about 24 times as soluble as O2 in the barrier and only slightly heavier, so its diffusion constant is about 20 times higher. Per mm Hg of gradient it crosses about 20 times faster, which more than makes up for a gradient about a tenth as large. That is why CO2 is almost never diffusion limited.

A healthy runner’s DL is higher during a race than at rest. Which part of the diffusing capacity changed, and why?


Answer

The hemoglobin part, θ·Vc. Exercise raises cardiac output and pulmonary pressures, which recruit closed capillaries and distend open ones, so capillary blood volume (Vc) rises and more hemoglobin is exposed to alveolar gas. The membrane is unchanged. (The larger exposed surface from recruitment also helps DM a little.)

In a resting subject, N2O uptake doubles when cardiac output doubles. Why? Would a moderately thickened alveolar barrier change N2O uptake?


Answer

N2O does not bind hemoglobin, so blood can hold only a little of it, and capillary PN2O reaches alveolar PN2O early in the capillary. After that the gradient is zero and nothing more crosses. Each milliliter of blood leaves carrying the same small amount, so uptake is set by how much blood passes: twice the flow carries away twice as much. A higher cardiac output shortens the transit time somewhat, but N2O equilibrates so early that the shorter time is still enough. A moderately thickened barrier slows equilibration, but as long as the blood still reaches alveolar PN2O before it leaves the capillary, uptake does not change. Only a barrier so thick that equilibrium is never reached would make N2O uptake depend on the barrier.

If alveolar PO2 and arterial PO2 are both about 100 mm Hg, where is the gradient that moves O2 into the blood?


Answer

Along the capillary. Blood enters at a mixed venous PO2 of about 40, so the gradient is about 60 mm Hg at the start, and it shrinks to almost zero about a third of the way along as hemoglobin fills. P2 in Fick’s law is capillary PO2 averaged along the capillary, not the arterial value.

Why does capillary PO2 rise slowly over the first part of the capillary, then quickly, then level off?


Answer

Only dissolved O2 sets PO2. At first the blood is on the steep part of the dissociation curve, so most of the O2 that crosses binds to hemoglobin and PO2 rises slowly. Once PO2 passes about 60 mm Hg, hemoglobin is nearly full, little O2 is bound per mm Hg, and PO2 rises fast. It levels off as it nears alveolar PO2 and the gradient closes.

title: 25  Transport of O2 and CO2 in the Blood
text:
25.1 The loop
Alveolar Ventilation brought O2 to the alveolus at a PO2 of about 100 mm Hg: 0.21 × (760 − 47) ≈ 150, minus 40/0.8 = 50. Diffusion moved it into the pulmonary capillary blood. This chapter follows it in the blood to the tissues, then follows CO2 back from the tissues to the lungs.
Keep one question in mind. A patient with heart failure and normal lungs has a PaO2 of 100 mm Hg. We give O2 and the PaO2 rises to 200. How much more O2 reaches the tissues? The answer comes in the section on O2 content.
Blood leaves the lungs with a PO2 of about 100, gives O2 to the tissues, and returns with a PO2 of about 40. Arterial blood has an O2 content CaO2, and mixed venous blood, returning to the lungs, has a content CvO2. Content is measured in mL of O2 per dL of blood, a volume of gas per volume of blood, which is awkward units but the ones everyone uses. The tissues take up O2 at a rate V̇O2 and give off CO2 at a rate V̇CO2, both in mL/min, and Q is the cardiac output. At steady state the lungs take up exactly as much O2 as the tissues use, and give off exactly as much CO2 as the tissues make.
Keep the sizes straight. At rest, cardiac output is about 5 L/min and minute ventilation about 6 to 7.5 L/min, flows of blood and of air. V̇O2 is much smaller, about 250 mL/min, and V̇CO2 about 200 mL/min. V̇O2 and V̇CO2 are gas exchange rates, not ventilation.
Arterial PO2 is a little lower than end-capillary PO2, about 95, because a small amount of blood bypasses gas exchange (bronchial and thebesian veins) and because ventilation and perfusion are not perfectly matched. That gap is the A–a gradient, and the Ventilation and Perfusion chapter covers it. In this chapter, round arterial PO2 to 100.
crumbs: 25  Transport of O~2~ and CO~2~ in the Blood

title: 25  Transport of O2 and CO2 in the Blood
text:
25.2 Dissolved O2 is not enough
Henry’s law says the concentration of a gas dissolved in a liquid is its solubility times its partial pressure:
\[[O_2]_{dissolved} = 0.003\ \frac{\text{mL O}_2}{\text{dL} \cdot \text{mm Hg}} \times P_{O_2}\]
At a PaO2 of 100 only 0.3 mL/dL is dissolved. (The small group keys use 0.0031. The difference does not matter.) The amount dissolved depends only on the partial pressure, not on how much gas the liquid touches. Dissolved O2 is also the only O2 that sets the PO2 and drives diffusion; O2 bound to hemoglobin does not count toward PO2.
Delivery of dissolved O2 is cardiac output times dissolved content:

At rest: 5,000 mL/min × 0.3 mL/100 mL = 15 mL O2/min
In heavy exercise, at a cardiac output of 25 L/min: 75 mL O2/min

A resting 70 kg person uses about 250 mL O2/min. One of the highest V̇O2max values ever reported, the cross-country skier Bjørn Dæhlie’s 96 mL/kg/min, is about 6,700 mL/min at 70 kg. Dissolved O2 cannot cover even resting needs. We need a carrier.
crumbs: 25  Transport of O~2~ and CO~2~ in the Blood

title: 25  Transport of O2 and CO2 in the Blood
text:
25.3 Hemoglobin
Adult hemoglobin (HbA) is a tetramer of two α and two β globin chains, each holding a heme group with a ferrous (Fe2+) iron. Each heme binds one O2, so one hemoglobin molecule carries up to four, loosely and reversibly. At a hemoglobin concentration of 15 g/dL, blood carries about 20 mL O2/dL bound to hemoglobin, roughly 65 times the dissolved amount.

25.3.1 The HbO2 dissociation curve
The O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve plots the percentage of heme sites occupied by O2 (saturation) against PO2 (Figure 25.1). It is sigmoid because binding is cooperative. Hemoglobin with no O2 is in the tense (T) state, with a low affinity. Each O2 that binds moves the molecule toward the relaxed (R) state and raises the affinity of the hemes still empty.






Figure 25.1: The HbO2 dissociation curve (maroon) with the course’s anchor points, and a protein with the same P50 and no cooperativity (dashed gray). The tan band is the loading zone in the lungs, where the curve is flat; the blue band is the unloading zone in the tissues, where it is steep. Curve from a Hill equation (P50 27 mm Hg, n 2.8), which passes through all four anchor points. Course figure.



Cooperativity shows most in the steep middle of the curve, about 10 to 40 mm Hg, where molecules are switching from T to R, so a small change in PO2 moves many molecules between nearly empty and nearly full. On the flat top almost every molecule is already full, so a big change in PO2 barely changes saturation. Compare the dashed curve, a protein with the same P50 and no cooperativity. At 100 mm Hg, hemoglobin is about 98% saturated and the non-cooperative protein only about 79%. From 100 down to 20 mm Hg (exercising muscle), hemoglobin gives up about 67 points of saturation and the non-cooperative protein about 36. Cooperativity buys two things: hemoglobin stays nearly full in the lung even if PAO2 falls a fair amount, and tissue can take a lot of O2 for a small fall in PO2.
Myoglobin, the O2-binding protein of muscle, has one heme and no cooperativity. Its curve is hyperbolic with a P50 near 3 mm Hg, so it holds its O2 until muscle PO2 is very low.
The loading zone (lungs, PO2 about 100). The curve is flat. PaO2 can fall from 100 to about 60 while saturation only drops from 97.5% to 90%, so content is largely kept. That is why moderate altitude is well tolerated.
The unloading zone (tissues, PO2 about 40 and below). The curve is steep. Resting mixed venous blood sits at the top of this zone (40 mm Hg, 75%). Exercising muscle pulls PO2 down to 20 mm Hg or lower, deep into the steep part, and hemoglobin gives up much more.

Clinicians watch 90% for that reason. During a difficult intubation the oximeter can sit in the 90s for minutes, and once it reaches the knee it can drop into the 80s within about 30 seconds.
P50, the PO2 at which hemoglobin is half saturated, is the standard index of affinity. A higher P50 means a lower affinity and a curve shifted to the right.

title: 25  Transport of O2 and CO2 in the Blood
text:
25.4 O2 content
Arterial O2 content is the O2 bound to hemoglobin plus the O2 dissolved in plasma:
\[C_{aO_2} = (1.39 \times \text{Hb} \times S_{aO_2}) + (0.003 \times P_{aO_2})\]
Know this equation. 1.39 is the mL of O2 carried by 1 g of fully saturated hemoglobin. Hb is in g/dL and SaO2 is a fraction, so the first term comes out in mL O2/dL, the same units as the dissolved term.
With Hb 15 g/dL, SaO2 0.97 and PaO2 100:
\[C_{aO_2} = (1.39 \times 15 \times 0.97) + (0.003 \times 100) = 20.2 + 0.3 \approx 20.5\ \text{mL/dL}\]
The dissolved part is a rounding error. Hemoglobin carries the O2.
Back to the opening question. Raising PaO2 from 100 to 200 adds 0.3 mL/dL of dissolved O2, and saturation can only rise from about 97.5% to 100%. Content goes from about 20.6 (at 97.5%) to about 21.4 mL/dL, about 4%. For a patient with normal lungs and a low cardiac output, O2 helps a little. The real gains come from cardiac output or hemoglobin.






NoteIf you are comparing with the small group keys



Some texts use 1.34 or 1.36 mL O2/g in place of 1.39, and the small group keys use 0.0031 for the dissolved O2 coefficient. This course uses 1.39 and 0.003. The differences change a content by less than 1 mL/dL. The Small Group 2 key, Case 2, says “normal CaO2 is about 20.1”; with its own Case 1 numbers (SaO2 100%) it is about 21. Either way, a normal CaO2 is about 20 mL/dL.



25.4.1 Content curves show what saturation curves hide
Plot content instead of saturation and you get a curve of the same shape, scaled by hemoglobin (Figure 25.2). The dissolved line, 0.003 × PO2, barely shows at normal PO2. Above 100 mm Hg it is the only part still rising.






Figure 25.2: O2 content against PO2 for a normal hemoglobin (15 g/dL), anemia (7.5 g/dL) and polycythemia (20 g/dL), with the dissolved O2 line. The dots are arterial (100 mm Hg) and mixed venous (40 mm Hg) blood at a normal hemoglobin. All three blood samples have the same saturation curve; only the plateau differs. Course figure.



Anemia lowers the plateau and polycythemia raises it, while the saturation curve is the same in both. Small Group 2 uses this in its teaching case of a climber at 8,400 m on Everest (PB 272; the Diffusion chapter compares him with the measured climbers at the same camp). On his blood gas, SaO2 is 68% at a PaO2 of 30 mm Hg. With a normal hemoglobin his content would be 1.39 × 15 × 0.68 + 0.003 × 30 ≈ 14.3 mL/dL. Over weeks at altitude his hemoglobin has risen to 20.2 g/dL, and his content is 1.39 × 20.2 × 0.68 + 0.09 ≈ 19.2 mL/dL, nearly normal despite a very low saturation. Polycythemia defends content; it cannot change saturation.
Methemoglobin, in which the heme iron has been oxidized from Fe2+ to Fe3+ (spontaneously or by drugs such as nitrites), cannot bind O2, and it shifts the curve of the remaining hemoglobin to the left. An enzyme in red cells, methemoglobin reductase, normally keeps it near 1%.
crumbs: 25  Transport of O~2~ and CO~2~ in the Blood

title: 25  Transport of O2 and CO2 in the Blood
text:
25.5 What shifts the curve
The curve is not fixed. Conditions in the blood change hemoglobin’s affinity for O2 (Figure 25.3).






Figure 25.3: Shifts of the HbO2 curve. The normal curve (P50 27 mm Hg) is solid; the dashed curves are shifted right (P50 about 36) and left (P50 about 20) for illustration. A right shift means lower affinity: at the same PO2, hemoglobin holds less O2 and gives more to the tissues. Course figure.



A right shift (higher P50, lower affinity, more unloading at a given PO2) comes from:

a higher temperature;
a higher PCO2 and a higher H+ concentration (lower pH), which together are the Bohr effect;
more 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) in the red cell.

Working muscle is warm and makes CO2 and acid, so it has the first three. That is the point of the system: high metabolism promotes unloading where O2 is needed. Because the top of the curve is flat, a right shift costs little loading in the lung; the gain is on the steep part, in the tissues. Try it on Figure 25.3: at 100 mm Hg the shifted curves are close together, and at 20 to 40 mm Hg they are far apart.
2,3-DPG is made by glycolysis in the red cell and binds deoxygenated hemoglobin. It rises over hours to days with chronic hypoxemia (altitude, chronic lung disease) and with chronic anemia, which helps those patients unload O2. It falls in stored blood, so transfused red cells hold O2 tightly until they rebuild it.
A left shift (lower P50, higher affinity) comes from the reverse: lower temperature, lower PCO2 and H+ (alkalosis), less 2,3-DPG. Carbon monoxide, fetal hemoglobin and methemoglobin also shift the curve left. A left shift helps loading and hurts unloading. When you hyperventilate and feel lightheaded, the main reason is that a low PaCO2 constricts the brain’s arterioles and lowers its blood flow. The left shift from the alkalosis adds a little, because the brain’s blood gives up O2 less easily.






WarningA common mistake



In a single bout of exercise the right shift comes from temperature, PCO2 and H+. 2,3-DPG does not rise meaningfully in one bout. It changes over hours to days, as at altitude, in anemia or in chronic lung disease.








NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



Slide 15 is titled “Dissociation Curve - Bohr Effect” and lists temperature, pH, PCO2 and 2,3-DPG, and in lecture all four were called the Bohr effect. Strictly, the Bohr effect is the effect of PCO2 and H+ on O2 affinity, as the slide’s notes say. Temperature and 2,3-DPG also shift the curve right, but they are not the Bohr effect. This course uses the name the same way.



25.5.1 The curve at altitude
At altitude, hyperventilation starts within minutes, and the respiratory alkalosis it causes shifts the curve to the left first. That helps the blood load O2 in the lung at a low PAO2. Red cell 2,3-DPG then rises over hours to days, stimulated by the hypoxemia and by the alkalosis, and shifts the curve back to the right. At moderate altitude the two roughly cancel. At extreme altitude the alkalosis wins and the curve stays left of normal. The Small Group 2 climber shows it: at a pH of 7.55 his SaO2 is 68% at a PaO2 of 30, where a normal curve gives about 57%.






NoteIf you are comparing with the small group keys



The Small Group 2 key (Case 1, polycythemia question) says that at moderate altitude the curve “initially shifts to the right due to 2,3-DPG” and then back to the left from the respiratory alkalosis. The order is the other way around, as described above: the alkalosis comes first, within minutes, and 2,3-DPG follows over hours to days.
crumbs: 25  Transport of O~2~ and CO~2~ in the Blood

title: 25  Transport of O2 and CO2 in the Blood
text:
25.6 Carbon monoxide
Carbon monoxide (CO) binds hemoglobin about 240 times more tightly than O2 does. Hemoglobin is half saturated with O2 at 27 mm Hg and half saturated with CO at about 0.1 mm Hg. Most of that affinity comes from CO leaving hemoglobin very slowly; it combines somewhat more slowly than O2 but lets go far more slowly still. That is why trace amounts are dangerous. Air with 0.1% CO has a PCO of about 0.7 mm Hg. Competing against an alveolar PO2 of 100, that is enough to put more than half the hemoglobin in the carboxy form (carboxyhemoglobin, COHb) once it reaches equilibrium, which takes hours.
CO harms O2 transport in two ways:

It takes heme sites away from O2, so saturation and content fall.
The hemoglobin that still carries O2 shifts left, so it gives up its O2 poorly in the tissues.

PaO2 stays normal, because PaO2 is dissolved O2 and CO does not change it, and the A–a gradient is normal too. The problem is tissue hypoxia from low content and poor unloading, not hypoxemia. A measured saturation (co-oximetry on an arterial sample) is low. A pulse oximeter can read falsely normal; you do not need the reason for this course.
Figure 25.4 compares 50% COHb with anemia at half the normal hemoglobin. Both have about half the normal O2 capacity. The anemic patient can walk around. A COHb of 50% is often fatal. The difference is the left shift: with CO, the O2 that is bound will not come off at tissue PO2.






Figure 25.4: O2 content against PO2 for normal blood, anemia with half the normal hemoglobin, and blood with 50% carboxyhemoglobin. The two abnormal curves have the same plateau, but the COHb curve is shifted far to the left, so between lung and tissue PO2 it gives up almost no O2. The COHb curve is illustrative (half the hemoglobin, P50 moved to about 10 mm Hg). Course figure.



CO binding is reversible. The COHb half-life is about 5 hours on room air, about 1 hour on 100% O2, and shorter still on hyperbaric O2. At very high PO2, dissolved O2 starts to count. Small Group 2 works this through for a man found confused in his car in a closed garage, with a PaO2 of 100 and a saturation of 50%:

Room air: 1.39 × 15 × 0.50 + 0.003 × 100 ≈ 10.7 mL/dL
100% O2 in Chicago: PAO2 = (747 − 47) − 36/0.8 ≈ 655, using his PaCO2 of 36, and PaO2 is close to it: 10.4 + 2.0 ≈ 12.4 mL/dL
Hyperbaric O2 at 3 atmospheres: PAO2 = (2,280 − 47) − 36/0.8 ≈ 2,190: 10.4 + 6.6 ≈ 17 mL/dL

His blood gas also shows a metabolic acidosis, from lactic acid made by hypoxic tissue.






NoteIf you are comparing with the notes and keys



The 2025 Transport notes (section X) say small amounts of CO “can cause major hypoxemia,” and the Small Group 2 key says the left shift causes decreased unloading “resulting in hypoperfusion.” CO causes tissue hypoxia with a normal PaO2, so it is not hypoxemia, and it does not reduce blood flow. Read “hypoxemia” and “hypoperfusion” in those places as tissue hypoxia. The notes’ section XXI says SaO2 is “falsely normal”; a measured SaO2 is low, and it is the pulse oximeter (SpO2), or a saturation calculated from PaO2, that can read falsely normal.
crumbs: 25  Transport of O~2~ and CO~2~ in the Blood

title: 25  Transport of O2 and CO2 in the Blood
section: 25.7 Venous O2, delivery and the Fick principle
text:
25.7 Venous O2, delivery and the Fick principle
The same content equation works for mixed venous blood. With PO2 40 and saturation 75%:
\[C_{vO_2} = (1.39 \times 15 \times 0.75) + (0.003 \times 40) = 15.6 + 0.12 \approx 15.8\ \text{mL/dL}\]
Arterial minus venous is about 20.5 − 15.8, roughly 5 mL/dL. At rest the tissues take about a quarter of the O2 delivered, and the other three quarters are a reserve.




Arterial

Three flows, all in mL O2/min, describe the loop (Figure 25.5):

Delivery (QO2 in the small groups) = Q × CaO2 = 5,000 mL/min × 20/100 ≈ 1,000
Return = Q × CvO2 = 5,000 × 15/100 ≈ 750
Uptake (V̇O2) = delivery − return ≈ 250







Figure 25.5: O2 delivery, return and uptake at rest. Cardiac output carries about 1,000 mL O2/min to the tissues, which take 250, and about 750 returns to the lungs. Contents are in mL/dL, so divide by 100 to multiply by a cardiac output in mL/min. Course figure.



Uptake is delivery minus return, not delivery itself. Grouping the terms gives the Fick principle:
\[\dot{V}_{O_2} = (Q \times C_{aO_2}) - (Q \times C_{vO_2}) = Q \times (C_{aO_2} - C_{vO_2})\]
With the rounded values, 5,000 mL/min × 5 mL/100 mL = 250 mL O2/min. Rearranged, Q = V̇O2/(CaO2 − CvO2). Measure any two terms and you can solve for the third. Measure V̇O2 at the mouth, draw arterial and mixed venous blood, and you have the cardiac output. The cardiac catheterization lab and the exercise lab both use this. (This V̇O2 is the resting value, not V̇O2max.)
Read the equation the other way too. CvO2 falls when delivery falls (a low cardiac output, anemia, a low SaO2) or when consumption rises (fever, seizure, exercise). Either way the tissues extract more of what they get. That is the Small Group 3 patient in septic shock, with an SvO2 of 42%. Raising delivery or lowering consumption raises it again. The V/Q chapter shows why a low mixed venous O2 makes the hypoxemia from a shunt worse.
crumbs: 25  Transport of O~2~ and CO~2~ in the Blood

title: 25  Transport of O2 and CO2 in the Blood
text:
25.8 CO2 transport
CO2 diffuses from the tissue cells into the plasma and on into the red cell. It travels in three forms (Figure 25.6):

Dissolved, in plasma and in the red cell. CO2 follows Henry’s law with a solubility of 0.067 mL/dL per mm Hg, more than 20 times that of O2, so at a PCO2 of 40 about 2.7 mL/dL is dissolved.
As carbamino compounds. CO2 binds reversibly to the N-terminal amine groups of proteins, mostly the α and β chains of hemoglobin, not the heme: Hb–NH2 + CO2 ⇌ Hb–NH–COO− + H+. Deoxygenated hemoglobin forms carbamino compounds more readily than oxygenated hemoglobin.
As bicarbonate. Inside the red cell, carbonic anhydrase speeds the hydration of CO2:

\[CO_2 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_2CO_3 \rightleftharpoons H^+ + HCO_3^-\]
The first step is slow in plasma, which has almost no carbonic anhydrase, and fast in the red cell. The second step is fast without help. Hemoglobin buffers the H+, and deoxygenated hemoglobin is the better buffer. The HCO3− leaves the red cell through an anion exchanger (band 3) in exchange for Cl−, the chloride shift. So most bicarbonate is made in red cells but carried in plasma. This is the same reaction that sets blood pH, which the Pulmonary Acid Base chapter builds on.
Blood carries about 48 mL/dL of CO2 at a PCO2 of 40, more than twice its O2 content.






Figure 25.6: Two ways to count the forms of CO2 in blood. Of all the CO2 in arterial blood, about 90% is bicarbonate and about 5% each is carbamino and dissolved. Of the roughly 4 mL/dL that the tissues add and the lungs give off, about 60% is bicarbonate, 30% carbamino and 10% dissolved. Carbamino CO2 is a small share of the total but a large share of the exchange, because deoxygenated hemoglobin forms it so much more readily. Course figure.



The lecture’s percentages, 10% dissolved, 30% carbamino and 60% bicarbonate, are shares of the CO2 given off in the lung, the venous-arterial difference. They are not shares of the total CO2 in blood, which is mostly bicarbonate.






NoteIf you are comparing with the notes



The table in the 2025 Transport notes (section XII) labels the 10, 30 and 60% column “% of Total CO2”, and the summary slide (slide 34) shows the same numbers without saying what they are a share of. They are shares of the CO2 exchanged in the lungs. Of the total CO2 in arterial blood, about 90% is bicarbonate, 5% carbamino and 5% dissolved.
crumbs: 25  Transport of O~2~ and CO~2~ in the Blood

title: 25  Transport of O2 and CO2 in the Blood
text:
25.9 The Haldane effect
The Haldane effect is the effect of O2 on CO2 carriage: at any PCO2, deoxygenated blood holds more CO2 than oxygenated blood. It is driven by O2 saturation, not by PCO2. It mirrors the Bohr effect:

Bohr: CO2 and H+ change how hemoglobin binds O2.
Haldane: O2 changes how blood carries CO2.

Two properties of deoxygenated hemoglobin cause it. It forms carbamino compounds more easily, and it buffers H+ better, which pulls the carbonic anhydrase reaction toward bicarbonate. So in a systemic capillary, as hemoglobin gives up O2 to the tissue, it takes up H+ and binds CO2, and more CO2 goes into bicarbonate. Unloading O2 makes room for CO2. In the lungs everything runs backward: loading O2 helps the blood give CO2 up.
Figure 25.7 shows two CO2 dissociation curves, one for arterial blood (saturation 97.5%) and one for venous blood (75%). Real blood moves from the arterial point a (PCO2 40, about 48 mL/dL) to the venous point v (PCO2 46, about 52 mL/dL). The path from a to v is steeper than either curve. Of the 4 mL/dL of CO2 the tissues add, about half comes from the rise in PCO2 along one curve and about half is the Haldane effect, the jump up to the venous curve as hemoglobin gives up O2. The Haldane effect is not a minor effect. Over this range the CO2 curve is steep and has no plateau, and the Haldane effect adds about as much again, which is why a 6 mm Hg change in PCO2 carries all the CO2 the body makes (4 mL/dL × 50 dL/min = 200 mL/min).






Figure 25.7: CO2 dissociation curves for arterial blood (SO2 97.5%) and venous blood (SO2 75%). Moving from a to v in the tissues, blood picks up about 4 mL/dL of CO2: about 1.9 from the rise in PCO2 along the arterial curve and about 2.1 from the shift to the venous curve as hemoglobin gives up O2 (the Haldane effect). In the lungs the same path runs backward. Curves are illustrative, fitted to the course’s two points. Course figure.



Clinically, when a patient with severe COPD who retains CO2 is given a lot of O2, PaCO2 can rise. Much of that is worse V/Q matching as O2 releases hypoxic vasoconstriction in poorly ventilated regions, part is the Haldane effect (fully saturated hemoglobin holds less CO2), and a small fall in ventilation contributes a little. Control of Ventilation returns to these patients.






WarningA common mistake



Supplemental O2 does not lower PaCO2. PaCO2 is set by CO2 production and alveolar ventilation (PaCO2 ∝ V̇CO2/V̇A, from the ventilation chapter). The Haldane effect changes how CO2 is loaded and unloaded inside the blood, not how much the body makes or how much the lungs clear. In the COPD patient above, O2 raises PaCO2 because effective alveolar ventilation falls as V/Q matching worsens (more of each breath goes to units that exchange little), and because the Haldane effect raises blood PCO2 that a patient who cannot breathe more cannot clear. The equation still holds; what changed is V̇A.
crumbs: 25  Transport of O~2~ and CO~2~ in the Blood

title: 25  Transport of O2 and CO2 in the Blood
text:
25.10 The whole path of O2
The lecture closes on one chain from air to tissue. Each link is a lecture in this block, and when a patient is hypoxemic or O2 delivery is low, you can walk down it and ask which link failed.

PB, FiO2 and PaCO2 set PAO2 (the alveolar gas equation; Alveolar Ventilation).
Diffusion and V/Q matching set how close PaO2 gets to PAO2 (Diffusion; Ventilation and Perfusion).
Hb, SaO2 and PaO2 set CaO2 (this chapter).
O2 delivery = Q × CaO2, and the tissues take out V̇O2, leaving CvO2 (this chapter, with cardiac output from the cardiovascular block). Metabolic activity (temperature, physical activity, infection) sets V̇O2.







NoteBackground: hemoglobin types, sickle hemoglobin and chronic anemia





Most adult hemoglobin is HbA (α2β2). HbA2 (α2δ2) is about 2.5%, and fetal hemoglobin (α2γ2) is under 1% in adults. Glycated forms (HbA1a, A1b, A1c) form without an enzyme and irreversibly, at a rate set by blood glucose. A red cell lives about 120 days, so HbA1c reflects average glucose over the past 2 to 3 months, which is why it is checked in diabetes. HbA1c binds O2 a little more tightly, partly because it binds 2,3-DPG less well, but at 6 to 9% of total hemoglobin the effect on the whole curve is small.
Sickle hemoglobin (HbS) comes from a single amino acid substitution in the β chain: valine replaces glutamate at position 6. Oxygenated HbS is normally soluble, but deoxygenated HbS is much less soluble than HbA and polymerizes into long, stiff fibers that distort the red cell into the sickle shape. Sickled cells are fragile and block small vessels, which causes the pain and organ damage of a sickle cell crisis, and they hemolyze (lifetime under 20 days), which causes chronic hemolytic anemia. Sickle blood also has a right-shifted curve.
In anemia that develops over a long time, 2,3-DPG rises and shifts the curve to the right, so hemoglobin releases O2 to the tissues at a higher PO2. This happens only with chronic anemia, not with a sudden fall in hemoglobin.
crumbs: 25  Transport of O~2~ and CO~2~ in the Blood

title: 25  Transport of O2 and CO2 in the Blood
text:
25.11 Check your understanding

A patient’s oxygen saturation falls from 97.5% to 90%. Roughly how far has her PaO2 fallen? If her PaO2 then falls another 20 mm Hg, what happens to her saturation, and why is the second fall worse?


Answer

From about 100 to about 60 mm Hg: a 40 mm Hg fall for 7.5 points of saturation, because she was on the flat top of the curve. Another 20 mm Hg brings her to 40, where saturation is about 75%, a further 15 points. Below the knee the curve is steep, so each mm Hg costs much more saturation and content.

During a race, the blood in a leg muscle’s capillaries is warmer, has a higher PCO2 and a lower pH. Which way does the curve shift? Why does that help the muscle without costing much O2 in the lungs?


Answer

All three shift the curve to the right (higher P50, lower affinity), and the PCO2 and pH part is the Bohr effect. At the low PO2 in working muscle, on the steep part of the curve, a right-shifted curve gives up much more O2. In the lungs, blood is cooler and has a lower PCO2 and a higher pH, so it is back near the normal curve, and on the flat top even a right-shifted curve stays nearly saturated.

A patient receives several units of blood that has been stored for weeks. Which way is the transfused blood’s curve shifted, why, and what does that mean for the tissues over the first hours?


Answer

To the left, because 2,3-DPG falls in stored red cells. The transfused hemoglobin loads O2 normally in the lungs but holds it more tightly at tissue PO2, so it unloads less until the cells rebuild their 2,3-DPG, which takes hours to days.

A patient with a hemoglobin of 10 g/dL receives a transfusion of fresh red cells that raises it to 13 g/dL. Her lungs and her cardiac output (5 L/min) do not change. Which way do her PaO2, SaO2, CaO2 and O2 delivery move, and by roughly how much?


Answer

PaO2 does not change. It reflects the dissolved O2, which depends on the alveolar gas and the lung, not on hemoglobin, so it stays about 100 mm Hg. SaO2 does not change either: saturation depends on PO2 and on hemoglobin’s affinity, not on how much hemoglobin there is, so it stays about 97%. CaO2 rises with the bound term, from about (1.39 × 10 × 0.97) + 0.3 ≈ 13.8 to (1.39 × 13 × 0.97) + 0.3 ≈ 17.8 mL/dL, close to a 30% rise. Delivery = Q × CaO2, so at 5 L/min it rises from about 690 to about 890 mL O2/min.

A patient’s cardiac output falls by half while his V̇O2 stays the same. Using the Fick principle, what happens to the arteriovenous O2 difference and to his mixed venous saturation?


Answer

V̇O2 = Q × (CaO2 − CvO2). If Q halves and V̇O2 is unchanged, the arteriovenous difference must double, from about 5 to about 10 mL/dL. With CaO2 unchanged at 20, CvO2 falls to about 10 mL/dL, and mixed venous saturation falls from 75% to about 50%. The tissues compensate by extracting more of the O2 they are given.

Carbamino compounds are only about 5% of the CO2 in arterial blood but about 30% of the CO2 given off in the lungs. Explain the difference.


Answer

The 5% is a share of the total CO2 carried, and the 30% is a share of the small amount exchanged between venous and arterial blood (about 4 mL/dL). Deoxygenated hemoglobin forms carbamino compounds much more readily than oxygenated hemoglobin, so carbamino CO2 changes a lot as blood gives up O2 in the tissues and takes it up in the lungs. That is part of the Haldane effect.

title: 26  Pulmonary Acid Base
text:
26.1 A blood gas
The earlier chapters followed air into the alveoli and gas across the barrier. This one looks at a consequence in the blood. CO2 is an acid, and the lung sets how much of it stays in the body, so every change in ventilation changes the blood’s pH. Clinicians look at blood gases constantly: in an emergency on any ward, someone will hand you one and ask whether to worry. The goal here is narrow and practical. You should be able to look at a blood gas with one disorder, say what the primary problem is, and say what the body is doing about it. The kidney’s side is treated as a black box here; the renal block opens it.
The lecture opens with a 27-year-old woman found unresponsive after heroin use. She does not wake to a sternal rub and her pupils are pinpoint. While she is being treated with naloxone, an arterial blood gas comes back:
A blood gas is always reported in that order. Blood is usually drawn from the radial artery, because arterial blood has just left the lungs and heart; venous blood has had acid added and O2 removed by whatever tissue it drained, so it says less about gas exchange. All the values are arterial (“little a”), because the alveolus cannot be sampled.
Memorize the normal values now. You will use them for the rest of the block.
Laboratories differ on how wide the normal pH range is. The lecture slides call a pH below 7.37 low and above 7.42 high; the course notes use 7.35 and 7.45. Both center on 7.40, and for the gases in this chapter the direction away from 7.40 is what you read.
PaCO2 and alveolar PCO2 are essentially equal, so a blood gas gives you PACO2 directly. PaO2 is not always equal to alveolar PO2. You calculate PAO2 with the alveolar gas equation and compare the two: the difference is the A–a gradient. In a healthy lung both gases equilibrate across the barrier, and PaO2 still ends up a few mm Hg below PAO2 because a small share of the blood bypasses gas exchange and V/Q varies across the lung. Those lower PaO2 far more than they raise PaCO2. The Ventilation and Perfusion chapter explains why.

26.1.1 Hypoventilation causes hypoxemia with normal lungs
Work through her oxygen first. In Chicago, with PB 747 mm Hg, R 0.8 and room air:
\[P_{AO_2} = (P_B - P_{H_2O})\,F_{IO_2} - \frac{P_{aCO_2}}{R} = 0.21\,(747 - 47) - \frac{85}{0.8} \approx 147 - 106 = 41 \text{ mm Hg}\]
Her PaO2 is 42. The A–a gradient is essentially zero (the PaO2 sitting a hair above PAO2 comes from assuming R is exactly 0.8). Her chest X-ray is clear. Nothing is wrong with her lungs. She is breathing so little that CO2 has built up in her alveoli, and at a fixed total pressure, more alveolar CO2 leaves less room for O2 (Figure 26.1).






Figure 26.1: Partial pressures in alveolar gas, from the alveolar gas equation with PB 747 mm Hg, PH2O 47 and R 0.8. In the opioid overdose, PACO2 rises from 40 to 85 and PAO2 falls from 97 to 41, with normal lungs. On 30% O2, PAO2 rises to about 104 and her saturation would look fine, but PACO2 is still 85. Course figure.



The low saturation is what gets attention. Put O2 on her and her saturation rises to normal, because raising FiO2 raises PAO2. Her PaCO2 has not changed, and the acidemia that comes with it can kill her. The fix for her is to make her breathe: naloxone reverses the opioid. With every blood gas, ask three things: what is the oxygen, what is the CO2, and does the patient look able to keep this up?

title: 26  Pulmonary Acid Base
text:
26.2 Why pH matters
Proteins work over a narrow pH range, and receptors, enzymes and channels all change shape when it moves.

Too acidemic (pH too low): cardiac function is depressed, tissues stop responding to catecholamines (the body’s own and those given as drugs), and the patient can die. Critical acidemia is a common final pathway in the ICU.
Too alkalemic (pH too high): muscle tightening (tetany), seizures, arrhythmias and death. This is less common.

In health the pH stays very close to 7.40.

title: 26  Pulmonary Acid Base
text:
26.3 The CO2 and bicarbonate buffer
An acid is a molecule that can give up a proton:
\[\text{HA} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{A}^-\]
The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation relates pH to the ratio of the base form to the acid form: pH = pK + log([A−]/[HA]). (The course notes print this ratio upside down; the base form goes on top, as in the bicarbonate form below.) A buffer resists changes in pH when acid or base is added. It does that best within about one pH unit of its pK (Figure 26.2).






Figure 26.2: The bicarbonate buffer: pH against the share of the buffer present as HCO3−, from the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation with pK 6.1. Adding acid moves the point left; adding base moves it right. Normal blood sits at 7.4, high on the curve, where HCO3− outnumbers dissolved CO2 by 20 to 1. Adapted from Ward, Ward and Leach, The Respiratory System at a Glance [1], as used in the 2026 lecture.



The buffer that matters for the lung is CO2 and bicarbonate:
\[\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \;\overset{\text{CA}}{\rightleftharpoons}\; \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{HCO}_3^-\]
Carbonic anhydrase (CA) speeds the first step. Plasma has almost none, so the reaction runs mostly inside red cells (see Transport of O2 and CO2). Say “bicarb” for bicarbonate; everyone does.
Written for this buffer, with 0.03 the solubility of CO2 in blood (mmol/L per mm Hg):
\[\text{pH} = 6.1 + \log\frac{[\text{HCO}_3^-]}{0.03 \times P_{aCO_2}} = 6.1 + \log\frac{24}{0.03 \times 40} = 6.1 + \log 20 = 7.40\]
The arithmetic checks out, and that is all it is here: a check. Clinicians who read thirty blood gases a day never calculate it, and you will not have to either. Read the equation for its directions:

HCO3− is on top. Raise it and pH rises; lower it and pH falls.
PaCO2 is on the bottom. Raise it and pH falls; lower it and pH rises. CO2 behaves as an acid.
pH depends on the ratio. If both rise or both fall, pH moves back toward 7.40.

The pK of 6.1 is far below 7.40, so blood sits near the top of the buffer curve, outside the range where a buffer works best (Figure 26.2). On its own the pair would be a weak buffer at 7.40. It works because the body controls both halves of the ratio, with two controllers. The lungs set PaCO2 and can change it within seconds to minutes by breathing faster or deeper. The kidneys set HCO3−, using transporters you will meet in the renal block, and they need hours to days. Strictly, the lungs stand for the whole respiratory system (lungs, chest wall and the muscles that move them) and the kidneys for the whole metabolic side, including the tissues that make acid. So the disorders are called respiratory and metabolic, not “lung” and “kidney”.

Compensation always acts on the other variable and moves it in the same direction as the primary change, because that restores the ratio. If PaCO2 is high, the kidney raises HCO3−; if HCO3− is low, the lung lowers PaCO2. Figure 26.3 shows all four as paths on a plot of HCO3− against PaCO2.






Figure 26.3: The four primary disorders on a plot of HCO3− against PaCO2. Gray lines join points of equal pH (from Henderson-Hasselbalch). Solid arrows are the primary change from normal; dashed arrows are compensation, which moves the point back toward the 7.4 line without reaching it. Compensation for a metabolic alkalosis is the smallest. Course figure.



Compensation never restores a normal pH. It moves the pH toward 7.40 and stops short. That makes blood gases easier to read, because compensation never overshoots. If a patient with a primary acidosis turns up alkalemic, a second process is present. A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis who is breathing as hard as she can will still be acidemic; if her gas shows an alkalemia, look for something else, such as vomiting (a metabolic alkalosis) or an ingestion that drives breathing.
Respiratory compensation is fast. Renal compensation takes hours to days, so the size of the HCO3− change tells you how long a respiratory problem has been going on. A patient with a PaCO2 of 80 and a very low pH has a new problem and needs the ICU. A patient with the same PaCO2 and a pH near normal has had time to compensate and may not need immediate action. There are formulas for the expected compensation. They belong to the renal block and are not part of this lecture.
The lung’s two responses are not equal. It can blow off a great deal of CO2 to compensate for a metabolic acidosis. Its compensation for a metabolic alkalosis is small. The high pH does lower the chemoreceptor drive, ventilation falls and PaCO2 rises, but hypoventilation also lowers PaO2, and the falling PaO2 drives ventilation back up through the peripheral chemoreceptors. The Control of Ventilation chapter covers those receptors.






NoteIf you are comparing with the lecture



In the recording, the small compensation for a metabolic alkalosis is explained as breathing less being “unnatural”, something you have to do consciously. The response is automatic: the chemoreceptors sense the higher pH and drive falls. It stays small because hypoventilation lowers PaO2, and hypoxemia limits it, as the course notes say.

title: 26  Pulmonary Acid Base
section: 26.5 Emia, osis, and what the body does
text:
26.5 Emia, osis, and what the body does
Read every blood gas with three questions.

What is the emia? Is the pH low (acidemia) or high (alkalemia)? This is the net result of everything going on.
What is the primary osis? A low pH means either a high PaCO2 (respiratory acidosis) or a low HCO3− (metabolic acidosis). A high pH means either a low PaCO2 or a high HCO3−. Look at the PaCO2 first and see whether it matches the pH, then use the HCO3− as the check. You can also do it the other way round; both work.
What is the body doing to compensate? Has the other variable moved away from normal in the same direction?

A patient can have several processes at once: ketoacidosis, a pneumonia that limits CO2 clearance, and dehydration adding a metabolic alkalosis, all pulling the pH in different directions. Mixed disorders wait for the renal block. Each gas in this lecture has one primary disorder.

These are the lecture’s values, rounded; if you check them with Henderson-Hasselbalch, each pH comes out a few hundredths different, which changes no reading.
The first gas is the opioid patient. A metabolic acidosis comes from an added acid, such as lactic acid when tissues are poorly perfused or ketoacids in diabetic ketoacidosis. A metabolic alkalosis comes from loss of H+, as in vomiting, or from volume loss.
A PaCO2 of 45, as in the third gas, may be flagged as normal by some laboratories. The body controls pH so tightly that the small rise is still a real compensation: a healthy person who holds their breath until PaCO2 reaches 45 feels short of breath.
Practice these until the reading is automatic. This is a topic many students learn for the test, forget, and then need on the first day of the wards.

title: 26  Pulmonary Acid Base
text:
26.6 How the lungs change PaCO2
The lungs have two levers: breathe faster or breathe deeper. Together they make the minute ventilation:
\[\dot V_E = \text{RR} \times V_T\]
A normal tidal volume is about 500 mL. A true resting rate is 10 to 12 breaths per minute (hospital charts often record 18), which gives a V̇E of about 6 L/min; other lectures use 15 breaths per minute and 7.5 L/min. In distress, VT can pass 1 L and the rate can reach the 30s or 40s, so V̇E can rise from 6 to 30 L/min or more. That wide range is why the lung can compensate so strongly for a metabolic acidosis. (When you climb stairs fast, notice that you breathe deeper before you breathe faster.)
More ventilation lowers PaCO2. Breathing more washes CO2 out of the alveoli, which steepens the gradient from blood to alveolus, so more CO2 leaves the blood. Strictly, PaCO2 depends on the part of each breath that reaches the alveoli, the alveolar ventilation: PaCO2 ∝ V̇CO2/V̇A (Alveolar Ventilation). The chemoreceptors sense the change and adjust breathing: the peripheral chemoreceptors respond to pH and PCO2, and the central chemoreceptors mainly to PCO2 (Control of Ventilation).
The classic example is diabetic ketoacidosis. Patients take giant, effortful breaths (Kussmaul breathing), sometimes without feeling short of breath. If their breathing later looks much more comfortable, that is either very good (the acidosis has been treated) or very bad (they are too tired to keep compensating). The blood gas and the patient’s appearance together tell you which.

title: 26  Pulmonary Acid Base
text:
26.7 Respiratory acidosis: strength and load
Respiratory acidosis is a low pH from a high PaCO2, and the high PaCO2 means alveolar ventilation is too low for the CO2 the body makes. The lecture’s rule: if you say a respiratory acidosis is due to a strength-load imbalance, you will always be right. The work is then to say which strength and which load. Strength is the ability to do the work of breathing. Load is everything that work has to overcome (Figure 26.4).






Figure 26.4: Respiratory acidosis as a strength-load imbalance. When the load on the respiratory system outweighs its strength, alveolar ventilation falls and PaCO2 rises. Examples are from the 2026 lecture and notes. Course figure.




26.7.1 Strength
People divide strength in different ways. One common split is won’t breathe and can’t breathe.
Won’t breathe means the drive to breathe is too low, so breaths come too seldom or too small. Opioids are the most common cause; an overdose may breathe 4 to 6 times a minute. Sedatives, including those given for surgery, do the same. Strokes in the brainstem can lower drive, though they are uncommon and usually bring other serious problems. CO2 is normally a potent stimulus to breathe, so a high PaCO2 without faster breathing tells you the drive itself is depressed.
Can’t breathe means the drive is there but the pump cannot produce a normal tidal volume.

Nerves and muscles. Paralytic drugs (given during surgery so the patient does not move), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, high spinal cord injury and diaphragm weakness. Recall from Respiratory Statics that the muscles set how far up and down the pressure-volume curve the system can go. Weak muscles cannot pull as large a breath. Many patients with ALS eventually need a machine that helps push each breath in, and later a ventilator.
Fuel for the muscles. Malnutrition weakens muscle. Electrolytes matter too: muscles need phosphate to make ATP, so severe hypophosphatemia can cause respiratory failure (and arrhythmias). Low potassium and magnesium also weaken muscle.



26.7.2 Load

Metabolic load. More CO2 to clear: fever, sepsis, a hypermetabolic state, or an added acid load. A metabolic acidosis is not a primary respiratory problem, but it is still a load. A patient with normal lungs compensates by blowing off CO2. A patient who already has a respiratory acidosis cannot, and the extra acid makes the respiratory acidosis worse.
Airways. High airway resistance, as in asthma and COPD, makes it hard to move air in and out. CO2 retention is usually more marked in emphysema than in asthma: the airways collapse more easily, the patients breathe from already overfull lungs, and long illness often leaves their muscles weak.
Lung and pleura. Anything that makes the respiratory system stiffer adds load, and the lecture builds the list from the inside out. In the lung: scar (pulmonary fibrosis), pneumonia, fluid. In the pleural space: fluid (an effusion) or air (a pneumothorax). A large, dilated heart in chronic heart failure takes up space in the chest.
Chest wall and abdomen. Kyphoscoliosis, a sternotomy or other chest surgery, and obesity, the most common chest wall problem in the United States. Below the diaphragm: pregnancy, ascites, a distended bowel, even severe constipation. Anything that fills the abdomen makes it harder for the diaphragm to descend.
Dead space. Ventilated lung that has no blood flow, as in a pulmonary embolism. Air moved through it carries off no CO2, so the same work clears less. The Ventilation and Perfusion chapter covers it.

Real patients often have several factors at once. A patient with lung cancer might be malnourished after chemotherapy, have low phosphate, a starvation ketosis (another acid load), a malignant pleural effusion and a pneumonia. Each one is small; together they tip the balance, a pattern ICU teams call “death by a thousand paper cuts”. Fixing one factor may not be enough, and fixing all of them may be what gets the patient out of the ICU. The Think Like a Respiratory Consultant chapter uses the same framework.






NoteBackground: cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis





A student asked where these fit. Thick secretions and inflamed airways raise airway resistance, and lung tissue scarred by repeated infection can lower compliance. Neither is usually enough on its own to raise PaCO2 chronically, and many patients have normal blood gases, but either can add to other loads.





26.7.3 Asthma: the normal PaCO2 that should worry you
Asthma narrows airways unevenly. Some close down and others stay open, and a patient in an attack breathes harder, so the open airways overventilate their alveoli. Early in an asthma attack PaCO2 is therefore usually low: a respiratory alkalosis. Small Group 3 follows a woman who presents at pH 7.45 with a PaCO2 of 33 (alkalemic by the slides’ cutoff of 7.42; wider normal ranges are also used) and later, as she tires, has pH 7.28 with a PaCO2 of 54 (Figure 26.5).






Figure 26.5: A schematic course of PaCO2 in a worsening asthma attack, using the presenting and later gases from Small Group 3. On the way from a low PaCO2 to a high one, the gas passes through normal. Course figure.



On the way from alkalosis to acidosis the PaCO2 passes through 40. A patient with asthma who is working hard to breathe and has a normal PaCO2 should be hyperventilating. If she is not, she may be tiring and close to failing. A normal gas in a patient who looks better is good news; the same gas in a patient who looks worse is not.

title: 26  Pulmonary Acid Base
text:
26.8 Respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis is a high pH from a low PaCO2: ventilation is more than the body’s CO2 production requires. The causes are more of a grab bag.

Hypoxemia. A low PaO2 (below about 60 mm Hg) stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors, ventilation rises, and PaCO2 falls. The alveolar gas equation shows why that helps: with less CO2 subtracted, PAO2 is higher. At the top of Everest, PB is low, hypoxemia drives her carotid bodies, and she hyperventilates; PaCO2 is the one term she can change, and lowering it raises her PAO2.
Pain and anxiety. A healthy person having an arterial blood gas drawn usually shows a slight respiratory alkalosis, because a needle is coming.
Ingestions, salicylates in particular, which stimulate the respiratory center.
Some central nervous system injuries.
Pregnancy. Progesterone stimulates breathing. The enlarged abdomen is also a load, so a pregnant patient with another cause of respiratory acidosis has less reserve.
Compensation for a metabolic acidosis. The PaCO2 is low, but the pH is still acidemic, because compensation stops short.







NoteIf you are comparing with the lecture



In the recording, salicylate toxicity is once called a cause of metabolic alkalosis. Salicylates cause a respiratory alkalosis, as the slide lists, and often a metabolic acidosis at the same time; they do not cause a metabolic alkalosis. The recording also says hypoxia causes alkalosis “via the alveolar gas equation”. The trigger is the peripheral chemoreceptors; the equation shows why the lower PaCO2 raises PAO2. Early in the recording, the gap between PaO2 and PAO2 is put down to O2 binding Hb. Both gases equilibrate in a normal lung, and the small gap comes from the normal shunt and V/Q scatter.

title: 26  Pulmonary Acid Base
text:
26.9 Oxygenation and ventilation come together
The block began by separating oxygenation from ventilation. Here they meet in both directions. In the opioid patient the primary problem was ventilation, and it caused hypoxemia with normal lungs. In the climber the primary problem was hypoxemia, and the response to it caused a respiratory alkalosis. They interact because O2 and CO2 share the same alveolar gas: when PACO2 rises, PAO2 falls, and the reverse.

title: 26  Pulmonary Acid Base
text:
26.10 Check your understanding

Why does compensation never carry the pH past 7.40? What would you conclude if a patient in diabetic ketoacidosis had an alkalemic blood gas?


Answer

The compensating system responds to the pH error, and the response shrinks as the error shrinks, so it never gets the pH all the way back, let alone past normal. An alkalemic gas in a primary metabolic acidosis means a second process is pushing the pH up, such as a metabolic alkalosis from vomiting or a respiratory alkalosis from an ingestion.

Sort each of these into strength or load, and say which kind: a sedative overdose, myasthenia gravis, severe hypophosphatemia, high fever, morbid obesity, a large pleural effusion, a pulmonary embolism.


Answer

Strength: sedative overdose (drive, “won’t breathe”), myasthenia gravis (neuromuscular, “can’t breathe”), hypophosphatemia (muscle fuel, “can’t breathe”). Load: high fever (metabolic, more CO2 to clear), obesity (chest wall), pleural effusion (pleura, lower compliance), pulmonary embolism (dead space).

The opioid patient is given O2 by face mask and her saturation rises to 98%. What has not been fixed, and why does the O2 not fix it?


Answer

Her PaCO2 is still high and her pH still low. Raising FiO2 raises PAO2 (the first term of the alveolar gas equation), which fixes the oxygen. CO2 leaves only with ventilation, and her ventilation has not changed. Only more breathing, here by reversing the opioid, lowers PaCO2.

Early in an asthma attack, the airways are narrowed, yet PaCO2 is usually below 40. How can that be?


Answer

The narrowing is uneven. The patient breathes harder, and the airways that are still open carry extra air, so their alveoli are overventilated and lose extra CO2. Total alveolar ventilation is high, so PaCO2 falls. Only when the open units can no longer make up the difference, usually because the muscles tire, does PaCO2 rise.

Why is the lung’s compensation for a metabolic alkalosis so much smaller than its compensation for a metabolic acidosis?


Answer

Compensating for an alkalosis means breathing less. As ventilation falls, PaCO2 rises, but PAO2 and PaO2 fall too, and hypoxemia stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors, which drives breathing back up. Nothing like that limits hyperventilation, and V̇E can rise about fivefold, so compensation for an acidosis can be large.

A climber spends a week at high altitude, and her kidneys lower her HCO3− to compensate for the respiratory alkalosis. She flies home, and on her first day at sea level her PaCO2 is back to 40 mm Hg. Is her pH above, at or below 7.40, and why? What does the kidney do next?


Answer

Below 7.40. The kidney took days to lower her HCO3− and needs days to raise it again, so on the first day her HCO3− is still low. With a normal PaCO2 and a low HCO3−, the ratio is below 20 to 1 and she is acidemic. Her gas looks like a metabolic acidosis, although it is the leftover of a compensation and not a new disease. Over the next few days the kidney raises HCO3− and the pH returns to 7.40.

title: 27  Ventilation and Perfusion
text:
27.1 Ventilation, dead space and alveolar ventilation
The heart and lungs work as one system: they bring O2 to the tissues and carry CO2 away and out of the body. Doing that takes two flows. Ventilation is the convective movement of air that exchanges gas between the atmosphere and the alveoli. Perfusion is the convective movement of blood that carries dissolved gases to and from the lung. Gas exchange works only where the two meet in the right proportion. Earlier chapters covered each piece on its own (Alveolar Ventilation, Diffusion, Transport of O2 and CO2), and the CV block covered the pulmonary circulation (Pulmonary Circulation). This chapter puts them together, first in the normal lung and then in disease, where a mismatch between air and blood is the most common reason a patient is hypoxemic.
A quick review of the numbers from Alveolar Ventilation:
The 350 mL of fresh gas mixes into the 2 to 3 L already in the lung at FRC. The muscles do the work of moving all of V̇E, but only V̇A takes part in gas exchange, and it is close to pulmonary blood flow, about 5 L/min. Dead space is ventilated but does no gas exchange (the trachea has a blood supply, but no gas crosses its wall).
