27.1.1 Fast or deep
The lecture reviews why, for the same V̇E, deep breaths give more alveolar ventilation than fast, shallow ones: the dead space is a smaller fraction of each breath (Figure 27.1 B; the arithmetic is in Alveolar Ventilation). In a sick patient whose muscles are tiring, rapid, shallow breathing is a recipe for respiratory failure: much of the work goes into moving air in and out of the dead space.






Figure 27.1: (A) Anatomic dead space is the conducting airways. Alveolar dead space is alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused. Together they make the physiologic dead space. (B) Two breathing patterns with the same V̇E of 15 L/min, using the lecture’s numbers. Deep breathing gives more alveolar ventilation because the dead space is a smaller fraction of each breath. Course figure.





27.1.2 Anatomic, alveolar and physiologic dead space
In a healthy person almost all dead space is anatomic: the conducting airways from the nose and mouth to the terminal bronchioles. In disease, alveoli that still get air can lose their blood flow. Air moved into them does no gas exchange, so they add alveolar dead space. The two together are the physiologic dead space. The classic example is a pulmonary embolism: a clot blocks a pulmonary artery, and the alveoli it supplied are ventilated but not perfused.
Fowler’s method measures the anatomic dead space. The subject takes a single breath of 100% O2 and then breathes out through a nitrogen meter. The O2 that filled the conducting airways comes out first and has no nitrogen. Once alveolar gas, still carrying nitrogen from earlier room-air breaths, starts to arrive, nitrogen rises. The volume exhaled before the rise is the anatomic dead space. It is a laboratory method, not a bedside one, and you need the concept, not the tracing.
Bohr’s method measures the physiologic dead space, anatomic plus alveolar, and uses a gas that matters to physiology: CO2. Inspired air has essentially no CO2. Only perfused alveoli add CO2 to the gas, and their PCO2 is close to PaCO2. Gas from the conducting airways and from unperfused alveoli comes out with no CO2 and dilutes the rest. So the more dead space, the lower the PCO2 of the whole exhaled breath. Any CO2-free inspired gas works, and room air is the usual one; the method does not need 100% O2. The Bohr equation:
\[\frac{V_D}{V_T} = \frac{P_{aCO_2} - P_{\bar{E}CO_2}}{P_{aCO_2}}\]
PĒCO2 is the mixed expired PCO2, the average PCO2 of all the gas exhaled in a breath, measured by collecting the gas. PaCO2 from a blood gas stands in for alveolar PCO2. With a PaCO2 of 40 and a PĒCO2 of 28:
\[\frac{V_D}{V_T} = \frac{40 - 28}{40} = 0.3\]
Normal is 20 to 35% of each tidal breath. In a healthy person there is so little alveolar dead space that the Fowler and Bohr methods give nearly the same number.






Figure 27.2: The PCO2 of exhaled gas across one 500 mL breath. Gas from the anatomic dead space comes out first, with no CO2. (A) In a healthy lung the alveolar plateau sits at PaCO2 (drawn idealized; in a real lung end-tidal PCO2 is a few mm Hg below PaCO2). The mixed expired PCO2 averages the whole breath, 28 mm Hg, and gives VD/VT 0.3. (B) If half the alveoli lose their blood flow, their CO2-free gas dilutes the plateau to 20 and the mixed expired PCO2 falls to 14, so VD/VT is 0.65. Adapted from Boron and Boulpaep, Medical Physiology [1], as used in the 2026 lecture.



At the bedside, a capnograph measures end-tidal PCO2 (PETCO2): the PCO2 of the last gas out, which comes from the alveoli. In a healthy lung it is a few mm Hg below PaCO2, about 35 to 38 when PaCO2 is 40. When part of the lung loses its blood flow, the alveolar gas is diluted and end-tidal PCO2 falls well below PaCO2 (Figure 27.2 B). That gap is the bedside sign of alveolar dead space. A patient on a ventilator whose end-tidal PCO2 falls from about 38 to 20 while PaCO2 rises has added alveolar dead space, and an embolism is a classic cause.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The slide 12 notes say mixed expired PCO2 can be measured by capnography, and in the recording end-tidal PCO2 goes into the Bohr equation with a normal value of “28, 30 or so”. The 28 on slide 13 is the mixed expired value, which the Bohr equation uses. A bedside capnograph shows end-tidal PCO2, normally close to PaCO2; the arterial to end-tidal gap estimates alveolar dead space, not total VD/VT. The slide 10 figure (and the recording) label the breath 100% O2. Any CO2-free gas works, including room air, as the slide 10 notes say.


You can often spot extra dead space without a calculation. Sitting in class you breathe about 12 times a minute at half a liter and hold your PaCO2 at 40. A patient taking big breaths 35 times a minute with a PaCO2 of 40 is doing a great deal of breathing for very little CO2 clearance; unless he is making far more CO2, his dead space is up. The extra work is one way dead space leads to respiratory failure (Pulmonary Acid Base).


27.1.3 CO2 and alveolar ventilation
With CO2 production steady at about 200 mL/min, PACO2 ∝ V̇CO2/V̇A: halve alveolar ventilation and PaCO2 doubles, double it and PaCO2 halves (Alveolar Ventilation). A patient breathing fast and hard with a normal or high PaCO2 has a low alveolar ventilation, whatever the V̇E.

title: 27  Ventilation and Perfusion
text:
27.2 The V/Q ratio
Picture the ideal lung as a single alveolus with a single capillary. Mixed venous blood arrives, equilibrates with alveolar gas, and leaves with the alveolar PO2 and PCO2. For that to work, the air brought to the alveolus has to match the blood carried past it. The ventilation-perfusion ratio is:
\[\dot V / \dot Q = \frac{\text{alveolar ventilation (L/min)}}{\text{pulmonary blood flow (L/min)}}\]
For the whole lung it is about 0.8 to 1. A V̇A of 4 to 5.25 L/min over a cardiac output of 5 to 6 L/min gives anything from about 0.7 to 1.05. Real lungs have millions of units, each with its own ratio, and in health they cluster around that average.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The V/Q lecture’s slides use 0.8 (slide 28), and the Ventilation lecture uses about 1. Both come from the same arithmetic with different inputs (4.2 L/min over 5 gives 0.84; 5.25 over 5 gives 1.05). What matters is the direction: apex high, base low, and disease pushing units toward 0 or infinity.



27.2.1 Ventilation is greater at the base
In an upright person, pleural pressure is more negative at the apex (about −10 cm H2O) than at the base (about −2.5). The weight of the lung hangs from the top, like a Slinky held by its top coil: the upper coils are stretched and the lower ones bunched. So at FRC the apical alveoli are already well inflated and the basal ones are small.
Ventilation is about the change in volume during a breath, not the volume. The small basal alveoli sit on the steep part of the lung’s pressure-volume curve, and the stretched apical alveoli sit near the flat top (Respiratory Statics). The same fall in pleural pressure during inspiration therefore adds more volume at the base. Ventilation per unit of lung falls steadily from base to apex.


27.2.2 Blood flow is greater at the base, by more
The pulmonary circulation is low pressure, low resistance and highly compliant, and its capillaries are recruited and distended as flow rises (Pulmonary Circulation). Because its pressures are low, gravity has a large effect on them: arterial pressure is higher at the base, where the column of blood above adds to it, and lower at the apex. Blood flow therefore falls from base to apex too, and it falls more steeply than ventilation.
So V/Q rises from base to apex (Figure 27.3). At the base, both are high but blood flow is higher, and V/Q is about 0.6. Near the middle they are about equal. At the apex both are low, but blood flow is much lower, and V/Q is about 3.






Figure 27.3: (A) Alveolar ventilation and blood flow in three slices of an upright lung, with their ratio, from the values on the 2026 lecture slide. Both fall toward the apex, blood flow more steeply. (B) Each region’s alveolar gas, plotted as PO2 against PCO2. A unit with V/Q of 0 has the gas of mixed venous blood; a unit with infinite V/Q has the gas of inspired air. Panel B values adapted from Costanzo, Physiology [2], as used in the 2026 lecture.



A unit’s V/Q sets its alveolar gas. At the high-V/Q apex, PAO2 is about 130 mm Hg and PACO2 about 33. At the low-V/Q base, PAO2 is about 90 and PACO2 about 42. The base has the lowest PAO2 and highest PACO2 of the upright lung, even though it gets the most air, and because it also gets most of the blood, its gas counts most toward the arterial blood.


27.2.3 The West zones and gas exchange
The West zones, defined by the order of alveolar pressure (Palv) and the pressures in the pulmonary arteries (Pa) and veins (Pv), are taught in the CV block; see the West zones figure. What they add to V/Q is this. In zone 1 (Palv > Pa > Pv) the capillaries are closed, so a zone 1 region is ventilated but not perfused: alveolar dead space. Healthy lungs have little or none, matching the point that healthy people have almost no alveolar dead space. Zone 1 appears when vascular pressures fall (acute hypovolemia, such as bleeding) or alveolar pressures rise (air trapping in asthma, or high ventilator pressures). Most matched gas exchange happens in zone 3, where the capillaries stay open. The zones move with position: lying on the back, the posterior, dependent lung gets the most blood flow, because gravity sends more blood to whatever part of the lung is lowest.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The Costanzo figure on slide 28 labels the apex point “Zone 1, V/Q highest”, the middle “Zone 2” and the base “Zone 3”. Read these as apex, middle and base. In the West zones (slide 27), zone 1 has no blood flow, so its V/Q is infinite, and the normal upright lung has little of it. The apex has the highest finite V/Q of the normal lung, about 3, with the highest PAO2 and lowest PACO2.

title: 27  Ventilation and Perfusion
text:
27.3 Oxygen: from air to tissue
What matters for life is how much O2 reaches the tissues, the O2 delivery: cardiac output times arterial O2 content. At rest the tissues extract about 25%, so mixed venous blood returns about 75% saturated. Getting O2 from air into the alveoli takes three steps.

Ambient air. PO2 = PB × FiO2, with FiO2 0.21 for room air.
Inspired air. The upper airway humidifies the air completely, even cold, dry air in fast breathing. Water vapor at body temperature takes 47 mm Hg, so PIO2 = (PB − 47) × FiO2.
Alveolar gas. CO2 arriving from the blood takes its share:

\[P_{AO_2} = (P_B - P_{H_2O})\,F_{IO_2} - \frac{P_{aCO_2}}{R}\]
R is the respiratory exchange ratio, the CO2 the body puts out divided by the O2 it takes up, about 0.8 on a typical Western diet. At sea level, (760 − 47) × 0.21 = 150, and 150 − 40/0.8 = 100 mm Hg. In Chicago, with PB 747, PAO2 is about 97.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The case slides write PAO2 = 0.21 (700 mm Hg) − PaCO2/R. The 700 is already PB − PH2O (747 − 47), so do not subtract 47 again. The V/Q notes do, which is where their ranges (“31–40”, “236–255”, “96–106”) come from; the slide values below are right.

title: 27  Ventilation and Perfusion
text:
27.4 Case 1: a comatose patient
A comatose young woman arrives in the emergency department. Her saturation is 75%. Her blood gas on room air is 7.08 / 85 / 42 / 75%: an acute respiratory acidosis and a low PaO2. Did she aspirate and get a pneumonia? The alveolar gas equation answers without an X-ray:
\[P_{AO_2} = 0.21\,(747 - 47) - \frac{85}{0.8} = 147 - 106 \approx 41 \text{ mm Hg}\]
Her PaO2 of 42 matches it. The A–a gradient is essentially zero, so whatever O2 reaches her alveoli is getting into her blood. Her lungs are fine; she is not breathing enough. Her gas is the same as the opioid patient’s in Pulmonary Acid Base, and the lecture treats her as an opioid overdose. Global hypoventilation is enough to cause hypoxemia, and clinicians often miss it: they see a low saturation and assume the lungs are the problem.
A few liters of O2 would raise her saturation but not lower her PaCO2. The fix is to make her breathe. If she goes from 4 to 6 breaths a minute to 10 to 12, alveolar ventilation roughly doubles, PaCO2 halves back toward 40, and PAO2 rises to about 97 with no extra O2.

27.4.1 Causes of a low alveolar PO2
Each term in the alveolar gas equation points to a cause:

Low PB: high altitude.
Low FiO2: suffocation, as in a confined space where O2 has been used up or displaced.
High PaCO2: global hypoventilation.

The history usually makes the first two obvious. In all three the A–a gradient is normal.

title: 27  Ventilation and Perfusion
text:
27.5 The A–a gradient
The A–a gradient is PAO2, calculated, minus PaO2, measured on a blood gas. In a young adult it is under 10 mm Hg. PAO2 at sea level is about 100, but a healthy PaO2 is more often about 90. About 5% of the cardiac output is a normal anatomic shunt that never meets alveolar gas: bronchial veins draining into the pulmonary veins, and thebesian veins draining the heart muscle into the left ventricle. A little V/Q scatter in the normal lung adds to the gap. Neither raises PaCO2 noticeably. Mixed venous PCO2 (46) is only 6 mm Hg above alveolar PCO2 (40), while mixed venous PO2 (40) is 60 below alveolar PO2. The shapes of the curves matter more. Blood mixes by content, and because the top of the O2 curve is flat, a small loss of O2 content lowers PO2 a lot; the CO2 curve is steep and nearly straight, so the same mixing barely moves PCO2 (see the two-alveolus model below).
The gradient rises with age. The slide 44 notes give an estimate, (age/4) + 4, which comes to about 10 at 24 and about 21 at 68.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



Course materials give less than 10 mm Hg (small-group keys, slide 44, the lecture), 5 to 15 (Ventilation notes) and (age/4) + 4 (slide 44 notes). They differ only for gradients between 10 and 15 mm Hg, and none of the course’s cases falls there. This book uses under 10 for a young adult, as the small groups do. In the recording, “anything less than ten is a problem” is a slip for more than ten.


A raised gradient means O2 is reaching the alveoli but not getting into the arterial blood. The causes are:

Diffusion limitation, where a thickened barrier slows O2 transfer, most of all in exercise (Diffusion).
V/Q mismatch, mainly units with low V/Q.
Shunt, blood that passes the lung without meeting ventilated alveoli.

A low mixed venous saturation does not belong on this list by itself. It makes shunt and low V/Q worse, as a later section shows, but it does little in normal lungs.

title: 27  Ventilation and Perfusion
text:
27.6 The V/Q spectrum
V/Q runs from 0 to infinity (Figure 27.4).






Figure 27.4: Three units on the V/Q spectrum. Capillary values are PO2 / PCO2 in mm Hg. A unit with no ventilation (shunt) leaves blood as it arrived: mixed venous. A matched unit brings blood to the alveolar gas, PO2 100 and PCO2 40. A unit with no blood flow (dead space) keeps the gas it breathes in, PO2 150 and PCO2 0. Low V/Q units sit between the first two, and high V/Q units between the last two. Course figure, after the lecture slide.



A low V/Q unit is ventilated, but less than its blood flow needs, so blood leaves it with a PO2 below 100 and a PCO2 above 40: blood going where there is not enough O2. A high V/Q unit has more air than its blood can use: gas going where there is no blood to use it. Healthy lungs have little dead space and only the small anatomic shunt. Diseased lungs are a mixture skewed toward one end or the other; as the course notes put it, “we live in the middle”.

title: 27  Ventilation and Perfusion
text:
27.7 Case 2: pneumonia on 40% O2
A 34-year-old woman has had cough, fever and shortness of breath for four days, and her chest X-ray shows pneumonia. On 40% O2 her blood gas is pH 7.48, PaCO2 30 and PaO2 65 mm Hg: she is hyperventilating. A PaO2 of 65 might not look alarming, but compare it with what her alveoli hold. She is breathing 40% O2 and blowing her CO2 down to 20, so:
\[P_{AO_2} = 0.40 \times 700 - \frac{30}{0.8} = 280 - 37.5 \approx 243 \text{ mm Hg}\]
Her A–a gradient is about 243 − 65 = 178 mm Hg (slide 44 calls it the A-a difference), far above 10. Always ask what the PaO2 should be at the FiO2 the patient is on. On supplemental O2, even a PaO2 of 100 or 150 can hide a very large gradient.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



Slides 43 and 44 give the gas as 7.40 / 20 / 65. A pH of 7.40 with a PaCO2 of 20 implies an HCO3− of about 12 mEq/L, a mixed disorder the case does not discuss, and the lecture noted the numbers need fixing. The course errata replace it with 7.48 / 30 / 65, which is used here. The A–a gradient is a little smaller (178 rather than 190 mm Hg), and the conclusion is the same.

title: 27  Ventilation and Perfusion
text:
27.8 The two-alveolus model
The lecture explains the causes of a raised gradient with two alveoli side by side, each with its own capillary, the blood from both mixing in the pulmonary veins. In the normal model both alveoli have PAO2 about 102 and PACO2 40; mixed venous blood arrives at PO2 40 and PCO2 46 and leaves both units at the alveolar values.

27.8.1 Shunt
Anatomic shunt is blood that bypasses the lung through a channel: the normal bronchial and thebesian veins (about 5%), an abnormal connection inside the heart, or an arteriovenous malformation in the lung. The lecture focuses on physiologic shunt, where blood flows past alveoli that get no air. Either the airway is blocked completely (a tumor, a foreign body, a mucus plug) or the alveoli are filled with something other than air: blood, pus or water. Collapsed alveoli (atelectasis) and the flooded lung of ARDS are shunt too.
Blood that leaves a shunted alveolus is still mixed venous blood. The breathing centers respond to the low PaO2 by driving more ventilation, so the good alveoli get extra air and a higher PAO2, but the blood passing the shunted alveolus never meets it. Mixing gives an arterial saturation below 100% (Figure 27.5 A).
With equal flow through the two units, blood leaves the shunted unit at 75% and the good unit at 100%, and the mixture is about 88%. Averaging saturations works here: when two streams with the same Hb mix, the O2 content of the mixture is the flow-weighted average of the two, and on room air almost all the O2 is bound to Hb. PO2 is the value you cannot average, because the dissociation curve is not straight. Blood at 88% has a PO2 of about 55 mm Hg, not the average of 100 and 40.






Figure 27.5: The two-alveolus model with half the blood flow through a shunt. (A) On room air, blood leaving the shunted unit at 75% mixes with blood at 100% for an SaO2 of about 88%. (B) On 100% O2 the good unit’s PAO2 is 663, but its Hb was already full; only the dissolved O2 rises, and SaO2 reaches only about 92%. (C) If mixed venous saturation falls to 50%, the same shunt gives about 79% even on 100% O2. (D) Arterial saturation against shunt fraction on room air and on 100% O2 (Hb 15 g/dL, PaCO2 40, sea level). Mixed values come from averaging O2 contents, with O2 content = 1.39 × Hb × SO2 + 0.003 × PO2. The ventilated unit is taken as fully saturated, as on the slides. Course figure, after the lecture’s two-alveolus slides.





27.8.2 Shunt is refractory to O2
Give this patient 100% O2. The good alveolus now has a PAO2 of about (760 − 47) × 1.0 − 40/0.8 = 663 mm Hg. Its blood was already 100% saturated, and Hb cannot carry more than full. The extra PO2 adds only dissolved O2, 0.003 × 663 ≈ 2 mL/dL. The shunted blood never sees the extra O2 and still leaves at 75%. The mixture rises only to about 92% (Figure 27.5 B). Shunt is refractory to supplemental O2, and that failure to respond is how you recognize it.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



Slides 49 and 54 average saturations on 100% O2 to get 87.5% and 75% (and write “75 + 100/2” for (75 + 100)/2). The dissolved O2 in the ventilated stream makes the true values about 92% and 79%. Either way the shunt is refractory, which is the slides’ point. The V/Q notes and the Small Group 3 key call averaging saturations “not mathematically correct”; it is close enough on room air, and averaging PO2 is the mistake to avoid.


Figure 27.5 D shows why shunt size matters. The lecture’s slide 52 makes the same point with PaO2: above about a 30% shunt, an FiO2 of 1.0 cannot bring PaO2 to 100.


27.8.3 Case 3: cough and fever, on room air and then 100% O2
A 68-year-old man with cough and fever has a chest X-ray with widespread white opacities. On room air his gas is 7.35 / 33 / 40 / 75%:
\[P_{AO_2} = 0.21 \times 700 - \frac{33}{0.8} \approx 147 - 41 = 106 \text{ mm Hg}\]
His A–a gradient is 106 − 40 = 66. On 100% O2 his saturation rises only to 88%: shunt physiology. It rises more than a pure shunt would, because some alveoli are only partly filled and still take some air, and those low-V/Q units respond to O2.


27.8.4 Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
The body has its own way to reduce a shunt. Small pulmonary arteries that supply poorly ventilated, hypoxic alveoli constrict. The response is present even in isolated lung tissue; its exact mechanism is still unclear. With cardiac output unchanged, blood that would have gone to the bad region goes to better-ventilated lung, so the shunt fraction falls and PaO2 rises. In the lecture’s example, moving the flow through a shunted unit from half to a quarter raises SaO2 from about 88% to about 94% (Figure 27.6 C).
It helps most when the disease is regional. A patient who suddenly plugs a bronchus with mucus may drop to a saturation of 60 to 70%, with a whited-out lung on X-ray, and over about 15 minutes the saturation climbs back. Suctioning may get the credit, but the repeat X-ray often still shows the whited-out lung; vasoconstriction diverted the blood. When less than about 20% of the lung is affected, total resistance barely changes. When the disease is diffuse, or the whole lung is hypoxic as at altitude, the vessels constrict everywhere, pulmonary vascular resistance can double, and the right ventricle faces an afterload it tolerates poorly.






NoteBackground: when inflammation overrides the response





In a bacterial or other strongly inflammatory lung lesion, the inflammation dilates the local vessels and brings blood to the infected region, so the bad lobe can get more blood flow, not less, and the shunt is worse than its size suggests. This was taught in the 2026 lecture. The Small Group 3 key marks it as not on the exam.





27.8.5 A low mixed venous saturation worsens shunt
The blood that passes a shunt leaves with whatever O2 it arrived with. Mixed venous O2 depends on how much O2 is delivered to the tissues and how much they take out. If cardiac output falls, as in heart failure, or the tissues extract more, as with fever, a high work of breathing or sepsis, mixed venous blood comes back less saturated. In a patient with a shunt, that lower saturation goes straight into the arterial blood. The slides and lecture call this mixing venous admixture (slide 54, “Poor venous saturation/admixture”): poorly saturated venous blood that passes the shunt mixing into the arterial blood. Without any change in the shunt, SaO2 falls further (Figure 27.5 C), and hypoxemia lowers delivery further, a downward spiral.
In normal lungs a low mixed venous saturation does little, because blood that passes well-ventilated alveoli reaches the alveolar PO2 whatever it started at. It matters when there is shunt, low V/Q, or a diffusion-limited barrier, as in exercise.
So with a severe shunt, the levers are to lower the shunt fraction, raise O2 delivery and lower O2 consumption (treating fever, resting the respiratory muscles).


27.8.6 O2 delivery
\[\dot Q_{O_2} = \dot Q \times C_{aO_2} = \dot Q \times \left[(1.39 \times S_{aO_2} \times \text{Hb}) + (0.003 \times P_{aO_2})\right]\]
Each gram of fully saturated Hb carries 1.39 mL of O2, and each mm Hg of PO2 adds 0.003 mL/dL dissolved. With a cardiac output of 5 L/min (50 dL/min), SaO2 1.0, Hb 15 g/dL and PaO2 97:
\[\dot Q_{O_2} = 50 \times \left[(1.39 \times 1.0 \times 15) + (0.003 \times 97)\right] = 50 \times 21 \approx 1050 \text{ mL O}_2/\text{min}\]
O2 content is Hb, saturation and, slightly, PaO2. Cardiac output is not part of content; it multiplies content to give delivery. Raising cardiac output helps a patient with a shunt by raising delivery, which lowers extraction and raises the mixed venous O2.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The slide 54 notes say “oxygen content relies on hemoglobin and cardiac output” and then give the content equation, which has no cardiac output in it. Content depends on Hb and saturation (and slightly on PaO2); delivery is cardiac output times content, as slide 56 shows.

title: 27  Ventilation and Perfusion
text:
27.9 Case 4: low V/Q in asthma
A 24-year-old man has cough, wheezing, shortness of breath and a subjective fever. His saturation is 85% on room air and 97% on 30% O2. His X-ray shows big lungs with flat diaphragms and not much white. A few liters of O2 fixed his saturation, so this is not shunt.
Air goes preferentially to units whose airways are open, so the units behind narrowed airways get less ventilation for the same blood flow: low V/Q, with a lower PAO2 and a higher PACO2 (Figure 27.6 A). They are still ventilated, so raising FiO2 raises their PAO2 too and their blood saturates (Figure 27.6 B). Low V/Q responds to O2.






Figure 27.6: (A) Low V/Q in the two-alveolus model, with the lecture’s values. Behind a narrowed airway, PAO2 is 77 and PACO2 45; the other unit gets extra ventilation, with PAO2 105 and PACO2 36. Mixed pulmonary venous PO2 is about 89, while PCO2 is back near 40. (B) On 30% O2, PIO2 rises by about 64 mm Hg in every ventilated unit, and both units now saturate their blood. (C) Hypoxic vasoconstriction in a shunt: halving the flow to the airless unit, from 50% to 25% of the total, raises SaO2 from about 88% to about 94%. Course figure, after the lecture slides.



The low-V/Q unit in Figure 27.6 A raises its PCO2 to 45, but the extra ventilation of the other unit lowers its PCO2 to 36, and the mix comes back near 40. The same extra ventilation cannot rescue the O2. Blood leaving the well-ventilated unit is already nearly saturated, so a PAO2 of 105 instead of 100 adds almost nothing; the flat top of the O2 dissociation curve leaves nothing to gain. The CO2 curve is nearly straight over this range, so extra ventilation removes extra CO2 in proportion. That is why V/Q mismatch lowers PaO2 much more than it raises PaCO2, and why a high PaCO2 usually means total alveolar ventilation is too low: the patient is tiring, or cannot raise ventilation enough, as in severe COPD.






NoteIf you are comparing with the notes



The V/Q notes say V/Q mismatch spares PaCO2 because CO2 diffuses about 20 times faster than O2. Both gases equilibrate fully in a normal capillary; the reason is the shapes of the two dissociation curves.


Opening the airways improves oxygenation, but the more immediate danger in asthma is the work of moving air through narrowed tubes. Hypoxic vasoconstriction plays a small part in low V/Q; once the patient gets O2, the stimulus goes away.

27.9.1 What disturbs V/Q
Airway problems: asthma, COPD (bronchitis and emphysema), secretions, bronchiectasis, foreign bodies and masses. Alveolar problems: pneumonia, interstitial lung disease and edema. Vascular problems: high or low pressures in the pulmonary circulation. Pneumonia and edema cause low V/Q where the alveoli are partly filled and shunt where they are filled completely. Atelectasis, where the alveoli have collapsed, is shunt.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



Slide 59 lists atelectasis with pneumonia, interstitial lung disease and edema as alveolar problems that disturb V/Q, and the lecture presented the list as problems that “don’t totally sock in” the alveoli, that is, low V/Q. Collapsed alveoli get no air, so atelectasis is shunt, as the slide 47 notes say.

title: 27  Ventilation and Perfusion
text:
27.10 The approach to hypoxemia
Every patient with a low saturation goes through the same steps (Figure 27.7). Calculate PAO2, measure PaO2, and take the A–a gradient. If the gradient is normal, gas exchange works and too little O2 is reaching the alveoli: look for hypoventilation, altitude or a low FiO2. If it is raised, give O2. A good response means low V/Q (or diffusion limitation); keep the O2 on while you treat what is lowering ventilation. A poor response means shunt.






Figure 27.7: The approach to hypoxemia, from the 2026 lecture. The A–a gradient separates a low alveolar PO2 from a gas-exchange problem, and the response to supplemental O2 separates low V/Q from shunt. A low mixed venous O2 worsens shunt and low V/Q. Course figure.



Low V/Q is by far the most common reason a patient is hypoxemic.






NoteBackground: the shunt toolbox





For severe shunt the lecture described, as physiology, what ICU teams do: positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) holds flooded alveoli open and turns shunt into O2-responsive low V/Q; diuresis removes lung water; turning a patient with ARDS onto the belly evens out ventilation and perfusion; and laying a patient good lung down lets gravity send blood to the ventilated lung.

title: 27  Ventilation and Perfusion
text:
27.11 Check your understanding

A person pants, with a very high rate and a tidal volume close to the anatomic dead space. The mixed expired PCO2 of the gas collected from his breaths falls toward zero, yet his PaCO2 rises. Explain both changes.


Answer

Each breath first fills and empties the conducting airways, which add no CO2. With VT close to VD, almost all of each exhaled breath is dead space gas, and the little alveolar gas in it is diluted, so the mixed expired PCO2 falls toward zero (in the Bohr equation, VD/VT approaches 1). Meanwhile alveolar ventilation, (VT − VD) × RR, stays small however high the rate goes. CO2 leaves the body only with alveolar ventilation, so removal falls below production and PaCO2 rises.

In an upright person, the base gets the most ventilation. Why does it still have the lowest PAO2?


Answer

Blood flow rises toward the base even more steeply than ventilation, so the base has the lowest V/Q (about 0.6). Each unit of blood there is matched with less fresh air, so more O2 is taken out of the alveolar gas and more CO2 added to it, and PAO2 ends up lowest and PACO2 highest.

Breathing 100% O2 raises a healthy person’s PaO2 from about 100 to about 600 mm Hg. With a hemoglobin of 15 g/dL, roughly how much does CaO2 rise, and why so little for a sixfold rise in PaO2?


Answer

About 2 mL/dL, from about 20.5 to about 22.6 mL/dL, roughly 10%. Hemoglobin is already about 97% saturated at a PaO2 of 100, on the flat top of the curve, so the bound term can rise only to 100%: about 1.39 × 15 × 0.03 ≈ 0.6 mL/dL more. The rest is dissolved O2, 0.003 × 500 = 1.5 mL/dL. Almost all the O2 in blood rides on hemoglobin, and once hemoglobin is full, extra PO2 adds only the small dissolved amount.

Why does V/Q mismatch lower PaO2 much more than it raises PaCO2?


Answer

The patient breathes more, and the well-ventilated units blow off extra CO2. The CO2 curve is nearly straight, so their lower PCO2 offsets the high PCO2 of the low-V/Q units. Extra ventilation cannot add O2 to blood that is already nearly saturated, because the O2 curve is flat at the top, so nothing offsets the poorly saturated blood from the low-V/Q units.

text:
27.12 Key equations

VD/VT = (PaCO2 − PĒCO2)/PaCO2

title: 27  Ventilation and Perfusion
text:
27.13 Sources
This chapter follows the 2026 Ventilation and Perfusion I and II lectures for MEDC 30504 and draws on the course’s V/Q notes, Small Group 3 and the 2018 course notes, corrected and updated. All figures were drawn for this book.


1. Boron WF, Boulpaep EL. Medical Physiology. 2, updated ed. Saunders; 2012.


2. Costanzo LS. Physiology. Philadelphia: Saunders Elsevier.

title: 28  Control of Pulmonary Ventilation
text:
28.1 Rhythm generation: the medulla
This is the last lecture of new material in the block. The earlier chapters followed the gas from the air to the alveolus (statics, dynamics, ventilation), across the barrier (diffusion), into the blood (transport), through the matching of air and blood (ventilation and perfusion), and on to the tissues as O2 delivery, cardiac output times O2 content. All of that runs without conscious effort, and it has to change from moment to moment as we sleep, talk, eat and exercise. This chapter is about the control system. The lecture builds it in four parts around one diagram (Figure 28.6, at the end of the chapter):
The basic drive to breathe comes from the brainstem: the medulla, which sits on top of the spinal cord, and the pons above it. Six structures matter for this course (Figure 28.1). Four are in the medulla, and they generate the rhythm. Two are in the pons, and they shape it.
Pre-Bötzinger complex (pre-BC): the “go” button. Its neurons are autorhythmic. Like the cells of the sinus node in the heart, they depolarize on their own at a regular rate, and each burst of firing starts a breath. That is why you breathe all day, and all night, without thinking about it. Recording electrodes moved through the brainstem pick up these rhythmic bursts most strongly at the pre-BC. Different groups of its neurons produce different patterns: ordinary tidal breaths (eupnea), sighs (a longer, deeper inspiration), and gasps (a sudden, abrupt inspiration). Other inputs shift which pattern dominates. Profound hypoxia, for example, shifts the pre-BC toward gasping, which is the gasp of someone who has been held underwater too long.
Bötzinger complex (BC): the “stop” button. It sits right next to the pre-BC and sends mostly inhibitory signals to it. The cycle has phases: pre-inspiration, when the inspiratory neurons begin to ramp up at the end of expiration; inspiration; a brief post-inspiration transition; and expiration. Toward the end of inspiration the BC fires and shuts off the inspiratory drive, so the inspiratory muscles relax and you breathe out. Go, stop, go, stop: the pair sets the rhythm.
Dorsal respiratory group (DRG): tidal breathing. The DRG carries out the rhythm for quiet breathing. It signals the primary muscles of inspiration, the diaphragm and the external intercostals. It sits beside the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), where much of the sensory feedback arrives (below), so that feedback acts on it directly.
Ventral respiratory group (VRG): augmented breathing. The VRG recruits the secondary muscles of inspiration and expiration. It is most active when breathing has to be augmented: deeper, fuller inspirations, or forced expirations.

title: 28  Control of Pulmonary Ventilation
text: Figure 28.1: The six brainstem centers that control breathing. In the medulla, the pre-Bötzinger complex starts each breath and the Bötzinger complex ends inspiration. The dorsal respiratory group drives the primary muscles for quiet breathing, and the ventral respiratory group recruits the secondary muscles when breathing must be augmented. In the pons, the apneustic center drives inspiration and the pneumotaxic center restrains it. Course figure, after the lecture’s diagram.

title: 28  Control of Pulmonary Ventilation
text:
28.2 Rhythm modulation: the pons
The two pontine centers do not start breaths. They shape the breath that the medulla starts: how deep it is, and how the cycle divides between inspiration and expiration. Their output is graded, set by the feedback they receive.
Apneustic center (AC). It sits at the junction of the pons and the medulla, caudal to the pneumotaxic center. It augments inspiration: it takes the signal from the pre-BC and ramps it up. Left to itself it would drive every inspiration as long and as deep as possible.
Pneumotaxic center (PC). It sits higher in the pons and inhibits the apneustic center, which ends inspiration on time and prevents overdistension. It receives the sensory feedback from the stretch receptors in the lungs, so it is the center that says “that’s enough stretch.” With both working, breaths are smooth and of normal size. (The slide notes give the PC’s anatomical names, the Kölliker-Fuse and parabrachial nuclei. You do not need them.)

28.2.1 What the transection experiments showed
The functions of these centers were worked out in animals by cutting the brainstem at different levels and watching the breathing pattern, with the vagus nerves left intact or cut. The vagi matter because they carry the stretch-receptor signals from the lungs (next section), which also help end inspiration. Figure 28.2 shows the results.






Figure 28.2: Breathing patterns after the brainstem is cut at four levels, with the vagus nerves intact (left) or cut (right). Level I, above the pons; level II, between the pneumotaxic and apneustic centers; level III, between the pons and medulla; level IV, below the medulla. Course figure, after the transection figure used in the lecture.




Level I (above the pons). Breathing stays close to normal, perhaps a little slower without the higher inputs. Cutting the vagi as well makes breaths slower and deeper, because the stretch signal that helps end inspiration is gone.
Level II (below the pneumotaxic center). The apneustic center now runs without its brake. Breaths are slower and deeper, and if the vagi are also cut, inspiration is held for a long time before a brief expiration: apneustic breathing, or apneusis.
Level III (between the pons and the medulla). Only the medullary centers are left. The pre-BC and BC still switch breathing on and off, but the breaths are irregular gasps, with or without the vagi. The pons is what turns that on-off signal into a smooth tidal breath.
Level IV (below the medulla). No breathing at all. The rhythm generator has been cut off from the spinal cord.

The gasping pattern comes from the firing of the medullary neurons, not from the mechanics of the lung or chest wall. You will see it at the bedside as agonal breathing, in patients who are dying or in cardiac arrest, when the higher centers have failed and the medulla is the last thing still working. It can look like breathing, which is why bystander CPR teaching now asks “is the person breathing normally?” rather than “is the person breathing?” A gasping person found collapsed needs CPR. Gasps can also continue for a time after death, which is distressing for families and staff, and knowing where they come from helps you explain them.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The lecture notes (section I.C) and the recording describe losing the pneumotaxic center as producing apneustic breathing, with breaths “held at inhalation.” The transection figure (slides 23 to 27) shows that apneusis appears only when the vagi are cut as well. With the vagi intact, the stretch-receptor signal still ends each inspiration, and breathing after a level II cut is slower and deeper. The figure is the version to learn. The course errata make the same correction.

title: 28  Control of Pulmonary Ventilation
text:
28.3 Muscles of respiration
The rhythm centers act through the respiratory muscles, which are skeletal muscle, so they can also be driven voluntarily (see “Higher brain centers,” below).









Inspiration
Expiration




Primary muscles (eupneic breathing), driven by the DRG
Diaphragm, external intercostals
None. The lung’s elastic recoil returns the system to FRC.


Secondary muscles (forced or augmented breathing), driven by the VRG
Upper airway muscles (nares, tongue, pharynx, larynx), which hold the airway open and lower its resistance; neck muscles (sternocleidomastoids, scalenes); chest muscles (pectoralis minor and major)
Internal intercostals, abdominal muscles



The ribs move like bucket handles, hinged at each end. The external intercostals pull them up and out, which enlarges the chest and lowers pleural pressure. The internal intercostals pull them down and in, which is only needed when expiration has to be forced. Quiet expiration uses no muscle at all, as the statics chapter explained: the inspiratory muscles relax and recoil does the rest. A person working hard to breathe, sitting forward with hands on knees and the neck muscles standing out with each breath, is using the secondary muscles that the VRG recruits. The skin pulling in above the collarbones and between the ribs shows how negative the pleural pressure has become.






NoteBackground: the motor nerves





The diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve, whose motor neurons sit in the spinal cord at C3 to C5. That is why an injury to the cervical cord above that level stops breathing, while an injury below it spares the diaphragm. The pathways from the brainstem groups to the spinal motor neurons belong to the neurobiology course.

title: 28  Control of Pulmonary Ventilation
section: 28.4 Sensory receptors in the respiratory system
text:
28.4 Sensory receptors in the respiratory system
As you breathe, the respiratory tract reports back. Its receptors lie throughout the system, from the nose and pharynx down to the alveoli and pleura.









Receptor
Where
Stimulus
Effect




Irritant receptors (rapidly adapting receptors, RARs)
Nerve endings between epithelial cells of the upper and lower airways
Smoke, dust, noxious gases, cold air
Airway constriction (bronchospasm), cough, sighs. In asthma this response is exaggerated.


Pulmonary stretch receptors (slowly adapting receptors, SARs)
Airway smooth muscle, lung parenchyma, pleura
Stretch as the lung inflates
Inspiration cut short to prevent overinflation: the Hering-Breuer reflex


Bronchopulmonary C fibers
Throughout the airways and lungs
Pain; temperature, including cold; very large stretch
Rapid, shallow breathing; part of the sensation of dyspnea


Juxtacapillary (J) receptors
Alveolar walls, next to the capillaries
Capillary distension and interstitial edema
Rapid, shallow breathing; the discomfort of pulmonary edema, as in heart failure



Rapidly adapting means the response fades if the stimulus continues. The first cigarette makes a person cough hard; a regular smoker hardly coughs at all, because the irritant receptors have adapted.
Slowly adapting means the opposite. The stretch receptors keep firing as long as the lung is overstretched; we never really get used to overdistension. The Hering-Breuer reflex is strong in infants, whose breathing it largely sets; in adults it acts only when tidal volume is several times normal. That is the vagal signal that the transection experiments removed.
The C fibers are unmyelinated, slow-conducting fibers, like the pain and temperature fibers elsewhere in the body. The C fibers and J receptors both produce rapid, shallow breathing: faster breaths that avoid stretching the lung further. Their signals reach the cortex too, which is part of why a patient with pulmonary edema feels short of breath.
The route. Almost all of these signals travel up the vagus nerve (CN X) to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) in the medulla, beside the DRG. From the NTS the feedback acts on the DRG and on the rhythm and pattern centers: the pre-BC and BC, which set rate and rhythm, and the pneumotaxic center, which restrains the apneustic center and so sets the depth of each breath.

title: 28  Control of Pulmonary Ventilation
text:
28.5 Central and peripheral chemoreceptors
The lung receptors report on mechanics. The chemoreceptors report on gas exchange: the O2, CO2 and H+ of the blood. You met them in the cardiovascular block, where the chemoreceptor reflex acted on the heart with breathing held fixed (ANS and Extrinsic Control). Here their main job, driving ventilation, takes center stage.

28.5.1 Central chemoreceptors
The central chemoreceptors lie near the ventral surface of the medulla (the slide names the medullary raphe, the ventrolateral medulla and the retrotrapezoid nucleus). They sit right next to the respiratory centers, which makes sense for a sensor whose job is to tell those centers how breathing is going.
They detect H+ and CO2, and the blood-brain barrier decides what reaches them. The capillaries of the brain have tight junctions between their endothelial cells, plus extra supporting cells, so much less crosses than elsewhere in the body. Water and small uncharged molecules such as CO2 cross freely. Charged ions such as H+ cross poorly. So the central chemoreceptors cannot sense the blood’s H+ directly. Instead, CO2 diffuses into the brain, and carbonic anhydrase in the brain tissue converts it, by the reaction you saw in the acid-base chapter:
\[\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{HCO}_3^-\]
A rise in arterial PCO2 therefore raises the H+ around the chemoreceptors within moments. Bicarbonate reaches the brain fluid more slowly, through the choroid plexus and transporters, and it sets how much H+ a given CO2 makes. That is why a person whose bicarbonate has risen over time, as in chronic CO2 retention, can tolerate a higher PaCO2 without much extra drive (below). It also means a change in the blood’s H+ alone, as in a metabolic acidosis, is sensed first by the carotid bodies, which sit in the arterial blood.


28.5.2 Peripheral chemoreceptors
The peripheral chemoreceptors are the carotid bodies, at the bifurcation of each common carotid artery, and the aortic bodies, on the aortic arch. The cells that do the sensing are the glomus cells. These are small organs next to the baroreceptors, but they are not the same thing: the baroreceptors are in the wall of the carotid sinus and the aortic arch.

Carotid bodies signal through the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). They sense O2 more than CO2, and they also sense pH. They are more sensitive than the aortic bodies.
Aortic bodies signal through the vagus (CN X). They also sense O2 more than CO2, and they are less sensitive.

The peripheral chemoreceptor afferents reach the NTS, the same relay as the lung receptors, and act from there on the DRG and the rhythm centers. The carotid bodies carry the fast ventilatory response to an acute metabolic acidosis, because H+ in the blood reaches them directly and reaches the central chemoreceptors poorly. The peripheral chemoreceptors respond to the PO2 of arterial blood, not to its O2 content. A patient with anemia or carbon monoxide poisoning can have a normal PaO2 and so gets little ventilatory drive from these receptors, even though the tissues are short of O2 (Transport of O2 and CO2).






NoteIf you are comparing with the recording



At one point the recording places the peripheral chemoreceptors “in the carotid sinus.” They are in the carotid bodies; the carotid sinus holds baroreceptors. The recording also says the peripheral chemoreceptors are “not going to be sensitive to pH” and then, a few sentences later, that the carotid body does detect pH. The slide is right: the carotid bodies respond to arterial H+, and the aortic bodies respond little to it.

title: 28  Control of Pulmonary Ventilation
section: 28.6 How ventilation responds to O2 and CO2
text:
28.6 How ventilation responds to O2 and CO2
Hold your breath as long as you can. O2 falls and CO2 rises. Which one finally forces you to breathe? CO2. Figure 28.3 shows why.






Figure 28.3: Minute ventilation as arterial PO2 (A) or arterial PCO2 (B) changes while the other gas is held constant. (A) Ventilation barely changes until PaO2 falls to about 60 mm Hg, then rises steeply, and the rise is larger when PaCO2 is higher. (B) Ventilation climbs steeply as PaCO2 rises through the normal range, and hypoxemia makes the climb steeper. Curves from a simple model scaled so that a person at PaO2 100 and PaCO2 40 mm Hg breathes 7.5 L/min. Course figure, after the response curves in the lecture and the course notes.



The response to O2 (panel A) is flat over a wide range. With PaCO2 held constant, PaO2 can fall from 100 to about 60 mm Hg with little change in ventilation. Below 60 the curve turns sharply upward. Recall the O2 dissociation curve: a PaO2 of 60 still gives a saturation of about 90%. So PaO2 can fall a long way, while saturation barely changes, before minute ventilation picks up much. The body tolerates a broad range of PaO2.
The response to CO2 (panel B) is steep. Normal PaCO2 is 40 mm Hg. Even 41 or 42 mm Hg raises minute ventilation sharply, and the breaking point of a breath-hold comes only a few mm Hg above normal. PaCO2 is held in a narrow window because it is tied to pH.
So in a healthy person, CO2 is the primary stimulus for breathing, sensed mainly by the central chemoreceptors and in part by the carotid bodies. O2 becomes a large stimulus only when PaO2 falls below about 60 mm Hg.

28.6.1 Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome
In congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (“Ondine’s curse”), the chemosensitivity to CO2 and H+ is impaired from birth. The cause is developmental, sometimes in the CO2 sensors and sometimes in the brainstem centers. Without the CO2 drive, these children breathe shallowly or stop breathing when voluntary control lapses, most dangerously during sleep. Unless it is recognized early it can be fatal, and many of these children need breathing support, often through a tracheostomy with a ventilator. The name comes from a folk tale in which a water nymph cursed her unfaithful husband to stop breathing if he ever fell asleep.


28.6.2 Chronic CO2 retention: a blunted response
The CO2 response is not fixed. In people who retain CO2 chronically, most often from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), it adapts over time. The response line shifts to the right and flattens (Figure 28.4): they need a higher PaCO2 before ventilation rises, and each extra mm Hg drives less breathing.






Figure 28.4: The ventilatory response to CO2 in a healthy person and in a person with chronic CO2 retention. The blunted line is shifted right and is flatter, so the same minute ventilation goes with a higher PaCO2. Course figure, after the lecture’s slide.



A person who has retained CO2 for years can sit comfortably with an arterial blood gas of about pH 7.37, PaCO2 52 mm Hg and HCO3− 29 mEq/L (an illustrative gas). At a PaCO2 of 52 most of us would be very short of breath. The bicarbonate is high, the mark of CO2 retained for a long time, so the pH is near normal and the central chemoreceptors are not strongly stimulated. Part of the blunting is this compensation. Part is mechanical: the drive to breathe may rise, but obstructed, overinflated lungs cannot turn it into ventilation (Think Like a Respiratory Consultant). In some patients the CO2 sensitivity itself is lower.
When the CO2 window widens like this, O2 becomes a larger part of what drives breathing. In some patients with advanced COPD, a falling PaO2 may be what finally raises ventilation.






NoteBackground: what this does and does not mean for oxygen therapy





You may hear that giving O2 to a CO2 retainer is dangerous because it “removes the hypoxic drive.” The blunted CO2 response is real, and it does make O2 a larger share of the drive. But when supplemental O2 raises PaCO2 in these patients, most of the rise comes from other effects: O2 relaxes hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, so blood flows back to poorly ventilated units and V/Q matching gets worse, and well-oxygenated hemoglobin holds less CO2 (the Haldane effect; see Transport of O2 and CO2). Loss of hypoxic drive is a small part of it.





28.6.3 The two signals interact
In real life O2 and CO2 change together, and each one changes the response to the other. When rising CO2 drives ventilation up, tidal volume rises first and then the rate. In panel B, the CO2 response line gets steeper as PaO2 falls: at a PaO2 of 47, and even more at 37, a small rise in PaCO2 drives a large rise in ventilation. In panel A, the hypoxic response is larger when PaCO2 is higher. Hypoxemia and hypercapnia together drive ventilation far harder than either alone.
The same interaction shapes the response to altitude. Low inspired PO2 lowers PaO2 below 60, and the carotid bodies drive ventilation up. The extra ventilation lowers PaCO2, which raises alveolar PO2 by the alveolar gas equation (Alveolar Ventilation). It also causes a respiratory alkalosis, and the low PaCO2 and high pH damp the central drive, which limits how far ventilation rises (Pulmonary Acid Base).

title: 28  Control of Pulmonary Ventilation
text:
28.7 Cheyne-Stokes breathing
When the CO2 response is very steep (hypoxemia is one cause, Figure 28.3 B; heart failure is another), a person can overreact to small changes in CO2. The result is Cheyne-Stokes breathing (Figure 28.5):

PaCO2 rises a little.
The exaggerated response produces deep, fast breaths that wax and then wane.
The overbreathing drives PaCO2 below normal.
With PaCO2 low, the drive to breathe disappears and the person stops breathing (apnea).
During the apnea CO2 builds up again, and the cycle repeats.

The cycle needs two things: a steep response, and a delay between the lungs and the chemoreceptors. Blood whose CO2 the lungs have just changed takes several seconds to reach the carotid bodies and the brainstem, so the controller is always acting on old information and each correction overshoots. In heart failure the slow circulation lengthens that delay, which is why heart failure is the classic setting.






Figure 28.5: Cheyne-Stokes breathing. Periods of deep, fast breathing that wax and wane alternate with apnea. PaCO2 falls below normal during each hyperpnea and builds during each apnea. Schematic. Course figure.



The usual settings are chronic heart failure, prematurity, sleeping at altitude, and other states of prolonged hypoxia. A stroke can also cause it, and it is common near the end of life. You will see it on the wards. Hypoxia is one setting, not the common thread: many patients with heart failure and Cheyne-Stokes breathing are not hypoxemic. What they share is a chemoreflex that overresponds and, in heart failure, the long delay.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



Slide 67’s first line, and the recording, present prolonged hypoxia as the usual setting. It is one setting, as at altitude, but many heart failure patients with Cheyne-Stokes breathing are not hypoxemic; what they share is the overresponding chemoreflex and the delay described above.
The slide and the notes also list “Drug use (Opiates).” Opioids work the other way: they blunt the drive to breathe. The usual result is slow, irregular breathing with central apneas, which clinicians classify separately, rather than the smooth crescendo and decrescendo of Cheyne-Stokes breathing. The rest of the slide, including its mechanism (an exaggerated response, then low CO2 and apnea), matches this chapter. The course errata make the same corrections.

title: 28  Control of Pulmonary Ventilation
text:
28.8 Baroreceptors
The baroreceptors also feed into breathing. The carotid sinus baroreceptors send their afferents in the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), and the aortic arch baroreceptors in the vagus (CN X), as in the baroreceptor reflex. Besides reaching the cardiovascular centers, these afferents reach the medullary respiratory centers. A sudden rise in arterial pressure can briefly reduce ventilation, and a fall can increase it. The lecture showed an experiment in which raising the pressure in the carotid sinus slowed the respiratory rate a little.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



Slides 69 to 71 label the baroreceptor input “Vagal (X) Afferents,” the recording says the baroreceptors feed back “through vagus afferents,” and the notes describe it as a parasympathetic response. The carotid sinus baroreceptors travel in CN IX and the aortic arch baroreceptors in CN X, the same split as the carotid and aortic bodies on slides 50 to 52. The effect on breathing is a connection within the brainstem to the respiratory centers, not a parasympathetic efferent effect.

title: 28  Control of Pulmonary Ventilation
text:
28.9 Higher brain centers and integration
So far the system runs on its own: the medulla and pons generate the rhythm, and feedback from the lungs, chemoreceptors and baroreceptors adjusts it. But we also need to take control of breathing. Higher brain centers can override the rhythm center:

Motor cortex: voluntary breathing. You can take a deep breath, hold your breath, or blow out candles.
Prefrontal cortex: planning. Breathing can rise in anticipation of exercise, before any CO2 has been produced.
Hypothalamus and amygdala: emotion. Fear, excitement and pain change the rate, depth and pattern of breathing, much as they act on the autonomic nervous system.

These inputs let us pause or reshape breathing to speak, give lectures, sing, go underwater, and hold the breath while swallowing so that food is not aspirated. In sleep they fall away and the automatic system runs alone.
All of these inputs compete for one rhythm center and one set of lungs. In exercise, the drive to breathe more says “bigger breaths,” and the stretch receptors say “enough.” Which wins depends on which signal is stronger: tidal volume rises a long way, and near its ceiling the rate takes over (Physiology of Exercise). In a breath-hold, the chemoreceptors say “breathe” and the cortex says “not yet.” The cortex wins, but only to a point: hold your breath long enough and the rising CO2 wins, or you pass out.
Figure 28.6 puts all four parts together.






Figure 28.6: The control of breathing as one loop. The brainstem rhythm generator drives the muscles, the muscles move the lungs, and gas exchange sets the arterial blood gases. Central and peripheral chemoreceptors, baroreceptors and lung receptors report back to the rhythm generator. Higher brain centers act on the rhythm generator and can also drive the muscles directly. Course figure, after the lecture’s integration diagram.



The next chapter, Physiology of Exercise, puts this system under the largest load a healthy person faces.

title: 28  Control of Pulmonary Ventilation
text:
28.10 Check your understanding

Experimenters cut the brainstem just below the pneumotaxic center and then cut both vagus nerves. What breathing pattern do they see, and why does cutting the vagi make the difference?


Answer

Apneusis: long, held inspirations with brief expirations. The cut removes the pneumotaxic center, which normally restrains the apneustic center. With the vagi intact, the stretch receptors still help end each inspiration, so breaths are only slower and deeper. Cutting the vagi removes that second brake, and the apneustic center holds inspiration on.

A patient develops an acute metabolic acidosis: the blood’s H+ rises while PaCO2 is at first normal. Which chemoreceptors raise ventilation first, and why do the central chemoreceptors respond less at first?


Answer

The carotid bodies, which sit in the arterial blood and respond to its H+. The central chemoreceptors are behind the blood-brain barrier, which H+ crosses poorly; they respond to the H+ that CO2 makes in the brain fluid. Once the extra ventilation lowers PaCO2, the brain fluid becomes less acidic, which damps the central drive.

Why does a fall in PaO2 from 100 to 70 mm Hg change ventilation very little, when a rise in PaCO2 from 40 to 45 mm Hg makes a person breathe much harder?


Answer

The ventilatory response to O2 is nearly flat until PaO2 falls to about 60 mm Hg, and at 70 the saturation is still above 90%. The response to CO2 is steep near 40, because PaCO2 is tied directly to pH, which the body holds in a narrow range. CO2 is the main stimulus to breathe in health.

After surgery that removes both carotid bodies, a patient breathes 12% O2 for a few minutes, and on another day 5% CO2. Compared with before the surgery, what happens to the rise in ventilation with each gas, and why?


Answer

The response to 12% O2 is nearly lost. The carotid bodies are the main O2 sensors. The aortic bodies also sense O2 but are less sensitive, and the central chemoreceptors do not sense O2. So a PaO2 well below 60, which would normally drive ventilation up steeply, now raises it very little. The response to 5% CO2 is mostly kept. CO2 is sensed mainly by the central chemoreceptors in the medulla, which are intact, so ventilation still rises steeply with PaCO2. It rises somewhat less than before, because the carotid bodies supplied part of the CO2 response.

Two people breathe the same 7.5 L/min. One has a PaCO2 of 40 mm Hg, the other a PaCO2 of 52 mm Hg with a high bicarbonate. On Figure 28.4, which line is each on, and what happens to each one’s ventilation if PaCO2 rises by 5 mm Hg?


Answer

The first is on the normal line, the second on the blunted line of chronic CO2 retention, shifted right and flatter. A 5 mm Hg rise raises ventilation a lot in the first person and much less in the second. The high bicarbonate keeps the second person’s pH near normal, which is part of why the CO2 drive is blunted.

During Cheyne-Stokes breathing, is PaCO2 highest during the deep breaths or during the apnea? Explain the order of events.


Answer

It is highest at the end of the apnea, just as breathing restarts. CO2 builds during the apnea; the exaggerated response then produces deep, fast breaths that drive PaCO2 below normal; once it is low, the drive disappears and the next apnea begins.

title: 28  Control of Pulmonary Ventilation
text:
28.11 Sources
This chapter follows the 2026 Control of Pulmonary Ventilation lecture for MEDC 30504 and its 2026 recording, and draws on the course’s lecture notes and the 2018 course notes, corrected and updated. All figures were drawn for this book.

title: 29  Physiology of Exercise
text:
29.1 The system, end to end
If you want to know how a system works and where its limits are, push it to the extreme. The cardiovascular block did that for the circulation. Cardiovascular Adaptation to Exercise covers the cardiovascular reflexes, the Guyton curves in exercise and the redistribution of blood flow, and this chapter does not repeat them. It adds the other ends of the chain: what the muscle burns, how much CO2 it makes, how breathing keeps up, what happens to gas exchange, and how a clinical exercise test measures all of it.
Start with the simplified model the lecture used. Air brings O2 into the lungs, the blood carries it away, and the tissues, mostly muscle during exercise, use it. Three relations describe the flows:
\[\text{O}_2 \text{ delivery} = \text{CO} \times \text{CaO}_2 \qquad \text{O}_2 \text{ returned} = \text{CO} \times \text{CvO}_2 \qquad \dot{V}\text{CO}_2 = \dot{V}\text{O}_2 \times R\]
The difference between what is delivered and what returns is what the tissues used, V̇O2 (the Fick principle from Transport of O2 and CO2). The tissues send back CO2 in proportion to the O2 they use, scaled by R.
The ratio of CO2 produced to O2 consumed by the cells is the respiratory quotient (RQ), and it depends on the fuel they burn. Measured at the mouth for the whole body, the same ratio is the respiratory exchange ratio, R, the symbol used in the alveolar gas equation. In a steady state the two are equal.
Figure 29.1 lays out the “drive train” that moves O2 from the air to the mitochondria and CO2 back out. Exercise steps up every link.

title: 29  Physiology of Exercise
text:
Figure 29.1: The drive train of exercise. O2 moves from the air to the mitochondria (top), and CO2 from the mitochondria to the air (bottom). Under each step is how it is increased during exercise. Course figure, after the lecture’s diagram.




Lungs: larger tidal volumes, then a faster rate.
Pulmonary circulation: parallel vessels are recruited, so pulmonary vascular resistance falls and the lungs take a large rise in flow with little rise in pressure (Pulmonary Circulation).
Heart: heart rate and stroke volume rise.
Systemic circulation: arterioles in working muscle dilate, veins constrict, and the muscle pump pushes blood back to the heart.
Muscle: more O2 is extracted from each milliliter of blood, and the fuel, and with it R, changes.

title: 29  Physiology of Exercise
section: 29.2 Bioenergetics: the fuel sets the CO2 load
text:
29.2 Bioenergetics: the fuel sets the CO2 load
Muscle contraction runs on ATP. The muscle can make ATP aerobically from fat or glucose, or anaerobically from glucose alone, by converting pyruvate to lactate. Aerobic metabolism does most of the work. The anaerobic pathway is a backup, and the more of it you use, the closer you are to your limit.










Fuel
Reaction (classic yields, as on the slide)
ATP per O2
CO2 per O2 (R)
CO2 per ATP




Fat (palmitate)
23 O2 + C16H32O2 → 16 CO2 + 16 H2O + 130 ATP
5.65
about 0.7
0.12


Glucose, aerobic
6 O2 + C6H12O6 → 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + 36 ATP
6
1.0
0.17


Glucose, anaerobic
C6H12O6 → 2 lactic acid + 2 ATP, then buffered by HCO3−
no O2 used
not defined (no O2 term); “lots of CO2”
1.0



Each row is a trade-off. Fat gives the most energy per gram but uses the most O2 per ATP, and it makes the least CO2 for the O2 it uses. Aerobic glucose gets slightly more ATP from each O2 but makes more CO2: one CO2 for every O2. Anaerobic glycolysis needs no O2 at all, which looks ideal until you see what it costs.
Where the anaerobic CO2 comes from. Lactic acid is a strong acid, and the bicarbonate in blood and tissue buffers it:
\[\text{lactic acid} + \text{NaHCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{sodium lactate} + \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2\]
Each lactic acid buffered releases one CO2, with no O2 consumed. One glucose makes two lactic acids and two ATP, so anaerobic metabolism releases about one CO2 for every ATP, against 0.12 to 0.17 for aerobic metabolism. The lungs have to clear all of it.






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The table on slides 8 and 9 lists anaerobic glucose as 1 CO2 and 2 ATP, a CO2 per ATP of 0.50. One glucose gives two lactic acids, and buffering each releases one CO2, so it is 2 CO2 for 2 ATP, a ratio of 1.0 (the lecture: anaerobic metabolism makes “a lot of CO2 per ATP”). Either way, anaerobic metabolism makes several times as much CO2 per ATP as aerobic metabolism, which is the point of the table. (The slides round aerobic glucose to 0.16; 6/36 is 0.17.)
The recording also describes the lactate itself being turned into water and CO2. The extra CO2 comes from the bicarbonate that buffers the acid, not from the lactate. The lactate anion is left in the blood, as sodium lactate on slide 8, and later the heart, other muscles and the liver use it, consuming O2 as they do.


What R tells you. On a fat diet R is about 0.7, on pure carbohydrate 1.0, and on a mixed Western diet about 0.8, the value used in the alveolar gas equation (slide 22 draws 0.85). During steady aerobic exercise, R stays in that range. Once anaerobic metabolism adds CO2 without adding any O2 use, the numerator of R grows and R rises above 1, to 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 or more. An R above 1 during exercise is the sign that buffered acid is being blown off.
Endurance athletes work just below the point where this starts. A marathon runner holds a high, steady O2 delivery for hours. A 200 m sprinter goes past it and builds up lactic acid within seconds, which is why the sprint cannot be sustained.






NoteBackground: diet and the CO2 load





Because glucose makes more CO2 per O2 than fat, a carbohydrate diet means slightly more breathing for the same work. The difference is modest, and in health it does not matter: we have plenty of respiratory reserve, and marathon runners load carbohydrate because muscle glycogen runs out in a long race and because glucose gives more ATP per O2, not to change their CO2 load. In a patient with severe lung disease and no reserve, a continuous glucose infusion can occasionally add enough CO2 to worsen respiratory failure.

title: 29  Physiology of Exercise
text:
29.3 The cardiovascular response, briefly
The cardiovascular block covered this in full (Cardiovascular Adaptation to Exercise; for the Guyton curves, Control of Cardiac Output). In one paragraph: an autonomic surge constricts veins, which raises mean systemic filling pressure (Pms) and venous return; the heart beats faster and harder, which by itself would lower right atrial pressure (with venous return rising at the same time, Pra ends about unchanged); deeper breaths make intrathoracic pressure more negative, which pulls blood back toward the heart (the respiratory pump); metabolic vasodilation in working muscle lowers SVR and resistance to venous return; and the muscle pump pushes blood back to the heart. The cardiac function and vascular function curves both shift, and cardiac output rises from about 5 or 6 L/min to 20 to 25 L/min, and to 35 or 40 L/min in a well-trained athlete. In the lungs, recruitment of parallel vessels keeps pulmonary arterial pressure low despite the huge rise in flow, which protects against pulmonary edema.








Effect of maximal exercise

About 3-fold increase

About 2-fold increase

The table’s 6- to 8-fold rise in cardiac output is the top of the range. The same lecture’s own numbers (about 6 L/min to 20 to 25 L/min, or 35 to 40 L/min in a well-trained athlete) and the cardiovascular lecture’s healthy young adult (4.9 to 19.8 L/min) give about fourfold for a typical person, with 6- to 8-fold reached by trained athletes. Renal blood flow is the one place the slide needs correcting. The slide groups renal with CNS flow as “constant”, but only brain flow stays about constant. As sympathetic activity rises with workload, renal and splanchnic arterioles constrict and their flow falls, which frees cardiac output for working muscle and skin, as the cardiovascular exercise chapter shows.

29.3.1 Delivery first, then extraction
The bottom line of the slide is “drastic increase in QO2 before increased O2 extraction.” At rest, arterial blood is about 100% saturated and mixed venous blood about 75%, so the tissues take about a quarter of the O2 that passes them. In exercise, cardiac output rises first, so delivery rises steeply. Then extraction rises too, and working muscle takes most of the O2 that reaches it. The lecture describes extraction becoming limiting at a mixed venous saturation around 50%; at maximal exercise SvO2 can fall further, to about 25 to 30%. The arterial-venous O2 difference widens as work increases, and in the lecture’s data, trained rowers reached a wider difference than average-fit subjects, extracting another 10 to 15% of the O2 delivered.


29.3.2 In health we are cardiac limited
Everyone has heard of a maximum heart rate (roughly 220 minus age). Nobody worries about reaching a maximum respiratory rate or a maximum minute ventilation, because in health we never get there. A healthy person who exercises as hard as possible stops because the cardiovascular system has reached its limit, and still has breathing capacity left over. In health we are cardiac limited, with plenty of respiratory reserve. A person who stops exercising because the lungs ran out first has lost so much ventilatory capacity that the lungs, not the heart, have become the weakest link. Severe obstruction is the usual example. If narrowed airways limit how fast air can leave, a faster rate leaves no time to empty the lungs. Air is trapped, the lungs ride up toward TLC, and tidal volume cannot rise either. The ceiling on ventilation comes down, and the patient reaches it before the heart reaches its limit. The exercise test at the end of this chapter is built to tell those two apart.

title: 29  Physiology of Exercise
text:
29.4 The respiratory response

29.4.1 Alveolar ventilation follows CO2 output
The respiratory system’s job in exercise is to keep PaCO2, and with it pH, near normal while CO2 output rises tenfold. From the alveolar ventilation equation in Alveolar Ventilation, PaCO2 ∝ V̇CO2 / V̇A, so holding PaCO2 at 40 mm Hg means raising V̇A in proportion to V̇CO2 (Figure 29.2 A). At rest, V̇CO2 is about 200 mL/min and V̇A about 4 to 5 L/min. In heavy exercise, V̇CO2 reaches about 2000 mL/min, and V̇A has to rise about tenfold, to roughly 40 L/min. Total ventilation rises 10- to 20-fold.






Figure 29.2: (A) The alveolar ventilation needed to hold PaCO2 at 30, 40 or 50 mm Hg as CO2 output rises, from V̇A = 0.863 × V̇CO2 / PaCO2. A person whose PaCO2 falls from 40 toward 30 during exercise has moved to a steeper line: ventilation is rising faster than CO2 output. (B) CO2 output for a given O2 consumption depends on R. Course figure, after the lecture’s slides.



The lines in panel A show what it means when PaCO2 changes during exercise. Breathing that holds PaCO2 at 40 stays on the middle line. If PaCO2 starts to fall (40, then 37, then 34, then 30), ventilation has moved onto a steeper line, and in exercise the usual reason is a metabolic acidosis: the person has reached the limit of O2 delivery, is making lactic acid, and is compensating by blowing off extra CO2. The opposite shift happens in a person with a metabolic alkalosis, say after days of vomiting: the compensating PaCO2 is higher, so that person breathes on the 50 line, with less ventilation for the same CO2 output. Panel B shows the other half of the CO2 load: for the same O2 consumption, a higher R means more CO2 to clear.
What drives the rise in ventilation? The full mechanism of exercise hyperpnea is not settled. In moderate exercise, PaO2 and PaCO2 stay near normal, so the arterial chemoreceptors are not seeing a large error signal. Most of the rise is attributed to neural drive, from the motor cortex (central command) and from receptors in working muscles and joints, and it is matched closely to the rising CO2 load, so V̇A rises in proportion to V̇CO2. Above the anaerobic threshold, the CO2 released by bicarbonate buffering adds to the load, and later the falling pH stimulates the carotid bodies and drives ventilation higher still (Control of Pulmonary Ventilation).






NoteIf you are comparing with the slides



The exercise notes say “The fall in CvO2 drives the respiratory response.” The fall in mixed venous O2 content reflects greater extraction by working muscle, but it does not drive ventilation. The chemoreceptors sense arterial blood, not venous blood. Low CvO2 matters to gas exchange instead, through the A–a gradient (below).




29.4.2 Breathe deeper, then faster
Minute ventilation is V̇E = VT × RR, but what clears CO2 is alveolar ventilation, V̇A = (VT − VD) × RR. Every breath first fills the anatomic dead space, so more breaths means more dead space ventilation. The slide compares two ways to breathe 15 L/min:
